exp.12:37:
Jesus asks Peter a question: "Will you lay down your life for me?" He then solemnly tells him (using the word "Verily, verily") that before the rooster crows, Peter will deny him three times.

Jesus speaks with his disciples at the Last Supper, shortly before he is arrested. Peter has just sincerely said that he would give his life for Jesus. Jesus does not doubt his affection, but he knows his weakness. The four Gospels later tell how Peter denied him, and John 21 shows how Jesus restored him with love.

For today: let us not rely only on our own strength or good intentions. If we have failed, let us remember that Jesus knows our weaknesses and still forgives us and lifts us up. Let us ask him daily for help to be faithful to him.
exp.9:4:
What it says: Jesus explains that the sheep do not follow a stranger but flee from him, because they do not recognize his voice. The word "but" is used here instead of an older form, and "rather" stands in its place where the verse says "will flee," while "stranger" means someone unknown, who is not trustworthy.

Context: Jesus speaks in a parable about the shepherd and the sheep. He addresses the Pharisees, whom he had just confronted after healing a blind man (ch. 9). The true shepherd is known by his sheep, and they trust him. John says that the listeners did not understand the parable, so Jesus clarifies it right away, saying that he is the door.

For today: Knowing well the voice of Jesus helps us detect false teachings. Read the Gospels regularly and pray; that way, when someone speaks to you in God's name, you will be able to compare their message with what Christ actually said.
exp.7:18:
The Pharisees ask Jesus, "Where is your Father?" He answers that they know neither him nor his Father. He explains that if they truly knew him, they would also know the Father.

Jesus had just said that his Father bears witness to him. The Pharisees, thinking of a human father, ask where he is. Perhaps they said it mockingly or out of incomprehension; the text does not make this clear. Jesus was teaching in the temple, and no one could seize him because his hour had not yet come.

For today: if we want to know God, we must look to Jesus. It is not enough to hold religious ideas about God. We can read the Gospels calmly and ask God to show us what he is like through Christ.
exp.1:14:
Jesus made a whip out of cords and drove the merchants out of the temple, along with their sheep and cattle. He also threw the money of the money changers on the floor and overturned their tables.

It was near the Passover, when many pilgrims were arriving in Jerusalem. In the temple, animals were sold for the sacrifices and money was exchanged. Jesus calls the temple "my Father's house," and his disciples remembered Psalm 69: "Zeal for your house consumes me." Scholars debate whether the whip was used only on the animals or also on the people; the text does not fully clarify this.

Today we can ask ourselves whether there are things in our life of faith that get in the way of sincere worship. Let us ask God to show us what to remove.
exp.3:53:
This verse says that the healing of the official's son was the second sign that Jesus did. A "sign" is a miracle that points to who Jesus is. The words "á" and "y" appear with old spelling; today we would write "a" and "and". It says that Jesus did it after returning from Judea to Galilee.

The one speaking here is the writer of the Gospel, John, who gives a brief summary. Earlier, Jesus had turned water into wine in Cana of Galilee, and that was the first sign. Now, also in Galilee, he healed from a distance the son of a royal official, only by his word. John tells this so that the reader will believe in Jesus.

For today: Jesus does not need to be present to act. Trust his word even when you don't yet see the result, as that father did, and let your faith reach your family too.
exp.10:43:
This verse tells that Lazarus, who had been dead for four days, came out of the tomb with his hands and feet bound with strips of cloth, and with his face covered by a cloth wrapped around his head. Then Jesus gave the command: "Loose him," that is, take off the wrappings, "and let him go," or in other words, let him walk free.

Jesus is the one speaking. He had just prayed to the Father out loud so that the people present would believe that God had sent him. Then he called Lazarus by name. After this, many believed in Jesus, but others went to tell the Pharisees, which shows that people react differently to the same miracle.

For today: Jesus gives life, but he also invites others to take part in setting someone free. We can walk alongside a person who is beginning a new life with patience and kindness, helping them let go of old bonds, without judging them or leaving them alone.
exp.0:33:
John the Baptist says that he saw Jesus, and that is why he can state with certainty that he is the Son of God. The words "bare record" mean that he spoke as a witness, telling what he had seen with his own eyes. "I saw" refers to what he saw at the baptism of Jesus.

Here John the Baptist is speaking. God had given him a sign: the Spirit would come down and rest on someone, and that person would be the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit. John saw that sign on Jesus. So he does not speak from opinion, but from what God had shown him. The next day he again points to Jesus as the Lamb of God.

For today: our faith does not need complicated words. We can simply tell what Jesus has done in our lives and what the Bible says about him, like a witness who shares what he knows.
exp.4:45:
Jesus says that if the Jewish leaders truly believed Moses, they would also believe in him. The reason is that Moses wrote about him. Some older words in the source text: the word for "believed" there is "believed," and the word "to" is "to," and "he wrote" is "he wrote."

Jesus speaks with certain religious leaders from Jerusalem who were questioning him after he healed a sick man on the Sabbath. They trusted in Moses and in the Law, but they rejected Jesus. He tells them that Moses himself accuses them, because his writings point to Christ. Scholars often think of passages such as Deuteronomy 18:15, although the text does not cite one in particular.

For today: reading the Bible is not enough if it does not lead us to Jesus. We can ask God that, as we read, he would open our hearts to recognize Christ and to obey him with humility.
exp.12:35:
Simon Peter asks Jesus where he is going. Jesus answers that Peter cannot follow him now, but that he will follow him later. Here "follow" means going the same way with Jesus.

Jesus is with his disciples at the Last Supper, shortly before his arrest. He has just given them the new commandment to love one another. He speaks of his departure, that is, his death and his return to the Father. Many understand that the "later" for Peter refers to his own martyrdom, although the text gives no further detail. Peter does not yet understand and promises to lay down his life, but Jesus warns him that he will deny him.

Following Jesus is a path walked in his time and with his strength, not ours. If you fail today, do not give up; Jesus keeps calling you and restores you.
exp.5:7:
This verse introduces a new character who enters the conversation. The phrase "saith unto him" is an older way of saying "says to him." John notes that one of the disciples, Andrew, is about to speak, and he identifies him as the brother of Simon Peter.

Jesus had just asked Philip how they would feed the crowd, but he asked to test him, because he already knew what he would do. Philip answered thinking only about the money. Now Andrew steps in and, in the next verse, points out that there is a boy with five barley loaves and two small fish. He himself doubts that this will be enough.

For today: Andrew did not have the solution, but he brought to Jesus the little that he had. We can do the same with our limitations, trusting that Jesus can do much with what we hand over to him.
exp.5:42:
Jesus is speaking to those who were grumbling against him, and he asks them to stop. "Murmur" means complaining or protesting under one's breath, out of doubt or anger. "Said" simply means "told them."

Jesus is speaking in Galilee with a group of Jews. He had just said that he is the bread that came down from heaven, and they were offended because they believed they knew his family. They could not understand how someone so ordinary could come from God. Jesus does not argue with their complaint. Instead, he helps them see that knowing God requires being drawn by the Father and being willing to learn from him.

When something about Jesus makes us uncomfortable or does not fit with what we think, instead of complaining, we can bring that doubt to God in prayer, read his Word with humility, and ask him to teach us.
exp.4:24:
Jesus says with great certainty that a time is coming, and has already begun, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear it will live. The phrase "Verily, verily" is the same as the emphatic word "truly" used to introduce his statement. The word "hear" is a form of the verb "to hear," which here means to listen and respond. Many understand "the dead" as people who are spiritually dead; others also see a reference to the final resurrection.

Jesus speaks in Jerusalem, after healing a sick man on the Sabbath. He defends the fact that his authority comes from the Father. Shortly before, he said that whoever believes his word passes from death to life. He then explains that the Father gave him life in himself and the power to judge.

For today: listen to the voice of Jesus in the Gospels with a heart ready to obey. Read one passage each day and ask him to give you new life, hope, and strength to do what he shows you.
exp.0:44:
Philip finds Nathanael and tells him: "We have found the one of whom Moses wrote in the law, and the prophets too: Jesus, the son of Joseph, from Nazareth." The words "found" and "found" mean "found" and "found" in the verse you read, and "tells him" is the same as "says to him."

Philip has just been called by Jesus, and he immediately runs to share the news with his friend. He speaks with excitement, like someone who has discovered what Israel was waiting for. By "the law and the prophets" he means the Hebrew Scriptures. Nathanael will doubt, because Nazareth did not have a good reputation, but Philip does not argue and simply invites him to see for himself.

When we come to know Jesus, it is natural to speak of Him with the people we love. We do not need to have all the answers or win debates. We can invite simply, as Philip did: "Come and see." Think of someone close to you and pray for an opportunity to share what Christ has done in your life.
exp.19:0:
This verse tells that on Sunday, the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene went to the tomb very early, while it was still dark. When she arrived, she saw that the stone that had closed the tomb was no longer in its place.

It is the beginning of John's account of the resurrection. The narrator is John himself, who tells what happened after Jesus died. Mary does not yet know that Jesus has risen; the next part of the text shows that she thinks someone has taken the body, and that is why she runs to tell Peter and the other disciple.

For today: Mary sought Jesus even in the darkness and in the middle of her grief. We can do the same when we do not understand what is happening: keep drawing near to God, even when we do not yet see the complete answer.
exp.4:15:
This verse says that the Jewish leaders were persecuting Jesus and wanted to kill him. The reason given is that he was healing and doing other works on the sabbath day. "Persecuted" means that they harassed him and pursued him with hostility. "Sought" means that they were looking for a way to do it. "Kill him" means to put him to death.

Here the narrator is John. Jesus had just healed a man on the sabbath, a man who had been sick for thirty-eight years by the pool of Bethesda. That man then told the leaders who had healed him. They understood the sabbath as a strict day of rest, and they saw that work as a violation. Later Jesus will say that his Father is working and that he is working too, which made them even angrier.

For today: sometimes we defend our customs so strongly that we stop rejoicing when God does good. Let us ask for a humble heart, one that loves people and recognizes God's work, even when it comes in a way we did not expect.
exp.18:40:
This verse says that near the place where Jesus was crucified there was a garden. In that garden there was a new tomb, that is, a tomb that no one had used yet. The word "tomb" here refers to a burial place cut into rock or built as a grave, and a "garden" is a piece of land with trees and plants.

Here John speaks as an eyewitness who tells what happened as a narrator. He explains where they laid Jesus' body after his death. Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus buried him in a hurry, because the Passover was about to begin. Many believe John points out that the tomb was new to show that no one else had been buried there, although the text does not explain this directly.

For today: Jesus was treated with respect in his burial, and that reminds us that God cares about the details. If you are going through a time of loss or silence today, trust that God is still at work even when you cannot see it. After that Sabbath of waiting came the resurrection.
exp.7:0:
This verse says that Jesus went to the Mount of Olives. The Mount of Olives is what we today call the Mount of Olives, a hill next to Jerusalem, covered with olive groves.

The speaker is the narrator, John, who tells of a movement of Jesus. After the debates in Jerusalem, everyone returned to their home, and Jesus withdrew to that mountain, probably to rest and pray. The Gospels mention that Jesus went to that place on other occasions. It should be said that many scholars note that this passage (7:53 to 8:11) is missing from some of the oldest manuscripts, and for that reason its origin is debated. Even so, the church has read it for centuries.

For today: before facing intense days, Jesus sought a quiet place. Set aside time too for silence and prayer to regain your strength.
exp.5:35:
Jesus says that, although the people have seen him with their own eyes, they still do not believe in him. "But" means "but," and "I told you" means "I already told you." Seeing Jesus is not the same as trusting him.

Jesus speaks with a crowd that followed him after the feeding of the bread. They had just asked him for "this bread," but they were looking for him mainly for the food. He tells them that he is the bread of life and shows that their hearts do not yet trust him. Right after, he adds that whoever comes to him will not be cast out.

For today: we can know a great deal about Jesus, or receive his blessings, and still not trust him. Today you can say to him sincerely: "Lord, I want to believe you and come to you, not only for what you give me, but for who you are."
exp.1:12:
This verse says that the Passover, the great Jewish feast that remembered Israel's deliverance from Egypt, was near. Then Jesus went up to Jerusalem. It says "went up" because the city is located on higher ground, and also because it was a very important place for the Jews. The verse is the one that speaks of Jerusalem.

Here the narrator, John, speaks. After the wedding at Cana and some days in Capernaum, John recounts the first trip to Jerusalem that he records. This prepares the next scene, where Jesus cleanses the temple. Many pilgrims came to that feast, and the temple was full of people.

For today: Jesus gave a central place to worship and to times of meeting with God. We can ask ourselves whether we give real space in our week to seek him with sincerity.
exp.11:14:
Here John quotes an ancient prophecy that announces the arrival of a king. He tells the people of Jerusalem, the daughter of Zion, a poetic way of naming the people of Jerusalem, not to be afraid. Their King comes sitting on a young donkey, that is, a little donkey, the colt of a female donkey.

John writes this as he tells of Jesus' entrance into Jerusalem. The crowd received him with palm branches and shouts of praise. John takes words that seem to come from the prophet Zechariah (9:9) to show that Jesus fulfills what was announced. A king on a donkey suggests humility and peace, not war. The disciples understood this later, when Jesus was glorified.

For today: if Jesus is a humble and near King, we can trust Him without fear. And we can also imitate His simplicity, serving others without seeking applause.
exp.11:24:
Jesus says that whoever holds on to their life, putting it above everything, ends up losing it. On the other hand, whoever hates their life in this world, that is, values it less than God and his calling, will keep it forever. Here "hate" does not mean hating oneself, but loving something less in comparison with Christ.

Jesus speaks shortly before his cross, when some Greeks wanted to see him. He announces that his hour has come and uses the image of the grain of wheat that dies to bear fruit. In this way he explains his own death and calls his followers to walk the same path of self-giving.

Today we can ask ourselves what we are guarding too anxiously: comfort, reputation, or control. Today you can let go of some of that out of obedience to God, for example by serving someone without expecting anything in return.
exp.3:44:
He says that when Jesus came into Galilee, the people there welcomed him warmly. They did so because they had seen everything he did in Jerusalem during the feast, since they too had gone to that celebration.

The one telling the story is John. Shortly before, Jesus had been in Jerusalem, where he performed signs during the Passover (John 2:23). Then he passed through Samaria and continued on to Galilee. There seems to be a tension here: Jesus had said that a prophet is not honored in his own country, yet the Galileans receive him. Some think John is pointing out that this welcome was based mainly on the miracles, and not on a deep faith.

For today: examine why you follow Jesus. It is good to thank him for his favors, but ask him for a faith that seeks him himself, even when you see no miracles.
exp.6:11:
This verse says there was much murmuring, that is, a lot of quiet talk, about Jesus among the crowd. Some thought he was a good man. Others said no, that he was rather deceiving the people. The word "people" here refers to the crowd in general.

We are at the Feast of Tabernacles, in Jerusalem. Jesus had gone up in secret, and the Jewish authorities were looking for him. Those who are speaking are ordinary members of the crowd, divided between sympathy and suspicion. The following verse makes clear that no one spoke openly for fear of the leaders. That is why the opinions were passed around in low voices.

Today there are also many opinions about Jesus. Instead of settling for rumors or for what most people say, we can read the Gospels sincerely and come to know him for ourselves.
exp.10:24:
Jesus says: "I am the resurrection and the life." He is not speaking only of a future event but of himself. Whoever trusts in him, even though he dies, will live again.

Jesus speaks with Martha, who is grieving because her brother Lazarus died four days ago. She believes in the resurrection on the last day, as many Jews of her time did. Jesus takes her further: hope is not only a future day but a present person. Afterward Martha confesses that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.

When you face a loss or a fear of death, do not cling only to an idea about the future. Trust in Jesus himself. Bring him your pain honestly, as Martha did, and answer his question: "Do you believe this?"
exp.11:8:
This verse tells that a large crowd of Jews learned that Jesus was in Bethany. They went to see him, but they also wanted to see Lazarus, whom Jesus had raised from the dead.

The one who narrates is the apostle John. This happens shortly after Mary anointed Jesus with perfume, six days before the Passover. Lazarus's resurrection was the great news among the people. His new life was a living sign of Jesus's power, and for this reason many believed in him, although the religious leaders reacted with anger and fear.

Today, our lives changed by Jesus can also awaken curiosity in others. It is not necessary to be famous or to speak perfectly: it is enough to live with gratitude and simplicity, and to point with love toward Christ, who is the one who gives life.
exp.10:5:
This verse says that when Jesus learned that Lazarus was sick, he did not go right away. He stayed two more days in the same place. The "heard" refers to his receiving the message, and "still stayed" means he remained there for the time being.

The one telling the story is John. Lazarus's sisters, Martha and Mary, had sent word to him. The text stresses that Jesus loved them, so the delay was not indifference. Jesus had already said that this sickness would serve God's glory. Later Lazarus dies and Jesus raises him. Some think the danger in Judea also played a part, but the text does not say so clearly.

For today: when God seems slow to answer, his delay does not mean a lack of love. We can keep trusting and praying, even when we do not understand his timing, because he may be preparing something greater than what we asked for.
exp.1:13:
This verse says that Jesus, on entering the temple in Jerusalem, found people selling oxen, sheep, and doves. There were also money changers sitting at their tables. The word "changers" in the verse refers to men who exchanged money.

Here the narrator, John, is speaking. The Passover was approaching, and many people were traveling to Jerusalem. The animals were used for sacrifices, and money exchange was used to pay the temple offering. These things were useful, but they were being done inside the temple. That is why, in the verses that follow, Jesus reacts firmly and calls the temple "my Father's house."

For today: let us examine whether anything has taken the place of sincere worship in our lives, such as the pursuit of money or empty religious routine. Let us ask God to cleanse our hearts and teach us to approach Him with reverence and simplicity.
exp.5:23:
This verse tells that the people saw that Jesus and his disciples were no longer in the place where they had eaten the bread. So they got into small boats and crossed the lake to Capernaum, looking for Jesus. The word for the boats is not in the verse above, so the explanation's comment on it is removed, and the sea of Galilee is referred to simply as the lake.

The narrator is John. The crowd had just been fed with loaves and fish. When they noticed that Jesus was not there, they searched for him with great effort. But in the next verse Jesus tells them that they were looking for him because they had eaten and been satisfied, not because they understood the signs. Seeking him was good, but their motives needed correcting.

For today: ask yourself why you seek God. It is right to ask him for help with your needs, but also open yourself to knowing him, not only to receiving his blessings.
exp.14:15:
Jesus says that the disciples did not choose him first, but that he chose them. He set them apart so that they would "go and bear fruit," and that this fruit would last. The words "you" and "you" are plain modern English, and "chose" is the word the verse uses. If they ask the Father in Jesus' name, the Father will give it to them.

Jesus speaks to his disciples the night before his crucifixion. He has just called them friends, not servants, because he shared with them what he heard from the Father. He explains that their relationship with him begins with Jesus' love, not with anything they earned. Right away he commands them to love one another, and he warns them that the world will reject them, as it rejected him.

For today: if God chose you, you do not have to earn his affection. Live thankfully, and let that love show in how you treat others. Pray for things that serve his purpose.
exp.12:7:
Peter says to Jesus with force, "Thou shalt never wash my feet." Jesus answers him that if he does not wash him, Peter will have no part with him, that is, he will have no fellowship or union with him.

Jesus is at the last supper with his disciples and takes the place of a servant to wash their feet. Peter feels uncomfortable, because it seems unworthy to him that his Master should do that. But Jesus shows him that he needs to receive his service and his cleansing. Many also see here a sign of his self-giving on the cross, though it can be understood in several ways.

For today: learn to receive. Sometimes we find it hard to accept help, forgiveness, or God's love out of pride. Humble yourself and let Jesus serve you and cleanse you.
exp.1:9:
Here the headwaiter, who was in charge of running the feast, speaks to the bridegroom. He tells him that the usual practice is to serve the good wine first, and when the guests have already drunk enough, to bring out the lesser wine. But this bridegroom did the opposite: he kept the best wine until the end.

The headwaiter does not know that the wine comes from Jesus, since only the servants knew. He thinks the bridegroom had set it aside, and he congratulates him without knowing the truth. John records this as the first miracle of Jesus, and the following text says that in this way he showed his glory and that his disciples believed in him.

For today: Jesus often works quietly and generously, and many times those who serve him notice it before anyone else. We can trust that he gives the best, even when we do not see it right away, and obey him in simple things, as the servants did.
exp.3:41:
The Samaritans tell the woman that they no longer believe only because of what she told them. Now they have heard Jesus with their own ears, and they are convinced that he is "the Saviour of the world," the Christ, that is, the Messiah.

The speakers are the people of Sicar, in Samaria. The woman had told them about her meeting with Jesus by the well, and they went to see him for themselves. They asked him to stay, and he remained with them for two days. It is remarkable that people whom many Jews looked down on recognized Jesus as the Saviour of the whole world, not only of Israel.

For today: the testimony of others can lead us toward Jesus, but our faith grows when we know him personally. Set aside time to listen to him in his Word and in prayer, and share with others what you have experienced with him.
exp.6:42:
This verse says that the people were divided because of Jesus. The word "division" in the verse means a split or a disagreement, a clash of opinions. Some thought one thing and others thought the opposite, and they could not agree about who he was.

We are at the Feast of Tabernacles, in Jerusalem. Jesus had just been teaching and inviting those who were thirsty to come to him. Some in the crowd believed he was the Christ, that is, the Messiah. Others doubted because they thought he came from Galilee, and the Scripture said the Messiah would be born in Bethlehem, of the family of David. They do not mention that Jesus was indeed born there; the text does not clarify this in this passage.

Today too there are different opinions about Jesus. Instead of deciding based on what others say or on assumptions, we can turn to the Bible with humility and honesty, and seek the truth about him for ourselves.
exp.1:23:
It says that Jesus did not trust those people, meaning he did not give them his confidence or let himself be led by them. The reason is that he knew everyone. The phrase "did not commit himself unto them" sounds old, but it means that he did not put himself into their hands. The word "because" gives the reason.

The writer of this Gospel, John, speaks here. He tells that in Jerusalem, during the Passover, many believed in Jesus when they saw the signs he performed. But John makes clear that this faith, based on what was impressive, was not firm, and Jesus knew it. Interpreters explain in several ways how genuine that faith was, but the text emphasizes that Jesus saw into hearts.

Today we can remember that God knows us completely, better than we know ourselves. That invites a sincere faith, not one merely excited by what we receive, and to trust his judgment with humility.
exp.8:3:
Jesus says that it is necessary for Him to do the works of God the Father, who sent Him. He must do this while the day lasts, that is, the time available. Then the night comes, when no one can work anymore.

Jesus speaks with his disciples in front of a man who had been blind from birth. They asked who was to blame for that blindness. Jesus rejects that idea and says that God wants to show his work in that man. For this reason he feels a sense of urgency to act. Some think that the night refers to his approaching death; others, to any limit of human time.

Today we can learn not to put off doing good. Instead of looking for someone to blame in the face of another's suffering, let us help with whatever is within our reach, while we still have the opportunity.
exp.1:17:
The Jews answer Jesus and ask him what sign he gives them to prove that he has the right to do what he did. A "sign" is a miraculous proof that confirms his authority.

Jesus has just driven the sellers and money changers out of the temple, saying that his Father's house should not be a marketplace. Those who speak are the Jewish leaders or authorities, who felt challenged. They do not ask him to explain whether the trading was wrong, but demand proof of his authority. Jesus will answer by speaking about the temple and his resurrection, although they did not understand it that way at that moment.

Today we can ask ourselves whether, when God corrects us, we respond with humility or ask for excuses and proof so that we do not have to change. A willing heart listens, recognizes the truth, and obeys.
exp.0:40:
Andrew, after spending the day with Jesus, first finds his brother Simon. He tells him with joy: "We have found the Messiah." The text clarifies that "Messiah" is a Hebrew word meaning "Christ," that is, the Anointed One, the one sent by God.

The one speaking is Andrew, one of the two disciples of John the Baptist who followed Jesus. He had just accepted Jesus' invitation to come and see. After spending time with Jesus, he became convinced of who he was. The first thing he does is tell his brother, and then he brings him to Jesus. That Simon would later be known as Peter.

For today: if you have come to know Jesus, don't keep the news to yourself. Begin with those closest to you, such as your family or your friends. You don't need complicated arguments; it is enough to share what you have lived and invite them to come and see.
exp.10:29:
This verse makes clear where Jesus was. He had not yet entered Bethany, the village, and was still in the same place where Martha had come out to meet him. The parentheses show that this is a note by the writer to help the reader locate the scene. "Had met" means that she had come upon him there.

The author, John, tells how Martha secretly called her sister Mary to let her know that Jesus was calling for her. John explains this because the people who were comforting Mary followed her, thinking she was going to the tomb. So many witnessed what Jesus did afterward. We do not know for certain why Jesus stayed outside the village; the text does not say.

Jesus knows how to wait for us where we are, and he calls us by name. If you are grieving, you can come to him honestly, as Mary did.
exp.6:34:
The Jewish leaders wonder aloud where Jesus might plan to go so that they cannot find him. It occurs to them that perhaps he will go to the Jews scattered among the Greeks, that is, to Jews living dispersed in lands shaped by Greek culture, and that he may also teach the Greeks, meaning the non-Jews.

They are speaking among themselves during the Feast of Tabernacles, annoyed with Jesus. He had just said that he would soon return to the Father who sent him. They understood only in a physical sense and did not grasp the spiritual meaning. Without realizing it, they mentioned something that would later happen: the message of Jesus would reach the Gentiles.

For today: let us not judge the words of Jesus with limited ideas. Let us ask him for humility to understand him, and let us remember that his invitation to drink from him remains open to everyone.
exp.10:55:
These words are spoken in the temple, where people were looking for Jesus and asking one another, "What do you think? Will he not come to the feast?" The explanation of the word "sought" means they were searching for him, either with their eyes or through their questions. "Feast" refers to the Passover.

The speakers are pilgrims who had gone up to Jerusalem to purify themselves before the Passover. They were in the temple, talking over the news. Jesus had withdrawn to Ephraim, near the wilderness, because the religious leaders wanted to arrest him. The next verse says the leaders had given orders that anyone who knew where he was should report it. The people did not know whether Jesus would dare to come, and the text does not make clear whether they were looking for him with good or bad intentions; probably there was a mix of both.

Today too there are people who wonder about Jesus, even if they do not say it aloud. We can listen to those doubts with kindness and, when the moment is right, share simply who he is. And we can ask ourselves: are we truly seeking him, or are we only keeping up a religious custom?
exp.10:28:
This verse says that Mary, as soon as she heard that Jesus was calling her, got up at once and went to him. The word "quickly" in the verse above means the same thing as "as soon as," so no separate note is needed for it. "As soon as she heard that" simply means "when she heard it."

Martha had just confessed her faith in Jesus as the Christ, the Son of God. Then she called her sister secretly and told her that the Teacher was there. The one telling the story is John. Lazarus had died, and the family was in mourning. Jesus was still outside the village, and that is why Mary went out to look for him.

When we sense that Jesus is calling us, whether in his Word or in prayer, there is no need to wait until we feel better. We can come to him quickly, even in pain, and bring to him what we are carrying.
exp.5:18:
This verse tells us that the disciples had rowed about three or four miles when they saw Jesus walking on the sea and coming near the boat. They were afraid. A furlong was about 220 yards, so twenty-five or thirty furlongs come to roughly three and a half miles.

The one telling the story is John. After the feeding of the five thousand, Jesus went up the mountain alone, and the disciples crossed the lake at night, with a strong wind and without Jesus. John shows that they were tired and struggling when Jesus arrived, and that their first reaction was fear, not joy.

For today: sometimes Jesus draws near in the middle of the storm, and we do not recognize him, because fear clouds our sight. When you are in difficulty, stop and ask him to help you see him near, and listen to his voice saying: "It is I; do not be afraid."
exp.1:8:
The ruler of the feast, that is, the one in charge of the banquet, tasted the water that had already become wine. He did not know where it came from, but the servants, who had drawn the water, did know. Then the ruler of the feast called the bridegroom.

John tells this at the wedding in Cana, where the wine ran out. Jesus commanded that the jars be filled with water, and the miracle happened without noise or spectacle. The one who narrates is John, and he wants to show that Jesus manifested his glory. Those closest to the work, the servants, were the main witnesses.

For today: God often works in what is simple, and sometimes those who do the humble tasks are the first to see what He is doing. Obey Jesus in small things, even when no one notices, and trust that He can transform the ordinary.
exp.3:47:
Jesus says to this man: "Unless you see signs and wonders, you will not believe." The words "viereis" and "creeréis" are old forms of "vieren" and "creerán." He is speaking in the plural, not only to him, but to those who were around him.

A royal official came from Capernaum, distressed because his son was dying. Jesus listens and answers with a sentence that sounds harsh. Many believe it points to a faith that depends only on seeing miracles, though the exact tone is not known for certain. Even so, Jesus grants what he asks: "Go, your son lives." The man believed his word and went on his way.

For today: do not wait to see a sign before you trust Jesus. Even without seeing answers yet, you can believe what he says and take the next step in faith.
exp.3:46:
This verse tells how a man who served the king heard that Jesus had come back from Judea to Galilee. He went to find him and kept begging him to come down to Capernaum to heal his son, who was at the point of death. The words "begged" and "come down" mean that he pleaded with him again and again to go with him.

Here the narrator is John. This man was someone in the king's service, perhaps an official at the court of Herod Antipas, though the text gives no further details. Cana was in a higher place than Capernaum, which is why the verse speaks of "coming down." His desperation led him to walk to Jesus, without regard for his position.

For today: when a need overwhelms you, do not wait until everything is settled. Go to Jesus with humility, bring him your pain with sincerity, and keep asking with confidence.
exp.3:40:
This verse says that many more Samaritans believed in Jesus, and that they did so after hearing his own words. "His word" refers to what Jesus taught them personally. They no longer believed only because of what others told them.

John tells the story. Earlier, a Samaritan woman spoke with Jesus at the well and returned to her city saying that he had told her everything she had done. Many believed because of her testimony. Then the Samaritans asked Jesus to stay, and he stayed for two days. There they heard him themselves, and afterward they told the woman that they now believed because they had heard him directly.

For today: the testimony of others can awaken our faith, but it should not stop there. Read the Gospels, listen to Jesus for yourself, and let his word strengthen your trust in him.
exp.6:43:
Some in the crowd wanted to arrest Jesus, but no one did. The explanation of the words "arrest" and "lay hands on" has been removed here because the verse itself uses neither wording.

Here we are at the Feast of Tabernacles, in Jerusalem. Jesus had just been teaching, and the crowd was divided: some believed he was the Prophet or the Christ, while others doubted him because he came from Galilee. The authorities already wanted to seize him. The text does not explain why no one dared to act; the Gospel suggests that his hour had not yet come (John 7:30), and this shows that God guided the timing of events.

Today we can trust that our circumstances do not slip out of God's hands. When we face opposition or fear, let us remember that he still reigns, and let us remain faithful with peace.
exp.3:37:
Jesus tells his disciples that he sent them to reap something they had not worked for. Others sowed and tended the field, and now they gather the result. "Reap" means to gather a harvest; "labour" means to work the land; and "labours" are the fruits of that work.

Jesus speaks with his disciples by the well at Sychar, after talking with the Samaritan woman. He uses the image of a field to explain God's work: many take part, each in their own time. The verses that follow show a real harvest, for many Samaritans believed, first because of the woman's testimony and then after hearing Jesus himself. Who the earlier sowers were is understood in several ways: the prophets, John the Baptist, or Jesus himself.

Today we can give thanks to those who sowed faith in us, such as parents, teachers, or friends. And if you see fruit in your service, remember that it did not begin with you: do your part with humility and without competing.
exp.15:16:
Here some of his disciples ask one another what Jesus meant by "a little while." He had said that in a short time they would not see him, and then again they would see him, because he was going to the Father. The words "á" and "unos á otros" simply mean "to" and "one another." They did not understand how all of that fit together.

Jesus speaks on the last night with his disciples, before his arrest. He is preparing them for his death and his departure. The disciples, confused, talk among themselves instead of asking him directly. Interpreters explain "ye shall see me" in different ways: his resurrection, the coming of the Spirit, or his final return. Perhaps it includes more than one.

When you do not understand what God allows or says, do not keep turning it over alone. Bring your confusion to Jesus with sincerity. He knows your questions and has patience to answer.
exp.6:5:
Jesus tells them that his time has not yet come. Your time, by contrast, is always ready: that is, it is always at hand, and you can act at any moment without consequences.

The speaker is Jesus, and he is answering his brothers, who did not believe in him. They were urging him to go up to the Feast of Tabernacles and show himself in public. Jesus knew that his time referred to the moment appointed by God for his decisive work, which would later include his death. That is why he did not let himself be pressured. Besides, the world rejected him because he told the truth about its evil deeds.

For today: we should not always act when others press us. We can ask God for wisdom to wait for his timing and do what is right, even when others do not understand our decision.
exp.17:8:
This verse says that Jesus took care of his disciples at the moment of his arrest, and that this fulfilled what he had already said to the Father. "Lost" means to let someone be lost or drift away. "Might be fulfilled" means that it would become reality.

John writes this in the garden, when soldiers come to arrest Jesus. He gives himself up and asks that the disciples be allowed to go. John connects this moment with Jesus' words in his prayer (John 17:12). It can be understood as physical protection in that moment, and also as care for their faith. Interpreters explain it in both ways.

Today we can trust that Christ still cares for his own. When you feel fear or weakness, remember that your faith rests not only on your own strength, but on his faithfulness. Rest in him and pray with confidence.
exp.7:28:
Jesus says that the Father, who sent him, is with him and has not left him alone. The reason is that Jesus always does what pleases the Father.

Jesus is speaking with Jewish leaders who did not understand that he was talking about the Father. He tells them that when they lift him up, they will know who he is. Many interpret this as a reference to the cross. Jesus affirms that he depends completely on the Father, and after these words many believed in him.

For today: when you feel alone for doing what is right, remember that God accompanies those who seek to please him. Let your daily decisions, even the small ones, come from a desire to honor him, trusting that he does not abandon you.
exp.17:1:
Este versículo dice que Judas, el discípulo que traicionó a Jesús, conocía bien el huerto al que Jesús había ido. Lo conocía porque Jesús se reunía allí muchas veces con sus discípulos. La palabra "traicionar" significa que lo estaba entregando, es decir, lo ponía en manos de sus enemigos.

Juan, quien escribe este relato, cuenta lo que pasó después de la última cena. Jesús cruza el arroyo de Cedrón con sus discípulos y entra a un huerto. Juan quiere que veamos que Jesús no fue sorprendido: iba a un lugar conocido, y luego sale a enfrentar a quienes venían por él, sabiendo todo lo que le esperaba.

Para hoy: a veces nos hiere la traición de alguien cercano, que conocía nuestros lugares y hábitos. Jesús lo vivió primero. Podemos llevarle ese dolor en oración, confiando en que él nos entiende y que nunca pierde el control.
exp.5:15:
When evening came, Jesus's disciples went down to the sea. The phrase about it becoming late means that night was already falling. The sea is the Sea of Galilee, also called the Lake of Tiberias.

John is the one who tells this. Jesus had just fed a crowd, and the people wanted to make him king by force. He withdrew alone to the mountain. The disciples went down to the sea to cross over to Capernaum, without Jesus. The verses that follow show that darkness and a storm came upon them.

For today: sometimes we have to move forward through the night without feeling Jesus close by. That does not mean he has forgotten us. Keep obeying what you already know God has asked of you, and trust that he sees you even when you cannot see him.
exp.10:49:
Caiaphas tells the Jewish leaders that it is better for one man to die for the people than for the whole nation to perish. The phrase "nor consider" in the verse means "you do not even consider" or "you do not realize," and "perish" means to be destroyed.

Caiaphas, the high priest that year, speaks at a meeting of the council. After the raising of Lazarus, they feared that everyone would believe in Jesus and that the Romans would take away their place and their nation. Caiaphas gives a political and practical argument. John explains later that, without Caiaphas understanding it, his words were a prophecy: Jesus would die for the nation and for the scattered children of God.

God can carry out his plan even through people with wrong intentions. When you see injustice or selfish decisions, remember that God is still at work and that his purpose does not stop. Trust in him.
exp.6:9:
He says that Jesus waited until his brothers had gone up to Jerusalem for the feast, and only then went up himself. But he did not go openly, that is, in a way that drew attention.

John tells us this. His brothers had urged him to show himself publicly at the Feast of Tabernacles, and Jesus told them his time had not yet come. The Jewish leaders already wanted to kill him, and the crowds were divided over who he was. Jesus did not act under the pressure of others, but followed the Father's plan and timing.

For today: do not let the opinions or expectations of others rush you. Before taking an important step, pray and ask God for wisdom to act in his time and in his way.
exp.2:35:
Whoever trusts in Jesus, the Son, already possesses eternal life, that is, a life with God that begins today and does not end. Here "unbeliever" refers to the one who rejects the Son or does not submit to him. That person "will not see life" means he will not live it. "The wrath of God" is his righteous opposition to sin, which remains on the one who rejects the rescue he offers.

The context is the testimony about Jesus that follows the conversation with Nicodemus. Many believe the speaker is John the Baptist; others think it is the evangelist John himself who is commenting. Both options are possible. Either way, the point is that Jesus speaks the words of God, and the Father has given him everything.

Today, do not treat Jesus as an optional topic. Trust him sincerely, and let that trust show in how you obey him each day.
exp.20:1:
This verse tells us who was gathered together by the lake. It names Simon Peter, Thomas (called Didymus, which means "the twin"), Nathanael, who was from the town of Cana in Galilee, and the sons of Zebedee. In addition, there were two other disciples whose names are not given. "The sea of Tiberias" is another name for the Sea of Galilee.

John is the one telling the story, and he recounts an appearance of the risen Jesus. The disciples are back in Galilee, their home region. John does not explain who the other two were, and we do not know their names. He also does not say why they were together, but that setting prepares the fishing and the meeting with Jesús that follow.

Today we can learn that Jesus lets himself be found among people who are gathered together, even in times of doubt or waiting. He seeks the company of other believers, so do not wait alone.
exp.13:22:
Jesus says that whoever loves him will obey his word. Because of this, the Father will also love that person, and the Father and Jesus will come to live with that person. To keep his word means to carry out and treasure what Jesus teaches. To make our home with someone means to set up one's house, one's permanent place of residence.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples at the Last Supper, shortly before he is arrested. Judas, not Iscariot, has just asked him why he will reveal himself to them and not to the world. Jesus answers that his closeness is experienced in a relationship of love and obedience. Shortly after, he also promises the Holy Spirit to accompany them.

For today: love for Jesus shows itself in everyday life. Choose one of his teachings, for example forgiving or speaking the truth, and practice it this week, remembering that God desires to dwell with you, not merely to visit you.
exp.18:29:
This verse tells of Jesus' final moments on the cross. He received the vinegar, a sour drink that was offered to him on a sponge. Then he said, "It is finished," and he bowed his head and gave up his spirit, that is, he died.

Jesus had earlier said, "I thirst." John explains that Jesus knew that everything had now been accomplished, and that this happened so that the Scripture would be fulfilled. With "It is finished," Jesus declares that he completed the work the Father had given him. Many Christians understand this to refer to the work of salvation, though other shades of meaning are also discussed.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love through perfect effort. Rest in what Christ has already done, and serve God out of gratitude, not fear.
exp.13:10:
Jesus asks his disciples to believe him when he says that he is in the Father and the Father is in him. If they find it hard to accept this on his word alone, he suggests they believe because of the works they have seen. The phrase "or else" in the verse means "if not, or even if that still is hard for you to accept."

Jesus is speaking with his disciples at the last supper. Philip asked him to show them the Father. Jesus replies that seeing him is seeing the Father, because his words and his works come from the Father who lives in him. The miracles were a sign pointing to that union.

Today, when you doubt who Jesus is, look at what he has done: his love, his care, and the changes he has brought into real lives. Trust what you have seen of him, even if you do not understand everything.
exp.5:31:
Jesus says that Moses was not the one who gave the manna, the bread from heaven, to your ancestors. It is his Father who now gives the true bread from heaven. "Gave you" is the same as "gave to you," and "but" means "rather." Jesus corrects the people's idea and points out that the true bread is greater than the manna.

Jesus speaks with a crowd that had just eaten bread that had been multiplied and was looking for him again. They ask him for a sign like the manna in the desert, so they can believe him. Jesus leads them to see that God is the one who gives, and that now he offers something that gives life to the world. Later they will ask for that bread, though they do not yet understand that he is speaking of himself.

For today: let us not seek God only for what he gives us for the day. Rather, let us ask him for what feeds the soul, which is knowing Jesus and trusting in him. We can begin each day by thanking God and reading a passage from the Gospels.
exp.0:35:
The explanation says that John the Baptist saw Jesus walking nearby and pointed him out with a very important statement. The phrase that follows is not carried over into English here, and the sentence that explained the walking place is removed for the reader.

John is speaking to two of his disciples. A day earlier he had testified that Jesus is the Son of God. Now he wants his followers to focus their attention on Jesus. Calling him the Lamb recalls the sacrifices of the people of Israel, and many Christians understand that he speaks of Jesus as the one who takes away sin (John 1:29). Upon hearing this, the two disciples followed Jesus.

Today we can learn from John: a good testimony does not point to itself, but helps others to look to Jesus. Today, with your words or your example, try to invite someone to get to know him.
exp.13:26:
Jesus leaves his disciples his peace as a gift. The words "I leave" sound like a farewell, like someone passing on an inheritance. This peace is not like the peace the world offers, which depends on everything going well. That is why he tells them not to let their hearts be troubled, that is, not to be filled with anguish, nor to be afraid.

Jesus speaks at the last supper, the night before his crucifixion. The disciples are sad and confused because he tells them he is going away. He has just promised them the Holy Spirit, who will teach them and remind them of his words. His peace is connected to that promise that they will not be left alone.

For today: when worry comes, pause and pray sincerely. Ask Jesus for his peace and remember that he is with you through his Spirit, even when circumstances do not change right away.
exp.20:14:
Jesus, after breakfast with his disciples, asks Peter: "Do you love me more than these?" Peter answers that yes, and that the Lord knows he loves him. Jesus gives him a charge: "Feed my lambs," that is, take care of them and nourish them. The reader sees "saith unto him" in place of the verb of speaking, so the words of the question are introduced as Jesus speaking to Peter.

"Than these" may refer to the other disciples or to the things of his life as a fisherman; it is interpreted in several ways.

Jesus, now risen, appears beside the lake. Peter had denied him three times on the night of the arrest. Now Jesus asks him three times whether he loves him, and so gives him the opportunity to reaffirm his love and be restored. Peter receives a new task: to care for the people of Jesus.

For today: love for Christ is shown in caring patiently for the people whom he loves. If you have failed, Jesus does not reject you; he restores you and entrusts you with something again.
exp.0:50:
Jesus speaks with great certainty: "Verily, verily, I say unto you," which means "I tell you the truth." He promises that from now on they will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man. "Son of man" is a title Jesus uses for himself.

Jesus speaks with Nathanael, who has just recognized him as the Son of God and King of Israel after feeling known by him. Jesus answers that he will see greater things. This image recalls Jacob's dream in Genesis 28, with a ladder between heaven and earth. Many understand that Jesus is that bridge between God and people, though this is explained in several ways.

For today: do not settle for a small faith. If you already trust in Jesus, ask him to show you more of himself, because in Christ heaven is open to you.
exp.5:16:
They got into a boat and crossed the sea toward Capernaum. By now it had grown dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them. Here, "boat" means a fishing boat, "the other side of the sea" means the far shore of the lake (the Sea of Galilee), and "dark" means that night had already fallen.

The writer, John, tells what happened after Jesus fed the crowd. The people wanted to make him king by force, so Jesus withdrew alone to the mountain. The disciples left without him. John does not explain why Jesus did not go with them, but the account shows that he was watching everything from afar.

Sometimes we have to keep moving through the night, when we do not see Jesus near and things become hard. Keep obeying and trusting. That you cannot see him does not mean he has left you; he knows where you are and will arrive in time.
exp.13:2:
Jesus says that he will go away and prepare a place for his disciples. Then he promises to come back and take them with him, so that they may be where he is. "Prepare" means to get something ready. "I will receive you to myself" means that he will welcome them to be with him. "If I go" is the same as "if I am going."

Jesus speaks with his disciples at the Last Supper, shortly before his death. They are sad and confused because he has announced that he will leave them. That is why he begins by saying, "Do not let your hearts be troubled." Christians have understood in different ways how and when this promise of his return will be fulfilled, but all agree that it is a promise of companionship.

When you feel fear or uncertainty about the future, remember that Jesus does not leave you without hope. Trust that he is preparing your place and that his goal is to be with you. That can bring you peace today.
exp.8:24:
Here the man who had been blind answers with simplicity. He says he does not know whether Jesus is a sinner, as the Pharisees claim, but he does know one certain thing: before he could not see, and now he sees. The phrase about being blind means "even though I was blind," and "to become his followers" is the idea behind the reference to becoming his disciples.

The speaker is the man healed by Jesus, in John 9. The religious leaders press him to say that Jesus is a sinner, because he healed on the Sabbath. His parents, out of fear, passed the responsibility on to him. He does not argue with theories; he simply tells what happened to him.

For today: you do not need to have all the answers to speak about Jesus. When someone questions you, you can tell with humility and honesty how He has changed your life. A sincere testimony has great strength.
exp.3:27:
This verse tells us that the Samaritan woman left her waterpot, or water jar, and went away into the city. There she began to speak to the people. The explanation here mentions an old form of the verb, but since your reader sees the King James wording, the verse reads "went her way into the city, and saith to the men," so the sentence that explained the old wording is omitted.

Jesus had just told her that He is the Christ, the Messiah. She had come to the well to draw water, but when she met Jesus, her priorities changed. Some think she left the jar because she was in a hurry and planned to return; others see in it a sign that something more important now filled her heart. The text does not explain it.

When we truly find Jesus, we do not need to have everything figured out in order to speak about Him. This woman was no expert, but she shared what she had experienced, and her simple testimony led others to seek Jesus. Today too we can honestly tell what He has done in our lives.
exp.12:18:
Jesus tells them ahead of time what is going to happen. He says "from now on" and "before it takes place" so that, when it happens, they will believe "I am he." That phrase echoes the divine name God gave himself in the Old Testament, and many understand that Jesus is affirming who he is.

Jesus speaks at the Last Supper, after washing his disciples' feet. He has just quoted Psalm 41:9, about the friend who betrays him, and soon he will say that one of them will hand him over. He warns them of the pain in advance so that the betrayal will not destroy their faith but will confirm it.

For today: when difficult moments or disappointments come, remember that Jesus is not caught off guard. What he said beforehand can sustain your trust, so read it and keep it in your heart before the storm.
exp.3:14:
What it says: The woman asks Jesus to give her this water. She wants her thirst taken away for good, so that she will not have to come back to the well to draw water.

Context: A Samaritan woman speaks with Jesus beside Jacob's well. Jesus has just spoken to her of a water that gives eternal life. She seems to think of literal water, which would spare her the daily work, though some believe she already senses something deeper. Jesus answers by touching her personal life, to lead her toward a deeper need.

For today: Often we ask God to relieve the discomfort of the moment, and He wants to give us much more: His life and His peace. Today you can pray sincerely, "Lord, give me what I truly need," and let Him touch what you usually keep hidden.
exp.8:5:
Jesus has just said that he is the light of the world. Then he spits on the ground, makes mud with his saliva, and spreads it over the eyes of a man who had been blind from birth. The word "anointed" means that he spread it on or applied it with his hand.

The narrator, John, shows us Jesus in action. Earlier, the disciples asked who had sinned so that this man was born blind. Jesus answers that this is an opportunity to show the works of God. The text does not say why he used mud; some think it recalls the creation of man from the dust, but that is an interpretation.

Today we can learn to obey Jesus even when his ways seem strange to us. He can act in our need in unexpected ways, and our part is to trust and take the next step.
exp.10:45:
This verse says that, after seeing Lazarus raised from the dead, some of the people who were there went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done. The Pharisees were an influential religious group among the Jews.

It is part of the account given by the narrator, John. Faced with the same miracle, the people were divided: many believed in Jesus, but others went to the leaders. It is not stated with certainty why they did this. Some think they wanted to report with good intentions; others think they were hostile. What follows shows that the leaders reacted with fear and began to plan against Jesus.

For today: the same clear sign from God can produce either faith or resistance. Ask God for an open heart, so that when you see his work you respond with trust and humility, not with fear or calculation.
exp.6:41:
This verse recalls what the Scripture taught: the Christ, that is, the Messiah, would be a descendant of King David and would come from Bethlehem, the town where David was born. "Seed" means descendants, and "town" means a small place.

The speakers are people from the crowd in Jerusalem, during the Feast of Tabernacles. They were listening to Jesus and were divided. Some thought he could not be the Messiah because they knew him as someone from Galilee. They quote the prophecy well (Micah 5:2), but they do not seem to know that Jesus was born in Bethlehem. Their conclusion was hasty.

Today, knowing the Bible is very good, but quoting it is not enough; we must investigate with humility. Before rejecting someone or something out of prejudice or incomplete information, it is wise to ask, to listen, and to seek the truth with a sincere heart.
exp.15:5:
Jesus says that when the disciples heard that he was leaving, their hearts were filled with sorrow. The word "filled" here means filled completely, so that their hearts had no room for anything else, not even for asking him where he was going.

Jesus speaks with his disciples at the last supper, shortly before the cross. He warns them that hard times are coming and that he is going to the Father. They focus on the loss and do not see what is coming. For this reason Jesus promises them the Comforter, the Holy Spirit, and assures them that his departure is for their good.

When pain fills our hearts, we can end up looking only at what we are losing. Even so, we can speak honestly to God and ask him what he wants to do in the middle of this. He does not leave us alone: he walks with us through his Spirit.
exp.10:16:
This verse tells how Jesus came to Bethany and found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb for four days. A tomb is the place where a dead person is laid. The phrase about four days stresses that Lazarus's death was a complete and obvious fact.

John is the one telling the story. Jesus had waited before going, and he told his disciples that this would happen so that they might believe. Thomas, somewhat discouraged but loyal, said: "Let us also go, that we may die with him." Many Jews of that time thought that after three days there was no hope left. Some scholars believe John highlights this to show how great the miracle was; others read it mainly as a detail of realism.

For today: when you feel that it is already too late in some situation, remember that Jesus comes even when everything seems finished. Trust in him, and keep walking toward him with honesty.
exp.17:28:
Pilate comes out of the praetorium, which was the residence of the Roman governor, to speak with the Jewish leaders who were standing outside. He asks them a formal question: what charge do they bring against Jesus?

It was early morning. The Jewish leaders had taken Jesus from the house of Caiaphas to Pilate. They would not enter the praetorium because, according to their custom, entering the house of a foreigner would make them unclean for the Passover. Pilate, as a Roman authority, wants to know the grounds for the case before he acts.

For today: Pilate asks for clear reasons, and this reminds us that we should be fair and not judge without knowing the facts. It also invites us to examine whether we care for religious appearances while neglecting justice and compassion.
exp.0:48:
Nathanael speaks to Jesus with great emotion. He calls him "Teacher," and then declares that he is the Son of God and the King of Israel.

Nathanael had just come to know Jesus through Philip. Jesus told him that he had seen him under the fig tree before Philip called him. Nathanael was impressed and recognized Jesus as the expected Messiah. Scholars explain in several ways what these titles meant to him at that moment, but Jesus then promises that he will see "greater things."

For today: God knows us and sees us in what is hidden. When we feel that Jesus truly knows us, we can answer him with honesty and confidence, and keep learning from him.
exp.19:5:
He says that Peter arrived after the other disciple, went right into the tomb, and saw the linen cloths lying there, that is, the strips of linen in which the body of Jesus had been wrapped. The word "saw" in this verse is the same as the one used for "seeth" in the King James wording, and the word for the tomb is the burial place itself. Peter did not stay outside; he went in.

It is the morning of the resurrection. Mary Magdalene had reported that the tomb was open and that she did not know where the body was. John, who tells this account, describes what he and Peter saw. Here the narrator is speaking, not Jesus. The verses that follow mention the face cloth, folded up separately, and that John "saw and believed."

For today: when you have doubts or news you do not understand, do not just stand back and watch from a distance. Come near with courage, as Peter did, and calmly examine the facts of the faith. God knows how to work in the one who seeks sincerely.
exp.10:35:
The Jews who were present say that, seeing Jesus weep, one can tell how much he loved Lazarus. The word "Behold" is an invitation to notice: "look" and "see." "How he loved him" speaks of the affection Jesus felt for his friend.

The speakers are Jews who had come to comfort Mary and Martha over the death of their brother Lazarus. Jesus had just asked where they had laid him and, on arriving, he wept. The verses that follow show that not everyone thought alike: some saw love in his tears, and others doubted him and asked why he had not prevented that death.

Jesus is not ashamed to weep with those who suffer. When you are in pain, you can draw near to him with confidence, knowing that he understands you. And when someone around you is suffering, accompany them with presence and tenderness before offering explanations.
exp.9:21:
This verse says that in Jerusalem the feast of the dedication was being celebrated, and that it was winter. The word "dedication" is how the King James Version names the feast that many today know as Hanukkah, which commemorated the renewed consecration of the temple after it had been defiled.

The one who narrates is John. He marks the time and the setting: months have passed since the earlier scenes, and the people are still divided about Jesus. Some say he has a demon; others say that his works do not belong to a man possessed. This feast recalled the temple, and Jesus walks right there, setting up the direct question they will put to him about whether he is the Christ.

For today: Jesus is present in times of celebration and also in the cold seasons. Even when there is doubt or division around you, draw near to him with sincerity and look at what he does, not only at what others say.
exp.8:0:
This verse says that Jesus was walking along and noticed a man who had been blind since birth. In the text it was written in an older form of the word for "saw," and the shorter form is what modern readers use. Jesus did not walk past: he stopped to look at someone many others ignored.

Here the narrator of the Gospel, John, speaks. He introduces the start of an important scene. As the story continues, the disciples wondered whether the blindness was a punishment for some sin. Jesus answers that it is not about that, but that God would show his work in this man. The text does not say exactly where they were, but what follows shows that Jesus took the initiative.

For today: Jesus saw a person, not just a problem. Today we can ask God for attentive eyes to notice those who suffer near us, without judging them, and to offer help, companionship, or a sincere prayer.
exp.11:1:
They prepared a dinner for Jesus there in Bethany. Martha was serving the guests, and Lazarus was seated at the table with Jesus. "At the table" describes the custom of reclining to eat.

John, the narrator, tells this six days before the Passover, shortly before Jesus' death. Lazarus had just been raised from the dead, and his presence at the table was a living sign of Jesus' power. Martha is still the one who serves, as in Luke 10. The text does not say who organized the dinner or whose house it was; some think it was in their home, but that is not certain.

For today: serving and simply being with Jesus are two ways of loving him. Give thanks for what he has done in your life, and offer him your service or your time simply, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.17:12:
They led him away first to Annas, because he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was the high priest that year.

John, who tells the story, makes clear who was who so the reader can follow the scene. Jesus had just accepted his arrest and had told Peter to put away the sword, because he had to drink the cup the Father had given him. Annas had been high priest before, and his family still held a great deal of influence. Scholars explain in several ways why they took him there first.

Jesus walked toward his suffering with resolve and not with fear. When you face unjust or difficult situations, remember that God is still at work even in the middle of them. You can trust him and respond with calm, without seeking revenge.
exp.17:29:
The Jewish leaders answer Pilate with irritation: "If this man were not a criminal, we would not have handed him over to you." The explanation of the wording is not needed here, since the phrase is already clear in the verse.

They are the accusers of Jesus, who brought him early in the morning to the praetorium, the residence of the Roman governor. Pilate asked them for a formal charge, but they give no specific accusation; they only ask him to trust their word. They wanted Pilate to approve the sentence, since, as they say later, they were not allowed to put anyone to death. John notes that in this way what Jesus had said about his death was being fulfilled.

For today: let us not condemn anyone simply because others do it or because they hold authority. Before judging, let us seek facts, listen with fairness, and ask God for humility so that we do not repeat the mistake of accusing without evidence.
exp.6:51:
The leaders answer Nicodemus with mockery: "Are you also from Galilee? Search and see that no prophet has ever come out of Galilee."

Nicodemus, a leader who had earlier gone to Jesus by night, asked that the law be followed: no one should be judged without first being heard. The Pharisees did not respond to his argument. Instead, they attacked him with a prejudice against Galilee, the region Jesus came from. Moreover, their claim was doubtful, since the Scripture says that the prophet Jonah was from Gath-hepher, which was in Galilean territory.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we judge people by where they come from, instead of listening to them fairly. Let us do as Nicodemus did: seek the truth honestly, even when others mock.
exp.18:22:
This verse tells that, after crucifying Jesus, the soldiers divided his clothing into four parts, one for each of them. There was also the tunic, the garment worn under the outer cloak. It was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom. The word "garments" here means items of clothing, and the chief priests are the leaders of the priests.

The one who tells the story is John, an eyewitness to the scene. Roman soldiers followed a common custom: they kept the belongings of the one executed. John recounts it in detail because, in the verses that follow, he connects it to Psalm 22:18. Some see the tunic as a symbol, but the text does not explain this, so we should be careful.

For today: Jesus gave up everything, even his clothing. Ask yourself what it costs you to let go of, and offer it to God in prayer, trusting that he keeps his promises even in the hardest moments.
exp.14:11:
Jesus says that his commandment is that we love one another, and that we do it with the same kind of love with which he loved us.

Jesus speaks with his disciples the night before his crucifixion, in the discourse of the vine and the branches. He has just told them to remain in his love by obeying him, just as he obeys the Father. He wants them to have complete joy. Right away he explains that the greatest love gives its life for friends.

For today: think of a person who is hard to love in your home, workplace, or church. Today, do something concrete for them without expecting anything in return: listen to them patiently, help them, or forgive them. In this way, the love of Christ becomes action, not just feeling.
exp.0:20:
The priests and Levites continue questioning John the Baptist. First they ask him whether he is Elias, and he says he is not. Then they ask whether he is that prophet, and he also answers no. The question "What then?" means "So what are you?" "That prophet" refers to the one many were expecting, as announced in Deuteronomy 18:15.

The authorities in Jerusalem sent these men to find out who John was, since he was baptizing and drawing crowds. They were expecting Elias because of what Malachi 4:5 says. John answers with few words and denies every great title. Later he will say that he is only a voice preparing the way of the Lord.

For today: John did not seek fame or try to appear to be more than he was. We can serve God with humility, without competing for recognition, and always point to Christ.
exp.10:25:
Jesus says that whoever is alive and believes in him shall never die. The word "never" means that death will not have the final say over that person. Then Jesus asks Martha a direct question: "Believest thou this?"

Jesus speaks with Martha, the sister of Lazarus, who has just died. She believed in a resurrection far off in the future, at the last day. Jesus leads her to trust in a person: "I am the resurrection and the life." She answers with faith, though she does not yet know that Lazarus will be raised.

For today: when grief comes or the fear of death arrives, do not rest only on ideas about the future. Answer Jesus' question personally, "Believest thou this?", and rest in the fact that your hope is in him.
exp.5:44:
Jesus quotes the prophets (Isaiah 54:13 and similar passages): God himself will teach his people. He says that everyone who hears the Father and learns from him comes to Jesus. "Taught of God" means instructed by God; "hear" and "learn" speak of listening to and receiving the truth.

Jesus speaks in Capernaum, after saying that he is the bread of life. Some Jews were grumbling because they would not accept that he had come down from heaven. He answers them that coming to him is not merely a human achievement: the Father draws and teaches the heart. Christians understand in different ways how this drawing of God relates to human freedom, but the text emphasizes that God takes the initiative.

Today, come to God with a heart ready to learn. Read the Bible and pray, asking: "Lord, teach me." If something in you is drawing near to Jesus, give thanks for it: God is already at work.
exp.9:38:
The explanation says that the Jewish leaders were trying once more to seize Jesus, but he slipped away from them. Their attempt to arrest him and his escape from their grasp are the two points the verse highlights.

Jesus was in Jerusalem at the Feast of the Dedication. He had just said that he and the Father are one, and some wanted to stone him for what they understood to be blasphemy. He invited them to believe at least because of his works. John does not explain how he got away, so we do not know the details. What is clear is that no one had power over him before his appointed hour.

For today: even when opposition seems stronger than we are, we can trust that God is in control. If you face pressure for your faith today, pray and keep doing good with calm, knowing that your life is in God's hands.
exp.2:5:
This verse says that what is born of the flesh, that is, of natural human life, is flesh: fragile, limited and mortal. But what is born of the Spirit is spirit, a new life that God himself gives. "Flesh" here speaks of our human nature, not only of the body.

Jesus speaks with Nicodemus, a teacher of the Jews who visited him at night. Nicodemus took being born again in a literal sense. Jesus makes clear to him that this is not another physical birth, but a new birth that only God produces, and he then compares it to the wind.

For today: we cannot manufacture spiritual life by effort, a good family or religion. Ask God humbly for that new life, and trust that he can transform you from within.
exp.14:12:
This verse says that the greatest love there is, is to give up one's own life for one's friends. "To lay down one's life" means to give it willingly, not to have it taken from us by force. The word "any" in the verse means "one person."

Jesus speaks with his disciples the night before his crucifixion. He has just commanded them to love one another as he has loved them. This verse explains the measure of that love: total self-giving. Shortly afterward he calls them friends, not servants, because he has shared with them what he heard from the Father. Christians see in this a reference to the cross.

For today: loving this way does not always mean dying, but it does mean giving of oneself. This week, give time and attention to someone who needs it, even if it costs you comfort or rest.
exp.11:15:
This verse says that at first the disciples did not understand what was happening when Jesus entered Jerusalem riding on a young donkey. But after Jesus was glorified (that is, after his death, resurrection, and return to the Father), they remembered that the Scripture had already spoken of this.
