Here John speaks as the writer of the Gospel, as a witness who remembers. Jesus enters Jerusalem and a crowd receives him. John quotes the prophet Zechariah (9:9) and explains that the disciples only grasped the full meaning later, when they saw everything God had fulfilled.

For today: sometimes we do not understand what God is doing in our lives. Do not despair or abandon your faith. Keep following Jesus, read his Word with patience, and trust that, in time, God can give you light and understanding.
exp.4:26:
The explanation says that the Father gave Jesus the authority to judge. The word "given" is the verb for giving, and "authority" here means the power or right to judge. Jesus holds this right as the Son of man, a title he used for himself, which recalls the vision in Daniel 7, where one like a son of man receives dominion. Some also see in it an emphasis that Jesus is truly human.

Jesus speaks to Jewish leaders who were challenging him because he had healed on the Sabbath and was making himself equal to God. He explains to them that the Father has entrusted him with giving life and also with judging. What follows announces a resurrection of all people.

For today: the final Judge is the same Jesus who became human and knows our weaknesses. We can live with reverence, but without paralyzing fear, trusting in him, listening to his voice, and obeying it every day.
exp.3:24:
Here the Samaritan woman says that she knows the Messiah is coming, the one also called the Christ. She states that when he comes, he will explain everything to them clearly.

She is speaking at a well in Samaria, right after Jesus had talked with her about worshiping God in spirit and in truth. The Samaritans also expected a messenger who would teach the truth. Perhaps she, feeling confused or moved by what she had heard, sets the matter aside until the Messiah arrives. Jesus answers her right away: "I am he, the one speaking with you."

For today: we often wait for answers from God in the future, but he is already near, speaking to us. Today you can open the Bible expecting to hear Jesus, not just to learn facts.
exp.5:43:
Jesus says that no one can come to him on their own. First, the Father, who sent him, must draw the person. The phrase "draw him" in the King James wording is the verb that this explanation discusses, and "I will raise him up" means that he himself will lift up from death whoever comes to him, "at the last day," that is, the final day.

Jesus is speaking to Jews who were complaining because he had said he was the bread that came down from heaven. They knew his family and could not understand how he could have come from God. He answers that believing does not depend on what a person knows from the outside, but on God himself opening the heart. Christians discuss how this divine drawing relates to human freedom.

For today: if your faith is weak, do not lose heart. Ask God to keep drawing you, and thank him each time you feel a desire to seek him.
exp.11:21:
Philip went and told Andrew that some Greeks wanted to see Jesus. Then Andrew and Philip together brought the message to Jesus. The words that the explanation quotes from the source wording mean "told him" and "tell him" in the verse above, so the phrase here is about Philip and Andrew passing a message from one person to another. It is a simple account of people carrying a message from one to the next.

The one telling the story is John. Some Greeks, who had come to Jerusalem to worship at the Passover feast, asked Philip to meet Jesus. Philip consulted Andrew, and the two of them carried the request to Jesus. Jesus answers by speaking of his hour and of the seed that dies to bear fruit, and many think this announces that his death would bring blessing to all peoples. That interpretation is common, though the text does not state it directly.

Today we can do the same as Philip and Andrew: if someone wants to know Jesus, they do not need to have all the answers. It is enough to bring them to him, simply and in the company of others.
exp.4:0:
This verse says that, after the events told earlier in the Gospel, there came a feast of the Jews and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. The word "went up" is used because Jerusalem is in a high place, so one is said to "go up" toward it. "Jerusalem" is Jerusalem.

Here the narrator, the apostle John, presents a new moment in the life of Jesus. He does not say which feast it was, and scholars have identified it in several ways, so it is best not to claim anything certain. What matters is that Jesus follows the customs of his people. Right after this, John tells that Jesus meets a sick man beside a pool.

For today: Jesus was going to the feast, but on the way he stopped before the need of others. We can ask him that, even in our religious or daily routines, he would make us attentive to those who suffer near us.
exp.13:5:
Jesus says that he is the way, the truth, and the life, and that no one comes to the Father except through him. The phrase "no one comes to the Father, but by me" means that only through Jesus can we draw near to God. In this older wording, the small word for "to" is simply the ordinary "to," and the word for "says to him" means "tells him."

Jesus is speaking with his disciples during the Last Supper, shortly before his arrest. He has told them that he is going away, and Thomas, confused, asks how they can know the way. Jesus answers that the way is not a place or a route, but himself. He then says that knowing him is knowing the Father.

For today: when you feel lost or far from God, you do not need to make some complicated journey. Come to Jesus with confidence, read about him in the Gospels, and speak to him sincerely. He is the open way to God.
exp.6:49:
Nicodemus, the same man who once went to see Jesus at night, now speaks. The text makes clear that he was "one of them," that is, part of the group of Pharisees and leaders. The explanation also notes that the old wording quoted here is simply the sense of "he says to them" and "came to him" as they appear in the verse above.

The religious leaders had just mocked the common people and rejected Jesus. Nicodemus had talked with Jesus in John 3. Now, from inside the group, he dares to step in. We still do not know whether he already believed fully in Jesus; the text only shows that he begins to defend fair treatment. Some see here a step on his path of faith.

For today: when everyone speaks with prejudice, we can ask for calm and justice, even when it costs us. A small step of courage, such as listening before judging, can open the way to the truth.
exp.6:26:
Here some residents of Jerusalem reason that Jesus cannot be the Christ because they "know where he is from": they know his origin, his hometown, and his family. According to this idea, the Messiah would appear in a mysterious way, with no one knowing where he came from.

Some of those who lived in Jerusalem are speaking, during the Feast of Tabernacles. They notice that the authorities want to kill Jesus, yet he teaches openly and no one stops him. They doubt and become confused. Jesus answers that they know him according to the flesh, but they do not know God, who sent him. His true origin is in the Father.

Today we can fall into judging Jesus or others only by what we think we know about them. Let us ask God for humility to listen, to let go of our fixed ideas, and to truly know Christ.
exp.7:53:
Jesus says that if he gave glory to himself, that glory would be worth nothing. The one who truly honours him is his Father, whom they call "your God." "I glorify myself" means "I give myself honour." "Is nothing" means that it has no value.

Jesus is speaking with Jewish leaders who have just accused him of having a demon. They ask him with contempt who he thinks he is, since Abraham and the prophets died. Jesus does not defend himself with pride, but points to the Father as the witness of who he is. Even so, they say they know God, but they do not truly know him.

Today we can learn not to live seeking applause or self-recognition. If we do what is right, we can trust that God sees us and will honour us in his time. Ask him to help you serve with humility.
exp.18:6:
The Jews answered Pilate that they have a law, and that according to that law Jesus must die. The reason they give is that he "made himself the Son of God." The word "answered" in the verse shows that they are replying to Pilate.

The ones speaking are the religious leaders and their helpers. Pilate had just said that he found no fault in Jesus. Then they change the accusation: it is no longer political, but religious. They probably have in mind the law about blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16), although the text does not say this directly. Jesus had indeed said that he was the Son of God, but they did not believe it. For this reason, this statement makes Pilate more afraid.

For today: before judging someone or defending "my truth," it is wise to ask myself whether I am seeking justice or only support for what I have already decided. Let us pray for humility to truly listen to Jesus.
exp.11:22:
Jesus answers that the time has come for the Son of man to be glorified. "Son of man" is a title Jesus uses for himself. "Glorified" means that his honor and his true worth will be shown. In this passage, that glory is tied to his death and resurrection.

Some Greeks wanted to see Jesus, and Philip and Andrew passed the request along. Jesus does not respond with a personal meeting, but by announcing that his hour has arrived. This suggests that his work would reach all peoples, and that it would pass through the cross. Right after this, he speaks of the grain of wheat that dies in order to produce much fruit.

For today: God often bears fruit through surrender and service, not through quick success. Think of one area where you can let go of your comfort or pride for the sake of others, and trust that God can bring something good from it.
exp.2:13:
Jesus says that just as Moses lifted up a serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of man, who is Jesus himself, must be lifted up. "Must" shows that this was part of God's plan. "Lifted up" points to his death on the cross.

Jesus speaks with Nicodemus, a Jewish teacher who visited him at night. Jesus reminds him of the story in Numbers 21: the people, bitten by serpents, looked at the bronze serpent and lived. In the same way, whoever looks to Jesus in faith receives eternal life, as the following verses say.

For today: when you feel wounded by your mistakes or your guilt, do not try to save yourself by your own means. Look to Christ on the cross with simple faith, and trust that his sacrifice is enough to give you forgiveness and life.
exp.0:7:
This verse makes clear that John the Baptist was not the light. His work was to point to the true light, which is Jesus. The phrase "to bear witness" means to speak about what he knew and tell it to others, like a witness.

The one speaking is the apostle John, the author of the Gospel, at the beginning of his book. He presents Jesus as the light and the Word of God. He mentions John the Baptist so that no one confuses the messenger with the One he announced. Then he says that the true light gives light to every man.

For today: our task is not to draw attention to ourselves, but to Jesus. We can serve in the church, in the family, or at work, and ask ourselves: "Do my life and my words help others look to Christ?" Being a witness is simply telling, in plain words, what He has done in us.
exp.19:14:
Jesus asks Mary Magdalene why she is weeping and who she is looking for. She thinks he is the gardener, that is, the person in charge of the garden. She asks him that, if he has carried the body away, he tell her where he has laid it, because she herself will take it.

It is the morning of the resurrection. Mary has come to the empty tomb and is full of grief. Her eyes do not recognize Jesus, even though he is standing right in front of her. He questions her with tenderness, and in the next verse he calls her by her name. Then she recognizes him. The text does not explain why she did not recognize him before; some think it was because of her tears or the dim light, but that is a guess.

Sometimes we are so focused on our pain that we fail to see that Jesus is near. We can tell him honestly what hurts us, and he listens to us and knows us by name.
exp.11:39:
It says that God left these people unable to see or understand. "Blinded" means he took away their sight, and "hardened" means he made their heart stubborn. The phrase "so that they cannot see" is understood as "so that they should not see." If they saw and understood with their heart, they would turn back to God and he would heal them.

John here quotes Isaiah 6:10 to explain why many did not believe in Jesus, despite his signs. John says that Isaiah saw the glory of Christ. Scholars explain in several ways how God acts here: some see a judgment on a hardness that already existed, others see a plan of God being fulfilled. But the text that follows shows that some leaders did believe, though out of fear they stayed silent.

For today: do not harden your heart when God speaks to you. Answer him with humility, and do not let fear of what others think keep you silent.
exp.13:30:
Jesus says he is going to do what the Father commanded him, and he does it so that the world may know that he loves the Father. The word "that" here introduces the purpose of his action. The phrase about the commandment means that the Father had entrusted him with a mission. Then he invites his disciples: "Arise, let us go hence."

Jesus is speaking with his disciples at the Last Supper, shortly before he is arrested. He has just said that the prince of this world is coming, meaning Satan, who would act through the people who would bring him to the cross. Jesus does not go to the cross defeated, but out of obedience and love. As for where they went when they got up, some think they left the upper room and that the discourse that follows continued on the road; others explain it in other ways.

For today: our obedience to God can also show love, even when it costs us. Today, obey in some specific thing God has shown you, without waiting to feel ready.
exp.15:19:
Jesus says with great seriousness that his disciples will weep and mourn, while the world rejoices. But their sorrow will not last forever: it will be turned into joy.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples on the last night before his crucifixion. They do not understand what he means. He announces his death, which will bring grief, and his resurrection, which will bring joy. Then he uses the example of a woman giving birth: the pain is real, but it ends in joy.

For today: when you go through a time of sorrow, do not deny it or feel ashamed of weeping. Bring it honestly before God, and remember that, in the hands of Jesus, sorrow does not have the last word.
exp.18:0:
Then Pilate took Jesus and had him flogged. Flogging means striking someone with a whip, and among the Romans it was a very cruel punishment. The explanation's comment about the old wording is left out here, since the reader's verse uses different words.

Here the narrator speaks, the apostle John. Pilate had already said that he found no fault in Jesus. Even so, the Jewish leaders kept pressing for him to be condemned. Some think Pilate hoped this punishment would stir the crowd to pity; the text does not say so with certainty. What we do see is that Jesus suffered unjustly.

For today: when you suffer without deserving it, remember that Jesus understands you, because he suffered out of love for us. Bring your pain to him in prayer and trust that he is with you.
exp.8:36:
Jesus answers the man: "You have already seen him, and the one who is talking with you is he." The old-style words, the quoted phrases, are dropped here because the verse your reader sees does not use them. Jesus presents himself directly as the Son of God.

The man had been born blind, and Jesus had healed him. Because he defended what had happened to him, the religious leaders threw him out of the synagogue. Jesus looks for him and finds him. Jesus had not been seen by him with his eyes before, and now he sees him for the first time. The man asks sincerely, and Jesus answers him with clarity. Afterward he believes and worships him.

Jesus goes out to seek those who have been rejected for following him. If today you feel alone or misunderstood because of your faith, remember that he finds you and makes himself known. Speak with him sincerely, ask him what you do not understand, and listen for his answer in his Word.
exp.19:23:
The explanation says that Thomas, one of the twelve apostles, was not with the others when the risen Jesus appeared to them. Thomas is also called Didymus, and in the original Aramaic that name, like Thomas itself, means "twin."

The narrator here is John. He has just told how Jesus came to the disciples on the night of the resurrection, gave them peace, and sent them out. John points out Thomas's absence to set up the next scene, where Thomas doubts and then Jesus meets him with tenderness and leads him to believe. The text does not explain why Thomas was missing, so it is best not to invent a reason.

For today: do not neglect meeting with other believers, because faith is often strengthened there. And if you ever have doubts, bring your questions honestly to Jesus; he knows how to meet you.
exp.8:33:
It says that the religious leaders answered the man who had been healed: "You were born full of sin, and do you want to teach us?" And they threw him out. The words "They answered" and "cast him out" are the ones that appear in the verse, so the explanation's comment on those words is left out here. It probably refers to expelling him from the synagogue, although the text does not spell this out.

The Pharisees are speaking, the ones who were investigating the healing of the man born blind. He had answered them plainly: if Jesus were not from God, he could do nothing. Having no arguments left, they attack him with contempt, since in their time it was commonly thought that such a condition came from some sin. Shortly afterward, Jesus seeks him out and finds him.

For today: when you are rejected or mocked for your faith or for speaking the truth, remember that Jesus does not abandon you. He seeks you, receives you, and invites you to trust Him more.
exp.10:10:
Jesus tells his disciples that their friend Lazarus is "sleeping," and that he is going to "awake him out of sleep." The word "sleeping" here is a gentle way of speaking about death.

Jesus speaks with his disciples after learning that Lazarus, from Bethany, had fallen ill. They understood his words as ordinary sleep, and thought that if he was sleeping, he would recover. For this reason the text makes clear right away that Jesus was speaking of death. He is preparing to show his power over it, and he calls Lazarus "friend," which shows his affection.

For today: when we suffer a loss, we can remember that Jesus sees death differently, with authority and tenderness. We can bring him our grief with confidence, because he is a faithful friend and has hope for those we love.
exp.16:15:
"They are not of the world" means that the disciples do not belong to the world's system, that is, to the ways of thinking and living that stand against God. Jesus says that their origin and their identity are different, just as his are. He is not talking about whether they live on earth, but about who they belong to.

Jesus is praying to the Father the night before his crucifixion. He prays for his disciples, who are going to remain in a world that will reject them, as it rejected him. He asks that God keep them from evil, not that he take them out of the world, because later he sends them into it.

Today we can remember that our identity comes from Christ, not from the approval of others. That helps us live with humility and firmness at work, at school, and in the family, loving people without copying what does harm.
exp.18:21:
Pilate answers the chief priests of the Jews firmly. He tells them that the sign he placed over the cross will not be changed. The chief priests are the leading priests. The sign is the notice stating the charge against Jesus.

Pilate had ordered a sign written that said Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews, in three languages. The priests wanted it to say only that Jesus claimed to be king. Pilate refused. We do not know his exact reasons: it may have been wounded pride, mockery toward them, or weariness at being pressed. Even so, without realizing it, he proclaimed the truth about Jesus before everyone.

God can use even the decisions of people who do not know him to proclaim the truth. Today we can trust that the truth of Christ does not depend on the intention of those who speak it. And we are called to be firm in what is good, not stubborn.
exp.6:46:
The Pharisees react with anger and answer the temple guards with a question: "Are ye also deceived?" In the Reina-Valera 1909, the guards are the temple officers or attendants, and the word "deceived" means led astray by an error.

Jesus was teaching in Jerusalem during the feast, and the religious leaders had sent these guards to arrest him. They returned empty-handed, impressed by his words. The Pharisees, annoyed that their plan had failed, dismiss the guards without examining what Jesus was saying. They prefer to rely on their own authority and on what most of the leaders thought.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we reject something only because it does not fit what we already think or what important people say. It is wise to listen with humility, compare it with Scripture, and let the truth speak, even when it makes us uncomfortable.
exp.18:35:
John says that what happened to Jesus on the cross fulfilled what the Scripture said: "A bone of him shall not be broken." The soldiers did not break his legs, as they did with the other people who had been crucified. The word "broken" here means that his bones would not be broken.

John, the narrator, was present and wants his readers to believe. The soldiers would break the legs of the crucified to hasten death before the day of rest, but Jesus had already died. Many connect this citation with the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:46) and with Psalm 34:20. John seems to present Jesus as the true Lamb.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even in the details. If he was faithful in this, you can trust that he also cares for you and that his Word is worthy of your confidence.
exp.18:2:
The explanation says that the soldiers were mocking Jesus. They called out to him "Hail, King of the Jews!", a greeting similar to the one given to the emperor, but said in mockery. "Hail" can be understood as "we salute you" or "long live." And "they smote him with their hands" means that they struck him in the face with their hands.

The soldiers speaking here are Roman soldiers. Pilate had already ordered Jesus to be scourged, and they placed a crown of thorns on him and a cloak of purple or dark red. They mocked the idea that Jesus was called a king. Afterward Pilate brought him out and said that he found no crime in him.

Jesus endured the contempt without answering with revenge. When someone mocks our faith or treats us badly, we can remember that Christ went through this first. Let us ask him for patience to respond with gentleness and to trust in God.
exp.0:8:
It says that Jesus, called here "the light," is the true light, the genuine one. This light "lighteth every man," that is, it gives clarity to every person who comes into the world. Some understand that the light reaches everyone through creation and conscience; others, that it is offered to everyone through the gospel.

The author, John, is writing the beginning of his Gospel. He has just said that John the Baptist was not the light, but a witness who pointed toward it. Now he makes clear who the true light is. He then explains that the world, which was made through Him, did not recognize Him, and that his own people did not receive Him.

For today: if Jesus is the light for everyone, I don't have to look for clarity elsewhere or feel too lost. Today I can ask Him to guide me in a concrete decision and live honestly with whatever He shows me.
exp.16:18:
Jesus says that he sets himself apart for his disciples, so that they too may be made holy in truth. "To sanctify" means to set apart for God, to dedicate to his purpose. The word "through" can be understood as a real and true holiness, not only an outward one.

Jesus speaks in prayer to the Father, the night before his arrest. He has just asked God to make the disciples holy in his truth, and he sends them into the world as the Father sent him. Many understand that Jesus sets himself apart to fulfill his mission, including the cross, and so makes their holiness possible. Interpreters explain the exact reach of that self-giving in various ways.

For today: do not seek to be holy by your own effort alone. Rest in what Christ has done for you, and let the Word of God shape you day by day, so that you live with integrity wherever you are.
exp.17:30:
Pilate tells the Jewish leaders to take Jesus and judge him according to their own law. They answer that it is not permitted for them to put anyone to death. The word "permitted" here means that it is not allowed.

It is early morning, in front of the praetorium, the residence of the Roman governor. The leaders had already arrested Jesus and wanted him dead. Pilate does not want a case without a clear accusation. The next verse explains that this fulfilled what Jesus had said about how he would die, namely by crucifixion. Historians debate how far their authority extended under Rome.

For today: when the heart has already decided, a person can look for legal excuses to justify themselves. Let us ask God for sincerity to act with justice, and not merely with the appearance of legality.
exp.7:1:
He says that Jesus, at dawn, went back to the temple in Jerusalem. Many people came to him, and he sat down to teach them. In that time, sitting was the normal posture of a teacher. The words "to him" and "taught them" are older forms, and we would say them today in the same way.

The one acting here is Jesus, and the one telling the story is John. Jesus had spent the night on the Mount of Olives, a place he used to go to be alone. Many scholars point out that this passage (John 7:53–8:11) does not appear in the oldest manuscripts, and some Bibles mark it. Even so, this scene sets up the encounter with the woman and the Pharisees.

Jesus began the day by teaching, and the people were eager to hear him. We can follow this by seeking God early, before the day fills with noise, and by coming to Jesus with a desire to learn. A brief time with his Word can give direction to everything else.
exp.8:29:
Here the man who had been born blind answers with courage. He says it is an astonishing thing: the religious leaders do not know where Jesus comes from, and yet Jesus opened his eyes. The phrase "in truth" would be a rendering of the earlier wording, but since it is not in the verse your reader sees, we simply note that the man's statement is one of surprise and certainty.

The Pharisees were questioning the man who had been healed. They had insulted Jesus and claimed to follow Moses, yet they doubted where Jesus came from. The man uses a simple argument: the fact of his healing is plain, and they cannot explain it or deny it.

For today: you do not need to know everything in order to speak about what God has done in your life. Your sincere testimony, given with respect and firmness, has value even when others do not understand it or do not accept it.
exp.7:3:
What it says: The scribes and Pharisees speak to Jesus and address him as "Master." They say this woman was caught in the very act of adultery. Their wording presents the case as if it were already proven, and the phrase "in the very act" describes her being caught while committing adultery.

Context: The religious leaders are the ones speaking, and Jesus is teaching in the temple in the morning. The text says they were doing this to trap him so they could bring an accusation against him. If Jesus said she should be stoned, he would clash with Roman authority and with his message of mercy; if he said no, he would seem to go against the law of Moses. Some scholars note that the man involved does not appear, although the text does not explain why. It is also known that this passage is missing from several ancient manuscripts, and its original place is debated.

For today: Let us be careful not to use the truth or the Bible as a weapon to expose others. Before pointing out someone else's sin, let us examine our own heart and seek restoration, not punishment.
exp.9:9:
The thief comes only to steal, to kill, and to destroy. "Steal" means to take secretly. By contrast, Jesus says that He came so that people may have life, and a life "in abundance," that is, full and overflowing.

Jesus is speaking to a group of Pharisees, after healing a blind man (ch. 9). He uses the image of a shepherd and his sheep. The "thieves" are the leaders who take advantage of the people instead of caring for them. Jesus presents Himself first as the gate and then as the good shepherd who gives His life for the sheep. Scholars debate whether "abundance" refers mainly to spiritual and eternal life or also to daily life; both ideas have been held.

Today we can ask ourselves which voices take away our peace and hope, and draw near to Jesus in prayer and Bible reading to rest in His care.
exp.0:2:
This verse says that everything that exists was created through the Word, that is, Christ. Nothing that was made appeared without him. The phrase repeats the idea in two ways to make clear that there is no exception.

Here the apostle John speaks, beginning his Gospel by presenting who Jesus is. Before telling of his life on earth, John shows him as the Word who was with God from the beginning. The verses that follow say that in him there is life and light for people, though the darkness did not understand it.

For today: if all things were made by Christ, your life and the lives of those around you are not an accident. You can treat people and creation with respect and gratitude, and trust that the one who made all things can also care for you.
exp.16:20:
Jesus prays that all who believe in him may be one, that is, that they may live united. This unity resembles the one between the Father and the Son: one in the other. And the goal is that the world may believe that the Father sent Jesus. The phrase "one thing" in the old wording means the same as "one," or "united" — but the verse above uses "one," so no further explanation is needed.

Jesus speaks on the night before his arrest, in a prayer to the Father. He has already prayed for his disciples, and now he also prays for those who would believe because of his message. He therefore includes believers of every age. Christians understand this unity in different ways, but all agree that it is something very important to Jesus.

For today: seek to care for unity with other believers. When there are differences, treat the other person well, listen with patience, and seek peace. Your kind treatment can be a witness before those who observe you.
exp.6:12:
Here is the translation of the explanation of John 7:13 into plain, modern English. It says that, although people talked a great deal about Jesus, nobody did so out loud or with courage. People spoke in hushed voices because they were afraid of the authorities.

The author, John, describes the atmosphere in Jerusalem during the Feast of Tabernacles. Here "the Jews" does not mean the whole people, but the religious leaders who opposed Jesus and were looking for him (verses 1 and 11). The crowd was divided: some said he was a good man, and others said he deceived the people. Out of fear of those authorities, everything stayed in whispers.

Today we too can keep our faith quiet out of fear of what others will say. This verse invites us to ask God for courage to speak about Jesus with respect and sincerity, without letting fear silence us.
exp.20:24:
This verse says that Jesus did many more things than were written down. If each one had been recorded in detail, the writer thinks the whole world would not have room for so many books. The phrase "would have room" is the point to notice here. It is a way of speaking with exaggeration, common in that time, to express that Jesus is immensely great.

The one speaking is the author of the Gospel, the disciple who gives testimony, and Christian tradition identifies him as John. Some scholars think that other people also took part in closing the text, since it says "we know that his testimony is true." With this farewell, the author explains that he did not want to tell everything, but only what was needed for belief (John 20:31).

For today: do not be discouraged if you do not understand everything about Jesus. Read calmly what God has left written, trust in it, and keep getting to know him each day, for there is always more to discover about him.
exp.0:42:
The verse says that the next day Jesus decided to go out into Galilee. There he found Philip and said to him, "Follow me." The words "findeth" and "would go forth" in the verse above correspond to "find" and "go forth." "Follow me" is an invitation to go after Jesus as a disciple.

The narrator is John, who is recounting the first days of Jesus' ministry. Shortly before, Andrew and another disciple had come to Jesus, and Andrew brought his brother Simon. Now Jesus himself takes the initiative with Philip, who was from the same town, Bethsaida. Soon Philip will bring Nathanael with the same message.

For today: Jesus continues to invite each person, and following him is not only believing ideas but walking with him every day. Whoever has been found by Christ can, like Philip, invite others with simplicity. Today you can say to Jesus, "Here I am, guide me," and share with someone close to you what he has done in your life.
exp.17:38:
Pilate reminds the Jews of a custom: each Passover he would release one prisoner.

He is speaking as the Roman governor. He has just questioned Jesus and has declared that he finds no crime in him. Instead of deciding justly, he tries to get out of the difficulty by letting the crowd choose. The Gospels mention this custom, but we have no other reliable source that confirms it. The crowd asks for Barabbas.

For today: when we know what is right, we should not hide behind the opinion of others or the pressure of the group. Let us ask God for the courage to act in truth, even when it costs us.
exp.11:13:
Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it. "Little donkey" means a small donkey, and "as it is written" shows that John wants us to see here the fulfillment of a prophecy from Scripture.

The one speaking is John, the narrator. The crowd has just welcomed Jesus as King with palm branches and shouts of "Hosanna!" John makes clear that Jesus does not enter on a warhorse but on a young donkey, and he quotes the prophet Zechariah (9:9). In this way he shows that Jesus is a humble and peaceful king. The disciples understood this only after the resurrection and glorification of Jesus.

For today: Jesus shows that true greatness is expressed with humility. Today we can ask ourselves where we seek to be seen or to impress, and ask him to teach us to serve with simplicity and peace.
exp.17:35:
Jesus says that his kingdom does not belong to this world. If it were a kingdom like those of the earth, his servants would fight to keep him from being handed over to the Jews.

Jesus speaks before Pilate, the Roman governor. The Jewish leaders accused him of wanting to be king, and that sounded like rebellion against Rome. Jesus makes clear that his kingdom is not a political threat, but he does affirm that he is king, and that he came to bear witness to the truth.

Today we can remember that Christ's kingdom advances through truth, love, and service, not through violence or force. Before we defend our faith, let us ask ourselves whether we do so with the spirit of Jesus: firmness, respect, and gentleness.
exp.5:33:
Here the people ask Jesus: "Lord, evermore give us this bread." The people who ask this are the ones who followed Jesus after the feeding of the multitude. They speak of the bread that comes down from heaven and gives life, which Jesus had just been talking about.

Those speaking are the people who followed Jesus after the feeding of the multitude. Jesus had explained to them that the true bread from heaven comes from the Father. They ask for that bread, but it seems they still think of physical food. Jesus answers them at once: "I am the bread of life." Some understand this request as sincere, others as a misunderstanding; the text does not make this entirely clear.

We can ask Jesus for what we need, but it is good to ask Him first for Himself. Today, before asking for things, take a moment to seek Him in prayer and in His Word.
exp.4:35:
Jesus says he has a greater witness than that of John the Baptist. That witness is the works the Father gave him to accomplish: healing, giving life, teaching, and showing compassion. These works show that the Father sent him. "Greater" means bigger, and "accomplish" means to carry something out until it is finished.

Jesus is speaking with religious leaders who were questioning him after he healed a sick man at the pool of Bethesda. He reminds them that John was a light they enjoyed for a while, but they did not fully believe. Now he points them to something they can see with their own eyes: what he does.

For today: it is not enough to admire Jesus or good teachers. Look at how Jesus has worked in the Bible and in your life, and let that lead you to trust him. Let your own life also reflect his works.
exp.18:36:
This verse says that another Scripture foretold that people would look on the one they pierced. The word "pierced" means that they ran through him or wounded him with something sharp. Here it refers to the spear that a soldier thrust into the side of Jesus after he had already died.

The one speaking is the author of the Gospel, John, who tells what he saw at the cross. Earlier he cited the Scripture that says not one of his bones would be broken, and now he adds another Scripture. Almost everyone thinks this one is taken from Zechariah 12:10. John wants his readers to see that what happened was no accident, and that in this way they may believe in Jesus.

For today: look at Jesus with attention and without rushing. Reflect on what he suffered for you, and let that lead you to trust him more and to thank him sincerely.
exp.4:25:
This verse says that the Father has life in himself, meaning his life does not depend on anyone. In the same way, the Father granted the Son to have that same kind of life in himself.

Jesus speaks with Jewish leaders who were criticizing him because he healed on the Sabbath and said that God was his Father. He explains that his authority comes from the Father. For this reason he can give eternal life to those who believe, and later raise the dead and judge.

For today: our life is borrowed, but Jesus' life is full and his own, and he shares it with those who trust in him. Today you can come to Jesus with your fears, your weariness, or your grief, knowing that he is the source of life and it never runs out.
exp.10:3:
Jesus receives the news that his friend Lazarus is sick. He answers that this sickness is "not unto death," meaning that it would not end in death as its final result. His purpose is the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.

Lazarus's sisters, Martha and Mary, send word to Jesus because they love him and trust him. Jesus answers the messengers, and the text makes clear that he loved that family. Then he stays two more days where he was. Lazarus dies, but Jesus raises him afterward (John 11). So his words point to the outcome, not to Lazarus not dying.

When a difficulty drags on and it seems that God is slow, we can keep trusting his love. His silence does not mean abandonment. We can ask him that, even in what hurts, he would accomplish his purpose and show himself great in our lives.
exp.6:50:
Nicodemus asks whether the law allows a person to be condemned without first hearing him and knowing clearly what he has done. In this verse, "judge" means to condemn. The old forms "hear" and "understand" are replaced here by the plain words of the verse: first a person is heard, then understood, and only after that is he judged.

We are in Jerusalem, at the Feast of Tabernacles. The Pharisees are angry with Jesus and look down on the ordinary people who follow him. Nicodemus, a Pharisee who had earlier gone to see Jesus at night, speaks with caution. His colleagues do not answer his argument; they mock his Galilean origin and bring the meeting to an end. The law he refers to is probably connected with principles such as those in Deuteronomy 1:16 and 17:6, although the text does not quote an exact passage.

Today, before you give an opinion or criticize someone, listen to them patiently and look for the facts. Justice and love begin with listening.
exp.5:20:
Here the text says that the disciples, who had been afraid earlier, were willing to receive Jesus into the boat. The word "willingly" means they did it gladly, eagerly. Then the boat immediately reached the shore where they were heading. Some understand this as an additional miracle; others think the text only emphasizes that they arrived quickly and safely. The text gives no further details.

John tells what happened at night on the Sea of Galilee, after Jesus fed the crowd. The disciples were rowing with difficulty and were frightened when they saw him walking on the water. Jesus said to them: "It is I; do not be afraid." John wants to show who Jesus is and what his power is.

For today: when you feel fear or weariness, do not wait for everything to calm down before inviting Jesus. Receive him with confidence into your "boat," that is, into your situation, and leave the course in his hands.
exp.0:4:
This verse says the light shines in the middle of the darkness, but the darkness did not grasp it. That word can mean to understand, and it can also mean to seize or overcome. So some read it this way: the darkness could not understand the light. Others read it this way: the darkness could not put it out. Both ideas fit well. "Shines" means that it gives light.

Here the apostle John speaks as he begins his Gospel. He is talking about Jesus, called the Word, who gives life and is the light for people. John wants us to know who Jesus is before he tells his story. The verses that follow introduce John the Baptist, sent to point to that light.

For today: when problems or confusion surround you, remember that the light of Christ still shines and no darkness puts it out. Ask him to guide you today in one specific step.
exp.11:20:
These verses tell of some Greeks who had come to Jerusalem to worship at the feast. They approached Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee. Respectfully, they said, "Sir, we would see Jesus."

The writer, John, tells this right after Jesus enters Jerusalem. The Pharisees were complaining that the whole world was going after him. These Greeks were probably foreigners who worshiped the God of Israel. Philip tells Andrew, and the two of them tell Jesus, who answers that the hour has come for him to be glorified. The text does not say whether they actually spoke with him at that time.

Today, we can have the same sincere desire to see Jesus. Seek him by reading the Gospels with an open heart. And if someone tells you they want to know him, do as Philip and Andrew did: go with them and bring them to Jesus.
exp.14:4:
Jesus says that he is the vine, that is, the main plant, and that his followers are the branches. Whoever remains joined to him, and he in that person, bears much fruit. He adds that, apart from him, they can do nothing.

Jesus speaks to his disciples the night before his crucifixion, at the Last Supper. He is preparing them for his departure. He teaches that life with God depends on being united to him, just as a branch lives only if it is joined to the plant. Some understand "fruit" as character and love; others also as service to others.

Today, before you strive to do good things, seek to be close to Jesus: pray every day, read his word, and trust in him. From the bond with him, fruit is born.
exp.5:1:
The explanation says that a great crowd was following Jesus because they had seen the signs he performed in healing the sick. The word for "followed" is rendered as "was following him," and the signs are miracles that showed God's power. The Sea of Galilee is the lake of Galilee, also called the Sea of Tiberias.

The writer, John, tells what happened after Jesus' teaching in Jerusalem. Jesus crosses the lake, and the people follow him. John says that the crowd was moved by the miracles, but he does not say that everyone understood who Jesus was. Later in the chapter, Jesus speaks to them about the bread of life, and many become confused or turn away.

We can come to Jesus with our needs, and he receives us. But let us also ask him to teach us to seek him himself, and not only his favors. In this way our faith will grow beyond the good moments.
exp.2:28:
He who has the bride is the bridegroom. The bridegroom's friend does not take his place: he stands by, attentive, listening. When he hears the bridegroom's voice, he is overjoyed. The phrase "rejoices greatly" means he feels a deep joy, and "fulfilled" means complete, full.

John the Baptist is the one speaking. His disciples were worried because many people were now going to Jesus to be baptized. John makes clear to them that he is not the Christ, but the one who was sent before him. In the image of the wedding, Jesus is the bridegroom and John is only his friend. Many understand that the bride represents the people of God.

For today: our joy does not depend on being the center of attention or on visible success. We can serve gladly, even when no one notices us, and rejoice when Christ is honored and others come to Him. Today, ask yourself: am I happier when I am recognized, or when Jesus is glorified?
exp.10:8:
Jesus answers with a question: does the day not have twelve hours? He means that the day has a limited amount of light. Whoever walks during that time does not stumble, because he sees the light of the sun. The word "walk" in the verse is the same idea as "walk" here.

The disciples warn him that in Judea the Jews wanted to stone him, and they do not understand why he is going back. Jesus answers them with this image: he has a time appointed by the Father, and while it lasts, he can walk with safety. Many understand that he is speaking of his mission and of God's will as the light that guides him.

Today we can learn to follow what God shows us, even when there are risks. Walking in obedience and trust in him gives us clarity and peace. Let us ask him each day for light to take the next step.
exp.13:28:
Jesus says that he told them about these things before they happened. "I have told you before it comes to pass" means "I told you beforehand." His purpose is that, when everything takes place, they will believe in him. "When it is come to pass" means "when it happens."

Jesus speaks with his disciples at the Last Supper, shortly before he is arrested. They are sad and confused because he has announced that he is going to the Father. He comforts them with his peace and explains in advance what is coming, so that his departure will not destroy their faith but strengthen it by reminding them that he had already said so.

For today: when difficult or unexpected moments come, remember what God has already said in his Word. Reading it calmly now prepares you to trust him later, when the trial arrives and you do not understand everything.
exp.4:30:
Jesus says that if He were the only one speaking in His own favor, His testimony would not be true. Here "not true" means it would not be valid or sufficient as proof before a court. He does not say that Jesus is lying, but that one voice alone, with no other witnesses, is not enough.

Jesus is speaking with Jewish leaders who were persecuting Him for healing on the Sabbath and for calling Himself the Son of God. The law required more than one witness to confirm something. That is why Jesus points to others who support Him: the Father, John the Baptist, and later, His works and the Scriptures. He says that He does not act on His own, but in unity with the Father.

Today: it is not enough for me to say that I am a Christian; my faith should be seen in my life. And to know the truth, it is good to listen to God's Word, and not only to my own opinion.
exp.1:7:
Jesus tells the servants to now draw out some of the water from the jars and bring it to the one in charge of the feast. The "governor of the feast" is the person who directs the banquet, something like the head of the table. To "draw out" means to take some out, and "bear" means to carry or bring it to him, so "they bare it" means they carried it to him.

We are at a wedding in Cana of Galilee. The wine has run out, and Jesus ordered the jars to be filled with water. Now he speaks to the servants and asks them for an act of obedience without explaining the result. They obey, and so the water, now turned into wine, reaches the governor of the feast.

For today: sometimes God asks us to take a simple step of obedience without showing us the whole outcome. We can trust that when we do what He directs, He knows how to work beyond what we can see.
exp.12:19:
Jesus says that whoever receives the person he sends receives him. And whoever receives Jesus also receives God the Father, who sent him.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples at the Last Supper, just after washing their feet. He has just taught them to serve with humility. He has also mentioned that one of them will betray him. Here he reminds them that, as those he sends, they carry his authority and his message, even when some reject them.

Today, we can receive with respect and kindness those who faithfully share the word of Christ with us. And when we serve others in his name, let us remember that we represent Jesus himself.
exp.11:33:
The people answer Jesus with confusion. They know the teaching of Scripture that the Christ, that is, the Messiah, remains forever. But Jesus has just said that the Son of man must be lifted up. So they ask: how can that be? Who is this Son of man?

The crowd speaking here is the one listening to Jesus in Jerusalem. He had spoken of being lifted up from the earth, and John makes clear that he meant his death. The people could not understand how an eternal Messiah could die. Jesus does not answer their question directly, but invites them to believe in the light while they still have it.

For today: when something about God does not fit our ideas, let us not stop at only arguing. Let us come to Jesus with humility, and follow the light we have already received.
exp.7:23:
Jesus tells them that if they do not believe that "I am he," they will die in their sins. The words "I told you" recall what he had already said before. "You will die in your sins" means reaching the end of life without having been forgiven. "If you do not believe" means "if you do not believe."

Jesus is speaking with some Jewish leaders who reject him. They do not understand where he comes from, and they think he may be planning to take his own life. He explains that he comes from above, from heaven. With "I am" he affirms who he is, and many believe it recalls the name by which God revealed himself to Moses. They ask him, "Who are you?", because they do not grasp it.

Today, believing in Jesus is not only admiring him, but trusting in him as God's sent one to forgive us. Today you can ask him for forgiveness sincerely and rest in his grace.
exp.18:38:
It says that Nicodemus, the man who once came to see Jesus at night, also came to help with the burial. He brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds. Myrrh and aloes were fragrant perfumes and spices used to prepare bodies. A mixture means the two were combined. A hundred pounds was an enormous amount, and some think it showed great honor.

Here John speaks, telling what happened after Jesus' death. Nicodemus appears earlier in John 3, when he sought out Jesus in secret. Joseph of Arimathea was also a disciple who hid out of fear. Now both act openly, in plain sight of everyone, just after Jesus had died.

For today: our faith sometimes begins timidly, but God can give us courage. Today we can take one concrete step and openly show our love for Christ.
exp.17:9:
Peter had a sword and drew it. With it he struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his right ear. The text makes clear that this servant's name was Malchus.

It is the night Jesus is arrested, in a garden. An armed crowd has come to take him. Jesus has just asked that his disciples be allowed to go free. At this moment, John is the one telling what happened, and Peter reacts with violence to defend his Master. Right away Jesus orders him to put the sword away, because he must drink the cup the Father has given him.

Many times we want to defend God with anger or force, but Jesus shows us another way. Before we react, it is good to ask ourselves whether we are trusting God's plan or only following our impulse.
exp.11:10:
This verse says that many Jews were leaving their leaders and believing in Jesus because of Lazarus. The word "went away" means that they were turning away from the position of the religious leaders, and "because of him" refers to Lazarus, whom Jesus had raised from the dead.

The writer, John, reports this in the days before the Passover. Many were coming to Bethany to see Lazarus alive. The chief priests felt threatened, and for that reason they were planning to kill Lazarus as well. His life was a visible proof of Jesus' power, and that troubled them. Shortly afterward, the crowd welcomed Jesus into Jerusalem with palm branches.

For today: a life changed by Jesus speaks louder than many sermons. Tell someone, simply, what God has done in you. Your testimony can encourage others to draw near to Christ, even though some may be bothered by it.
exp.11:16:
The people who were with Jesus when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead kept telling what they had seen. They were witnesses to it, so they spoke about it openly.

John is the one telling the story. Jesus enters Jerusalem riding on a young donkey, and the crowd that had seen Lazarus raised tells others about it. Because of this, as the following verses show, many people go out to meet him. The Pharisees, on the other hand, are worried because they see that everyone is following Jesus.

For today: you do not need to be a great preacher to speak about Jesus. It is enough to simply tell what he has done in your life or what you have seen of him. A sincere testimony can awaken in others the desire to know him.
exp.11:41:
Although many did not believe, this verse says that several Jewish leaders did believe in Jesus. But they did not say so openly because they feared the Pharisees. They were afraid of being thrown out of the synagogue. The chief rulers were the authorities or leaders of the people.

Here the writer of the gospel, John, speaks. He has just explained that many did not believe in Jesus, and he quotes Isaiah. Then he shows that there were exceptions among the leaders. Being put out of the synagogue meant losing one's community and social standing. John points out that the fear of what others think weighed more heavily than their desire to please God.

For today: if you believe in Jesus, do not hide your faith out of fear of what people will say. Ask God for courage and look for a simple, humble way to speak of Him with those around you.
exp.0:34:
This verse says that the next day John the Baptist was again in the same place, and with him were two of his disciples. The phrase "the next day" refers to the day after John gave his testimony about Jesus. The word "stood" gives the idea that he remained there, firm in his work.

Here the narrator, John the apostle, is telling the scene. John the Baptist had already said that Jesus was the Son of God. This verse prepares the moment when he will say, "Behold the Lamb of God." The two disciples listen, and then they follow Jesus. The verse does not say who they were, although some think one of them was Andrew, who is mentioned later.

For today: John did not keep his followers for himself, but pointed them toward Jesus. We can ask ourselves whether our way of speaking and living helps others draw near to Christ, without seeking attention for ourselves.
exp.5:61:
Jesus asks a question that is left open: "What then if you see the Son of Man ascend to where he was before?" The word "viereis" is not used here; the question itself stands as the focus. "Son of Man" is a title Jesus uses for himself. It speaks of his return to heaven, from where he says he came.

Jesus is speaking in Capernaum, after saying that he is the bread of life. Many disciples were offended, that is, they stumbled, because his words seemed hard to them. Jesus knew what they were grumbling about and shows them that his origin is heavenly. Interpreters explain in various ways whether this points to the ascension or to his glory in general, but the point is that he is greater than they imagine.

For today: when a teaching of Jesus seems difficult to you, do not turn away right away. Trust in who he is and ask him for light to understand it.
exp.16:19:
Jesus says that his prayer is not only for the disciples who are with him, but also for all those who will believe in him later on. These people will come to faith through the message the disciples will proclaim. Here the word "Neither" in the verse, along with "these," refers to the eleven disciples who were present.

Jesus speaks with the Father in his final prayer before going to the cross. He has just prayed for his disciples, whom he is sending into the world. Now he widens his prayer to include the future generations of believers. He asks that all of them be one, so that the world may believe.

For today: if you believe in Jesus, you were included in this prayer. Someone shared the message with you, and you can share it with others. Pray for unity among believers and seek to get along well with your brothers and sisters in the faith, so that your life speaks well of Christ.
exp.7:48:
Jesus answers calmly to a serious accusation. He says that he does not have a demon, but that he honours his Father. Then he points out that they have dishonoured him. The word "but" here means "on the contrary," and "dishonoured" means that they have treated him without respect.

Jesus is in Jerusalem, speaking with Jewish leaders who reject him. They have just called him a Samaritan (an insult, since they looked down on Samaritans) and said that he has a demon. Jesus does not defend himself out of pride; he insists that his teaching comes from God. Right after, he adds that he does not seek his own glory, because God himself will take care of judging.

When someone treats you badly or insults you, you can respond without shouting or seeking revenge. Jesus shows us how to speak the truth with firmness and peace, and to leave the outcome in God's hands.
exp.16:3:
Jesus tells the Father that, while he was on earth, he honored him through his life and his works. He affirms that he finished the work the Father gave him to do. "Glorify" means showing how great and good someone is, and "finished" means completed.

These words are part of Jesus' prayer before going to the cross, on the night of the Last Supper. He speaks with the Father about his mission: to give eternal life to his own, which is to know the true God. Here he sees his ministry as already accomplished, and right after this he asks to be glorified together with the Father. Some think he refers to his whole work, including the cross that was still ahead; the text does not fully make this clear.

For today: God has also entrusted you with specific things in your home, your work, and your church. Do them faithfully, without comparing yourself to others, seeking that God be honored.
exp.13:27:
Jesus reminds his disciples of what he has already told them: he is going away, but he will come back to them. He says that if they truly loved him, they would rejoice, because he is going to the Father. And he adds: "for my Father is greater than I," meaning that the Father is greater than he is.

Jesus speaks at the last supper, shortly before his arrest. The disciples are sad and afraid because he will leave them. He wants them to look beyond their grief and trust. About how the Father is "greater," Christians have understood it in several ways: through the Son's obedience in his mission, or through the order of the relationship between the two.

When something hurts, we can trust that God is still at work. Ask him to give you his peace and a faith that looks beyond the difficult moment.
exp.0:21:
The envoys from Jerusalem had already asked John whether he was the Christ, Elijah, or the prophet, and he said no to all of them. Now they press him: "Who art thou?" They want to bring an answer back to those who sent them. They ask him to tell them about himself.

The ones asking are priests and Levites, sent by the Pharisees, or by the religious leaders of Jerusalem. John was baptizing and many people were following him, so the authorities wanted to know by what right he acted. John does not put himself at the center. In the next verse he describes himself as a voice preparing the way of the Lord.

For today: when someone asks you who you are, do not begin with your achievements or your image. Let your life point to Christ. You can live with humility, knowing that your worth comes from God and that your purpose is to serve him and point toward Jesus.
exp.14:14:
Jesus says that he will no longer call his disciples "servants," but "friends." He gives the reason: a servant only obeys orders without knowing the plans of his master, but Jesus has shared with his friends everything he has heard from his Father. The word "made known" in the verse means to make known, to reveal.

Jesus speaks to his disciples at the Last Supper, shortly before going to the cross. He has just said that the greatest love is to lay down one's life for one's friends, and he himself is about to do so. His friendship is an invitation to a close relationship, where obedience springs from love and not from fear. Then he reminds them that he chose them and asks them to love one another.

For today: draw near to God not as someone fulfilling a duty, but as a friend. Set aside time to listen to his Word and to speak to him with confidence, and let that affection move you to obey and to love others.
exp.3:0:
This verse says that Jesus became aware that the Pharisees had heard that He was gaining and baptizing more disciples than John the Baptist. The word "knew" here means that He found out or learned it. The Pharisees were a very strict Jewish religious group devoted to the law.

The one speaking here is the narrator, John, the author of the Gospel. The Pharisees were already watching John the Baptist, and now they were taking note of Jesus, whose ministry was growing. The next verse clarifies that it was His disciples who baptized, not Jesus Himself. Afterward, Jesus left Judea and went toward Galilee. The text says nothing more about His reasons, so it is best not to assume too much.

For today: Jesus did not seek fame or rivalry, and He acted wisely under pressure. We can learn to serve without comparing ourselves to others, and to ask God for discernment to know when to move forward and when to step away from unnecessary conflict.
exp.19:10:
Mary Magdalene, the explanation says, stood outside the tomb, weeping. While she wept, she bent down to look inside. The text adds nothing more, but it shows her grief and her desire to find Jesus.

John tells what happened on the morning of the resurrection. Peter and the other disciple had already seen the empty tomb and gone home. Mary remained alone, not yet understanding what had happened, since she thought the body had been taken away. Her weeping prepares the way for her meeting with the angels and then with Jesus himself.

For today: when you feel sadness or confusion, do not turn away from God. Stay close to Him, even while weeping, and keep seeking Him sincerely. Sometimes Jesus is nearer than we imagine.
exp.19:22:
It says that Jesus gives his disciples an authority connected with the forgiveness of sins. "To forgive" means to pardon or let go of a debt, and "to withhold" means not to forgive, leaving the debt in place. The words "forgive" and "withhold" are the verse's own wording, so no separate comment is needed on the older forms.

Jesus speaks after his resurrection, on the evening of Easter Sunday, with his disciples gathered together. He has just sent them as the Father sent him and has given them the Holy Spirit. Christians understand this passage in different ways: some see it as the Church's authority to absolve, others as the proclamation of the forgiveness that God gives through Christ.

For today: if someone asks you for forgiveness or needs to hear the gospel, tell them with confidence that in Christ there is forgiveness, and you too forgive without holding on to resentment.
exp.13:13:
Here it says that Jesus himself will answer whatever his disciples ask "in my name." The old word translated here as "ask" means "ask," so the phrase reads simply "if you ask." Asking in his name is not repeating a formula at the end of a prayer, but asking according to his character, his will, and his authority.

Jesus speaks with his disciples the night before his crucifixion. He is preparing them for his departure, since he is going to the Father. He promises that they will carry on his work and that they will not be alone. The purpose, the previous verse says, is that the Father be glorified in the Son. That is why the next passage joins asking with love and obedience, and announces the Holy Spirit.

Before you pray, ask yourself: "Does this honor Jesus?" Ask with confidence, but with a heart ready to obey him, and let him decide how and when to answer.
exp.15:2:
Jesus says that those who persecute his disciples will do so because they do not truly know the Father or him. The words "these things will they do unto you" refer to the expulsions and violence he has just announced. The word "unto" is an older way of saying "to," and "you" here means the disciples he is speaking to.

Jesus speaks with his disciples at the Last Supper, shortly before he is arrested. He warns them about the rejection that is coming so that they will not lose heart or stumble in their faith. Many persecutors would believe they are serving God, but Jesus explains that in reality they did not know him. In the Gospel of John, knowing God is more than knowing facts: it is a relationship with the Father through the Son.

Today, if someone rejects you or mocks you for your faith, remember that Jesus already anticipated this. Do not respond with hatred; pray for that person and examine your own heart, so that you may truly know God and reflect his love.
exp.17:13:
This verse reminds us who Caiaphas was: the high priest who had already advised the Jews that it was better for one man to die for the people. "High priest" is the title for the leading priest, and "advice" is an opinion or counsel given to others.

Here the writer, John, is speaking as he recounts Jesus' arrest. He points back to what was said earlier in John 11:49-52. There Caiaphas put it as a political calculation to avoid trouble with Rome. John explains that, without Caiaphas knowing it, his words said something true: Jesus would die for the people. So John shows us that Jesus was not dragged into this by surprise; God was still at work even in the midst of injustice.

For today: when you see injustice or human plans gone crooked, trust that God can accomplish his purpose without approving of the evil. Rest in Christ, who gave himself up for you.
exp.12:29:
Judas received the piece of bread that Jesus gave him and went out at once. The word translated as "sop" is that piece of bread dipped in the dish. "Then" is the same as "immediately." And the text adds: "and it was night."

Here the apostle John, who tells of the last supper, speaks. Jesus had just announced that one of them would betray him, and he gave the bread to Judas. The others did not understand what was happening and thought he was going to buy something or help the poor. Many see in the "night" something more than the hour: John often uses darkness as a sign of turning away from the light, although the text does not fully explain this.

For today: Judas was close to Jesus and still turned away. Let us examine our hearts with sincerity, and when God speaks to us, let us respond with humility and not with indifference.
exp.10:15:
Thomas, who is also called Didymus, says to the other disciples: "Let us also go, that we may die with him." The word "fellowdisciples" refers to his companions in following Jesus. It is not clear whether "him" means Jesus or Lazarus; many understand it to mean Jesus.

Jesus decides to return to Judea to go to Bethany, where his friend Lazarus had died. The disciples know that the Jewish leaders there had tried to stone Jesus. Thomas speaks with courage, but also with sadness and pessimism, because he thinks that going there means dying.

Thomas shows a sincere loyalty, although he did not yet understand everything God would do. Today we can follow Jesus even with doubts or fear, taking the next step of obedience. God can take an imperfect faith and make it grow.
exp.14:1:
Jesus says that the Father, as the gardener, takes care of the branches of the vine. A "branch" is a branch of the vine. The branch that does not bear fruit is taken away; the one that does bear fruit is pruned, that is, trimmed so that it bears more. Some understand "taken away" also as "lifting up" the branch off the ground so that it receives light; the Greek verb allows both meanings.

Jesus speaks to his disciples the night before his crucifixion, preparing them for his absence. He teaches them that their spiritual life depends on remaining united to him. Interpreters debate whether the branch that is "taken away" speaks of loss of salvation or of a faith that is only apparent.

Today, do not be alarmed if God corrects or prunes certain areas of your life; his purpose is that you bear more fruit. Spend time in his Word and in prayer, and remain united to Christ.
exp.12:13:
Jesus says that if He, being the Lord and the Teacher, washed the feet of His disciples, then they too ought to wash one another's feet. The words "you" and "ought" in the verse you are reading match the original wording as they stand here, so no comment is needed on them. The small accent mark on a letter is only an old way of writing a plain letter, and it does not change the meaning of the verse.

Jesus speaks with his twelve disciples during the last supper, shortly before he is arrested. Washing feet was a servant's task, since the roads were dusty. He accepts being called Teacher and Lord, and even so he takes the place of a servant. Some Christians understand this as a command to practice foot washing literally; others see it as a teaching about humble service. Both views exist.

Today we can look for a simple task that nobody wants to do, and serve someone with humility, without expecting recognition or applause.
exp.5:34:
Jesus says that he is the "bread of life." Just as bread feeds the body, he sustains the soul. "Coming to him" and "believing in him" go together: it means trusting in Jesus. The promise is that whoever trusts in him will not be left hungry or thirsty spiritually.

Jesus speaks to a crowd that had followed him after he multiplied the loaves and the fish. They kept asking him for bread, but they were thinking of physical food. Jesus leads them to see that he wants to give them something deeper: life with God. Shortly afterward he tells them that, although they have seen him, many do not believe.

For today: when you feel emptiness, anxiety, or weariness of soul, do not run first to what only comforts for a while. Come to Jesus in prayer and read his Word. Trust him with your needs and let him nourish you each day.
exp.6:27:
Jesus speaks out loud, with force, as he teaches in the temple. He tells them that they think they know him and know where he comes from. But he makes it clear that he did not come on his own: the Father sent him, and the Father is true. And they, although they consider themselves very religious, do not know the God who sent him.

We are at the Feast of Tabernacles, in Jerusalem. People were debating whether Jesus was the Christ. Some said they knew his origin (Galilee, Nazareth), and they believed the Christ would appear in a mysterious way. Jesus answers with irony and firmness: they know his place of origin, but not his true origin, which is God himself.

For today: we can believe that we know God only from habit, tradition, or inherited ideas. Let us ask the Lord to lead us to know him truly, by listening to Jesus in his Word and obeying him with humility.
exp.0:41:
Andrew brings his brother Simon to Jesus. Jesus looks at him closely and tells him who he is: Simon, son of Jonas. Then he gives him a new name: Cephas, an Aramaic word that means "A stone." In Greek it is Peter.

This happens at the beginning of Jesus' ministry. Andrew, who had followed Jesus because of the testimony of John the Baptist, is convinced that he has found the Messiah, and he tells his brother. Jesus speaks here, and his gaze shows that he knows Simon completely. The text does not explain everything the name means; that is developed later in the Gospels.

For today: Andrew did not do anything complicated; he simply brought someone to Jesus. You too can invite a family member or friend to know him. And remember that Jesus truly knows you, and still looks at you with hope.
exp.19:21:
After saying this, Jesus breathed on his disciples and told them, "Receive the Holy Ghost." The word "receive" is the verb the verse uses for taking in what is given. "Breathed" recalls the breath of life that God gave the first man in Genesis 2:7.

Jesus speaks on the evening of the day he rose from the dead. The disciples were shut in and afraid, but he shows them his wounds and gives them peace. Then he sends them as the Father sent him. Before sending them, he gives them the Spirit. Christians understand this moment in different ways: some see it as a real and present gift, others as a foretaste of Pentecost.

For today: you do not have to carry out what God asks of you by your own strength alone. Before you act, ask the Holy Spirit to guide you, give you courage, and help you bring his peace to others.
exp.10:31:
Then when Mary came to where Jesus was, and saw him, she fell down at his feet, saying to him, Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. She fell down at his feet, which means she threw herself down on the ground before him. "If you had been here, my brother would not have died" is her way of saying that her brother would still be alive.

Mary was from Bethany, the sister of Martha and Lazarus. Lazarus had already died and been buried. Martha had said the very same words to Jesus a little earlier. The Jews who were comforting Mary followed her, thinking she was going to weep at the tomb. She does not keep her pain to herself: she brings it directly to Jesus, and he responds with compassion.

For today: when you feel pain or confusion, you do not have to hide it from God. Bring him your complaints and your tears with honesty, as Mary did. He listens to you, and he draws near to you.
exp.7:7:
He says that Jesus bent down again and kept writing on the ground. The phrase for "bent down again" means he stooped once more, and "on the ground" means on the floor or in the dust.

The scribes and Pharisees brought him a woman caught in adultery. They wanted to set a trap to accuse him, whether he answered for or against the law. Jesus had already said, "Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone." Then he bent down again. The Bible does not say what he wrote, so we do not know; there are several guesses, but none is certain. His silence gave the accusers time to think.

Today: before pointing out other people's faults, pause and examine your own heart. Sometimes staying quiet and reflecting is better than answering right away.
exp.15:32:
Jesus says that he has told them all this so that they may have peace by being united to him. He warns them that in the world they will go through affliction, that is, suffering and difficulties. But he encourages them: "be of good cheer" means have courage, do not lose heart. And he gives the reason: he has already overcome the world, that is, he has already triumphed over everything that opposes God.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples on the night before his arrest. He has just told them that they will all flee and leave him alone, although the Father will be with him. Even knowing they will abandon him, he does not rebuke them; he offers them peace and hope for what is coming.

When you face problems, do not expect life to always be easy. Look for your peace in Jesus, not in everything turning out well. Today, tell him your worries in prayer and trust that he has the final victory.
exp.6:35:
Here the Jews repeat in confusion what Jesus had said. "What manner of saying is this?" means "What does this mean?" "Ye shall seek me" is "you will look for me," and "thither ye cannot come" is "you will not be able to go." They did not understand where Jesus was going.

Some Jews are speaking at the Feast of Tabernacles in Jerusalem. Jesus had told them that he would soon leave, and they thought of earthly things, such as going away to the scattered Greeks. Jesus was speaking of returning to the Father, although the text does not explain everything here. Soon after, on the last day of the feast, he invites everyone who is thirsty to come to him.

For today: you do not have to understand everything before you draw near to Jesus. Today he still invites you to come. Bring him your doubts and your thirst with sincerity, and he will receive you.
exp.15:13:
Jesus says that the Holy Spirit will glorify him. The word "glorify" means to show how great and valuable someone is. "He will take of what is mine" means that the Spirit will receive what belongs to Jesus, his truth and his work, and will make it known to us. "He will show it to you" means the Spirit will help you understand it.

Jesus speaks with his disciples the night before his arrest. They are sad because he is leaving. He promises them that they will not be left alone: the Spirit of truth will guide them and help them understand what they cannot yet grasp. And since everything the Father has also belongs to the Son, the Spirit brings us close to God himself.

Today, when you read the Bible, ask the Spirit to help you see Jesus in it. A good sign of his work is that your heart turns more toward Christ, not toward yourself.
exp.11:40:
