This verse says that Isaiah spoke these words when he saw the glory of Jesus, and that he spoke about him. The reader sees "saw" and "his glory" in the verse above, so no word needs explaining here; the phrase "his glory" refers to the divine splendor and greatness of Christ.

Here John, the writer of the Gospel, is speaking. He has just quoted Isaiah to explain why many did not believe in Jesus, despite his signs. John joins two passages from Isaiah, and the second recalls the vision of Isaiah 6, where the prophet saw the Lord seated on his throne. John understands that this glorious Lord was Christ. Some scholars debate how to fit the idea of hardening together with human responsibility, and the following context shows that many did not confess their faith because of fear.

For today: do not let fear of what others think silence you. Ask God for the courage to confess Jesus with simplicity and love.
exp.5:46:
Jesus states with great seriousness, saying "Verily, verily," that whoever believes in Him already has eternal life. Notice that the verse speaks of having life now, not merely of receiving it later: it is a life that begins now and continues forever. Believing here means trusting in Jesus, not just accepting facts about Him.

Jesus speaks in Capernaum, after multiplying the loaves. The crowd was looking for Him because of the food, and some doubted Him. He explains that God draws people to His Son, and that only Jesus has seen the Father. Soon He will present Himself as the bread of life, greater than the manna that their ancestors ate.

For today: life with God does not depend on what we accomplish, but on trusting in Christ. Today you can rest in that promise and bring your worries to Him with confidence.
exp.3:34:
Jesus asks his disciples whether they do not say that there are four months still to go before the harvest. Then he invites them to lift up their eyes and look at the fields, because they are already white, ready to be harvested.

Jesus speaks with his disciples beside the well at Sychar, in Samaria. He had just been talking with a Samaritan woman, and people from the town were coming toward him. He uses the image of the field to speak of people ready to hear God's message. Many understand the white fields as those people who were coming toward him.

For today: do not wait for the right moment to speak about God with others. Ask him to open your eyes to those who are near you, in your family, your work, or your neighborhood, and to give you love to share his hope with them simply.
exp.12:34:
Jesus says that the sign he will give the world to show who his disciples are is love for one another. The old words are easy: "know" and "recognize" both mean that people will see it, and "have" means the same. He does not say they will know it by their teaching, their rituals, or their reputation, but by how they treat one another.

Jesus speaks at the Last Supper, shortly before he is arrested. He has just washed his disciples' feet and announces that he is leaving. He gives them a new command: to love one another as he has loved them, that is, with self-giving and service. Right after this, Peter says he will lay down his life for him, not yet understanding what is coming.

Today, we can show this love in concrete ways: forgiving a brother or sister in the church with whom there is tension, helping them in a need, or treating them with patience. In this way, our love becomes a visible witness to others.
exp.3:28:
Here the Samaritan woman invites the people of her town: "Come, see a man who told me everything I have done." Then she asks: "Could this be the Christ?", that is, the promised Messiah. The word "perhaps" shows that she says it with caution, as an open question and not as a confident statement.

The woman speaks after talking with Jesus beside the well. He had shown her that he knew her life, and she felt seen and touched. For that reason she left her water jar, which was why she had come, and ran to the city. The Samaritans and the Jews were usually estranged, so her testimony was something unexpected. Many went out to see Jesus.

For today: you do not need to have all the answers to speak about Jesus. You can simply tell what he has done in you and invite others to come and see for themselves.
exp.6:15:
Jesus says that what he teaches did not originate with him, but with God the Father, who sent him. The word "doctrine" in the verse means teaching. "The one who sent me" refers to the Father.

Jesus speaks during the Feast of Tabernacles, in the temple in Jerusalem. The Jews were amazed that he taught with such wisdom without having studied under the recognized teachers of his time. Jesus answers that his authority does not come from a human school, but from God. He then adds that whoever truly wants to do God's will will be able to recognize whether his teaching comes from God.

For today: before we look for answers in the Bible, we can pray with a heart ready to obey. Understanding God does not depend only on being intelligent or educated, but on wanting to do what he says.
exp.3:39:
The Samaritans came out of their town and went to where Jesus was. They urgently asked him to stay with them, and he agreed. He stayed there two days.

The one telling the story is John. Shortly before, a Samaritan woman had spoken with Jesus by the well and told her people what he had said to her. Many believed because of her testimony. Now they want to know him in person. It is remarkable that some Samaritans would invite a Jew to stay, since there was great tension between the two peoples. Jesus accepts, and for that reason many more believe when they hear him directly.

For today: the testimony of others may awaken our curiosity, but faith grows when we spend time with Jesus. Invite him to stay with you in your day: make room for him in prayer and in the reading of his Word.
exp.1:19:
The Jews answer Jesus with amazement and mockery: the temple took forty-six years to build, so how could he raise it up in three days? The word for "was built" in the verse is the one the reader sees as "was," and the sentence in the explanation about the old wording is set aside here.

The ones speaking are Jewish leaders in Jerusalem. Jesus had just cleared the temple, and they were asking him for a sign that would prove his authority. They were thinking of the stone building, but John explains that Jesus was speaking of his own body, which would be raised. The forty-six years refer to the work of rebuilding the temple, which historians connect with Herod, although the details of the dates are debated.

Today we can learn not to stop at what we see. God's words sometimes have a deeper meaning, and with humility and time he helps us understand them, as he did with the disciples.
exp.4:4:
A certain man in this verse had been ill for thirty-eight years and was beside the pool. The phrase "he had been ill for thirty-eight years" means that his sickness had lasted almost an entire adult life. The text does not say what his ailment was.

The one speaking here is John, the narrator of the Gospel. He tells us that Jesus went up to Jerusalem for a feast and came to a place where many sick people waited to be healed. John focuses attention on this man, because Jesus will see him, understand his long situation, and ask him a direct question. Some ancient manuscripts do not include the part about the angel, and for that reason some Bibles leave it out or set it apart.

For today: when a difficulty drags on for years, we can feel forgotten. This passage reminds us that Jesus sees our whole story and draws near with compassion. Today you can honestly tell him about what you have been waiting for, for a long time.
exp.4:23:
Jesus says that whoever hears his word and believes in the Father who sent him already has eternal life. That person will not be condemned, because they have already passed from death to life. "Condemnation" means judgment that brings punishment, and "passed" indicates a change that has already happened.

Jesus speaks to Jewish leaders who were criticizing him for healing on the Sabbath and for calling himself the Son of God. He explains that the Father gave him authority to judge and to give life. So believing in the Son means believing in the one who sent him.

For today: if you trust in Christ, you can live with peace and not with fear of judgment. This new life does not depend on your merits, but on his word. Today, read a passage from the Gospel and respond to it with faith and simple obedience.
exp.19:11:
This verse tells that Mary Magdalene, looking into the tomb, saw two angels dressed in white. They were sitting, one where Jesus' head had been and the other where his feet had been.

John narrates what happened on the morning of the resurrection. Peter and the other disciple had already gone home, but Mary stayed behind, weeping, without understanding where the body of her Lord was. The angels appear in that moment of grief and ask her a question. John does not explain why they were sitting in that way; some see in it a sign of the place where Jesus had lain.

For today: when we weep over a loss or do not understand what God is doing, we should not walk away. Mary stayed close, and there God met her. Remaining near Him in prayer, even in tears, is a good place to wait.
exp.0:11:
This verse says that those who received Jesus, that is, those who believe in his name, received the right to be children of God. The phrase about "authority or right" needs no separate comment here, since the verse itself speaks of the power given to them. Being a child of God is not earned, it is received.

The author is John, who begins his Gospel by speaking of Jesus as the Word, the Word of God. Just before this, he says that many did not receive him, even though he came to his own people. By contrast, John highlights that others did receive him. He then makes clear that this new birth comes from God, not from family background or human effort.

Today we can rest in the fact that our identity before God does not depend on what we accomplish. If you trust in Jesus, you are received as a child. Today, pray addressing God as "Father" and trust in his love.
exp.2:20:
The person who practices the truth, that is, who lives with honesty and sincerity, comes to the light. He does so so that it may be seen clearly that what he does has been done in God, that is, with his help and according to his will.

Jesus speaks with Nicodemus, a teacher of Israel who came to him at night. He explains that the light, Jesus himself, has come into the world, and that some reject it because they do not want their evil deeds to be exposed. This verse shows the contrast: whoever lives in the truth is not afraid to be seen.

For today: if you want to live with integrity, invite God to look at your decisions. Pray with sincerity and, if needed, confess something you are hiding to someone you trust. God's light is not meant to shame you, but to heal you and guide you.
exp.14:2:
Jesus tells his disciples that they are already "clean." The word "clean" here refers to being purified, free from guilt, and it comes from the same root as the verb "to prune" in the verse before.

Jesus speaks with his disciples the night before his crucifixion, using the image of the vine and the gardener. He explains that the Father prunes those who bear fruit so that they will bear more. They have already been made clean by receiving and believing his teaching. Some scholars see here a reference to Judas, who had already left, but this is interpreted in different ways.

For today: spend time reading the Bible carefully. God uses his word to cleanse and shape us, so that we remain in Christ and bear fruit.
exp.8:10:
Here the man who was healed tells, step by step, what happened to him. He says that Jesus made clay, put it on his eyes, and told him to wash in the pool of Siloam. He obeyed and received his sight. Where the explanation says the clay was spread over his eyes, that means Jesus put the clay on his eyes. The explanation's remarks about the wording itself are left out here, since the verse above is what the reader has.

The one speaking is the man who had been born blind. His neighbors doubted whether it was really him, because now he could see. He answers simply and without embellishment: he tells only what he experienced. He does not yet know well who Jesus is; he calls him "a man that is called Jesus." Later in the chapter his faith will grow.

For today: you do not need to know everything to give testimony. Tell honestly what Jesus has done in your life, without exaggerating or hiding it. And when He points you to a step, take that step with confidence, even if you do not understand everything.
exp.7:8:
They heard his words, the explanation says, and were convicted by their own conscience. They felt that their own conscience accused them. "Convicted" here means rebuked or shown to be guilty of their wrong. They left one by one, beginning with the oldest and ending with the youngest, and Jesus was left alone with the woman, who was still standing in the middle of the crowd.

The scribes and Pharisees had brought a woman caught in adultery to test Jesus. He answered by inviting whoever was without sin to throw the first stone. Some think the older men left first because they were more aware of their own faults, but the text does not explain this. We also do not know what Jesus was writing on the ground.

Before pointing out the mistakes of others, let us examine our own hearts with humility. And when we fail, we can come to Jesus, who offers forgiveness and a new life.
exp.2:3:
Nicodemus asks Jesus how someone can be born when they are already old. Does he think of the physical sense: can a man go back into his mother's womb and be born again? "Saith" means "says." A "womb" is the place where a baby is formed before birth.

Nicodemus was a respected teacher among the Jews, and he came to Jesus at night. Jesus had just told him that a person must be born again to see the kingdom of God. Nicodemus takes the words in a literal way. Some believe he did not grasp the spiritual meaning; others think his question shows a sincere confusion. Jesus soon makes clear that he is speaking of being born of the Spirit.

For today: knowing a lot about God, or having a good religious reputation, is not enough. Ask God humbly to give you a new life through his Spirit, and do not be afraid to ask honest questions, as Nicodemus did.
exp.15:29:
The disciples tell Jesus that now they understand. They see that he knows all things, even what they are thinking, without anyone needing to ask him questions. For this reason they state that they believe he came out from God. "You have come out from God" means that his origin is God himself.

The disciples are speaking on the last night before the cross. Jesus had just spoken to them plainly, without figures of speech (the word for a figurative or puzzling saying means language that is veiled or hard to grasp). They are moved and declare their faith. But Jesus answers them with a question: "Do you now believe?" because soon they would all leave him alone. Their faith was sincere, though still fragile.

For today: It is good to confess our faith, but it is tested in difficulties. Ask God to strengthen your trust, and remember that Jesus does not let go of you when you falter.
exp.5:14:
He says that Jesus realized the crowd wanted to take him by force to make him king. For that reason he withdrew again to the mountain, alone, to be by himself.

Here the writer John speaks. The crowd had just eaten bread that had been multiplied, and they were saying that Jesus was the prophet who was to come. They wanted a king who would meet their needs and, probably, their political problems, although the text does not spell this out. Jesus did not refuse to be king, but he did not accept being king according to their plans. His kingdom would not come through human pressure.

For today: let us not seek Jesus only so that he will give us what we want. Let us allow him to be Lord in his own way, and, like him, look for times of solitude to be with God.
exp.20:9:
Jesus asks his disciples to bring some of the fish they have just caught.

Jesus has already risen and is on the shore of the lake, where he has prepared a fire, bread, and fish. Earlier, from the shore, he had told them where to cast the net, and the catch was enormous. Although he already has food ready, he asks them to bring some of their catch. In this way he includes them in the meal and shows them that their work matters to him. Some scholars also see here an invitation to take part in his work.

For today: what we have, even though God has provided it, he wants to receive and use. Offer him with confidence your time, your talents, and your effort, knowing that he invites you to work together with him.
exp.0:10:
This verse says that Jesus, the Word made flesh, came to what belonged to him: his world, his land, and his people. But his own people did not receive him, that is, they did not accept him or welcome him. "His own" can be understood as his own creation or, more closely, as Israel. Many interpreters see both ideas at once.

The speaker is John, the author of the Gospel, in the prologue. He explains who Jesus is, the true light, and shows that although the world was made by him, it did not recognize him. But right away hope appears: those who do receive him become children of God.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we give Jesus a real place in our lives. To receive him is to believe in him and open our hearts to him each day, without ignoring him or leaving him out.
exp.13:8:
Jesus asks Philip whether, after so long being together, he still does not know him. He says that whoever has seen him has seen the Father.

Jesus speaks with his disciples at the last supper, shortly before his death, to comfort them. Philip asks to see the Father, thinking that this would be enough to settle his mind. Jesus answers that in himself, in his words and in his works, who God is is already being shown. This connects with what John 1:18 says about the Son who makes the Father known.

If we want to know what God is like, let us look at Jesus: his compassion, his truth and his service. When we doubt his character, let us read the Gospels again and trust what we see of him there.
exp.17:7:
Jesus answers calmly: he has already told them who he is, "I am." Then he gives them a clear condition: if they are looking for him, they must let his disciples go their way. The old-fashioned word "Á" and "pontífice" are not used here; so I will simply note that the word "pontiff" refers to the high priest, which is not needed in this verse.

We are in the garden, on the night of the arrest. Jesus speaks with the soldiers and guards who have come for him. Although he knows what awaits him, he does not hide, and he places himself between them and his friends. John explains that this fulfills what Jesus said earlier: he would not lose any of those whom the Father had given him. Some see here physical protection, and others also see a reflection of his spiritual care.

For today: Jesus cares for his own with firm love and without fear. You can entrust your loved ones and your own life to his care. And, by imitating him, you can protect others with courage and simplicity.
exp.7:29:
This verse says that while Jesus was speaking, many people believed in him. The words "as he spake these words" refer to what he had just said: that he does what the Father taught him and that the Father is with him.

Jesus was speaking with a group of Jews in the temple, and he announced that they would lift up the Son of Man, that is, that he would be lifted up on the cross. However, the next verse shows that this faith was still fragile: Jesus tells them that they will be true disciples if they remain in his word. Some understand that their belief was sincere but incomplete, and others that it was shallow. The text does not make this entirely clear.

Believing in Jesus is a good beginning, but he invites us to stay with him. Today we can do this by reading his word every day and obeying it, so that our faith grows and does not remain only a moment of emotion.
exp.11:35:
Jesus invites the people to believe in the light while they still have it, so that they may become "children of light," that is, people who belong to God and live according to his truth. After saying this, he went away and hid himself from them.

Jesus speaks in Jerusalem, shortly before his death. The people did not understand how the Christ could be "lifted up," if they believed he would remain forever. Jesus calls himself the light and warns them that his time with them is short. Then he withdraws, and the text goes on to say that many did not believe.

For today: do not put off until tomorrow what God shows you today. If you sense that Jesus is inviting you to trust him, or to obey him in something, respond simply now, while you still have the light.
exp.18:9:
Pilate becomes irritated because Jesus does not answer him. He asks, "Do you not speak to me?" and reminds Jesus that he has power, that is, authority, to order that he be crucified or to let him go free. To release you means to set you at liberty.

Pilate was the Roman governor and was judging Jesus. He was already afraid, because the Jews said that Jesus called himself the Son of God. With these words he tries to assert his authority. Jesus answers at once that this power was given to him from above, that is, from God. Commentators agree that Jesus shows that God is still in control, even in the middle of this unjust trial.

For today: human power is limited and borrowed. If you have authority, use it with justice and humility. And if you feel you are in the hands of others, trust that God governs over all.
exp.6:7:
Jesus says to his brothers: "Go ye up unto this feast: I go not up yet unto this feast; for my time is not yet full come." The phrase "Go ye up" is the same as "Go up yourselves," and "yet" means "still." By "my time" he means the exact moment that God had set for him.

Jesus is speaking with his brothers, who were urging him to show himself publicly at the feast, and the text says that they did not believe in him. Jesus does not act under pressure but according to the Father's plan. Afterward he did go up, but in secret. Many understand that his "time" points to the hour of his death.

For today: do not let yourself be rushed by the opinions of others. Pray, wait for God's guidance, and act when the time is right.
exp.7:2:
The verse tells that the scribes and Pharisees brought before Jesus a woman caught in adultery. They set her in the midst, that is, at the front of everyone, in full view of the people gathered there. The scribes were the experts in the law of Moses, and the Pharisees were a group very strict in keeping it.

Jesus was in the temple teaching the people from early morning. These leaders were not seeking real justice. The verses that follow say they wanted to set a trap so they would have something to accuse him of. They used the woman as a tool for their purpose. It should be noted that many scholars point out that this passage does not appear in the oldest manuscripts of John, although the church has preserved it and read it for centuries.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we treat people as human beings or as arguments to win a discussion. God calls us to see each person with dignity and compassion.
exp.3:42:
He says that Jesus stayed two more days in Samaria and then left there to go to Galilee.

Here the narrator, John, is speaking. Jesus had just been in Sychar, where many Samaritans came to believe in him, first because of the woman's testimony and then because they had heard him themselves. After that, Jesus continues on his way. The next verse speaks of how "a prophet has no honor in his own country"; interpreters understand this in several ways, and it is not entirely clear which country is meant.

For today: the firmest faith comes from a personal encounter with Jesus, not only from what others tell you. Hear his word for yourself, and then keep going forward with him.
exp.2:30:
This verse says that Jesus, who comes from above, that is, from heaven, is above all. By contrast, the one who is from the earth belongs to the earthly and speaks from that human perspective. The word "earthly" means that he is from the earth, with a limited origin and outlook.

Here John the Baptist is speaking (although some scholars think that from verse 31 on these may be words of the author of the Gospel, and it is not known with certainty). John's disciples were concerned because many people were going to Jesus. John answers with humility: Jesus has an origin and an authority higher than those of any person, even his own.

For today: when you have doubts or make decisions, listen first to Jesus in his Word, and not only to human opinions. With humility, let him have the first place.
exp.13:7:
Philip says to Jesus, "Lord, show us the Father, and that is enough for us." Philip asks to see the Father, and he thinks that would leave them satisfied and at peace.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples the night before his crucifixion. He has just told them that he is the way to the Father and that they have already seen the Father by knowing him. Philip does not fully understand, so he asks for one clearer proof. Jesus answers him with kindness but also with firmness: whoever has seen him has seen the Father.

Many times we look for extraordinary signs in order to believe or to feel secure. This week, read a passage from the Gospels and notice how Jesus treats people. There we can see what God is like.
exp.12:28:
It says that some of the disciples thought Jesus was sending Judas to buy what was needed for the feast, or to give something to the poor. They thought this because Judas carried the bag, that is, the group's money.

The writer, John, explains why the disciples did not understand Jesus's words to Judas. It was the night of the Last Supper, shortly before the Passover. Jesus knew that Judas was going to betray him, but the others did not yet see it. Giving to the poor was a common practice at that feast, so the explanation seemed reasonable to them, though it was mistaken.

For today: we do not always see what is happening in the hearts of others, nor do we understand everything God is doing. Let us avoid judging by appearances, and ask God for wisdom and humility. Meanwhile, let us practice generosity toward the poor, which always pleases God.
exp.19:20:
Jesus repeats his greeting of peace to the disciples. Then he tells them that, just as the Father sent him, he now sends them. The phrase "to you" in the older wording is an old form; today we would say "to you" as well, in the same plain way the verse reads.

Jesus speaks as the risen Lord, on the evening of the day of the resurrection. The disciples were shut inside out of fear of the Jewish leaders. Jesus appears, shows them his wounds, and they rejoice. His peace calms that fear, and right away he gives them a mission. Then he breathes on them and speaks to them about the Holy Spirit. Interpreters explain in different ways the scope of his words about forgiving sins.

For today: Jesus does not call us to live hidden away out of fear. First he gives us his peace and his presence, and from there he sends us. Today you can ask him for courage to love, to serve, or to speak about him with someone close to you.
exp.17:27:
This verse tells that the Jewish leaders led Jesus from the house of Caiaphas, the high priest, to the praetorium, which was the residence of the Roman governor. It was early in the morning. They did not want to go inside, so as not to become unclean according to their law, and so that they could eat the Passover.

John, who narrates, shows the scene after the night of the arrest and Peter's denial. The leaders were Jews, and the praetorium belonged to Gentiles. Entering the house of a foreigner, according to their custom, made them unclean. Some think the Passover refers to the meal of that festival week; the exact detail is debated.

For today: let us make sure that religion is not only outward appearance. It is possible to keep external rules carefully while the heart remains far from justice and compassion. Let us ask God for a sincere heart.
exp.10:50:
This verse explains that Caiaphas said something deeper than he himself understood. Because he was high priest that year, his words served as a prophecy: Jesus was going to die for the nation.

The Jewish leaders feared that the Romans would destroy the country because of Jesus. Caiaphas proposed his death for political convenience. John, the writer, makes clear that God used those words to announce the true meaning of the cross: Jesus would die for the people and also for the scattered children of God. Scholars understand this as a sign that God works even through people with wicked intentions.

For today: even when you see injustice or twisted plans around you, trust that God is still in control and can accomplish his purpose of good. Rest in the knowledge that he does not lose his way.
exp.2:0:
This verse introduces a man named Nicodemus. He was a Pharisee, that is, part of a Jewish religious group very careful about the law of Moses. He was also a ruler of the Jews, a phrase meaning that he was a leader or governing figure among his people. He was probably part of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish council, although the text does not say so in those words.

Here the narrator, John, introduces a new scene. Up to this point Jesus had performed signs, and many people were paying attention to Him. Nicodemus appears as a religious leader with sincere questions. According to the following verses, he comes at night. Some believe it was out of fear or discretion, and others think he wanted a quiet conversation. The text does not clarify his reason.

For today: do not be ashamed to have questions about God. Even if you hold a position, have studied, or have experience, you can come to Jesus honestly. He welcomes whoever seeks Him, even with doubts.
exp.17:22:
Jesus answers the servant who struck him. He says to him: if what I said was wrong, prove with witnesses where the wrong was. But if I spoke well, why do you strike me?

Jesus is being questioned by Annas, before he is taken to Caiaphas. He had asked that those who heard him teach openly be questioned. A servant slapped him because he seemed disrespectful. Jesus does not get angry or take revenge; he asks for fair treatment that rests on the truth. The questioning itself did not follow a clean process, and Jesus calmly lets this be seen.

For today: when you are treated unjustly, you can answer with firmness and gentleness, without returning evil for evil. Ask for fair reasons, speak the truth calmly, and trust God, who judges with justice.
exp.1:16:
Explanation: It tells that, when they saw Jesus act this way in the temple, the disciples remembered a line of Scripture: "The zeal of your house has consumed me." The word "zeal" means an intense and burning love for something. The phrase "has consumed me" means it was eating him up inside, like a fire that filled him completely.

The writer, John, speaks and tells what the disciples thought. Jesus had just driven out those who were doing business in the temple. The line comes from Psalm 69:9. The disciples understood that his action showed a deep passion for the honor of God. Afterward, the Jews asked him for a sign to justify his authority.

For today: ask yourself how much you care about the honor of God. Ask God for a sincere love for Him, one that shows itself in humility, respect and obedience, not in anger or pride.
exp.3:38:
This verse says that many of the Samaritans of that town believed in Jesus because of what the woman told them. She gave her testimony and kept saying, "He told me all that ever I did." The phrase "believed on him" means they trusted Jesus as the Messiah, not merely that they respected him.

Here the narrator, John, is speaking. Jesus had just talked with this Samaritan woman by the well. She left her water jar and went to tell the people. Jesus had said that one sows and another reaps, and this is an example of it: she sowed with her testimony, and then many believed. Afterward, the Samaritans asked Jesus to stay, and many more believed when they heard him themselves.

For today: you do not need to be an expert to speak about Jesus. Tell simply what he has done in your life, and let him do the rest.
exp.3:43:
This verse says that Jesus himself stated a well-known truth: a prophet does not receive respect in his own homeland. The word "testified" means that he declared or affirmed something, and "honour" means respect and esteem.

The speaker here is the writer of the gospel, John, who recalls a saying of Jesus. The Samaritans had just come to believe in him, even though they were foreigners to the Jews. Then Jesus goes to Galilee. Scholars explain in several ways which "country" is meant: Galilee, where he grew up, or Judea, from which his family line came. What is clear is the contrast between the faith of the Samaritans and the little faith of those who knew him closely.

For today: do not grow used to what is familiar. Sometimes what is close to us, such as a church, a biblical text, or a wise person, stops amazing us. Ask God for a humble and attentive heart to value what he has already placed within your reach.
exp.20:12:
Verse 13 tells how Jesus comes to his disciples, takes the bread and gives it to them, and does the same with the fish. The explanation of the wording is removed here, since those phrases do not appear in the verse your reader sees. Jesus acts as the host and serves them the meal.

It is the morning after a night of fishing with no results. Jesus, already risen, had prepared a fire, bread and fish on the shore of the lake. The disciples did not dare to ask him who he was, because they knew he was the Lord. John narrates this simple and close moment, before the conversation in which Jesus restores Peter.

Jesus remains the Lord who serves with tenderness. Before asking anything of us, he feeds us and receives us. We can come to him with our weariness and failures, knowing that he waits for us with care and provision, and that he invites us to share his table.
exp.16:14:
Jesus asks the Father not to take his disciples out of the world, but to keep them from the evil. The word "keep" means to protect, to keep safe. "The evil" can be understood as the evil one, that is, Satan, or as evil in general; scholars translate it in both ways.

Jesus speaks in prayer, shortly before he is arrested. He is praying for his disciples, who will be hated by the world because they belong to God. He does not ask for them a life apart from others, for he will send them to share his message. He asks that God sustain them and make them holy by his truth.

For today: you do not need to flee from your work, your school, or your family in order to be faithful to God. Stay where he has placed you, pray asking for his protection, and fill yourself with his word, so that you may live with love and steadfastness in the midst of a difficult world.
exp.8:12:
They brought the man who had been blind to the Pharisees. The word "Pharisees" refers to a respected religious group that devoted itself to teaching and keeping the law of Moses. The text does not say who brought him or what their purpose was; it only reports the event.

Jesus had just healed this man, and his neighbors were amazed because they knew him as a blind beggar. Bringing him before the Pharisees was a way for the religious authorities to examine what had happened. Later on it is made clear that it was the Sabbath, and that will lead to a conflict.

For today: when God does something good in your life, do not be ashamed to tell it simply. This man just repeated what he had lived: "I now see." Your honest testimony has value, even when others question it.
exp.4:44:
Jesus tells his listeners not to think that he is going to accuse them before the Father. Someone else is already accusing them: Moses, the very one in whom they put their trust.

Jesus speaks with Jewish leaders who were criticizing him for healing on the Sabbath and for calling God his Father. They studied the Scriptures of Moses very carefully, thinking that in them they would find life. But Jesus shows them that those same writings point to him. If they truly believed Moses, they would receive him.

For today: we can know the Bible well and still not draw close to Christ. As we read it, let us ask God for a humble heart that seeks Jesus, and not merely information or the approval of others.
exp.6:31:
The Pharisees heard that the crowd was whispering such things about Jesus, that perhaps he was the Christ. Then they and the chief priests sent officers, the guards, to arrest him.

John, the narrator, tells this during the Feast of Tabernacles in Jerusalem. There is division: some believe because of Jesus' signs, and others reject him. The leaders feel they are losing control over the people and react with fear. Even so, the previous verse reminds us that no one could touch him, because his hour had not yet come. Jesus responds by saying that he will be with them only a little while longer.

Today we can ask ourselves how we react when Jesus challenges our ideas or our comfort. We can defend ourselves with pride, as these leaders did, or we can draw near with humility and listen to him. Moreover, it encourages us to know that God directs the times, even when others oppose him.
exp.5:32:
This verse says that the bread of God is the one who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world. Jesus is speaking of a bread that is not ordinary food, but a gift from God that gives true life. The idea of coming down means that he came from heaven, and giving life to the world means that this life is for all people, not only for one group.

Jesus speaks with a crowd that had just seen him feed thousands of people. They mention the manna that their ancestors ate in the desert. Jesus gently corrects them: the true bread from heaven is not the manna, but what the Father is giving them now. A little later, Jesus says that this bread is himself.

For today: we often ask God to solve what is urgent, such as work, money, or health. Today you can also ask him for what is most important: to draw near to Jesus, trust him, and find in him a life that does not end.
exp.18:32:
The explanation says that the soldiers came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, so they did not break his legs, as they did with the other two who were crucified. "They came to Jesus" means "they reached Jesus." Breaking the legs hastened death, because the crucified man could no longer push himself up to breathe.

John, the writer of the Gospel, tells what happened. The Jewish leaders asked Pilate to have the bodies taken away before the Sabbath, which was a very solemn day. John highlights this detail, and shortly afterward (verse 36) connects it with the Scripture that says not a bone of him would be broken. Many see this as an allusion to the Passover lamb.

For today: Jesus truly died, and by his own will, and nothing escaped God's care. You can trust that God keeps his promises, even in the most painful and confusing moments of your life.
exp.16:22:
He says that Jesus lives in his followers, and that the Father lives in Jesus. The goal is that they may become perfectly one, that is, fully united, complete in their unity. In this way the world will be able to recognize two things: that the Father sent Jesus, and that the Father loves believers with the same love with which he loves his Son.

Jesus speaks in prayer to the Father, on the night before his arrest, according to John. He prays first for his disciples and then for those who would believe through them. His desire is that the unity among them be a visible witness before the world.

For today: unity among believers is not an ornament, but a sign that speaks of Christ. This week, seek to be reconciled with or draw closer to a brother or sister with whom you have distance, and treat them with the love that God has shown you.
exp.18:8:
Pilate went back into the judgment hall, which was the place where he sat in judgment and stayed while he was in Jerusalem. There he asked Jesus, "Where are you from?" Jesus gave him no answer.

The Jews had just said that Jesus must die because he made himself the Son of God. When Pilate heard this, he became more afraid. His question may have been trying to find out whether Jesus had a divine origin, not only where he was born. Some think Jesus' silence shows his authority and his willing surrender. Later, however, he does speak to Pilate about the authority that comes from God.

Today we can learn that not all silence is weakness. When we are pressured or misunderstood, we ask for wisdom to know when to speak and when to be quiet, trusting that God is still in control.
exp.5:6:
Philip answers Jesus that not even two hundred denarii would buy enough bread to give each person even a little. "Denarius" was a Roman coin; it is generally understood to have equaled a day's wage for a laborer, so it was a large sum.

Jesus had just asked Philip where they could buy bread for the crowd. The text makes clear that he was asking to test him, since Jesus already knew what he was going to do. Philip responds with human calculations and sees only the limit of the money.

For today: when you face a need that is bigger than you are, do not rely only on your own calculations. Bring to Jesus what you have and what you lack, and trust that he can work beyond your resources.
exp.4:31:
Jesus says there is another who speaks in his favor, and that he knows the witness that other gives about him is true. The word "witness" here means a statement that confirms who someone is or what someone has done.

Jesus is speaking in a discussion with Jewish leaders who questioned him for calling God his Father and for healing on the Sabbath. He acknowledges that, according to the custom of the law, one person's witness about himself is not enough. So he points to another witness. Scholars usually understand this to mean the Father, though some think it could refer to John the Baptist, whom he mentions next.

For today: we do not have to prove ourselves to everyone. We can live in peace, trusting that God knows the truth and will confirm it in his time.
exp.9:25:
Jesus says that some people do not believe in him, and he explains the reason: they are not among his sheep. The word "you" here means "you all," and the phrase "as I said to you" means "as I already told you." The sheep are those who listen to him and follow him.

Jesus is speaking in the temple in Jerusalem, during the Festival of Dedication. Some leaders gather around him and demand that he say plainly whether he is the Christ. He had already spoken to them and shown signs through his works, but they did not trust him. Christians interpret in different ways how God's choosing and each person's responsibility relate here.

For today: it is not enough to ask for more proof; what is needed is a heart willing to listen. Set aside a few minutes each day to read the Gospels, and ask God to help you hear the voice of Jesus with humility and to follow him.
exp.15:25:
Jesus says that "in that day," meaning the time after his death and resurrection, his disciples will ask the Father in Jesus' name. And he adds: "I do not say to you that I will pray to the Father for you." With this he does not promise to stop interceding, but makes clear that they will have direct and confident access to the Father. The word "ask" is simply the ordinary word for "ask."

Jesus speaks on his last night with the disciples, before the cross. They feel confused and sad because he tells them that he is leaving. He explains that soon they will understand clearly, and the next verse gives the reason: the Father himself loves them.

Today you can pray without fear or feeling unworthy. Through Jesus, God receives you as a beloved child. Pray simply, trusting that the Father listens to you with affection.
exp.18:12:
Pilate hears that the Jewish leaders are accusing him of not being a friend of Caesar, and so he brings Jesus out of the palace. He sits down on the judgment seat, that is, the seat where sentences were handed down, in a place called the Pavement in Greek, and Gabbatha in Hebrew (Aramaic). Its exact location is not certain.

The Jewish leaders press Pilate with a political threat: if he releases a man who claims to be a king, he would look bad before the emperor. Pilate, who had earlier seen Jesus as innocent, gives in to fear for his position. That is why he sits down to judge, and the true Judge stands before a weak judge.

Today, this passage invites us not to decide out of fear of losing our position or approval. Ask God for the courage to do what is right, even when it costs us.
exp.10:33:
Jesus asks, "Where have ye laid him?" That is, "Where did you bury him?" They answer, "Lord, come and see." These are simple words: they invite him to come to the place where Lazarus was buried.

Jesus speaks, and some of those present in Bethany answer him. Lazarus had died, and Mary and others were weeping. Jesus was moved and troubled. His question does not show that he did not know something; many believe he wanted to draw near and share their sorrow. Right after this, the text says that Jesus wept.

Today, when we suffer, we can say to Jesus with confidence, "Lord, come and see." He does not turn away from our pain. Bring him your sorrow with sincerity, for he cares and walks with you.
exp.11:27:
Jesus prays asking that the Father's name be glorified, that is, that how great and good God is be shown. Then the Father answers with a voice from heaven: he has already glorified it, and he will do so again.

Jesus speaks only a few days before his crucifixion. His soul is troubled, yet he does not ask to escape the cross; he prefers that God be honored. The voice speaks of the Father himself, who had already revealed himself in Jesus' miracles and would reveal himself even more in his death and resurrection. Some who heard it thought it was only thunder, and Jesus explains that the voice was for them, to help them believe.

For today: when you go through difficult moments, you can be honest with God about your fear and still say to him, "Father, glorify thy name in this." That prayer shifts the focus of your distress toward trust in God.
exp.1:11:
This verse tells us that, after the wedding at Cana, Jesus went down to Capernaum with his mother, his brothers, and his disciples. They stayed there only a few days. Capernaum sat beside the Sea of Galilee, lower down than Cana, which is why the verse says he went down. "Brothers" is usually understood to mean close relatives of Jesus; some believers take them to be sons of Joseph and Mary, and others take them to be cousins or stepsons.

Here the narrator is John. After the first miracle, which strengthened the faith of the disciples, John shows a brief moment of rest with family. It is a pause before Jesus goes up to Jerusalem for the Passover and begins to act publicly in the temple.

For today: Jesus spent time with his family and friends before a demanding stage. We too can value those simple moments with our own loved ones and ask God for strength for what lies ahead.
exp.11:12:
The explanation says that the people took palm branches and went out to meet Jesus as he was arriving in Jerusalem. They cried out and called the one who comes in the name of the Lord blessed, and they proclaimed him King of Israel. "Clamaban" means they were shouting loudly.

Many visitors had come to the Passover feast and learned that Jesus was approaching. They had heard about him, partly because of the raising of Lazarus. Their cries recall Psalm 118:25-26. The palms were a sign of celebration. They probably expected a king who would free them from Rome, but Jesus arrives riding on a young donkey, like a humble king.

We can praise Jesus, but we can also ask ourselves whether we receive him as he is and not as we want him to be. Today, tell him sincerely: "Reign in my life in your way."
exp.15:28:
The disciples say to Jesus that now he is speaking plainly and no longer using figures of speech, that is, language that is figurative or hard to understand.

They are speaking on the last night before the cross. Jesus had just told them openly that he came out from the Father, came into the world, and now returns to the Father. They feel that at last they understand. However, the next verse shows that Jesus asks them, "Do you now believe?", for soon they would flee. Their enthusiasm was sincere, but still fragile.

Today we can rejoice when we understand something of God, but without trusting only in our own understanding or our own strength. True faith is tested in difficulties. Let us ask Jesus to sustain our faith when we do not understand everything.
exp.12:2:
This verse says that Jesus knew three things: that the Father had put all things into his hands, that he had come from God, and that he was returning to God. The quoted old spelling and the quoted phrase in the source are not needed for the reader, so the sentence about the old spelling is removed. The phrase "all things in his hands" means that he had full authority.

Here the writer of the Gospel, John, describes Jesus at the Last Supper, shortly before the Passover. Judas had already made up his mind to betray him. John points out that Jesus knew his origin, his power and his destiny, and right after this comes the surprising part: he rises, takes a towel and washes the feet of his disciples.

For today: true greatness does not need to show off. Someone who knows that their worth comes from God can serve with humility, even in tasks that others avoid. Today you can look for one simple act of service, without expecting recognition.
exp.5:49:
Jesus says that he is the bread that comes down from heaven, and that whoever eats of this bread will not die. The word that means "comes down" is not a term your verse uses, so there is nothing to explain there, and I have left out the sentence about the old word for "eat" since the verse above already uses "eat" plainly. Unlike the manna, which did not save anyone from death, this bread gives life that does not end.

Jesus speaks in the synagogue in Capernaum, after feeding the crowd. The people asked him for a sign like the manna given through Moses. He answers that he himself is the true food from God. Eating, here, is commonly understood as believing in him and receiving him, although some Christians also relate it to the Lord's Supper, and it is interpreted in several ways.

Today, it is not enough to admire Jesus from a distance. Every day you can feed on him: reading his Word, praying, and trusting in him, knowing that only he gives true and eternal life.
exp.3:51:
Here the father asks his servants at what hour his son began to get better. They answer that "yesterday at the seventh hour" the fever left him. The word "á" is an old way of writing "a," and "dejó la fiebre" means that the fever went away.

It speaks of a royal official from Capernaum who had asked Jesus to heal his son. Jesus told him, "Go, your son lives," and he believed and went on his way. By asking about the hour, he wants to confirm what happened. The seventh hour in the evening is reckoned according to the way time was counted back then, and some scholars understand it differently. Even so, the point is clear: it coincided with Jesus' word.

For today: when we trust in the word of Jesus, even though we do not see the result right away, we can keep walking in peace. And when we look back, we often discover that God was already at work.
exp.9:22:
It says that Jesus was walking in the temple in Jerusalem, in an area called Solomon's porch. It was a covered colonnade with columns, a place for passing through where people gathered and talked. The word "walked" means that he was strolling along calmly.

The writer, John, places the scene during the Feast of Dedication, in winter. That feast remembered the renewed dedication of the temple. Many were asking who Jesus was, and right away the leaders surrounded him to demand a clear answer. Jesus answers them that his works already speak about who he is.

For today: Jesus did not hide or avoid difficult questions. We can come to him with our honest doubts, and look at what he has done in the Bible and in our lives, so that we can trust him more.
exp.19:12:
The two angels ask Mary, "Woman, why are you weeping?" She answers that they have taken away her Lord and that she does not know where they have laid him. "Woman" was a respectful way of addressing someone in that time.

It is the morning after the Sabbath. Mary Magdalene came to the tomb and found it empty. She does not yet understand that Jesus has risen; she thinks someone has taken the body away. Her grief is real and her love for Jesus is great. Soon, Jesus himself will speak to her.

When we are sad, we sometimes fail to see that Jesus is nearer than we think. You can honestly tell him about your pain and your doubts, as Mary did. He listens, and he often answers us in ways we did not expect.
exp.14:25:
Jesus promises that he will send the Comforter, who is the Holy Spirit. The Spirit is called "the Spirit of truth" because he guides people into the truth, and he is said to come forth from the Father. His task is to bear witness to Jesus, that is, to show who he is.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the night before his arrest. He has just warned them that the world will hate them, as it hated him, even after seeing his works. He encourages them by saying that they will not be alone: the Spirit will speak of him, and they too will be witnesses.

For today: when you feel weak or afraid to speak of your faith, ask for the help of the Holy Spirit. You do not have to convince anyone by your own strength; simply rely on telling plainly what Jesus has done in your life.
exp.18:5:
It says that when they saw Jesus, the chief priests and the temple guards shouted, "Crucify him, crucify him!" Pilate answered them, "Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no fault in him." The chief priests are the main religious leaders, and the guards are the temple attendants or officers. "Fault" means a wrong or a guilt.

Pilate was the Roman governor. He had already declared Jesus innocent, and he brought him out wounded, wearing a crown of thorns, perhaps hoping to stir up pity. The religious leaders, however, wanted his death. Pilate tells them to crucify him themselves, although the Jewish leaders did not have the authority to carry out an execution, as is made clear in John 18:31. His words show that he did not want to carry the decision, but he did not stop it either.

For today: it is not enough to recognize what is right; we must act in accordance with it. Ask God for the courage to defend the truth, even when it costs you the approval of others.
exp.16:0:
Jesus finishes speaking with his disciples and lifts his eyes to heaven to pray. He says to God, "Father, the hour is come." He asks God to glorify him, so that he, in turn, may glorify the Father. The word "glorify" is explained in this way: it means to show his greatness and honor.

He speaks the night before his arrest, at the end of his teaching at the Last Supper. "The hour" refers to his suffering, death, and resurrection. This is a prayer addressed to the Father, which the disciples hear. Jesus is not seeking his own fame; his aim is that the Father be honored, and the verses that follow explain that this leads to eternal life, which is knowing God.

For today: before difficult moments, we can pray as Jesus did, looking to God with confidence. We can ask him that, in the midst of our trials, his name be honored through the way we live.
exp.8:34:
Jesus heard that they had cast him out, and he went to look for him. When he found him, he asked whether he believed in the Son of God.

The verse uses the phrase "cast him out" to mean that the man was driven out of the synagogue, that is, out of his religious community. Finding him means simply coming to meet him.

Jesus had healed this man, and the Pharisees questioned him. He answered plainly that Jesus came from God. They, angry, insulted him and threw him out. Jesus, the one speaking here, does not leave him alone: he seeks him out to lead him toward a fuller faith.

When someone pays a price for following the truth, Jesus does not abandon them. If you feel rejected for being faithful, remember that He seeks you and makes Himself known to you. Come to Him with sincerity.
exp.7:13:
Jesus answers the Pharisees that, although he speaks about himself, what he says is true. The reason is that he knows where he came from and where he is going. They, on the other hand, do not know this.

Jesus has just said, "I am the light of the world." The Pharisees object, saying that no one can be a valid witness on his own behalf. Jesus replies that his origin is in God the Father and that he returns to Him. For this reason his word has an authority that they do not understand. Later he will say that the Father also testifies about him.

For today: before we judge others or close our hearts to what they say, let us examine whether we truly know what lies beneath. Let us ask God for humility to recognize what we do not yet understand, and to let Jesus guide us, for he knows the whole way.
exp.8:14:
The explanation says that the Pharisees asked the healed man again how he had received his sight. He answered in few words: Jesus put clay on his eyes, he washed, and now he sees. Where the explanation comments on the wording, it would be "asked him again," which means the same as "he had received his sight" in this verse.

The one who speaks is the man who had been born blind. The Pharisees, religious leaders, question him because the healing happened on the Sabbath, and for them that was a problem. He gives no long explanations or theories; he simply tells what he experienced. Afterward the Pharisees are divided, and he states that Jesus is a prophet.

For today: you do not need to know how to answer every difficult question in order to speak about Jesus. You can tell, simply and honestly, what He has done in your life, and that sincere testimony has great value.
exp.20:0:
This verse says that Jesus appeared again to his disciples, this time on the shore of the Sea of Tiberias. The phrase "showed himself" means that he let himself be seen, that he made himself visible. The "Sea of Tiberias" is another name for the Sea of Galilee, and "in this way" signals that the author is about to tell how it happened.

The one writing is John, the disciple of Jesus. This chapter works like an epilogue to the Gospel, coming after the resurrection. John tells us that Jesus had already appeared before, and now he shows himself again in Galilee, the place where his followers had lived and worked with him. The disciples were in the middle of everyday life, waiting and not quite sure what would come next.

For today: Jesus does not wait for us to be in a special spiritual moment. He makes himself present in our work and in our daily routine. Today you can ask him to open your eyes so that you recognize him in the ordinary things of your day.
exp.7:41:
Jesus says that if God truly were the Father of those men, they would love him. The reason is that Jesus came forth from God and came from God's side. He did not come on his own, but the Father sent him.

Jesus is speaking with some leaders and people of Jerusalem who claimed to be children of Abraham and of God. Yet they were seeking to kill him. He shows them that their actions did not match what they professed. He says he has spoken the truth he heard from the Father, but they reject it. Shortly afterward, the conversation becomes even harder.

For today: it is not enough to say "I believe in God" or "I come from a believing family." If we truly love God, we will also receive Jesus and what he teaches with humility. Ask yourself today: does my life show love for Christ?
exp.0:49:
Jesus answers Nathanael with a gentle question: do you believe only because I told you I saw you under the fig tree?

Jesus is speaking early in his ministry. Nathanael has just been amazed because Jesus knew him without having met him before, and he called Jesus the Son of God and the King of Israel. Jesus does not reject that confession, but he shows Nathanael that he is only beginning to know him. In the next verse he speaks of seeing heaven opened. Scholars explain that image in several ways, but it points to Jesus joining heaven and earth.

Even if your faith is simple and only beginning, God does not stop there. Follow Jesus with an open heart, and he will show you more of who he is.
exp.5:11:
This verse says that when all the people had eaten until they were full, Jesus told his disciples to gather up the pieces of food that were left over, so that nothing would be wasted. The word for "filled" means they ate until they were completely full.

Jesus speaks right after multiplying five barley loaves and two fish for about five thousand men. Although he had the power to give in abundance, he asks them to take care of what was left. Then the disciples fill twelve baskets, and the people recognize the sign and think of the expected prophet.

For today: God gives generously, and we can respond with gratitude and careful stewardship. We can avoid wasting food, time, or money, and share what is left over with those who need it.
exp.16:5:
Jesus says that he has made known who God the Father is to the people the Father gave him out of the world. Those people already belonged to the Father, he entrusted them to Jesus, and they have obeyed his word. "Manifested" means to make known or show clearly. "Name" here refers to the person and character of God. "Kept" means that they obeyed and held on to his word.

Jesus speaks in prayer to the Father, the night before his crucifixion. He has just said that he finished the work he was given to do. Now he presents his disciples before the Father and explains that they received what he taught them and believed that he was sent by God.

For today: God knows us and has cared for us since before we sought him. We can live with security, and show that we know him by obeying his word in everyday life, through small, concrete steps.
exp.13:4:
Thomas tells Jesus that they do not know where he is going, so they cannot know the way either. The question is an honest one, asked plainly and without beating around the bush.

Jesus has just said that he is going to prepare a place for his disciples and that he will come back for them. He also told them that they already knew the way. Thomas, sincere, admits that he does not understand. That confusion leads Jesus to give one of his most famous answers: "I am the way, the truth, and the life." He speaks this on the night before his crucifixion, comforting his friends.

For today: you do not have to pretend you understand everything. You can bring your doubts to Jesus honestly, as Thomas did. He does not rebuke him, but answers him and offers himself as the sure guide.
exp.19:24:
The other disciples told Thomas, "We have seen the Lord." But Thomas replies that he will not believe unless he sees the marks of the nails in Jesus' hands, and puts his finger into them and his hand into his side. The word for "marks" here means a mark or print left behind. The word "put" means to touch with a finger or hand.

Thomas, one of the twelve, was not there when Jesus first appeared. His friends give him the news, but he is hurt and does not dare to hope so soon. He asks for concrete proof. A week later, Jesus himself appears and invites him to touch his wounds, showing that he knows Thomas's doubt and does not reject him.

For today: if you have doubts, do not hide them. Bring them honestly to God and stay close to other believers, as Thomas did by staying with the group. Jesus knows how to answer with patience those who seek him sincerely.
exp.8:28:
What it says: The Pharisees claim that they are certain God spoke to Moses, but as for Jesus, they do not know where he comes from, that is, who sent him or by what authority he acts. The word "as for" is the older way of saying "as for" in this sentence, and "this fellow" refers to Jesus.

Context: The religious leaders are speaking to a man who was born blind, whom Jesus had just healed. They question him because the healing took place on the Sabbath, and this troubles them. They hold on to Moses, whom they know, and reject Jesus, even though the miracle stood before them. The healed man answers them with simplicity and courage.

For today: It is easy to rely so much on what we know and on our traditions that we fail to recognize God when he acts in a new way. Let us ask for humility to examine what God is doing with an open heart, in the light of his Word.
exp.10:56:
The chief priests and the Pharisees had given an order: if anyone knew where Jesus was, he was to tell them so that they could have him arrested. The word "chief priests" here refers to the leading priests, and "arrested" means to take him into custody.

The one speaking here is the writer, John, and he explains what was happening in Jerusalem before the Passover. After Jesus raised Lazarus, the leaders decided that he had to die (John 11:53). People were arriving to purify themselves and wondering whether Jesus would come to the feast. Meanwhile, the leaders were already preparing to seize him.

For today: sometimes power and pride lead us to oppose what God is doing, even when we see clear signs. We can ask God for a humble heart, willing to receive his truth even when it disturbs us or changes our plans.
exp.17:31:
This verse explains that what was happening to Jesus fulfilled something He had already said. "Signifying" means "making known" or "pointing out." Jesus had announced the way He was going to die, and the account shows that this was coming true.

The Jewish leaders brought Jesus before Pilate, the Roman governor. Pilate told them to judge Him themselves, but they answered that they were not allowed to put anyone to death. So the case remained in Roman hands. John connects this with Jesus' words about being "lifted up" (John 3:14; 12:32-33), which point to crucifixion, a Roman punishment. Scholars debate how far Jewish authority extended at that time, but John emphasizes the fulfillment of what had been said.

For today: even when things seem unjust or out of control, God continues to guide His plan. We can trust that His words are fulfilled.
exp.12:9:
Jesus says that the one who has already bathed only needs to wash his feet, because the rest of his body is already clean. Then he tells the disciples, "you are clean, but not all." Where the explanation quotes or comments on the source wording, it is rendered here in the verse's own terms: the word "but" in "but not all" marks the exception, and the phrase "wash his feet" refers to the same washing the verse describes.

Jesus is with his disciples at the last supper and washes their feet. Peter resists and then asks to be washed completely. Jesus answers him with this image. Many understand that he is speaking of the spiritual cleansing they already have and of the daily forgiveness we still need. By saying "not all," he refers to Judas, who was going to betray him.

Today we can trust that God has forgiven us, and still draw near to him each day with humility, acknowledging our faults, without fear and without pride.
exp.16:8:
Jesus says that at this moment he is praying in a special way for his disciples. He makes clear that he is not asking on behalf of "the world," that is, those who reject him, but for those the Father has given him. He adds that these disciples belong to the Father: "they are thine."

Jesus speaks with the Father on the night before he is arrested. He is about to leave and wants to care for his disciples, who have received his words and believed that he was sent by God. Some think that here he is not excluding the world from God's love, since in other passages God loves the world; he is simply focusing this prayer on his own.

We can rest knowing that Jesus prays for those who belong to him. If you trust in him, you are not alone: you are God's, and he sustains you. This also invites us to care for one another and to pray for our brothers and sisters in the faith.
exp.4:39:
The explanation says that the people Jesus was speaking to did not want to come to him to receive life. The phrase "you will not come" speaks of a decision of the will, not a lack of information. "That you might have life" refers to eternal life, that is, a life with God that begins now.

Jesus speaks with Jewish religious leaders who were criticizing him because he had healed a man on the Sabbath and was saying that God was his Father. They studied the Scriptures with great care, but did not recognize that those same Scriptures pointed to Jesus. He shows them that knowing the Bible is not enough if the heart resists coming to Christ.

For today: reading the Bible is good, but it is not the goal. As you read, ask yourself: "How does this lead me to Jesus?" Come to him with humility and with a desire to receive what only he gives.
exp.8:8:
The neighbors are divided. Some say, "This is he." Others doubt, saying, "He is like him, but it cannot be." Then the man himself settles the question and says, "I am he." The word "said" here means that they were giving their opinions among themselves. His change was so great that many did not recognize him.

Jesus had just healed this man, who had been blind from birth. The neighbors knew him from seeing him beg every day. Now that he could see, his face and his bearing seemed different. That is why they argue. The man speaks simply and firmly, without hiding who he had been. Afterward he will tell how Jesus healed him.

For today: when Jesus works in your life, others will notice the change and may doubt or wonder. You do not have to defend yourself with great arguments. It is enough to say with humility and courage who you were and what Christ has done with you.
exp.14:17:
If the world hates you and treats you with hostility, the disciples are to remember that it rejected Jesus first. The word for "hates" here describes a strong rejection and opposition, not just a passing dislike.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples on the night before his crucifixion. He has just told them to love one another. Now he prepares them for the rejection that will come, because they belong to him and not to the system of values that opposes God. Here "the world" does not mean creation, but humanity turned away from God.

For today: if living faithfully for Christ brings mockery or rejection from others, do not become discouraged or bitter. Remember that Jesus experienced this first, and respond with love and humility.
exp.12:1:
It says that Jesus and his disciples were at the supper, which was already coming to an end. Before that, the devil had put into the heart of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, the idea of handing Jesus over. The explanation notes that this means the devil had planted that thought in him. It also says that this means Judas would betray him. Some translations say "during supper," and there are differences in the ancient manuscripts.

The one speaking here is the narrator, John. He is setting the scene for the washing of the feet. Even though Jesus knew what Judas was planning, and knew that his hour was near, he kept loving his own to the very end. The contrast is strong: betrayal on one side, humble service on the other.

For today: when someone hurts you or lets you down, you do not have to answer in kind. Ask God to give you a heart like Jesus', one that serves and loves even in the middle of pain.
exp.6:37:
Jesus says that whoever believes in him will have rivers of living water flowing from within them. "Belly" is an old way of speaking of a person's inner being, their heart or deepest self. "Living water" means fresh, moving water that gives life.

Jesus speaks on the last day of the Feast of Tabernacles, in Jerusalem, a time of great spiritual thirst among the people. He invites everyone to come to him and drink. The evangelist explains that he is referring to the Holy Spirit, which believers would receive after Jesus was glorified. It is not clear which exact passage of Scripture he has in mind; there are several possibilities in the prophets and the Psalms.

For today: when you feel dry or weary, go to Jesus in prayer and trust him. What you receive from him is not meant to be kept, but to flow out to others with kindness and help.
exp.6:44:
This verse tells us that the temple guards returned empty-handed. The "officers" were the guards or officials sent to arrest Jesus. The chief priests and the Pharisees, who were the religious leaders, confront them: "Why have ye not brought him?"

We are at the Feast of Tabernacles. There was division among the people about who Jesus was, and the leaders had sent the guards to seize him. Here the leaders speak, annoyed that their plan had not succeeded. In the next verse, the guards explain that they had never heard anyone speak the way Jesus does.

For today: when we listen sincerely to the words of Jesus, they can touch our hearts more than the pressure of others. We can read the Gospels with an open mind and let his voice speak to us, even when the atmosphere around us opposes it.
exp.0:15:
This verse says that everyone who believes has received something from the fullness of Christ, that is, from all that He is and has. "Have received" is the meaning here. The phrase "grace upon grace" can be understood in several ways: one grace after another, or a grace that takes the place of another, or grace on top of grace. Whichever reading one takes, the point is that God's favor comes again and again.

The speaker is John the apostle, at the beginning of his Gospel. He has just said that the Word, Jesus, came full of grace and truth. Now he explains that this abundance was not kept only in Him, but reaches those who trust in Him. Then he contrasts the law given through Moses with the grace and truth that came through Jesus Christ.

For today: do not live as someone who depends on his own strength. Each morning, ask Christ for what you need, remembering that His grace does not run out.
exp.4:14:
The man went away and reported to the Jewish leaders that it was Jesus who had healed him. The verb "told" in the verse means that he informed or announced it. "The Jews" here refers mainly to the religious authorities in Jerusalem, not to the whole people.

The one speaking is the narrator, John. Shortly before, Jesus had healed this man at the pool of Bethesda on the Sabbath. The leaders had already questioned him for carrying his mat. Now they knew who had healed him. It is not clear whether the man acted with ill intent, out of fear, or from simple obedience to the authorities. The Bible does not say, and it has been interpreted in several ways. What is evident is that this increased the opposition against Jesus.

For today: after receiving God's kindness, we can speak of Jesus with gratitude and clarity, taking care that our words honor the one who helped us and do not expose him to harm.
exp.9:35:
Jesus asks his opponents how they can accuse him of blasphemy when he, whom the Father set apart for his work and sent into the world, only said, "I am the Son of God." To "set apart" here means to separate or dedicate someone for a special purpose. To "blaspheme" means to speak against God or to claim for yourself what belongs only to him.

Jesus speaks in the temple during the Feast of Dedication. Some Jewish leaders wanted to stone him because he said, "I and the Father are one." He quotes Psalm 82:6, where human judges are called "gods," to show that their accusation has no foundation. Many interpreters believe that Jesus does not deny his divinity but reasons with them and leads them to look at his works.

Today, when someone doubts your faith, do not stop at arguments alone. Let your life, your acts of love, and your service point toward God.
exp.15:30:
Jesus answers his disciples with a question: "Do ye now believe?" In the King James wording, "Do ye now believe?" is the question. It is not a harsh scolding, but an invitation to think about whether their faith is as firm as they believe it is. It can also be read as a gentle statement: yes, they do believe, but their faith is going to be tested.

Jesus is speaking at the last supper. The disciples have just said that they now understand everything and believe that he came from God. Jesus knows that they will soon run away and leave him alone, as he says in the next verse.

For today: believing is easy when everything makes sense and things are going well. But true faith shows itself in difficulty. Acknowledge your weakness, do not rely only on your own strength, and remember that Jesus said: "Be of good cheer; I have overcome the world."
exp.20:11:
Jesus invites his disciples: "Come and dine." None of them dared to ask him, "Who art thou?" because they already knew it was the Lord.

Jesus, risen, appears by the Sea of Tiberias. The disciples had fished all night without success, and he told them where to cast the net. Now there is already a fire and bread on the shore. He receives them as a host, with closeness and care. His silence suggests reverence and wonder; the Bible does not explain more, and it can be understood in several ways.

Today, Jesus also invites us to draw near to him before we resolve everything. We can spend a few minutes being with him in prayer, resting in his company and receiving his care, without fear or doubt.
exp.18:16:
This verse tells that Jesus went out carrying his own cross to a place called "the place of a skull," which in Hebrew (or Aramaic) was called Golgotha. "Chief priests" are the leaders of the priests. "The sign" is the notice with the charge against him.

The one telling the story is John, a witness to these events. Pilate, the Roman governor, had just handed Jesus over to the Jewish authorities, who were shouting for him to be crucified and said, "We have no king but Caesar." John stresses that Jesus moved toward the cross, not as someone dragged along without direction. About the name of the place, some think it came from the shape of the hill; others, from the fact that condemned people were executed there. It is not known for certain.

For today: Jesus carried the cross out of love for us. When you face a hard road, you do not walk it alone; you can trust in the One who walked through suffering first.
exp.6:22:
It says that if a boy receives circumcision on the Sabbath, so as not to break the law of Moses, no one complains. Then Jesus asks why they are angry with him for making a man completely whole on the Sabbath. "Broken" means breached or disobeyed, and "made whole" means that he healed him.

Jesus speaks in Jerusalem, during a festival, before people who wanted to kill him. Earlier he had healed a sick man on the Sabbath (John 5), and many were scandalized. He shows them that they already accept doing good on the Sabbath, since they circumcise on that day. For this reason he asks them to judge with righteousness and not merely by appearances.

For today: before criticizing someone, it is good to look at what they actually do and why. Sometimes we defend rules and forget their purpose: to care for and give life. Let us ask God for a just and compassionate heart.
