exp.3:36:
It says there is a well-known and true saying: one person sows the seed and another person reaps the harvest. The word for "harvest" here means to gather in what has ripened in the field. The same person does not always do both tasks.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples by the well at Sychar, in Samaria. He has just spoken with the Samaritan woman, and she is already running to tell her people. Jesus uses the field as an image: people ready to believe are like ripe grain. He encourages them to see that opportunity and to value the work of others who prepared the way.

Today we can serve with humility, without fighting for the credit. Perhaps you sow with a kind word, a prayer, or a good example, and someone else will see the fruit. God sees each part, and everyone will rejoice together.
exp.15:7:
Jesus says that when the Holy Spirit comes, he will convict the world. The word that the King James Version uses here means to convince, to make the truth clearly seen, and it can also carry the idea of rebuking or bringing something into the open. The Spirit will make the world see three things: what sin is, what righteousness is, and what judgment is.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples on the night before his crucifixion. They are sad because he tells them he is going away. He promises them that the Comforter, the Holy Spirit, will come to help them. The verses that follow explain that the central sin is not believing in Jesus.

For today: when you sense that God is showing you a mistake, do not take it only as condemnation. It is an invitation to return to Christ. And when you speak about your faith with others, pray and trust that only the Spirit can open the heart.
exp.5:37:
Jesus says that he came down from heaven with a clear purpose: not to do what he himself wanted, but what the Father who sent him wants. The word "but" in the verse marks this contrast, and "came down" means that he came from heaven to earth.

Jesus speaks in Capernaum, after multiplying the loaves, to people who were looking for him because of the food. He tells them that he is the bread of life. Although they had seen him, many did not believe. Here he explains that his mission is to carry out the will of the Father, and that will is to care for everyone who comes to him and to give them eternal life.

For today: when you make decisions, ask yourself not only "What do I want?" but "What does God want?" Jesus gives us an example of a life entrusted with confidence to the Father, and we can rest in the knowledge that his will is good.
exp.1:20:
When he said "this temple," the explanation says, he was not referring to the stone building in Jerusalem but to his own body. The word "But" is used here, and the phrase "temple of his body" means that his body was the place where God dwelt.

Jesus had just cleared the temple, and the Jewish leaders asked him for a sign to prove his authority. He answered with mysterious words about destroying the temple and raising it up in three days. They thought of the building, but John explains that he was speaking of his death and resurrection. The disciples understood this after Jesus had risen.

Today we can learn that Jesus is the center of our faith, and that God draws near to us through him. If there is something in the Bible we do not understand, we can keep trusting; sometimes God gives us light over time.
exp.4:32:
This verse says that the Jewish leaders sent messengers to John the Baptist to ask him who he was, and that John spoke the truth about Jesus. Some older words in the wording: the form "ye sent" means "you sent," and "he bare witness" means "he gave witness."

Jesus is speaking, defending himself before leaders who were challenging him for healing on the Sabbath and for saying that God was his Father. He reminds them of a testimony they themselves had sought: that of John (see John 1:19-27). Jesus does not need it for himself, since his true support comes from the Father, but he mentions it so that they, by recognizing the truth of John's words, might believe and be saved.

For today: let us not ignore the honest voices God places in our path. If we seek the truth sincerely, it is not enough to admire a message; we must respond to it with faith and obedience to Christ.
exp.13:9:
Jesus asks Philip whether he does not believe that he is in the Father and the Father in him. He says that his words are not his own ideas apart from the Father, but that the Father, who dwells in him, is the one who does the works.

Jesus speaks with his disciples at the last supper, shortly before his death. Philip asked to see the Father, and Jesus answers him with some sadness: after so long together, Philip still has not recognized him. Jesus shows that his teaching and his miracles reveal the Father. Christians have understood this as a very deep union between the two.

If you want to know what God is like, look at Jesus: how he treated the poor, how he forgave, and how he told the truth. Read the Gospels calmly and trust that his character shows the heart of the Father.
exp.8:16:
The Pharisees, divided among themselves, ask the man who had been blind what he thinks of Jesus, the one who gave him back his sight. He answers simply: "He is a prophet." The word "blind" here refers to him before he was healed, and "gave him back his sight" means that Jesus restored his ability to see.

The Pharisees were arguing because Jesus had performed the healing on the Sabbath. Some said he did not come from God; others could not understand how a sinner could do such signs. Faced with the division, they ask the man who was healed for his opinion. He speaks only from what he has experienced, and he calls Jesus a prophet, someone sent by God.

For today: you do not need to know everything to bear witness to Jesus. Tell honestly what He has done in your life, even if others doubt or oppose it.
exp.20:20:
Peter turns around and sees that the disciple whom Jesus loved is following them. Then he asks, "Lord, and what shall this man do?"

Peter is speaking. Jesus has just restored him after his denials and has told him that his death would glorify God. Then he says, "Follow me." Peter, perhaps out of curiosity or concern, looks at John and wants to know what his path will be. Jesus answers that this is not Peter's concern: he must follow Jesus.

It is easy to look to the side and compare our lives with others': their work, their blessings, or their trials. Jesus calls us to personal faithfulness. Today, instead of asking "And what about him?", ask in prayer, "Lord, what do you want from me today?" and take the next step of obedience.
exp.17:0:
After Jesus had finished speaking these words, he left the city with his disciples and crossed the brook Kidron, a streambed that carried water mostly during the rainy season, and entered a garden, that is, an enclosed place with trees.

The one telling the story is John. Jesus had just said goodbye to his disciples and prayed for them (chapters 14 through 17), on the night before his crucifixion. John does not name the garden; other Gospels call it Gethsemane. Jesus knew that place, and the verses that follow say that Judas knew it too, since they often met there.

For today: Jesus did not run from what was coming, but went calmly to the place where he would be found. When you face something hard, you can seek a place of prayer and commit yourself to God with confidence, instead of running away.
exp.15:17:
The disciples repeat among themselves the words of Jesus: "A little while." They say they do not understand what he means. The phrase "They said therefore" is rewritten here as "They said then," meaning "they said at that point." The words confuse them, and they discuss them quietly among themselves, not yet daring to ask him directly.

This happens on the night before the cross, when Jesus is preparing them for his departure. He had told them that in a little while they would not see him, and then they would see him again. They do not understand that he is speaking of his death, his resurrection, and his return to the Father. Some interpreters also see here a reference to his future coming.

It is normal not to understand God at every moment. The disciples did not pretend to understand; they acknowledged their confusion. We can do the same: bring our doubts honestly to Jesus and trust that he will explain them in his time.
exp.16:2:
It says that eternal life consists in knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ, whom He sent. The word "empero," which means "but" or "now then," is not part of the English verse, so it needs no comment, and the small word "á" is simply "to," which is also not needed here. Here "know" does not mean only knowing facts, but having a personal and real relationship.

Jesus speaks with his Father in prayer, shortly before going to the cross. He asks to be glorified so that the Father may also be glorified. He says that the Father gave him authority to give eternal life to those who were given to him. With this phrase he explains what that life consists of.

Today, eternal life is not only something in the future; it begins when we come to know God. We can set aside a few minutes each day to read the Gospels and speak with God, seeking to know him better as a friend, not just to fulfill religious duties.
exp.15:12:
Jesus says that when the Holy Spirit comes, the one he calls "the Spirit of truth," he will guide the disciples into all truth. He will not speak on his own, but will say what he hears from the Father and the Son. He will also let them know the things that are going to happen, that is, what will take place later.

Jesus is speaking at the Last Supper, shortly before his arrest. The disciples are sad because he is leaving. He tells them that he still has much to teach them, but that they cannot yet bear it. The Spirit will carry on that work. Many understand that the promise refers above all to the apostles and their teaching, which was preserved in the New Testament.

Today you can ask the Spirit to guide you as you read the Bible. He does not contradict Jesus but makes him clearer. Read with humility and pray before opening the Word.
exp.11:42:
This verse says that some leaders wanted the applause and respect of people more than the approval of God. Here the word "glory" means honor, good name, or recognition, and "rulers" refers to the governing leaders of the people.

The speaker is the apostle John, who explains why many Jewish leaders believed in Jesus in their hearts but did not say so openly. They feared the Pharisees, who could put them out of the synagogue, which would mean losing their place in the community. John shows that the fear of rejection weighed more heavily than their faith. Afterward, Jesus calls everyone to believe in Him and in the Father who sent Him.

For today: ask yourself whom you are trying to please when you make decisions. Ask God for the courage to live your faith sincerely, even if it costs you some mockery or discomfort.
exp.3:35:
This verse says that the one who reaps, or gathers in the harvest, receives wages. Along with this, he gathers fruit that lasts into eternal life. In this way, both the one who sows and the one who reaps rejoice together. The word "gathereth" in the verse above means to bring together or collect.

Jesus speaks with his disciples by the well at Sychar, after talking with the Samaritan woman. They were thinking about food and about waiting months for the harvest. Jesus uses the picture of the field to show them that many people were already ready to hear God's message. Here the "harvest" stands for the people who believe.

For today: do not lose heart if you are only sowing, that is, if you speak of God kindly and see no results. And if your task is to reap, remember that others worked before you. We all share in the joy of God's work.
exp.6:10:
The explanation says that during the feast, the Jews were looking for Jesus and asking, "Where is that man?" The word "that man" sounds dismissive, as if they avoided saying his name. "Were looking for him" means they were searching for him. The feast is the Feast of Tabernacles, also called the Feast of Booths.

The one speaking is the narrator, John, who recounts what "the Jews" were saying. This term here usually refers to the religious leaders of Jerusalem. They were looking for him because there was already tension with Jesus and some wanted to arrest him (John 7:1). He had gone up secretly, so they could not find him. Among the crowd there were divided opinions about who he was.

For today: some people ask about Jesus with curiosity, others with distrust. We can seek him with a sincere heart, willing to listen to him and not only to offer opinions about him.
exp.4:16:
Jesus answers those who accuse him by saying that his Father is still working, and that he also works. The Greek-based phrasing of the verse is rendered in the King James Version as "My Father worketh hitherto, and I work," meaning that God has never stopped working.

Jesus speaks after healing a sick man on the Sabbath, a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years. Some Jewish leaders were pursuing him for this reason. Many understand Jesus to be saying that God continues to sustain and care for all things, even on the Sabbath, and that he acts in unity with the Father. The verses that follow show that his hearers understood this as a claim to be equal with God.

For today: God is still at work in your life, even when you do not notice it. Ask him to help you join his work, doing good without waiting for the perfect moment.
exp.8:15:
The Pharisees divide over the healing of the blind man. Some say Jesus is not from God because he does not keep the Sabbath, that is, he does not honor the day of rest. Others ask how a man who is a sinner could perform such miracles, which are wonders that point to God's power. The word "division" in the verse means a split or disagreement.

The ones speaking are Jewish religious leaders. Jesus had made mud and healed the blind man on the Sabbath, and many understood that kneading mud was forbidden work. Some held tightly to their rule; others could not deny the miracle. Shortly after, the man who was healed will say that Jesus is a prophet.

For today: when what God does does not fit our ideas, let us not close our eyes. Let us be humble enough to examine our opinions and let the facts and the Word correct us.
exp.0:25:
John answers the Pharisees that he baptizes with water, but that among them already stood someone they did not know.

Habla Juan el Bautista. The Pharisees sent from Jerusalem ask him by what authority he baptizes, if he is not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet. John does not speak about himself; he turns attention toward Jesus, whom he will soon present. His baptism with water was preparing the way, but it was not the main thing.

For today: sometimes Jesus is near and we do not notice, because we are distracted by other things. We can ask God for attentive eyes, and seek Christ in His Word, in prayer, and in the people He places beside us.
exp.11:34:
Jesus says that the light will be with them only a little while longer. He asks them to walk while they have the light, so that darkness does not overtake them. Being "overtaken" by darkness means it catches them suddenly. Whoever walks in the dark does not know where he is going.

Jesus is speaking to the people in Jerusalem, shortly before his death. He has just announced that he would be lifted up, and the crowd does not understand how the Christ could die if he is meant to remain forever. He does not answer their question directly, but calls them to respond in time. According to the context, the light is himself, and the verse that follows invites them to believe in the light.

When God shows you the truth, do not put it off for later. Today you can pray, read his Word, and obey what you already understand, instead of waiting until you feel ready.
exp.2:15:
It says that God loved the world so much that he gave his only Son, Jesus, so that everyone who believes in him will not be lost, but will have eternal life. "Gave" means he gave it as a gift. "Only" means one of a kind, the Son who was loved in a special way. Being lost speaks of being separated from God forever.

Jesus speaks at night with Nicodemus, a Jewish teacher who came to him with questions. Jesus explains to him that he must be born again. Earlier he mentions the snake that Moses lifted up in the desert: whoever looked at it was healed. In the same way, Jesus would be lifted up, and whoever trusts in him receives life. Some understand that this verse is still the words of Jesus, and others think it is a reflection by the author, John.

Today, you do not have to earn God's love. Trust in Jesus and receive his gift with gratitude.
exp.4:1:
This verse describes a place in Jerusalem: a pool next to the sheep gate, which in the local language was called Bethesda and had five covered colonnades or walkways. "Colonnades" here means those covered walkways. The word "tongue" refers to the language of the Jews, probably the Aramaic spoken at that time. The exact meaning of the name Bethesda is debated; it is often explained as "house of mercy," but this is not certain.

John is the one telling the story. Jesus has gone up to Jerusalem for a Jewish feast. The author sets the scene in detail to prepare the story that follows: the healing of a sick man, in a place full of people in need.

For today: Jesus goes where there is pain. We can ask him to give us eyes to see those who suffer near us, and the courage to approach them with compassion and simple help.
exp.18:24:
John tells us that standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother Mary, his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Cleophas (also called Clopas), and Mary Magdalene. It is not known for certain whether "his mother's sister" and "Mary of Cleophas" refer to one woman or to two different women; the Bible does not make this clear.

The one telling the story is John, who was there. After showing the soldiers dividing up the clothing with indifference, he shows these women who stayed with love and faithfulness. Right after this, Jesus, from the cross, will entrust his mother to the beloved disciple.

For today: being present matters. Perhaps you cannot take away someone's pain, but you can stay by their side, visit them, listen to them, and pray with them. Your faithful presence can be a very great comfort.
exp.16:7:
Jesus says that he gave his disciples the words that the Father gave him. They received them, that is, they accepted them with their hearts. Because of this, they knew for certain that Jesus came from God, and they believed that the Father sent him.

Jesus speaks in prayer to the Father, the night before his crucifixion, during the last supper with his disciples. He is praying for them before leaving them. He remembers what they have learned and what they have believed, because soon they will be sent into a world that will reject them.

For today: faith grows when we receive God's word with simplicity and do not merely hear it. Spend a few minutes each day reading a passage from the gospels, and ask God to help you believe and obey what you have read.
exp.0:0:
It says that before anything existed, the Word already existed. This Word was with God and, at the same time, was God. The phrase "was with" speaks of a close relationship, and "was God" speaks of his divine nature. Later, the text shows that this Word is Jesus Christ.

The one who writes is John, the disciple, according to Christian tradition. He opens his Gospel with a solemn introduction, almost like a hymn. He wants the reader to know from the beginning who Jesus is: not only a teacher, but the eternal God who created everything and who later became human. The following verses say that all things were made through him.

For today: if Jesus is God himself speaking to us, it is worth listening to him carefully. Today you can read a passage from the Gospels and ask yourself sincerely: "Lord, what do you want to tell me?"
exp.9:39:
This verse says that Jesus went away again to the other side of the Jordan River, to the same place where John the Baptist had been baptizing at the beginning, and he stayed there. The phrase about going back across the Jordan means that he returned to the region on the far side of the Jordan. The word for "stayed" simply means he remained.

Here the narrator is John the evangelist. Jesus had just escaped from leaders who wanted to arrest him, after saying that his works showed that the Father was with him. He withdrew to a quiet place, connected with John the Baptist's testimony. There the people remembered what John had said about Jesus, and many believed. The Bible does not explain in detail why he chose that place, but it fits the context.

For today: when there is rejection or pressure, it is not always necessary to fight. Sometimes it is wise to step aside calmly, return to what is essential, and give the truth room to speak in a simpler setting.
exp.13:25:
Jesus promises that the Father will send the Holy Spirit in his name. He calls this Spirit "the Comforter," a word that can also be understood as Helper or Advocate. He will teach all things and bring to mind what Jesus said. The phrase "in my name" means that he comes with the authority and mission of Jesus.

Jesus speaks with his disciples the night before his crucifixion. They are sad and confused because he tells them he is leaving. So he assures them that they will not be left alone. The disciples would remember his teachings through the work of the Spirit, and later many of them would be written down.

For today: when you feel lost or afraid, you are not alone. Ask the Spirit to guide you as you read the Bible, and trust that he helps you understand it and remember it when you need it.
exp.15:27:
Jesus sums up his story in a few words: he came forth from the Father, he came into the world, and now he leaves the world to return to the Father. He speaks of his divine origin, his mission on earth, and his return to heaven. "Leave" means "go away from" or "depart."

Jesus speaks with his disciples the night before his crucifixion. He has told them that he will soon go away and that they will feel sorrow. He wants them to understand that his departure is not a failure but part of the Father's plan. The disciples answer that now they understand clearly. Even so, the text shows that their faith would still be tested.

For today: when changes or farewells come that you do not understand, remember that Jesus knew where he came from and where he was going. You can trust that God is also guiding your path.
exp.5:17:
This verse tells us that the sea was stirred up because a very strong wind was blowing. "The sea rose" means the waves were growing higher. In that time, the word for "sea" was also used for the lake, which here is the Sea of Galilee.

John is the one telling the story. The disciples are in a boat heading toward Capernaum, and it is already night, and Jesus has not yet come to them. Earlier, Jesus had fed a crowd, and then he withdrew to a mountain. John does not say why Jesus let them sail on their own at that moment; some think it was to teach them to trust him.

For today: sometimes the wind blows hard even when we are doing what is right. That we cannot see Jesus in the middle of the storm does not mean he has forgotten us. We can keep rowing with faith, and the next verse reminds us that he comes and says, "It is I; be not afraid."
exp.2:18:
This verse says that God's judgment does not begin because He is harsh, but because the light has already come. That light is Jesus. The condemnation, meaning the verdict, is that many people chose spiritual darkness, that is, living far from God, because their actions were evil and they did not want to be exposed.

These words come from Jesus' conversation with Nicodemus, a Jewish leader who visited him at night. Some scholars think that from a certain point the text is an explanation by John himself, and it is not known with complete certainty where the voice changes. Even so, the message is clear: God sent his Son to save, not to condemn.

Today, we can ask ourselves which part of our lives we avoid showing to God. Bringing it honestly into his light, in prayer, is the first step toward being healed.
exp.3:52:
The passage tells us that the father realized something important: the hour when his son got better was the same hour in which Jesus had said to him, "Your son lives." So he believed, and his whole household believed too. The word "realized" here means that he recognized or understood it clearly. "Household" refers to his family and to those who lived with him, including the servants.

The one speaking is the narrator, John. This father was an official of the king, who had asked Jesus to heal his sick son in Capernaum. Jesus did not go with him; he only told him that his son was living, and the man believed Jesus' word and went on his way. On his return, his servants confirmed the healing to him, and the timing matched exactly.

His faith began by trusting the word of Jesus and grew as he saw what Jesus had done. Today we too can trust what God says, even before we see the result. And when you see his work in your life, tell it within your family, so that they too may come to know Jesus.
exp.0:47:
Nathanael is surprised that Jesus knows him without ever having met him before. Jesus answers that he saw him under the fig tree, before Philip called him. 

Nathanael had just doubted that anything good could come from Nazareth. Jesus welcomes him by calling him an Israelite in whom there is no deceit. Nathanael asks how Jesus knows him, and Jesus shows that he had seen him even from a distance. The Bible does not say what Nathanael was doing under the fig tree; some think he was praying or meditating, but that is only a guess. Even so, this leads him to confess that Jesus is the Son of God.

For today: Jesus sees you and knows you in what is hidden, even when no one else notices you. You can come to Him with sincerity, without pretending, and with the confidence that He knows you and receives you.
exp.18:37:
It tells that, after Jesus died, Joseph of Arimathea went to ask Pilate for the body of Jesus. Joseph had been a disciple of Jesus, but he had been one in secret, out of fear of the Jewish leaders. Pilate gave him permission, and Joseph went and took the body down.

The word "besought" means that he asked earnestly and insistently, and "take away" here means taking the body down from the cross.

John, the author, tells what happened after the crucifixion. It was important that someone take care of a dignified burial, because the Romans often left bodies on the cross. John shows us that Joseph acted with courage, even though before he had kept his faith quiet. About his motives, the text says nothing more.

For today: sometimes our faith stays silent out of fear. God can give us courage at the right moment. Ask Him to help you take one small step of courage for Jesus today.
exp.7:4:
The scribes and Pharisees speak about the law of Moses. They say it commanded that women like her be stoned, and they ask Jesus for his opinion. The phrase about "such women" means the same as "women like this," and the phrase "but what sayest thou?" in the King James Version carries the same sense as "and you, then?"

Those speaking are religious leaders, and they are not seeking justice but setting a trap, as the next verse makes clear. If Jesus said not to stone her, they could accuse him of going against the law; if he said to stone her, they could confront him with the Roman authorities. Moreover, the law required that both guilty parties be judged, yet here they bring only the woman. Some scholars point this out, though the text does not explain why.

Today we can take care not to use the Bible to point out others without looking at our own hearts. Before judging, it is wise to ask ourselves whether we seek the truth with humility and mercy, as Jesus did.
exp.9:12:
This verse says that the hired hand, that is, the one who works only for pay, runs away when danger comes. He does so because the sheep are not his own and he does not truly care about them. "Careth not" means that he does not care for them.

Jesus speaks here of himself as the good shepherd. He contrasts himself with those who look after the people only for their own gain. Many understand that Jesus has in mind the religious leaders of his time, although the text does not name them here. His point is that he, unlike the hired hand, lays down his life for the sheep.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we care for others only when it is convenient or whether we stand by them in difficulties. We can also be thankful that Christ never abandons us. If we lead or serve others, let us ask him for a shepherd's heart, not a hired hand's.
exp.9:30:
It says that the Jews who were with Jesus in the temple picked up stones again to kill him. The phrase "took up stones again" shows they had already tried this before (John 8:59). Stoning was the punishment the law of Moses gave to someone regarded as a blasphemer.

Jesus had just said: "I and the Father are one." His listeners understood him to be speaking of being equal with God, and that is why they reacted with violence. They themselves explain it afterward: they accused him of blasphemy because, though a man, he was making himself God. Jesus did not correct that idea; he invited them to look at his works.

For today: the words of Jesus leave no room for indifference; they call for a response. We can ask God for a humble heart that listens to Jesus attentively, without closing itself off through prejudice, and that trusts that his sheep are secure in the Father's hand.
exp.18:19:
This verse says that many of the Jews read the sign that Pilate had placed on the cross. Because the place of the crucifixion was near the city, many people passed by there. The sign was written in three languages: Hebrew, Greek, and Latin.

The one speaking here is John, who tells what he saw. Pilate had ordered it written, "Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews." The languages show that the message could be understood by different peoples: Hebrew for the religious, Greek for the cultural, and Latin for the official. The chief priests were upset and asked for it to be changed, but Pilate did not give in. Pilate's reasons are not clearly explained in the text.

For today: God can use even the unexpected to proclaim who Jesus is. Let us pray that our lives and our words will also make him known clearly, so that everyone can understand.
exp.10:4:
This verse says that Jesus loved Martha, her sister, and Lazarus. The text does not name the sister here; it only says "her sister." The word "loved" shows a constant love, not a passing one. It is a close and real friendship.

The one telling this is the author of the Gospel, John. He says it right after the sisters sent word that Lazarus was sick, and just before Jesus waits two more days. John makes clear Jesus's love so that we do not think the delay came from indifference. How Jesus acts during that wait is understood by reading on in the account.

For today: when God seems slow to answer, the love of Jesus is still true. We can trust his heart even when we do not understand his timing, and keep praying with sincerity.
exp.5:25:
Jesus says to them very plainly: "Verily, verily" is a way of saying "I assure you, it is true." He explains that they are looking for him, but not because they understood the signs, that is, the miracles that pointed to who he is. They seek him because they ate the bread and were filled, that is, fully satisfied.

Jesus speaks with the crowd that had just eaten the bread multiplied in chapter 6. The next day they follow him to Capernaum. He knows their motives: they are interested in easy food, not in what the miracle reveals. That is why he immediately invites them to seek the food that endures to eternal life.

For today: examine why you seek God. It is natural to ask him for help with daily needs, but it is also good to seek him himself, not only his blessings. Today you can pray: "Lord, teach me to love you more than your gifts."
exp.4:28:
Jesus says that all the dead will hear his voice and come out of their graves. Those who have done good will rise to life, and those who have done evil will rise to be judged and condemned. Condemnation means judgment with a sentence against the person.

Jesus is speaking in Jerusalem, defending that the Father gave him authority to give life and to judge. His hearers were scandalized that he made himself equal to God. He tells them not to be amazed, because an hour is coming when his voice will reach even the dead. Some debate how doing good relates to faith (see John 5:24), but in John, deeds usually show whether someone truly believes.

Today we can live with our eyes on that hour. Ask Jesus to help you trust in him and to show that faith through concrete acts of love and justice, without fear and without boasting.
exp.9:41:
It says that, in that place across the Jordan, many people put their trust in Jesus. "Believed" means they placed their faith in him, not merely that they listened to him out of curiosity. The word "there" points to the place where John the Baptist had baptized before.

The narrator, John the apostle, closes this chapter this way. Jesus had withdrawn to that place after people in Jerusalem wanted to stone him. The people remembered that John the Baptist did no miraculous signs, but what he had announced about Jesus proved true. Seeing Jesus, they compared what had been said with what they saw, and they believed.

For today: faith often grows when we honestly remember what God has said and what he has fulfilled. Think of a promise of God that you have seen come true, and let that strengthen your trust in Jesus, even if the atmosphere around you today is difficult.
exp.16:11:
Jesus says that, while he was with his disciples, he cared for and protected them in the name of the Father. Of those the Father had given him, none was lost, except "the son of perdition," a phrase understood to mean someone destined for ruin, which almost everyone connects with Judas. This happened so that the Scripture would be fulfilled. Keeping, in this sense, means caring for and protecting.

Jesus is praying to the Father shortly before his arrest, on the last night with his disciples. He knows he will soon leave, and he asks that the Father continue to care for them and that they remain united. About how the Scripture was fulfilled in Judas's case, there are different interpretations.

For today: If you belong to Christ, you are not alone. He cares for you and prays for you. Rest in that protection and, at the same time, seek unity with other believers, because Jesus asked that we be one.
exp.3:50:
As he was going down, his servants met him and brought him the good news: his son is alive. The words "the good news" simply mean the report that the boy was alive, and "going down" means he was traveling down, since Capernaum lay lower than Cana.

Here the narrator, John, speaks. A royal official had asked Jesus to heal his dying son. Jesus did not go with him; he only told him, "Go, your son is alive." The man believed the word Jesus spoke and set out on his way. The servants confirm that what Jesus said came true.

For today: we can trust what Jesus says even when we do not yet see the result. This father believed first and walked on calmly, and the confirmation came afterward. When we pray, let us rest in the word of Christ and keep going in faith.
exp.3:18:
The Samaritan woman says to Jesus, "Sir, I perceive that thou art a prophet." She recognizes that Jesus is not an ordinary man.

Jesus has just shown her that he knows her private life, something she had never told him. That is why she draws this conclusion. Then she shifts the subject to the question of where worship should take place, on the mountain of the Samaritans or in Jerusalem. Some think she wanted to steer the conversation away; others think she was genuinely seeking answers. The text does not make this clear.

When God shows us the truth about ourselves, we can turn away from it or respond with honesty. Today we can approach Jesus just as we are, hiding nothing, trusting that he knows us and still receives us with grace.
exp.14:7:
Jesus says that the Father is glorified, that is, honored and shown to be great, when believers bear much fruit. And that fruit shows that they are truly his disciples. The word "bear" in the verse means to give or produce.

Jesus speaks to his disciples the night before his crucifixion, using the image of the vine and the branches. He is the vine, the Father is the gardener, and they are the branches. He wants them to understand that without remaining joined to him they cannot bear fruit. The nearby verses speak of remaining in his love and obeying him. Some think the fruit includes character and love; others add witness. It probably includes all of that.

Today, seek to stay close to Jesus each day through his Word and prayer. Ask him to let his love be seen in how you treat others.
exp.10:39:
Jesus reminds Martha of something he had already told her: if she believes, she will see the glory of God. The phrase about believing refers to trusting him, and "the glory of God" refers to his power and his presence shown in a visible way.

Jesus speaks with Martha in front of the tomb of her brother Lazarus, who has been dead for four days. She hesitates to have the stone removed because of the smell. Jesus does not rebuke her harshly, but reminds her of what he said before (in John 11:4 and 11:25-26). Soon the stone is taken away, and Jesus prays to the Father so that the people will believe.

When a situation seems closed or beyond hope, we can trust the word of Jesus and take the step of obedience that is ours to take, even when we do not understand everything. God knows how to work where we no longer see a way out.
exp.2:17:
It says that whoever trusts in Jesus is not condemned. On the other hand, whoever does not believe is already condemned, because they have turned away from Jesus, the only begotten Son of God. "Name" here means his person and his authority.

Jesus speaks at night with Nicodemus, a teacher of the Jews who came to find him with sincere questions. Jesus explains to him that God did not send his Son to destroy the world, but to save it. Condemnation is not God's plan; rather, it is what remains when someone rejects the light that he offers.

Today, this invites us not to live in constant fear or guilt if we have placed our trust in Christ. It also invites us to let his light shine on the hidden areas of our lives, instead of hiding from him.
exp.18:13:
John notes that it was the day of preparation for the Passover, around the sixth hour, which would normally be noon. Then Pilate presents Jesus before the crowd and says: "Behold your King!" The word for "day of preparation" means the day before the Sabbath or a feast, and the Greek word for "about" is written in an older form.

Pilate is the one speaking. The Jewish leaders had been pressing him, saying that if he released Jesus, he was no friend of Caesar. Pilate, who knew Jesus was innocent, seems to say this with irony and to provoke them. As for the hour, scholars do not agree on how it fits with Mark 15:25.

For today: Jesus is King even when people reject him. Ask yourself whether, in practice, you give him that place, or whether, like that crowd, out of fear or convenience, you prefer other "kings." Today you can decide to obey him in something concrete.
exp.3:17:
She says the woman has had five husbands and that the man she now lives with is not her husband. Jesus adds: "in that saidst thou truly," meaning she spoke the truth, though only in part. The phrase "thou saidst truly" carries the sense of "you have spoken the truth."

Jesus speaks with a Samaritan woman by a well. She asks him for living water, and Jesus touches on her personal life. He does not do this to shame her, but to show her that he knows her. That is why she answers, "Sir, I perceive that thou art a prophet." The texts do not explain her motives or her circumstances, so it is best not to assume more than they say.

Jesus knows our whole story and still draws near with truth and kindness. Today we can stop hiding what shames us and come to him with sincerity, trusting that he receives us to heal us, not to destroy us.
exp.3:22:
Jesus says that a time is coming, and has already begun, when true worshippers will worship the Father "in spirit and in truth." Moreover, the Father himself seeks that kind of worshipper. "But" means "yet," and "such" means "of this kind."

Jesus speaks with a Samaritan woman at a well. She had asked him whether people should worship on Mount Gerizim or in Jerusalem. Jesus answers that what matters will no longer be the place, but the way of worshipping. Many understand "in spirit" as sincere worship from the heart, guided by the Spirit of God, and "in truth" as in line with what God is really like, revealed in Jesus. There are different ways of interpreting it.

For today: do not worry so much about the place or the form. Come to God with a sincere heart, without pretending, knowing that he seeks you first.
exp.12:15:
Jesus says with great seriousness ("verily, verily" means "I tell you the truth") that a servant is not greater than his master, nor is one who is sent greater than the one who sent him.

Jesus speaks at the last supper with his disciples. He has just washed their feet, work belonging to a servant. If he, being Lord and Teacher, humbled himself in this way, they have no reason to think themselves too important to serve others. He gives them an example to follow.

Today, this invites us to serve without seeking recognition. Think of a simple task that no one wants to do, at home, in your church, or at work, and do it gladly, following the example of Jesus.
exp.8:20:
The parents of the man who was healed say they do not know how he now sees, nor who opened his eyes. They leave the matter to him: he is of age, that is, he is an adult, so the authorities can ask him, and he will speak for himself.

The parents speak before the Jewish authorities who are investigating the healing. They confirm that he is their son and that he was born blind, but nothing more. The text explains that they were afraid: the authorities had decided to expel from the synagogue anyone who acknowledged Jesus as the Messiah. Perhaps they knew more than they said, but the account only states that they feared the consequences.

Today, the fear of being rejected can lead us to keep silent about what God has done. Let us ask for courage to bear witness with simplicity and truth, trusting that God sustains those who confess him.
exp.10:38:
Jesus asks that the stone covering the cave where Lazarus is buried be taken away. Martha, his sister, objects that by now there will be a bad smell, because he has been dead for four days.

Jesus stands before the tomb of his friend Lazarus, surrounded by people who are weeping and doubting. Martha speaks with honesty and practical good sense: she sees death as something already final. Some believe the four days also stress that there was no human hope left. Jesus will answer her by reminding her that if she believes, she will see the glory of God.

Many times God asks us to take a step of faith before we see the result, even when the situation seems lost. We can be honest like Martha about our doubts, but also obey what Jesus tells us, trusting that He can act where we no longer see a way out.
exp.20:15:
Here Jesus asks Peter a second time: "Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me?" Peter answers that yes, Jesus knows that he loves him. Then Jesus says, "Feed my sheep," that is, care for, nourish, and guide his people as a shepherd would.

Jesus had already risen and was with his disciples by the lake, after eating. Peter had denied him three times the night of the arrest. Many understand that these three questions restore him and give him a task again. Some note that in the original text there are different words for "love," but interpreters do not agree on how much meaning should be drawn from that.

Loving Jesus is not only a feeling; it shows itself in patiently caring for others, whether in the family, the church, or the community. If you have failed, he can still entrust you with something valuable.
exp.6:21:
Jesus says that Moses gave you circumcision, though he clarifies that it actually came from the patriarchs, that is, from Abraham and his descendants. And you circumcise a boy even on the Sabbath.

Jesus speaks in Jerusalem, during the Feast of Tabernacles. The leaders wanted to kill him because he healed a man on the Sabbath (John 5). The crowd, who perhaps did not know about those plans, accuses him of having a demon. He shows them their inconsistency: they accept breaking the rest of the Sabbath to circumcise, but they become angry because he made a whole person well.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we apply the rules with mercy. Before criticizing someone, it is good to look with justice and not only at appearances. Doing good to others should never seem like an offense to us.
exp.9:28:
Jesus says that the sheep, that is, those who follow him, were given by the Father, and that the Father is "greater than all," meaning more powerful than any force. For that reason no one can take them out of the Father's hand by force.

Jesus speaks in Jerusalem, during the Feast of the Dedication, and the Jewish leaders ask him to say plainly whether he is the Christ. He answers with the image of the shepherd and his sheep. Right after, he adds: "I and my Father are one," and for this reason they want to stone him. Interpreters debate how to explain that unity, but the listeners understood that Jesus was placing himself on the level of God.

If you trust in Christ today, your security does not depend on your strength, but on the hands that hold you. When you feel fear or doubt, rest in that promise and keep listening to his voice.
exp.7:21:
The Jews wondered whether Jesus planned to take his own life, because he had said, "Where I go, you cannot come." Their question suggests he might kill himself, and the quoted phrase in that question is simply a way of asking whether he is about to end his own life.

Jesús was teaching in the temple, near the place of the offerings, and he had said that he was going away and that they would look for him. The Jewish leaders understood his words in an earthly way and thought of death. Jesus was speaking of returning to the Father, and that is why he later tells them that he is "from above" and they are "from below."

For today: when a word from God sounds strange to us, let us not judge it by human ideas alone. Let us ask for humility to listen to Jesus and to believe in him, for he speaks to us of eternal realities.
exp.5:38:
Jesus says that the Father's will is that he should lose nothing of all that the Father has given him, but should raise it up again at the last day, that is, the final day. The words "the last day" in the verse refer to the final day. Here it speaks of a promise of complete protection until the resurrection.

Jesus speaks in Capernaum, after the feeding of the multitude. He presents himself as the bread that came down from heaven. He explains that he did not come to do his own will, but the will of the Father. For this reason, whoever comes to him is not cast out. Some ask how the action of the Father and the human decision relate to each other; the text affirms both.

For today: if you trust in Christ, you can rest in the knowledge that your salvation does not depend on your own strength, but on his faithfulness. When you feel weak or afraid, remember that Jesus cares for what the Father has entrusted to him.
exp.17:2:
Judas arrived at the garden bringing a group of soldiers and guards sent by the chief priests and by the Pharisees. They carried lanterns, torches, and weapons. The word "band" refers to a group of soldiers; some believe it was a Roman unit, but its exact size is not known with certainty.

The one telling this is John, who was present. After praying with his disciples, Jesus was in a garden that Judas knew well. The religious leaders wanted to arrest him at night and in secret, and Judas showed them where to find him. John highlights that Jesus knew everything that was going to happen.

For today: when you face fear, injustice, or betrayal, remember that nothing takes Jesus by surprise. He walked calmly toward what was difficult, trusting the Father. You can give your situation to him in prayer and ask him for courage to act with peace.
exp.16:25:
Jesus says he has made the name of the Father known to them, that is, who God is, his character and his heart. And he promises to keep doing so. The word "declared" means making known, and the phrase "will declare it" means he will keep making it known. The purpose is that the same love the Father has for the Son would be in the disciples, and that Jesus would live in them.

These are the final words of Jesus' prayer, the night before his crucifixion. He speaks with the Father and prays for his disciples and for those who would believe through them. He ends by asking that they live within the love that unites the Father and the Son. Some understand that "will declare it" points to the work of the Holy Spirit and to the cross.

Today we can let Jesus keep showing us what God is like, as we read the Gospels with an open heart. When we know ourselves to be loved by the Father, we can love others with patience, even when it is hard.
exp.20:7:
The other disciples came to the shore in the little boat, dragging the net full of fish. They were close to land, about two hundred cubits away, which is roughly ninety meters, since one cubit measured close to half a meter. The "little ship" here is a small fishing boat.

John tells the scene after Jesus' resurrection. The disciples had fished all night without catching anything, and Jesus, from the shore, told them where to cast the net. Peter threw himself into the water to reach Jesus first, while the others did the most practical thing: they brought the boat and the catch.

For today: not all of us express our love for Jesus in the same way. Some go with impulse, like Peter; others serve with steadiness, faithfully doing what falls to them. Both ways are valuable before Him.
exp.7:37:
Jesus says that He speaks what He saw beside the Father, that is, He teaches what He knows of God firsthand. By contrast, his hearers do what they heard from "their father." Here "with" means "in the presence of" or "alongside."

Jesus speaks with Jews who believed in Him in a shallow way, yet who wanted to kill Him because his word had no place in their hearts. They relied on being descendants of Abraham. Jesus shows that what a person does reveals whom they are learning from. Shortly afterward he will tell them more plainly who that other father is.

For today: ask yourself where you are receiving your ideas and reactions. Set aside time to listen to Jesus' Word with humility, and let it, not your habits or your pride, guide your decisions.
exp.0:36:
The explanation says that two disciples of John the Baptist heard his words about Jesus and decided to follow him. "Heard him speak" means they listened to what he said, and "followed Jesus" means they began to walk after him. It was not only going behind someone; it was the beginning of drawing near to him to get to know him.

The one speaking is John the Baptist, who had just pointed to Jesus and said, "Behold the Lamb of God." John was not trying to gather followers for himself, but to point toward Jesus. That is why his disciples left him to go after the Teacher. The text does not name one of them here; the other is mentioned later as Andrew.

For today: when we listen sincerely to what is said about Jesus, we can take a step and draw near to him, by praying or reading the Gospels. And if we speak about him to others, our aim is to point to him, not to gain attention for ourselves.
exp.18:3:
Pilate goes out again before the crowd and tells them that he is bringing Jesus out to them so that they may know he finds no fault in him. "Crime" here means guilt or grounds for condemning him.

Pilate, the Roman governor, speaks before the Jewish leaders. He had already questioned Jesus and saw no reason to condemn him. He had ordered him to be flogged, and the soldiers mocked him with the crown of thorns. Some think Pilate hoped to stir the people's pity by showing him wounded. The text does not say this with certainty, but his declaration of innocence is clear.

Today, this verse reminds us that Jesus suffered though he was innocent. When we feel treated unjustly, we can turn to him, who understands that pain. It also invites us not to stop at knowing what is right, as Pilate did, but to act with courage according to the truth.
exp.16:10:
He says that Jesus is about to leave the world, but his disciples will remain in it. He is going toward the Father. For this reason he asks the holy Father to care for them through your name, that is, through his power and his character. His desire is that they be one, meaning that they live united, just as the Father and the Son are. Keep them means protecting them and keeping them steady.

Jesus speaks on the last night with his disciples, before being arrested. This is his prayer to the Father. He knows that he will go away and that they will face difficulties and pressure. He does not pray for the world in general, but for those whom the Father gave him. He asks for protection and unity, so that they will persevere after his departure.

For today: do not rely only on your own strength to stay firm. Trust that Jesus prays for his own. And seek unity with other believers: forgive, listen, and serve in your church.
exp.2:8:
Nicodemus answers Jesus with a question: "How can these things be?" It means: "In what way can that happen?" Nicodemus does not understand how someone can be born again.

Nicodemus was a Pharisee and a Jewish leader who went to see Jesus at night. Jesus had just told him that it is necessary to be born again, and that the Spirit works like the wind: it cannot be seen, but its effects are noticed. Nicodemus, a very learned man, is left puzzled. Jesus will respond to him with surprise because he was a teacher of Israel.

Today we can bring honest questions to God when we do not understand something. Nicodemus did not leave; he stayed and kept listening. But we must also be willing to trust what Jesus says, even when we cannot explain everything.
exp.11:49:
Jesus says that the Father's commandment is eternal life. For this reason, everything he teaches he says just as the Father charged him, without adding anything of his own. The word "commandment" here refers to the charge or message the Father gave him.

Jesus speaks at the end of his public ministry in Jerusalem, shortly before his arrest. Many had not believed in him despite his signs. He warns that rejecting his words has consequences, because they are the very words of God. With this he concludes his teaching addressed to the crowd.

Today we can take seriously what Jesus says, not merely admire him. A practical way to do this is to read a passage from the Gospels each day and ask ourselves: "What is Jesus asking of me today?" Then we can obey that concrete step, trusting that his words lead to life.
exp.14:6:
It says that if a person remains united to Jesus and his teachings live within them, they can ask for whatever they wish and it will be granted. The word "abide" means "remain" or "stay." The word "branches" refers to the branches of the vine. "Ask what ye will" means "ask whatever they want." The condition is twofold: to be in Christ and to have his word in us.

Jesus speaks to his disciples the night before his crucifixion. He compares himself to a vine and them to the branches, to teach them that they can bear fruit only if they remain connected to him. The verses that follow show that the purpose is to bear fruit and to glorify the Father.

For today: read the Bible regularly and speak with God sincerely. In this way, your desires will gradually align with those of Jesus, and your prayers will seek what pleases him, not only what suits you.
exp.11:46:
Jesus says that if anyone hears his words and does not believe them, he does not condemn that person. He explains that he did not come into this world to judge it, but to save it. The words "hear" and "believe" in the verse are the plain forms of what the explanation discusses, and "judge" here means condemn.

Jesus speaks near the end of his public ministry, in Jerusalem, addressing the crowd. He has just said that he is the light that came to bring people out of darkness. Yet many did not believe in him. His main purpose was to offer salvation. Even so, the following verse makes clear that whoever rejects his message will be confronted by that same word on the final day.

Today we can come to Jesus without fear, with our doubts and failures. He invites us; he does not crush us. And when we speak about him with others, let us do so with the same attitude: offering hope, not condemnation.
exp.19:29:
John says that Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples that were not written in this book. The word "signs" refers to miraculous deeds that point to who Jesus is. In other words, what John wrote is only a selection, not everything Jesus did.

The one speaking is John, the author of the Gospel, and he says this right after the scene with Thomas, when Jesus blesses those who believe without having seen. The verses that follow explain the purpose: John chose certain signs so that his readers would believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in his name.

For today: we do not need to see everything to trust in Jesus. What is already written is enough to believe. Read the Gospels calmly, and ask God to strengthen your faith with what he has already given us.
exp.17:10:
Jesus orders Peter to put away his sword. The word "cup" refers to the suffering that God assigned to him, like a cup that must be drunk to the very end. The "sheath" is the scabbard of the sword. Jesus asks with firmness: will I not accept what the Father has given me?

It is the night of the arrest in the garden. Peter, wanting to defend Jesus, wounds Malchus, a servant of the high priest. Jesus speaks like someone who already knows what is coming and accepts it out of obedience to the Father. In Gethsemane, according to the other Gospels, he had prayed about this very cup.

Many times we want to settle things by force, with anger or with our own means. Jesus invites us to trust the Father's plan, even when it is painful, and to respond with peace instead of violence.
exp.9:33:
Jesus asks them whether it is not written in their own law: "I said, Ye are gods." He is quoting Psalm 82:6. "Law" here means the whole of the Old Testament Scriptures, not only the first five books. "I have shown you" means "I have taught you" or "I have made you see."

Jesus is speaking with Jewish leaders who want to stone him for calling himself God. He answers with an argument from the lesser to the greater: if Scripture calls "gods" men who received the word of God, why is it blasphemy for the Son, sent by the Father, to say "I am the Son of God"? Interpreters disagree about who the psalm refers to: judges of Israel, or the people themselves.

For today: trust that the Bible has full authority. Before arguing, return to what God says and read it with care and humility.
exp.13:16:
Jesus calls the Holy Spirit "the Spirit of truth," the Comforter whom the Father will send. The world cannot receive him because it neither sees nor knows him, but the disciples do know him. "Ye" means "you," and "but" is the word that introduces the contrast here.

Jesus speaks to his disciples the night before his crucifixion. They are sad and confused because he is leaving. He promises them that they will not be left alone: the Spirit will be with them always. Some understand "he dwelleth with you" as referring to the Spirit's work while Jesus was still present with them, and "shall be in you" as referring to his dwelling in them after Pentecost.

For today: when you feel alone or without direction, remember that the Spirit of God lives in those who trust in Christ. Ask him each day to guide you into the truth and to give you peace to obey Jesus.
exp.16:13:
Jesus says that he has given his disciples the word of the Father, that is, his message and truth. For this reason the world has hated them, which means it rejected them and treated them with hostility. The reason is that they no longer belong to the world, just as Jesus also does not belong to it. "The world" here refers to a way of living that turns away from God.

Jesus is praying to the Father the night before his crucifixion. He speaks about his disciples, since he will soon leave them and knows they will face rejection. He asks that God keep them, not that he take them out of the world, but that he protect them from evil.

For today: if following Christ brings mockery or discomfort, do not be surprised. Remember that you belong to God, hold fast to his word, and respond with love, without bitterness.
exp.17:11:
A group of Roman soldiers, their commander, and the guards of the Jewish leaders seized Jesus and tied him up. The commander was the military leader of a group of soldiers. The guards here are the temple guards. The word for "arrested" means they took him into custody.

The one telling the story is John, a witness to what happened in the garden. Jesus had just stopped Peter, who defended his Master with a sword. Jesus did not run away or resist, because he accepted the path the Father had set before him, the cup of suffering he was to drink.

For today: when life becomes hard or unfair, we can trust that God is still at work, even where we do not understand it. Instead of responding with violence or anger, let us ask for strength to obey with peace, as Jesus did.
exp.2:6:
Jesus tells Nicodemus not to be surprised by what he has just said. "Marvel" here means to be amazed or astonished. "Ye must" means "it is necessary for you," that is, everyone needs to be born again, to have a new beginning that comes from God.

Jesus speaks at night with Nicodemus, a respected teacher among the Jews who approached him with curiosity and respect. Jesus explains that entering the kingdom of God does not depend on inheritance or human effort, but on a work of the Spirit. Nicodemus does not understand, and so Jesus uses the image of the wind. Some understand "water and Spirit" in different ways.

Today we can stop trusting in our own merits and ask God humbly for a new life, even though we do not understand everything.
exp.12:16:
Jesus says that knowing or understanding what he taught is not enough: true happiness comes from putting it into practice. The archaic phrasing of the verse is simply a way of saying "if you do them." The "these things" are the humble service he has just shown.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples at the last supper. He has just washed their feet, work normally done by a servant, to teach them that leadership in his kingdom means serving. He reminds them that no servant is greater than his master, so if the Teacher serves, they must serve too. Shortly afterward he announces Judas's betrayal.

For today: do not stop at just listening to sermons or reading the Bible. Choose one concrete act of humble service today, without seeking recognition, such as helping someone with an uncomfortable task, and do it with joy.
exp.3:1:
It says that Jesus himself did not baptize people. Those who did it were his disciples. It is a brief clarification, in parentheses, that corrects what the previous verse says: that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John. The words "went" and "necessary" are not in the verse, so I have left out the comment on them.

Here the narrator speaks, the apostle John. The Pharisees had heard that large crowds were following Jesus, and that could bring tension. John makes clear that the baptizing was carried out by the disciples under Jesus' authority. Why Jesus did not baptize personally is not explained in the text; some have read it as a sign that his main task was teaching and proclaiming the kingdom.

For today: God often works through ordinary people who serve in his name. You do not need to hold the first place for your service to have value. Serve faithfully and let the recognition go to Christ.
exp.1:2:
It says that during the wedding feast the wine ran out. Then Mary, the mother of Jesus, told him: "They have no wine." The phrase about the wine running low means it was already running out or had already run out. She does not ask him for anything directly; she simply presents the need.

Mary speaks, and she was at the wedding in Cana together with Jesus and his disciples. In that culture, running out of wine was a serious embarrassment for the hosts. Christians understand in different ways what Mary exactly expected: some think she was hinting at a miracle, others that she simply trusted Jesus would know what to do. The Bible does not make this clear.

We can bring our needs to Jesus with simplicity and trust, without giving him instructions on how to meet them. It is enough to tell him what is lacking and let him act in his own time and in his own way.
exp.18:18:
John tells us that Pilate had a sign written and placed it above Jesus' cross. It read: "Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews." The word "title" here means a sign announcing the reason for the sentence. "Nazareth" tells us he came from the town of Nazareth.

The one speaking is the narrator, John, who was close to these events. Pilate was the Roman governor and ordered the sign. The verses that follow say it was written in Hebrew, Greek and Latin, and that the chief priests objected. We do not know for certain what Pilate meant: it may have been mockery, pressure on the Jewish leaders, or simply routine. Even so, John stresses that the sign told the truth about Jesus.

Today we can recognize that Jesus is King, even when the world rejects him or mocks him. We can ask ourselves: do I really let him govern my day, my decisions and my relationships?
exp.11:31:
Jesus says that when he is "lifted up from the earth," he will draw "all" people to himself. "Lifted up" refers to being raised up on the cross. The word "traeré" means "I will draw."

Jesus speaks shortly before his death. He has just heard a voice from heaven, and he says the time of judgment for this world has arrived. The text itself makes clear that he was referring to the kind of death he would face: crucifixion. The crowd is confused, because they thought the Messiah would remain forever. Some understand "all" to mean people from every nation, not every single individual without exception; others understand it more broadly.

Today, when you feel far from God or unworthy, look to the cross. There Jesus shows his love and invites you to come close to him. Respond today with a simple prayer.
exp.18:10:
Jesus tells Pilate that his authority over him would be nothing if God had not allowed it. The words used here refer to the authority he had, and the phrase "from above" points to God. For that reason, the one who handed Jesus over bears a greater guilt, a heavier sin, than Pilate does.

Pilate was proud of his power to crucify or to release. Jesus, who had been silent before, answers calmly and reminds him that this power has a limit. It is commonly understood that the one who handed Jesus over is Caiaphas, though some think it also includes Judas or the Jewish leaders in general. Even so, Pilate remains responsible for what he decides.

Today we can rest in the fact that no human authority is outside God's control. When we face injustice, we can act with calm and confidence, knowing that God is still in control and that each person will answer for their own decisions.
exp.12:3:
He gets up from the supper table and takes off his outer garment. Then he takes a towel and ties it around his waist. The word "girded" here means he wrapped it tightly around his body, the way a servant would do to get a task done.

The writer, John, tells what happened at the last supper. Before this act, he points out that Jesus knew the Father had given him all things, that he had come from God and was going back to God. He also mentions that Judas was already planning to betray him. Even so, Jesus, with all his authority, chooses to do the work of a servant, washing feet, something usually done by the lowest-ranking servant.

For today: serving does not make us less. Someone who is secure in their identity in God can help with humility, even in simple tasks or ones nobody applauds, and do it with love.
exp.19:4:
He says that the other disciple, who arrived at Jesus' tomb first, bent down to look inside and saw the linen wrappings lying on the ground. But he did not go in. The explanation's word for the wrappings and its note about an old form are not needed here, since the verse already says "linen clothes" and "saw."

The one telling the story is John, who refers to himself as "the other disciple." Mary Magdalene had reported that the tomb was empty, and the two of them ran to check it for themselves. John does not explain why he did not go in; some think it was out of reverence or fear, but the text does not say so. Peter did go in right away.

For today: when faced with something we do not understand, we can approach it with respect and honesty, without being ashamed of our doubts. And, like Peter, we can take the step of going in to look for answers, trusting that God allows himself to be found.
exp.18:26:
From the cross, Jesus says to his beloved disciple: "Behold thy mother." From that very moment, that disciple took Mary into his home and cared for her as part of his family. The phrase "took her unto his own home" means that he welcomed her into his household. Traditionally this disciple is thought to be John, although the text does not give his name.

Jesus speaks in the middle of his suffering. Mary was standing beside the cross, and Jesus, before dying, is concerned for her. Since she was a widow, she probably needed someone to look after her. Jesus gives her a son in the faith, and to the disciple he gives a mother. Some also see here a sign of a new spiritual family, but the text presents it mainly as an act of care.

Today, this verse invites us to care in concrete ways for those near us, especially elderly relatives or people who are alone. Love is not only a feeling, but opening the door of our home and taking responsibility.
exp.13:17:
Jesus tells his disciples that he will not leave them like children without a father or anyone to care for them. The word "orphans" refers to people who have been abandoned, with no one to protect them. "I will come to you" is a promise of nearness and care.

Jesus speaks at the Last Supper, shortly before his arrest. The disciples are sad because he has told them he is going away. He promises them the Holy Spirit, the Comforter. About how the promise "I will come" is fulfilled, some think it refers to the resurrection, others to the coming of the Spirit, and others to his final return. It may include more than one of these.

For today: when you feel alone or lost, remember that Jesus promised to be with you. Speak to him in prayer and ask that his Spirit give you peace and guidance today.
exp.3:48:
Here a man in the king's service pleads with Jesus: "Sir, come down before my child dies." The "nobleman" here refers to an official of the royal court. The word "come down" means to go down, or to come with me, since Cana lay at a higher elevation than Capernaum.

The one speaking is a desperate father. His son is dying, and he has traveled to Jesus. Jesus had just said that people only believed when they saw signs. The man does not argue; he insists with urgency, though he seems to believe that Jesus must be present to heal. Jesus answers him: "Go, your son lives."

For today: we can bring our urgent needs to Jesus with sincerity. Even when we ask in our own way, He invites us to trust His word, even when we do not yet see the answer.
exp.0:16:
This verse compares two great gifts of God. The law was "given" through Moses, meaning God handed it to his people through him. By contrast, grace and truth "came into being" through Jesus Christ, that is, they arrived and became real in him. Grace is God's undeserved favor; truth is the reality of who God is.

The speaker is the apostle John, the author of the Gospel, in the introduction where he presents Jesus as the Word made flesh. He has just said that from the fullness of Christ we have received grace upon grace. He does not say the law is bad, but that Jesus shows God in a complete way, as the next verse explains.

Today we can stop trying to earn God's love through efforts and lists of merits. This week, when you fail, come to God honestly, trusting that his grace receives you and his truth guides you to change.
exp.4:37:
Jesus says that his hearers do not have the word of God remaining in them, meaning that it does not live or stay in their hearts. The proof is that they do not believe in the one God sent. The explanation of "ye" is that it means "you," and the one sent refers to Jesus himself.

Jesus is speaking with religious leaders from Jerusalem who were questioning him after he healed a man on the Sabbath. He presents witnesses: John the Baptist, his works, and the Father. Then he shows them that they know the Scriptures, but they do not let them reach the heart, because they reject the one they point to.

For today: it is not enough to read or know the Bible; we must let it lead us to Jesus. As you read, ask yourself: "What does it show me about Christ, and how do I respond today with trust and obedience?"
exp.7:43:
Here Jesus says that those who reject him follow the desires of the devil, not the desires of God. He calls him a murderer from the beginning and a liar, the origin of every lie.

Jesus speaks with certain Jews who were arguing with him in Jerusalem and boasted of being children of Abraham. But they would not accept his word and even wanted to kill him. Jesus shows them that being someone's child is seen in what a person does and loves. These are harsh words, aimed at those who hardened their hearts, not at an entire people.

For today: examine humbly which voices you follow. If there is lies, resentment or resistance to the truth in you, ask God to correct you, and seek to live in the truth of Jesus.
exp.17:17:
The explanation says that in the courtyard of the high priest's house there were servants and guards who had lit a fire of coals, because it was cold. Everyone was warming themselves by the fire, and Peter was there with them.

John, the narrator, tells what happened the night Jesus was arrested. Peter had already said he was not a disciple to the servant girl at the gate. Now he mixes in with the men who had arrested his Master. John shows Peter near the fire while Jesus is being questioned inside, and soon Peter will deny him again.

For today: sometimes, out of fear or for comfort, we draw near to fires that seem harmless but pull us away from Christ. Let us ask for courage to be faithful, and remember that Jesus forgave Peter and also restores us.
exp.9:36:
Jesus says that if He does not do the works of His Father, then they have no reason to believe Him. It is like putting Himself to the test before them. The phrase "do not believe me" is an older way of saying "do not believe me."

Jesus speaks in Jerusalem, during the Feast of Dedication, before Jewish leaders who accuse Him of blasphemy for calling Himself the Son of God. He does not ask them for blind faith. He invites them to look at His works: healings, signs, and acts of mercy that show the character and power of the Father. Then He adds that if they will not believe Him, they should at least believe the works.

Today we can believe with our eyes open. Christian faith is not closing the mind, but looking at who Jesus is and what He has done. It also challenges us: our works of love and kindness should point to the Father.
exp.8:4:
Jesus says that, as long as he is in the world, he is the light of the world. "As long as I am in the world" simply means "while I am in the world" or "for as long as I am in the world." "Light" speaks of what shows the way, drives away darkness, and lets us see clearly.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples, in front of a man who had been blind from birth. The disciples were asking who was to blame for the blindness, and Jesus answers that what matters is that God be revealed. He says that the work must be done while it is "the day," that is, while there is opportunity. Right away he heals the blind man, and so he shows by an action what he has just said.

For today: when you face suffering, your own or someone else's, instead of looking for someone to blame, come to Jesus and ask him for his light. And help others while you still have the opportunity.
exp.20:17:
Jesus tells Peter, very seriously, that when he was young he dressed himself and went wherever he wanted. But when he is old, he will stretch out his hands, someone else will tie him up or tie his clothes on him, and he will be carried where he does not want to go.

Jesus speaks with Peter after the resurrection, by the lake. He has just asked him three times whether he loves him and told him to take care of his sheep. The next verse explains that Jesus was pointing to the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God. Many understand this as a reference to his martyrdom, although the text gives no further details.

For today: loving Jesus can cost us something and does not always follow our plans. We can hand Him our future and follow Him with confidence, even when the road is hard.
exp.12:17:
Jesus says that his earlier words about the blessing of obedience do not include everyone. He knows the ones he has chosen, and he knows that one of them will betray him. This fulfills what Psalm 41:9 says: the one who shares the table with him "hath lifted up his heel against me," that is, turns against him, the way someone kicks another person. The word "hath lifted up" in the verse above is the phrase the explanation is describing.

Jesus speaks with his disciples at the Last Supper, after washing their feet. He teaches them to serve with humility. He warns them about Judas's betrayal before it happens, so that afterward, when they see it, they will believe in who he is and not lose heart.

For today: Jesus is not surprised when someone close to us fails or betrays us. If you suffer a wound like this, remember that he knows it well. Ask him to help you forgive and to keep serving with humility.
exp.13:11:
Jesus says with great seriousness that whoever believes in him will do the same works he does, and even greater works. The reason he gives is that he is going to the Father. The phrase "Verily, verily" means "truly, truly." The "works" are the deeds and signs that Jesus performed.

Jesus speaks to his disciples at the Last Supper, shortly before his death. They are sad and confused. He has just told them that the Father acts through him. Now he promises that this same power of the Father will continue working through them. Many understand "greater" to mean more extensive, since the message would reach more places and people, although some interpret it in other ways.
