For today: trust that God can use you in simple things, such as helping, praying, or sharing your faith, and ask him to do so in the name of Jesus.
exp.9:17:
Jesus says that no one takes his life from him by force: he gives it up by his own decision. He has the authority to give it and also the authority to take it up again, that is, to rise from the dead. The phrase "take it again" means "take it up once more." He also makes clear that he received this charge from his Father.

Jesus speaks in the discourse of the Good Shepherd. He has just said that he gives his life for the sheep, and that he will also bring in others who are not of that fold. Many understand this to refer to people from other nations, though some interpret it in other ways. His words divide his hearers: some think he has a demon, others do not.

For today: the cross was not an accident or a defeat for Jesus, but an act of freely chosen love. When you doubt whether God loves you, remember that Christ chose to give himself for you. Respond with gratitude, trusting him and placing your life in his care.
exp.5:52:
Jesus says with great seriousness ("Verily, verily") that whoever does not eat his flesh and drink his blood has no life in himself. The words "Verily, verily" are the King James phrase rendered as "Verily, verily, I say unto you," so this stress is shown in the verse itself.

Jesus speaks in Capernaum, after multiplying the loaves. He has just said that he is the bread from heaven, and the Jews are scandalized when they hear it. Many Christians understand these words as a picture of believing in him and depending on his sacrifice. Others relate them to the Lord's Supper, and churches interpret them in different ways.

Just as the body needs food every day, our spiritual life needs Christ. Today you can seek him in prayer and in his Word, trusting in what he did for you on the cross.
exp.13:15:
Jesus promises that he will pray to the Father, and the Father will send "another Comforter" to be with the disciples forever. "I will pray" means I will ask; "will give you" means will give to you; "you" refers to all of you. The Greek word (Paraclete) can be translated Comforter, Helper, or Advocate. "Another" suggests someone like Jesus.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples at the Last Supper, shortly before his arrest. They are sad and confused because he has told them that he is going away. So he assures them that they will not be left alone: the Holy Spirit will be with them, and the verse before connects love for Jesus with obeying him.

For today: when you feel alone or without strength, remember that, according to this promise, God does not leave you without help. Ask the Spirit to guide you, comfort you, and help you live what Jesus taught, beginning with one simple decision of obedience today.
exp.17:18:
Here the high priest means the chief priest. He questions Jesus about two things: who was following him and what he was teaching.

This takes place on the night Jesus was arrested. It is not known for certain whether the questioner is Annas or Caiaphas, and scholars understand this in different ways. Meanwhile, outside, Peter denies knowing Jesus. The priest looks for an accusation, but Jesus answers that his teaching was public and that he has nothing to hide.

Today we can learn from Jesus' openness: to live our faith with sincerity, without hiding it out of fear, so that anyone who observes us sees consistency between what we say and what we do.
exp.14:16:
Jesus says that his command is that we love one another. The phrase "these things I command" means "I order you," and "one another" refers to everyone among them, each toward the other. It is not a suggestion but the center of what He asks of his followers.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the night before his crucifixion, according to John's account. He has just called them friends, not servants, and reminded them that He chose them to bear fruit. Right after this he warns them that the world will reject them. For that reason, love among them would be their support and their distinguishing mark.

Today you can apply this by looking for a concrete act of love toward someone in your church, family, or workplace whom you find difficult: a phone call, forgiveness, or a practical help, without expecting anything in return.
exp.4:40:
Jesus says that he does not seek or accept applause, praise, or honor that comes from people. "Glory" here means honor, recognition, or fame. He does not need it in order to know who he is.

Jesus is speaking with some religious leaders who were questioning him after he healed a man on the Sabbath. He had already pointed them to several witnesses about himself. He makes clear that he is not speaking to them in order to win their approval. His aim is that they come to him and have life. The text that follows shows that they were in fact seeking human honor, and that is why they found it hard to believe.

Today we can ask ourselves whom we want to please. If we seek above all the approval of people, it will be hard for us to be faithful. Let us do what is right with humility, seeking to please God, even when no one applauds us.
exp.18:20:
The chief priests of the Jews, the men in charge of the temple, ask Pilate to change the sign on the cross. They do not want it to say "King of the Jews," but that Jesus claimed to be that king.

The people speaking are the leading priests of the Jews. It bothered them that the sign presented Jesus as their king, as if they accepted it. Pilate had already put the sign up, and in the next verse he refuses to change it. Scholars debate whether he did this to mock them, out of pride, or out of weariness; the text does not say. Even so, the sign stated a truth, and it was written in three languages.

For today: we may try to correct the truth when it makes us uncomfortable, but God sometimes leaves it written in plain view for everyone to see. Let us ask him for humility to accept what Jesus is, even when it does not fit what we expected.
exp.2:23:
This verse clarifies a point of timing: when Jesus and John were baptizing at the same time, John had not yet been put in prison. "Prison" is the jail. That is, John's ministry was still active.

Here the writer of the Gospel, John the apostle, speaks and adds a note for the reader. The other Gospels record the imprisonment of John the Baptist and begin Jesus' public work in Galilee after that. This explanation shows that there was a time when the two ministries overlapped. That prepares the discussion that follows between John's disciples and the Jews.

For today: God gives each person a time and a task. Let us serve faithfully while we have our moment, without competing with others, and let us rejoice when God makes someone else's work grow.
exp.11:3:
This verse introduces Judas Iscariot, one of the twelve disciples, and says of him that he was "Simon's son" and that he "would betray" Jesus, that is, that he would hand Jesus over. "Hand over" here means to deliver Jesus into the hands of his enemies. The phrase about betrayal announces what would happen later.

We are at a dinner in Bethany, where Mary has just anointed Jesus' feet with very expensive perfume. In the middle of that act of love, Judas speaks up to criticize it. John, telling the story, quickly makes clear that Judas did not truly care about the poor, but was taking money from the common purse.

For today: let us take care that our words of "good sense" do not hide selfish interests. Let us ask God for a sincere heart, one that knows how to value the generous devotion of others toward Jesus without criticizing it out of envy.
exp.7:33:
Jesus says this with great seriousness: "Verily, verily, I say unto you." In plain terms, he is saying, "I assure you of the truth." Whoever commits sin, or lives in it as a habit, is a servant, that is, a slave of sin. "Committeth sin" suggests a constant practice, not just an occasional slip.

Jesus is speaking with some Jews who believed in him, but they were offended when he told them that the truth would set them free. They answered that they were descendants of Abraham and had never been slaves to anyone. Jesus shows them that there is a deeper bondage than political oppression: the bondage of sin. He then explains that only the Son can truly set someone free.

Today, if there is a habit that dominates you and you cannot give it up, do not hide it or make excuses for it. Acknowledge it before God, ask Jesus to set you free, and seek the support of trustworthy brothers and sisters.
exp.10:32:
This verse tells us that Jesus saw Mary weeping, and the Jews who had come with her weeping too. Then he was deeply moved in his spirit and troubled. The words "groaned" and "was troubled" refer to a very deep emotion. The original Greek verb can also suggest anger or indignation, and scholars understand it in different ways: as deep sorrow, as anger at death, or as both together.

This happens after Lazarus has already died. Mary has just fallen at Jesus' feet, telling him that if he had been there, her brother would not have died. The narrator, John, shows us Jesus' inner reaction to so much grief.

For today: Jesus does not stay distant from our suffering. You can bring him your sadness with confidence, knowing that he has compassion. And when someone weeps beside you, stay with them with tenderness, without rushing them and without easy answers.
exp.0:30:
John the Baptist says that he did not know Jesus, that is, he had not recognized him as the Messiah. He explains that his reason for coming to baptize with water was so that Jesus would be shown to all the people of Israel.

The speaker is John the Baptist, giving public testimony about Jesus a day after calling him the Lamb of God. Scholars understand his not knowing him in various ways: he may not have known for certain that Jesus was the Messiah until he saw the sign of the Spirit, as the following verse explains. His task was to prepare the way, not to be the center.

Today we can ask ourselves whether what we do and say helps others come to know Jesus, or only draws attention to ourselves. Like John, we can serve with humility, pointing to Christ.
exp.3:30:
The explanation says that, while the people of the town were coming toward Jesus, the disciples kept urging him earnestly to eat. The word "prayed" means they were asking him again and again, not just once. The word "Master" is a respectful way of addressing him.

The disciples had gone into the town to buy food and had come back. Jesus was tired and thirsty beside the well, and he had just spoken with the Samaritan woman. They were concerned for his body, which is natural and kind, but they did not yet understand what was happening: a woman was bringing her town to Jesus. He will answer them with something deeper.

For today: caring for the needs of others is good, but let us not allow what is urgent to make us lose sight of what God is doing. Let us ask for eyes to see the people who are coming to Jesus.
exp.6:38:
This verse is the Gospel writer John's own explanation. He says that when Jesus spoke of "rivers of living water," he meant the Holy Spirit, which those who believed in him would receive. He clarifies that the Spirit "had not yet come," that is, had not yet been given in the full way that would come later. "Glorified" refers to Jesus' death, resurrection, and exaltation.

Jesus spoke on the last day of the Feast of Tabernacles, probably a very solemn moment, and offered to satisfy the spiritual thirst of whoever trusted in him. John adds this note so that his readers would understand the meaning of those words. After this, the crowd was divided: some thought Jesus was the Prophet, others that he was the Christ.

Today we can come to Jesus with our inner thirst: weariness, emptiness, or questions. Whoever believes in him receives the Spirit, who gives life and strength to love and serve others.
exp.8:31:
It says that since the beginning of time it had never been heard that anyone gave sight to a man born blind. The phrase "since the world began" means "since the beginning of the world" or "since forever," and "was it heard" is "has it ever been heard," while "opened" is "opened."

The man Jesus healed is the one speaking. The religious leaders were questioning him because Jesus had healed him on the Sabbath, and they doubted that Jesus came from God. The man, with simple reasoning, shows them that such a miracle points to God. They do not accept this and throw him out of the synagogue.

For today: when God works in your life, tell honestly what you have lived through, even if others do not understand or mock you. Your simple testimony can be steady, and God looks after those who are faithful to him.
exp.8:30:
Here the verse says that God does not listen to sinners, meaning those who live in rebellion against Him. Instead, He listens to the person who has reverence for God (who respects and honors Him) and does His will. The phrase that the verse renders as "him he heareth" means "this is the one He listens to."

The speaker is the man who had been born blind and whom Jesus healed. The religious leaders question him and say that Jesus is a sinner. He reasons simply: if Jesus opened his eyes, something that had never been heard of, then God must be with Him. Note: his statement reflects the common belief of his time, not a rule that explains every prayer.

For today: draw near to God with humility and obedience, not with pride. And when God has worked in your life, tell with courage what you have experienced, even if others do not understand it.
exp.2:9:
Jesus answers Nicodemus with a surprising question: "Are you a teacher of Israel, and yet you do not know this?" Jesus points out that Nicodemus, being a recognized teacher, should understand something about the new birth of the Spirit.

Nicodemus was a Pharisee and a Jewish leader who came to Jesus by night. He had just asked, "How can these things be?" Jesus does not mock him, but invites him to see that knowing the Scriptures is not enough; God must open the heart. Some think Jesus had in mind Old Testament promises about a new heart, though the text does not spell this out here.

For today: even if we know a great deal about the Bible, we need humility to keep learning. Let us ask God to fill not only our minds but to transform our hearts.
exp.5:51:
The explanation says that the Jews who were listening to Jesus began to argue among themselves. They could not understand how Jesus could give them his flesh to eat. "Strove" means that they argued with force.

Jesus had just said that he is the living bread that came down from heaven, and that this bread is his flesh, given for the life of the world. The people took his words literally and were scandalized. Jesus did not correct them by softening what he had said; instead he insisted that eternal life comes from him. Many Christians understand this as a picture of believing in Christ and receiving his sacrifice; others also connect it with the Lord's Supper.

Today, when something about Jesus does not sit well with us, we can ask him humbly instead of arguing or walking away. He invites us to trust and to keep listening.
exp.20:8:
He says that, when they stepped out of the boat and came ashore, the disciples found a fire of coals already prepared, with a fish on it and also bread. The word "fire of coals" refers to glowing embers. The phrase "came ashore" means reaching the shore. Nobody tells them who prepared it, but the reader understands that it was Jesus.

The narrator is John, who remembers this appearance of the risen Jesus by the lake of Tiberias. The disciples had spent the night fishing without success, until a man on the shore told them where to cast the net. Now, tired and wet, they are greeted with a breakfast. Some see here a gesture of care and closeness; the text does not explain more.

For today: Jesus goes ahead of our needs. When you feel tired or see no results, remember that He is already waiting for you with care, and you can come to Him with confidence.
exp.3:9:
Jesus tells the woman that if she knew what gift God offers, and who it is that is asking her for water, she would have asked him, and he would have given her living water.

Jesus is tired, sitting by the well at Sychar, and he speaks with a Samaritan woman. Jews and Samaritans kept away from each other, but Jesus breaks through that barrier. She understands that he is talking about the water in the well; Jesus is speaking of something deeper. Many understand that he is referring to the new life that the Spirit gives, something he himself explains later in the Gospel.

For today: Jesus not only asks, he also offers. Think about what you look for to fill your emptiness, and take a moment to ask Jesus to give you what truly satisfies.
exp.0:3:
It says that in the Word, that is, in Jesus Christ, was life. He does not merely have life; he is the source of all life. And that life is also "the light of men": what allows us to see the truth, know God, and find the way.

Here John the apostle speaks as he begins his Gospel. He has already said that the Word was with God and that through him all things were made. Now he explains that the very one who created is the one who gives life and light. Later he will mention that the darkness did not comprehend him, and he will introduce John the Baptist. Some understand "life" as physical and spiritual life at once.

For today: if you feel lost or without direction, draw near to Jesus in prayer and read his words in the Gospels. Ask him to give you light to make decisions and to give you new life where you feel weary today.
exp.15:9:
Jesus says that the Holy Spirit will show the world what true righteousness is. The reason is that Jesus is going to the Father, and his disciples will no longer see him. To convict means to convince, to make clear that someone is wrong. Righteousness is what is right and approved by God.

Jesus speaks in the upper room, the night before his crucifixion, preparing his disciples for his departure. They are sad, and he promises them the Spirit as Counselor. Many understand that his return to the Father confirms that he was the Righteous One, approved by God, even though the world condemned him. Others explain it somewhat differently, but almost all agree on this central idea.

When we feel disoriented or judged by the world, we can trust that Jesus is the Righteous One and that the Spirit guides us. Let us ask him to teach us to live uprightly, not for appearance, but following the example of Christ.
exp.5:63:
Jesus says that among those who were listening to him there were some who did not believe. The text makes clear that he knew this from the start, that is, from the beginning of his dealings with them. He also knew who would hand him over, referring to Judas. Handing him over means betraying him, putting him into the hands of his enemies.

Jesus is speaking in Capernaum, after saying that he is the bread of life. His words were hard, and many were offended. He explains that his words are spirit and life, and that believing is something the Father grants. Christians understand in different ways how God's grace and human choice relate to each other, but all of them see here that Jesus knows the heart.

For today: we do not need to pretend before Jesus. We can tell him our doubts honestly and ask him, "I believe; help my unbelief." He receives us just as we are.
exp.10:27:
Martha, after speaking with Jesus and confessing her faith, went away and quietly called her sister Mary. She told her that the Teacher had come and was calling for her. Some older words: "went away" means she left, "called secretly" means she did it apart, in private, and "Teacher" refers to Jesus as the one who teaches.

The speaker is Martha, sister of Mary and Lazarus, whose brother had died four days earlier. Jesus was still outside the village. The text does not explain why Martha spoke in secret; some think she wanted to avoid the attention of those comforting the family, but this is an interpretation. What is clear is that Jesus was calling Mary.

For today: when Jesus comforts you in the midst of pain, share that invitation with someone who is suffering. Sometimes a simple, caring sentence is enough: "Jesus is here and calling for you."
exp.11:9:
This verse says that the chief priests came to an agreement, or made plans, to put Lazarus to death as well. The chief priests were the most important priests, and the word "consulted" means they talked it over among themselves to decide it.

Here it is not Jesus speaking; it is the narrator, John, who is telling what was happening. Jesus had raised Lazarus from the dead, and because of this many people were going to see him and were believing in Jesus. The religious leaders already wanted to kill Jesus, and now they saw Lazarus as another threat to their authority. Their problem was not a lack of evidence, but that they did not want to accept what God was doing.

For today: sometimes the truth makes us uncomfortable because it changes the way we live. Let us ask God for a humble heart, one that prefers to obey him rather than defend our comfort or our pride.
exp.12:25:
Jesus answers the beloved disciple's question: the one who betrays him will be the one to whom he gives the dipped bread. Then he dips the bread in the dish and gives it to Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon.

We are at the Last Supper. Jesus has just said that one of the twelve would hand him over, and Peter asked to know who it was. Giving a morsel to a guest was a gesture of closeness and friendship. The verses that follow show that the others did not understand what was happening. Some think Jesus was offering Judas one last sign of love.

Jesus knew what Judas would do and still treated him with kindness. Today we can learn to respond with gentleness even to someone who hurts us, without giving up telling the truth, and trust that God is still at work even in the middle of betrayal.
exp.4:10:
The explanation says that the healed man answered the Jewish leaders who criticized him for carrying his mat on the Sabbath. His defense is simple: the one who had the power to heal him is the one who gave him the command.

The man speaking had been ill for thirty-eight years beside the pool of Bethesda. The Jewish leaders confront him because they understood that carrying a load on the Sabbath broke the law. He did not yet know who Jesus was, but he was clear about what he had experienced: he was healed and he received a command. Some interpret that he was trying to avoid blame; others, that he is simply saying what he knows.

For today: when someone questions your faith, you do not need to have all the answers. You can simply tell what God has done in your life, and keep obeying him with confidence.
exp.17:3:
He says that Jesus already knew everything that was going to happen to him: the arrest, the trial, and the cross. Even so, he did not hide or run away. He stepped forward and asked the crowd, "Whom seek ye?" That is, "Whom are you looking for?"

The one speaking is Jesus, in the garden across the Kidron brook, at night. Judas arrived with soldiers and temple guards, armed and carrying lights. John shows that Jesus was not caught off guard or overpowered: he gave up his life willingly, as he had said earlier (John 10:18).

For today: when difficult moments come that we cannot avoid, we can face them with confidence, knowing that God is still in control. Jesus teaches us to face things calmly and to surrender ourselves to the Father's will.
exp.5:47:
Jesus says that he is the bread of life. Bread was the basic food of everyday life, so he uses this simple image to say that he gives what the soul needs in order to truly live. The phrase "bread of life" means bread that gives life, not just bread that fills the stomach.

Jesus speaks in the synagogue at Capernaum, after feeding a crowd with bread. The people were looking for him because of the food, and he invites them to look beyond it. He reminds them of the manna their ancestors ate in the desert, which sustained them for a time but did not save them from death. Jesus presents himself as the food that gives eternal life to whoever believes in him.

Just as you cannot live without eating, the heart cannot live without God. Today, before rushing into your tasks, take a few minutes to read a passage from the Gospels and pray, seeking in Jesus your daily strength.
exp.15:1:
Jesus says that his disciples will be put out of the synagogues, that is, out of the places where the Jews gathered to worship and pray. And a time will come when whoever kills them will think he is offering service to God.

Jesus speaks in the upper room, the night before his crucifixion. He wants to prepare his friends for the rejection that is coming, so that they will not be caught off guard and fall away in their faith. He explains that their persecutors will act this way because they do not know the Father or him. He warns them so that, when it happens, they will remember that he had already said it.

Today we can learn that opposition does not mean God has abandoned us. If we suffer rejection for following Christ, let us trust his word and respond with love, without repaying evil with evil.
exp.5:10:
This verse tells how Jesus takes the five loaves, gives thanks to God, and hands them out to the disciples. They distribute them to the people who were sitting on the grass. He does the same with the fish, and everyone eats as much as they wanted.

John tells this miracle when a large crowd was following Jesus. Earlier, Andrew had pointed out that a boy had only five barley loaves and two small fish, and that this seemed like very little. Jesus tells the people to sit down and, before distributing the food, gives thanks. Afterward, twelve baskets are left over.

For today: What little we have, placed with gratitude in the hands of Jesus, can be a great blessing. Today you can thank God for what you have and offer it to serve others, even if it seems insufficient to you.
exp.8:27:
It says that the Pharisees, angered by the question of the man who had been healed, insulted him. The word "reviled" means to treat someone with mockery and contempt. They told him that he was a disciple of Jesus, while they presented themselves as followers of Moses.

It refers to a group of religious leaders who were questioning the man born blind for a second time. He had just answered them with irony, asking whether they too wanted to follow Jesus. Instead of considering the miracle, they felt attacked and resorted to insults and to their religious authority.

When a truth makes us uncomfortable, it is easy to defend ourselves with pride or with attacks. Today we can ask God for a humble heart, willing to acknowledge what He does, even when it does not fit what we expected.
exp.0:37:
Jesus turns around and sees that two men are following him. He asks them a simple question: "What seek ye?" They do not answer his question directly. Instead, they call him "Rabbi," which means Master, and ask where he is staying.

John the Baptist had just pointed to Jesus as the Lamb of God, and that is why these two disciples of John began to follow him. Jesus speaks first, not to rebuke them, but to invite them to express their desire. Their question about where he lives shows that they want to spend time with him and get to know him closely.

For today: Jesus also asks you what you are seeking. Before asking him for things, tell him honestly what is in your heart, and seek to be with him in prayer and in his Word. He invites you: "Come and see."
exp.4:42:
Jesus says he came with the authority of his Father, that is, sent by God and representing him, but his hearers do not accept him. On the other hand, if someone came speaking only in his own name, on his own authority, they would receive that person. The second sentence of that comment, explaining the verb forms, is removed because those forms do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

Jesus speaks with some Jewish leaders in Jerusalem, after healing a man on the Sabbath. He explains to them that his works and the Scriptures bear witness to him. He tells them that they do not have the love of God in them, and that for this reason they reject him. Some think he is referring to false messiahs in general; the text gives no name.

Today we can ask ourselves what weight we give: to what pleases people or to what comes from God. Before following any voice, it is wise to compare it with Jesus and his Word.
exp.15:3:
Jesus says that he has warned them about these things so that, when the difficult hour comes, they will remember that he had already told them. He explains that he did not mention these things before because he was with them.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the night before his crucifixion. He has just announced rejection and persecution. While he was present, he himself watched over them and bore the rejection. Now that he is going to the Father, he warns them so that the trial will not catch them by surprise or lead them to doubt him. Shortly afterward he promises them the Holy Spirit as their helper.

Today, God does not promise a life without difficulty, but he warns us honestly. When moments of rejection or pain come, we can remember his words and trust that he is still with us. Keeping Scripture in the heart prepares us for those days.
exp.8:19:
The parents of the man who was healed answer the authorities with what they do know: that this is their son and that he was born blind.

The Jewish leaders doubted the miracle and called the parents in to investigate. The parents confirm two facts that they are sure of, but in the verses that follow they avoid explaining how their son can now see, because they feared being put out of the synagogue. It was a very strong social and religious pressure, and that is why they speak with caution.

Today we can learn to say honestly what we know and no more. But this also invites us to ask ourselves whether the fear of what others think silences us when we should be giving testimony to what God has done.
exp.1:15:
Jesus tells the people selling doves to take their cages out of there. He asks them not to turn his Father's house into a "market house," that is, into a place of business. Some old words: the word for "to" is written in an older form, "take these things hence" means "take these things out," and "make not" means "do not make."

He speaks this at the beginning of his ministry, during the Passover in Jerusalem. Animals were sold in the temple for the sacrifices, and money was exchanged there. Doves were the offering of the poorest people. Jesus calls the temple "my Father's house," and in doing so he speaks of a unique relationship with God. His disciples later remembered Psalm 69:9, about zeal for the house of God.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our time with God, at church or alone, has been filled with interests, worries, or profits. Let us ask the Lord to help us give Him first place with a sincere heart.
exp.8:7:
This verse tells us that the man's neighbours, and others who had seen him before, were puzzled. They were asking whether this was the same man who used to sit and beg. "Begged" here means that he asked people in the street for money or help.

The speakers are people who knew the man. Jesus had just healed him, and the change was so great that some doubted it was really him. This sets up the next part of the story: the man himself will say that it is he, and he will have to explain how he was healed.

When God changes a life, others notice, sometimes with amazement and even with doubts. We can respond as this man did: plainly, honestly telling what Jesus has done in us, without embellishing or hiding anything.
exp.12:26:
It says that, after Judas received the dipped bread, Satan entered into him. Then Jesus told him to do quickly what he was about to do. The "sop" is the piece of bread, and "quickly" means "as fast as possible."

Jesus is eating supper with his disciples before his arrest. He had just pointed out Judas by giving him that bread, and he knew what Judas was planning. His words are not a command to do evil, but a sign that Jesus was in control and was moving toward the cross of his own free will. The others did not understand what was happening.

For today: evil can come very close to us, even in religious places. Guard your heart, do not harden your conscience, and remember that even in the worst betrayals, God still reigns and fulfills his purpose of love.
exp.11:36:
It says that Jesus did many signs, that is, miracles that showed the power of God, and he did them in front of the people. Even so, many did not believe in him. The word "though" in the verse above means "but" or "yet", and the phrase shows a sad contrast: so much evidence in plain sight, and so little faith.

Here John, the writer of the Gospel, is speaking. He has just told how Jesus invited the people to believe in the light while they still had it. With this verse, John sums up the reaction of many and prepares the quotation from Isaiah, which explains that this unbelief had already been foretold. Some did believe, but not the majority.

For today: seeing signs does not always produce faith; an open heart is needed. Today we can ask God for humility so that we do not harden ourselves, and to respond with trust when he speaks to us.
exp.17:20:
Jesus answers the high priest with a question: "Why do you question me?" He suggests that they should instead ask those who heard him teach, because they know well what he said.

Jesus is being questioned at night by Annas, before he is taken to Caiaphas. The high priest wanted to find some charge against him. Jesus points out that his teaching was public and that he had nothing to hide. According to Jewish law, an accused person was not to be forced to testify against himself, and witnesses were sought. Many scholars see here Jesus asking for a fair trial.

Today, we can live in such a way that our faith and our words are transparent. And when we are judged unjustly, we can respond with calm and truth, without fear or revenge.
exp.17:21:
He says that, after Jesus spoke, one of the guards or servants standing nearby struck him, that is, hit him on the face with the palm of his hand. He rebuked him, saying, "Answerest thou the high priest so?" The word "high priest" here is the usual term for the chief priest.

Jesus is being questioned at night, in the house of Annas, who was the high priest or had great influence. They asked him about his disciples and his teaching. Jesus answered that he had always spoken openly and that they could ask those who had heard him. The guard reacted with violence, wanting to defend the authority of the priest. Jesus then asked for a concrete proof of the supposed wrong.

For today: when we are treated unjustly, we can respond with calm and truth, without returning blow for blow. Jesus did not stay silent in the face of injustice, but he also did not let himself be carried away by anger.
exp.4:17:
This verse says that the Jewish leaders wanted to kill Jesus even more than before. They had two reasons: in their view, Jesus was breaking the Sabbath (that is, not keeping the day of rest), and he was also calling God his own Father, in a way that made him equal with God. The verse's wording "sought the more" means that they kept looking for a way to do it.

Here the writer of the gospel, John, is speaking. Jesus had just healed a sick man on the Sabbath and had answered: "My Father worketh hitherto, and I work". The Jews understood that Jesus was claiming a unique unity with God, and that is why they became even more angry. The verses that follow show that Jesus did not deny this, but explained his unity with the Father.

For today: Jesus did not back down in the face of rejection. We can come to him with confidence, believing that his work and his love perfectly reflect the heart of the Father.
exp.14:10:
Jesus says that he has spoken these things to them so that his joy may be in them and that their joy may be complete, that is, whole and full. The word for "you" in this verse is an older way of saying the plural "you," which the King James Version renders simply as "you."

Jesus speaks on the night before his crucifixion, in his farewell discourse to his disciples. He has just spoken about remaining in his love and keeping his commandments, as he keeps the Father's. Here he makes clear that his teaching is not meant to burden them, but to give them joy. Right after this, he asks them to love one another.

For today: instead of seeing obedience to Christ as a burden, take a few minutes each day to read a passage from the Gospels and ask him to fill you with his joy. That joy grows as we remain close to him and love those around us.
exp.14:8:
Jesus says that the love he has for his disciples is equal to the love the Father has for him. He invites them to remain in that love, that is, to stay, abide, and live in it. The explanation's note about old wording is removed here, since the reader's verse uses the modern "continue" and "love" directly.

Jesus speaks at the Last Supper, shortly before going to the cross. He has just used the image of the vine and the branches: his disciples must remain joined to him to bear fruit. Now he assures them that this bond is sustained by love. The verses that follow explain that obeying him is the way to remain in that love.

For today: when you feel tired or unworthy, remember that Christ has already loved you. Set aside a few minutes each day to pray and read his Word, not to earn his love, but to live close to him.
exp.11:11:
This verse tells that on the next day, many people who had come to Jerusalem for the feast (the Passover) heard that Jesus was coming toward the city. The word "Jerusalem" refers to Jerusalem, and the phrase "when they heard" means that the news reached them. The verse is incomplete, since the action continues into the next one.

The one telling the account is John, the apostle. Earlier, the religious leaders had wanted to kill Lazarus, because his being raised was leading many to believe in Jesus. So the crowd that goes out to receive him stands in contrast with the rejection of these leaders. John shows that the people responded when they heard the news about Jesus.

For today: When we hear about Jesus, we can respond with sincere interest. Hearing news about Him is not enough; we can draw near, seek Him, and receive Him with gratitude, even when others around us reject Him.
exp.10:52:
This verse says that, from the day Caiaphas spoke, the Jewish leaders agreed together to put Jesus to death. The phrase "took counsel together" means that they gathered to plan and decide. "Put him to death" means taking away his life.

The narrator, John, tells what happened after Jesus raised Lazarus. Many believed, and the leaders feared losing their power. Caiaphas, the high priest, said that it was better for one man to die for the people. John explains that, without knowing it, those words foretold that Jesus would die to save and gather together the children of God.

For today: the truth can make us uncomfortable and make us react with fear or with pride. Let us ask God for a humble heart to receive what He shows us, even when it changes our plans.
exp.3:31:
Jesus tells his disciples that he has a food they do not know about. "Food" here is what a person eats to sustain themselves. The phrase "you do not know" is an older way of saying it, and Jesus is speaking of something deeper than bread.

Jesus is tired and sits by the well in Samaria. His disciples had gone to buy food and, when they return, they find him speaking with a Samaritan woman. She has just gone into the town to tell what she has experienced. The disciples think of physical food, but Jesus is thinking of the mission his Father gave him. That is why he later explains that his food is to do the will of God.

For today: just as the body needs bread, the heart needs purpose. When we do what God asks of us, even when we are tired, he gives us strength and joy that nothing else can give.
exp.2:27:
John the Baptist reminds his disciples of something they themselves heard: he clearly said that he was not the Christ, that is, the Messiah. He said his role was to be "sent before him," that is, to prepare the way.

Ye yourselves bear me witness, that I said, I am not the Christ, but that I am sent before him.

His disciples were worried because Jesus was baptizing and people were going to him. John feels no jealousy. He responds with humility, remembering that his mission was always to point to Jesus, not to attract followers to himself. Shortly afterward he compares Jesus to the bridegroom and himself to the friend who rejoices for him.

For today: serve God without seeking applause or comparisons. If others grow or receive recognition, rejoice. Ask yourself whether your life points toward Jesus and not toward yourself.
exp.10:9:
It says that whoever walks at night stumbles, because the light is not in him. Jesus uses the image of walking in the dark: without light, a person cannot see the way and falls.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples, who were afraid to return to Judea because the Jews there had wanted to stone him. He answers that the day has twelve hours: as long as his appointed time has not yet come, he can walk safely. Many understand that the "light" refers to God's will that guides him, although some see it as a reference to Jesus himself. He is going to wake Lazarus.

For today: before deciding something important, seek God's guidance in prayer and in his Word. Walking in his light gives us security, even when the path seems risky.
exp.1:4:
What it says: Mary speaks to the servants at the wedding feast. She tells them to do whatever Jesus tells them. The servants are the attendants or helpers who serve the guests.

Context: We are at the wedding in Cana. The wine has run out, and Mary tells Jesus. He answers that his time has not yet come, which is understood in different ways, but points to his mission and to the cross. Mary does not argue: she trusts him and prepares the servants to obey him, without knowing what he will ask.

For today: Trusting Jesus includes obeying him even when we do not understand the whole plan. If today you feel a need, bring it to him simply, and then pay attention to what he asks of you, even if it seems small, like filling jars with water.
exp.9:16:
Jesus says that the Father loves him because he freely gives up his life, with the purpose of taking it back afterward. Giving up his life means laying it down for others. Taking it again means rising from the dead.

Jesus speaks in the discourse of the Good Shepherd. He presents himself as the shepherd who cares for his sheep to the point of giving his life for them, and he mentions other sheep who are not from Israel. He then makes clear that no one takes his life from him by force: he lays it down in obedience to the Father. His words caused division among the Jews who heard him.

For today: we can rest in the fact that Christ's love was not an accident, but a free giving of himself for us. This invites us to answer him with confidence and to love others generously, even when it costs us.
exp.6:2:
Jesus' brothers tell him to leave Galilee and head to Judea. There, they say, his disciples will also be able to see the works he does. The quoted phrases in the source wording are not part of the verse here, so the sentence explaining them is removed.

The brothers of Jesus are speaking. The Feast of Tabernacles is approaching, when many people went up to Jerusalem. They suggest that he show himself in public. The text makes clear that they did not yet believe in him, so their advice did not come from faith. Jesus was staying in Galilee because people in Judea wanted to kill him. Some understand their advice as mockery or pressure, and others as a simple idea that was poorly aimed. The text does not give details.

Today, we sometimes receive advice from people close to us that sounds logical but does not understand God's plan. Before acting, let us pray and seek God's guidance, not just the opinion of others.
exp.9:2:
This verse says that the true shepherd is recognized: the doorkeeper opens the gate for him, the sheep listen to his voice, he calls them one by one by name, and he leads them out. The doorkeeper is the one who watches over the entrance of the sheepfold. The phrase "leads them out" means he guides them outside, to the pasture.

Jesus is speaking, addressing the Pharisees after healing the man born blind (chapter 9). They had thrown that man out and believed themselves to be good guides for the people. Jesus presents himself as the rightful shepherd, in contrast to the thieves who do not enter by the door. Interpreters do not agree on who the doorkeeper represents: some think of God, others of the Holy Spirit or of John the Baptist.

For today: set aside time to read the Bible and to pray, so that you learn to recognize the voice of Jesus. The better you know him, the easier it will be to tell what comes from him apart from what only sounds appealing.
exp.8:23:
They called the man who had been blind a second time. They order him: "Give God the praise," and they state that Jesus is a sinner. "Give God the praise" was a solemn formula that, as it is understood, called for telling the truth before God. Here it sounds like pressure on the man to deny the miracle or to stop acknowledging Jesus.

The Pharisees are speaking, and they were already investigating the healing. The man's parents, out of fear, did not want to commit themselves, so now they press the healed man directly. They had already settled their conclusion: Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, and for that reason they judged him a sinner.

For today: when we have prejudices, we can close our eyes to what God is doing clearly. Let us ask him for humility to examine the facts honestly, and for courage to say what we have seen of him, even when others do not agree.
exp.10:1:
This verse is a parenthetical note. The author identifies Mary as the woman who poured perfume on the Lord and wiped his feet with her hair. "Ointment" refers to a fragrant perfume or oil. To anoint means to pour that oil on someone as a sign of honor. Her brother Lazarus was sick.

The one telling the story is John, the author of the Gospel. He writes as if his readers already know Mary, because this anointing will be described later, in John 12. So he identifies her before going on to the news of Lazarus's illness. Some scholars discuss how this account relates to other anointings in the Gospels, but here John is speaking of Mary of Bethany.

For today: God remembers and values simple acts of love toward Jesus. Mary also faced an illness in her family and went to him with confidence. When something hurts you, bring it to Jesus with that same sincerity.
exp.18:39:
It says that Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus took the body of Jesus and wrapped it in strips of linen cloth, placing aromatic spices between the layers. "Linen cloths" are pieces of linen fabric, and "spices" are perfumes and resins. Here the verb means simply "they wrapped it." John clarifies that this was how the Jews customarily buried their dead.

The one speaking is John, a witness to what happened. He explains this to readers who may not have known Jewish customs. The two men had been secret disciples out of fear, but now, after Jesus' death, they act with courage and treat him with great respect and care. The hundred pounds of spices show a great expense and much affection.

For today: it is never too late to set aside fear and show love for Jesus through concrete actions. If until now you have been timid in your faith, ask God for courage to take a simple step: pray aloud, serve someone, or confess Christ.
exp.13:14:
Jesus says that love for him is shown in obedience. "Keep" here means to carry out and obey, and also to treasure and care for what he teaches. "Commandments" are his teachings and instructions, not just scattered rules. He does not say that obeying buys his love, but that true love shows itself in what we do.

Jesus speaks with his disciples the night before his crucifixion. He is preparing them for his departure and promises them answered prayer. Right after this, he announces that the Father will give them another Helper, the Holy Spirit. So obedience is not left alone: God himself will give them help to live as Jesus teaches.

For today: think of a teaching of Jesus that you have set aside, such as forgiving or being honest. Ask the Spirit for strength, and take one concrete step of obedience today as a sign of your love for him.
exp.18:1:
The soldiers wove a crown of thorns and placed it on Jesus' head. They also dressed him in a robe of "grana," a deep red color, close to purple. The other Gospels also speak of a robe of this kind.

John is the one telling the story. Pilate had already ordered Jesus to be flogged, and the soldiers mocked him as if he were a pretend king. With the crown and the robe they were imitating an emperor. Then they greeted him with irony: "Hail, King of the Jews!" Pilate wanted to show that he found no guilt in Jesus.

For today: Jesus endured mockery and pain out of love for us. When someone mocks your faith or treats you badly, remember that he understands you. Ask him for patience to respond with gentleness and not with resentment.
exp.19:6:
This verse says that the cloth, the piece of linen that had covered the head of Jesus, was not lying with the strips of linen that had wrapped his body. It was rolled up or folded, in a place by itself. The "linen clothes" are the strips of cloth used for the burial.

John, the author, tells what Peter saw when he entered the empty tomb on the morning of the resurrection. The detail suggests order and calm, not the disorder of a hurried theft. Some think that the "wrapped together" means it was folded; the text only says it was rolled up and set apart, so it is best not to add more.

For today: God pays attention to details, and faith can grow as we notice carefully what He has already done. Take a moment to read the Bible slowly, without rushing, and ask Him to show you something new.
exp.0:5:
The explanation says that God sent a man named John. It is John the Baptist, not the apostle who wrote this Gospel. His origin is in God: he did not set out on his own, but was sent.

The one speaking is the apostle John, the author, as he begins his Gospel. After speaking of the Word, the life, and the light, he introduces this messenger. The verses that follow explain his mission: to bear witness to the light, who is Jesus, so that many would believe. John was not the light; he only pointed to it.

For today: all of us can be simple witnesses of Christ. We do not need to shine ourselves or draw attention. When we speak with humility about what Jesus has done in our lives, we help others see the true light.
exp.5:19:
Jesus speaks to his disciples, who are frightened in the middle of the storm. He tells them "It is I," plain words that mean "it is I, do not be confused," and he asks them not to be afraid. The word for distance here was an old unit of measure. Twenty-five or thirty of them are about five or six kilometers.

The disciples were crossing the lake at night, with strong wind and waves. When they saw Jesus walking on the water, they were terrified. Jesus identifies himself to calm them. Some see here also an echo of the divine name, "I am," although at this moment he mainly gives them security by his presence.

When the storm comes, do not look only at the wind and the waves; remember that Jesus is near. When you feel fear, pray and repeat: "Lord, you are with me." His presence can give you peace even if the situation does not change right away.
exp.19:15:
Context: Mary Magdalene is weeping beside the empty tomb. Up to that moment she believes Jesus is the gardener, that is, the man who looks after the garden. When he speaks her name, she recognizes him. John does not explain why she had not recognized him before. Afterward, Jesus sends her to tell the disciples that he is going to his Father.

For today: Jesus knows each person by name and draws near even when we weep without understanding what is happening. We can speak to him with confidence in the midst of pain, and expect that he will also speak to us, especially through his Word.
exp.10:30:
It says that the Jews who were in the house comforting Mary saw her get up quickly and leave. The word for "quickly" in the source is the one that means fast, immediately. They followed her because they thought she was going to her brother Lazarus's tomb to weep. In reality, she was going to meet Jesus.

Here the narrator, John, speaks. Mary had just learned, through Martha, that Jesus had arrived and was calling for her. Those who were with her did not know this and assumed what seemed most logical. Their mistake ended up bringing them also before Jesus, where they would see what He would do next.

For today: when grief pushes you to move, run to Jesus and do not stay alone in sadness. Also, sometimes the people around us do not understand where we are going or why, but God knows, and He can use even that for good.
exp.4:3:
It says that, at a certain time, an angel would go down to the pool and stir the water. The first one who stepped in after that was made well of whatever disease he had.

The one telling the story is John, describing why so many sick people waited beside the pool of Bethesda. Many early manuscripts do not include this verse, and some scholars believe a copyist added it later to explain why the sick were waiting. For that reason it is interpreted in different ways. What is certain is that Jesus healed the man with his word, not with the water.

For today: sometimes we feel that our hope depends on luck or on getting there first. Jesus invites us to something better: to come to Him with sincerity and trust His mercy, without competing for it.
exp.3:26:
Verse 27 says that the disciples came back just as Jesus was finishing his conversation with the Samaritan woman. They were surprised, or "marvelled," to see him talking with a woman. Even so, no one dared to ask him what he was looking for or why he was talking with her.

John tells this after Jesus had revealed himself as the Messiah to this woman. In that time, many teachers avoided talking alone with a woman, and even more so with a Samaritan. The disciples stayed silent, perhaps out of respect or because they did not understand what was happening. The text does not explain their exact reason. What we do see is that she leaves her water jar and runs to tell her town.

Today we can learn that Jesus values people whom others overlook. Let us ask God to free us from prejudice and to help us approach with kindness those whom people usually ignore.
exp.12:31:
Jesus says that if God is glorified in the Son, God will also glorify him in himself, and will do so right away. To glorify means to show the worth and honor of someone. The words about glorifying him refer to Jesus.

Jesus speaks at the Last Supper, just after Judas went out to betray him. With that departure, the cross was already very near. Jesus calls what is coming his glory: his death and his resurrection. Many understand that the love and obedience of the Son toward the Father shine through there. Right after this, he speaks to his disciples about his departure and gives them the command to love one another.

For today: even in moments of pain or sacrifice, God can be honored. Ask him that your concrete love for others, even when it costs you, may show what Jesus is like.
exp.5:64:
Jesus says that no one can come to him in true faith unless the Father grants it.

Jesus is speaking to many followers who were offended by his teachings about being the bread of life. He already knew that some did not truly believe. With these words he explains that faith does not arise only from human effort, but that God awakens it. Christians have understood in various ways how God's action and the person's responsibility fit together, but the text emphasizes that the initiative belongs to God.

For today: if you believe in Jesus, give thanks, because God drew you. And if someone close to you does not believe, pray for that person with hope, trusting that the Father can call them.
exp.5:3:
The verse says that the Passover was close at hand, the great annual feast of the Jews. There they remembered how God brought them out of slavery in Egypt. "Feast of the Jews" is the way John, the writer, presents it to his readers.

John is the narrator, and he gives this detail of the time just before the miracle of the bread and the fish. A large crowd was following Jesus because of the signs he was doing. Some think John mentions the Passover because the bread and the deliverance connect with what Jesus will later teach about himself as the bread of life. The text does not say this directly, so it is an interpretation.

For today: God works within time and in moments that he knows well. When you feel that the need is great, remember that Jesus already knows what he is going to do. Trust him and obey step by step.
exp.10:46:
The verse says that the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered in a council, that is, a meeting of leaders. They asked what they should do, because Jesus was doing many signs, that is, miracles that showed extraordinary power.

Shortly before this, Jesus had raised Lazarus. Many who saw it believed in him, and some went to tell the Pharisees. The leaders speak with concern: they feared losing their influence and that the Romans would react. Notice that they do not deny the miracles, but they do not ask whether Jesus is the Messiah.

We can see clear evidence and still resist it out of fear of losing comfort or control. Today I invite you to ask yourself with humility: what is it costing me to surrender to God? Ask him for a heart willing to believe and obey.
exp.5:45:
Jesus says that no one has seen the Father, except the one who comes from God, and that one is himself. The words "not that" would be rendered as "I do not mean that." Jesus clarifies that, although he was speaking about being taught by the Father, this does not mean that anyone has seen God face to face. Only the Son has seen him.

Jesus speaks in Capernaum to a crowd that was complaining because he said he was the bread that came down from heaven. They knew his family and doubted where he came from. He explains to them that coming to him is the work of the Father, and that only he knows the Father directly, because he comes from God.

For today: if you want to know what God is like, look to Jesus. Instead of imagining God in your own way, read the Gospels calmly, ask the Father to teach you, and trust what Christ reveals about him.
exp.9:40:
Many people kept coming to Jesus, and they remarked that John the Baptist did no sign, that is, no miracle, but that everything John said about this man proved to be true.

Jesus had withdrawn to the other side of the Jordan, to the place where John had been baptizing at the beginning, because in Jerusalem they wanted to arrest him. The ones speaking are the people of that region, who remembered John's testimony. Seeing Jesus, they compared what John had said with what they now saw, and this led them to believe, as the next verse says.

For today: God can use a simple and faithful witness, even if it is not spectacular. You do not need to do extraordinary things to help others believe; it is enough to speak truthfully about Jesus and to live in accordance with it. Over time, the works of Christ can confirm your words.
exp.12:21:
After Jesus announced that one of them would betray him, the disciples looked around at one another. They did not know whom he meant. The phrase "looked one on another" means that they were looking at each other, and "doubting" here means that they were puzzled, unable to understand who it would be.

This is the last supper, shortly before the cross. John tells us that Jesus was deeply troubled in his spirit and spoke with clarity. The disciples did not suspect any one man; no one pointed to Judas at once. This shows that Judas had hidden his intentions well, and that each of them felt the weight of the warning.

Today, instead of looking at others with suspicion, we can examine our own hearts and ask God to keep us faithful. A simple prayer: "Lord, keep me from betraying you, and show me if there is something in me that I should correct."
exp.7:5:
These words asked Jesus the question as a trap, so that they would have something to accuse him of. The word "tempting" here means testing him with bad intentions. Jesus did not answer right away: he bent down and wrote on the ground with his finger.

The religious leaders brought a woman caught in adultery. If Jesus said to let her go, he would seem to go against the law of Moses; if he said to stone her, he would look bad because of his mercy. The Bible does not say what he wrote, so any explanation is only a guess. What is clear is that he did not let himself be rushed.

Today we can learn not to answer in haste when someone provokes us. Before speaking, it is good to pause, pray, and seek wisdom. And let us remember that God seeks to correct with truth and mercy, not with traps or contempt.
exp.9:37:
Jesus says that if He does the works of His Father, even though people do not believe Him, they should at least believe the works. In this way they will be able to know and believe that the Father is in Him and He in the Father.

Jesus speaks in Jerusalem, at the Feast of Dedication, before Jewish leaders who accused Him of blasphemy for calling Himself the Son of God. He does not defend Himself only with words, but points to His miracles and His obedience to the Father as proof. Afterward, they tried to arrest Him, but He escaped from their hands.

Today, when you have doubts about who Jesus is, look honestly at what He did and continues to do. Read the Gospels calmly and ask God to open your heart to believe.
exp.3:49:
The speaker is Jesus, in Cana of Galilee. Standing before him is a royal official, the man described as "the nobleman" in the KJV's sense of a king's officer, who begs him for his sick son. Jesus had just said that the people demanded signs before they would believe. Yet this desperate father kept pleading, and Jesus answered him with a word of life.

Today, we sometimes want to see the answer first before we trust. This father teaches us to believe the word of Jesus and to take the next step in faith, even when we do not yet see the result. Trust, and walk on.
exp.0:22:
John answers with words from the prophet Isaiah. He says that he is only the voice crying out in the wilderness, that is, a messenger calling people to prepare. To make straight means to set things right, removing whatever gets in the way. The Lord is the one who is coming, and the way is being prepared to receive him.

John the Baptist is speaking with the messengers sent by the Pharisees, who wanted to know who he was. He had already denied being Elijah or the prophet. Now he does not speak of his own importance, but of his mission: to point to someone else. John quotes Isaiah 40:3 to explain that his task was to prepare the people's hearts for the Messiah.

For today: we can ask ourselves whether our lives point to Jesus or to ourselves. Ask God for humility to remove from the heart whatever stands in the way, such as pride or resentment, and let Christ have the first place.
exp.17:37:
Pilate asks Jesus, "What is truth?" Then he goes back out to where the Jews were and declares, "I find in him no fault at all."

Jesus had just said that he came to bear witness to the truth. Pilate, the Roman governor, answers with a question, and it is not certain what his tone was: it may have been sincere doubt, weariness, or irony. He does not wait for an answer and leaves. Even so, he declares Jesus innocent, but then the crowd asks for Barabbas.

Today we can ask Pilate's question with a heart willing to listen. Before deciding something important, it is not enough to recognize what is right; we must act in accordance with it. Let us ask God for courage to live out what we already know to be true.
exp.13:6:
Jesus says that knowing him is knowing the Father. The old verb forms in the source wording, which correspond to the phrase "if ye had known" in the verse above, are simply a past-tense form of the verb "to know." Here "from henceforth" means that from this point on, the disciples already know the Father and have seen him, because they have seen him through Jesus.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples at the Last Supper, shortly before his arrest. Thomas has just asked about the way, and Jesus answered that he himself is the way to the Father. Here he makes clear that the disciples still have not fully understood who he is, and Philip shows this when he asks him to show them the Father.

If you want to know what God is like, look at Jesus: his compassion, his truth, his patience. Today you can read the Gospels with this question: what does Jesus teach me about the heart of the Father?
exp.17:19:
Jesus says that his teaching was never secret. "Openly" means in plain view of everyone. He spoke in the synagogues and in the temple, where the Jews gathered, and he said nothing in secret.

The high priest interrogates Jesus about his disciples and his teaching. This takes place at night, after his arrest, while Peter warms himself outside. Jesus does not defend himself with lengthy speeches; rather, he points out that his message was public and that there are witnesses who can confirm it. Many understand that he is also questioning the irregularity of that interrogation.

For today: let us strive to live with transparency. May our faith and our words be the same in public and in private, so that we have nothing to hide.
exp.9:20:
He says that some of those listening to Jesus disagreed with those who accused him of having a demon. They reasoned that Jesus' words did not sound like those of someone possessed. And they asked: if a demon cannot give sight back to a blind man, how could Jesus be someone possessed? Being possessed means being controlled by a demon. Being divided means being split apart or in disagreement.

This was a group of Jews who were divided after Jesus' discourse about the good shepherd. Some said he was mad and possessed. Others remembered the miracle of John 9, when Jesus healed a man born blind. For them, the works of Jesus weighed more than the accusations.

For today: before repeating what others say about Jesus, look at what He does and teaches. Read the Gospels honestly, and let his words and works speak to you, instead of settling for other people's opinions.
exp.11:5:
Here the apostle John, who writes the Gospel, explains why Judas criticized Mary. A thief is someone who takes what belongs to others. The common box for the group's money was kept there.

We are in Bethany, six days before the Passover. Mary has just anointed Jesus' feet with a very costly perfume. Judas protests, saying it should have been sold to help the poor. John clarifies, looking back, that it was not sincere compassion but self-interest. Jesus defends Mary and receives her gesture with appreciation.

For today: let us review our motives. We can say good things, such as talking about helping the poor, but God looks at the heart. Let us ask him for sincerity, and that our generosity be real and not a mere appearance.
exp.9:24:
Jesus answers that he has already told them who he is, but they do not believe. He says that his works, the ones he does with his Father's authority, are the testimony that speaks about him. The explanation's quoted phrase "I told you" means "I already told you," and where it says "bear witness" it means "prove" or "confirm."

Jesus is in the temple in Jerusalem, at Solomon's Porch, during a feast. The Jewish leaders surround him and demand that he say plainly whether he is the Christ, that is, the Messiah. Jesus replies that the problem is not a lack of proof but a lack of faith. His miracles and the way he lives already showed who he was.

For today: we often ask for more signs before we believe, but God has already given us a great deal. Look at what Jesus has done in the Bible and in your own life, and respond with simple trust, without hardening your heart.
exp.9:26:
This verse says that those who belong to Jesus listen to his voice, he knows them personally, and they follow him. Jesus uses the image of a shepherd and his sheep. "Hear" here means to listen carefully and obey, not merely to perceive a sound.

Jesus speaks in the temple in Jerusalem, during the Feast of Dedication. Some Jewish leaders were asking him to say plainly whether he was the Messiah. He answers that his works already testify to who he is, but they do not believe. Then he contrasts that attitude with that of his sheep, who do recognize his voice and follow him.

Today we can set aside a few minutes each day to read the Gospels attentively, asking God to speak to us. In this way we learn to recognize the voice of Jesus and to follow him in our everyday decisions.
exp.19:28:
Jesus tells Thomas that he believed because he saw. Then he declares happy those who believe without having seen. The source's "bienaventurados," meaning "blessed," is the word in the verse itself, so no separate note is needed. Jesus does not rebuke Thomas harshly, but he points out that there is a kind of faith praised even more: the faith that trusts without seeing.

He is speaking as the risen Jesus, eight days after appearing to the disciples. Thomas was not present the first time and doubted their testimony. Upon seeing Jesus, he confessed, "My Lord and my God!" John explains afterward that he wrote his book so that readers may believe and have life in his name.

For today: we did not see Jesus in person, but we have the testimony of the apostles in the Bible. This week, read a passage from the Gospel and trust what Jesus says, even if you do not yet see the answer to your doubts.
exp.12:10:
This verse explains why Jesus said "not all of you are clean." John makes clear that Jesus knew who would betray him. "Betray" here means handing someone over to their enemies. So that statement was not about the dirt on their feet, but about the heart of one of the disciples.

Jesus is at the last supper, washing the feet of his disciples. Peter has just asked him to wash his hands and head as well. Jesus replies that someone who is already clean only needs to wash their feet. The eleven were clean, but Judas was not. Jesus knew this and, even so, he washed Judas's feet too.

For today: Jesus knows our hearts completely, and still he treats us with humility and kindness. This invites us to be sincere with God, without pretending, and to serve others even when they do not deserve it.
exp.20:22:
This verse tells us that a rumor spread among the brothers, that is, the believers, that the disciple whom Jesus loved would not die. The text makes clear that Jesus never said that. He only said: "If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?" The phrase "what is that to you" means "what does it matter to you?" To "remain" means to "stay."

The one speaking is the author of the Gospel, correcting a misunderstanding. Just before this, Jesus had restored Peter and told him, "Follow me." Peter, curious, asked about the future of John. Jesus redirected him to his own calling. Then people exaggerated his words.

For today: don't get distracted by comparing your path with that of others. God guides each person in a different way. And before repeating something as "spiritual," check that it really says what Jesus said.
exp.9:31:
Jesus tells the Jews that he has shown them many good works, and that all of them come from his Father. Then he asks them a direct question: for which of those works are they trying to stone him?

Jesus has just said, "I and the Father are one." Some of the Jews picked up stones because they understood him to be claiming to be equal to God. Jesus speaks to them calmly and reminds them of his healings and signs. With the question, he makes clear that his works show who he is, and that their anger has no fair reason behind it.

For today: when someone rejects or criticizes us, we can ask ourselves the same question with humility: what fruit does my life show? And if we serve God, let us keep doing good even when others do not understand us.
exp.3:2:
Jesus left Judea and went back to Galilee. The wording of the verse shows that he had already been in Galilee before. The narrator is the Gospel writer, John. He tells us that Jesus learned the Pharisees had heard that his disciples were baptizing more people than John the Baptist. The text does not state clearly why he left, but many believe he wanted to avoid a confrontation before the appointed time. That is an interpretation, not something the text states directly. His journey would take him through Samaria.

For today: not every withdrawal is weakness. Sometimes it is wisdom. We can ask God for discernment to know when to stay and when to step away, without ceasing to obey his call.
exp.11:17:
This verse explains why so many people went out to meet Jesus when he arrived in Jerusalem. The reason was that they had heard about the miracle he had done: raising Lazarus from the dead. A miracle like this points to something greater, and going out to meet him means going out to welcome him.

Here John, the narrator of the Gospel, speaks. He has just described Jesus' entry into Jerusalem, riding on a donkey. John makes clear that the crowd received him because of the testimony of those who saw Lazarus come out of the tomb. That fame angered the Pharisees, who felt they were losing control of the people.

For today: the testimony of what God does in a life can move others to seek Jesus. Tell simply what he has done for you. But it is good to go beyond the miracles and get to know Jesus himself, because following him is more than admiring what he did.
exp.19:9:
This verse says that Peter and the other disciple, who had already seen the empty tomb, went back home. The phrase "to their own home" means "to their own place" or "to where they were staying." The text does not speak of any command from Jesus; it is simply what they did.

The narrator is John, who refers to himself as "the other disciple." He had just seen the linen cloths in the tomb and had come to believe, though he still did not fully understand the Scriptures about the resurrection. Some think they returned to the other disciples, others that they went to their homes; the text does not make this clear. Meanwhile, Mary stays outside, weeping.

Today, we sometimes understand only part of what God is doing. We can return to our everyday lives with questions, but also with openness. Staying close to Jesus, as Mary did, lets us meet Him.
exp.7:24:
Here people ask Jesus, "Who are you?" He answers, "Even the same that I said unto you from the beginning." The phrase is difficult and can be understood in several ways: "the same thing I have told you from the start," or "why am I still speaking to you?" What matters is that Jesus says he is not saying anything new.

Jesus speaks with religious leaders who doubt him. He has just told them that if they do not believe, they will die in their sins. They ask who he is, but they do not accept what he has already shown them. Jesus makes clear that he speaks what he heard from the Father who sent him.

For today: we do not need to wait for a new answer about Jesus. We can return to what he has already said in the Gospels, read it with humility, and believe him from the heart.
exp.5:40:
The verse tells us that the Jews complained quietly about Jesus. "Murmured" means that they protested and found fault among themselves. What troubled them was that Jesus said, "I am the bread which came down from heaven", that is, that He came from God and gives life.

The one speaking here is the narrator, John, and he recounts the reaction of the people who had heard Jesus in Capernaum. Shortly before, Jesus had told them that whoever believes in Him has eternal life. They knew His family and could not accept that He had come from heaven. They looked at what was human and did not see what God was doing.

For today: when something about Jesus is hard for us to understand or makes us uncomfortable, let us not stay complaining. Better to bring our doubts to Him honestly and openly, asking Him to teach us to believe.
exp.19:25:
It says that a week later, the disciples were gathered together again in a house, and this time Thomas was with them. Although the doors were shut, Jesus came, stood in the middle of them, and said to them, "Peace be unto you." The phrase "after eight days" means a week later, counting the same day of the week.

John is telling what happened after the resurrection. Thomas had not been there the first time and doubted what the others said. Jesus returns and speaks peace, not rebuke. He wants to answer Thomas's doubt with care and closeness.

For today: when you have doubts, do not withdraw from the community of faith. Thomas stayed with the disciples, and there he met Jesus. Bring your questions with sincerity, and remember that Christ receives you with peace.
exp.6:8:
This verse tells us that Jesus, after speaking with his brothers, did not go with them to the feast but stayed in Galilee. It is a simple moment, but it shows that Jesus did not act under pressure.

Here John is the narrator. Jesus' brothers were urging him to show himself publicly in Jerusalem during the Feast of Tabernacles. Jesus answered them that the right time had not yet come, meaning the moment God had appointed. Afterward he did go up, but in secret, without drawing attention.

For today: we do not always have to move because of haste or the opinions of others. We can pray, wait for God's timing, and act when He guides us, even when others push us to hurry.
exp.19:2:
Peter and the other disciple, traditionally identified with John, set out from where they were and went toward Jesus' tomb. The word "went" here means they made their way there. They do not stop to discuss it; they simply get moving.

The narrator is John, who tells what happened that early Sunday morning. Mary Magdalene had just seen the stone taken away and thought someone had carried off Jesus' body. She gave the news to the two disciples, and they reacted at once. They did not yet understand that Jesus had risen; they only wanted to find out what was going on.

For today: when something unsettles you or fills you with questions about God, do not freeze. Take a step, go, and look. Even with doubts, drawing near to Jesus with sincerity is the best way to discover the truth.
exp.12:11:
He tells that Jesus finished washing his disciples' feet, put his outer garment back on, sat down at the table again, and asked them a question: "Do you understand what I have done to you?"

He speaks during the Last Supper, shortly before he is handed over. He had done the work of a servant, something no one else was willing to do. His question is not asking for information, but for them to think about the meaning of his action. Right away he explains that it is an example of humility and of serving one another.

For today: before looking for someone to serve us, let us ask ourselves whom we can serve in simple ways. It may be helping at home, listening to someone who is tired, or doing a task that no one wants to do, without expecting recognition.
exp.11:43:
