Jesus speaks out loud and says that whoever believes in him is not believing only in him, but also in God the Father, who sent him. The word "cried" means that he spoke loudly and firmly, so that everyone could hear him. The word "but" introduces the contrast in the sentence.

It is Jesus himself who speaks, toward the end of his public ministry. Shortly before, many leaders believed in him, yet they kept silent out of fear of the Pharisees and of being put out of the synagogue. Jesus makes clear that believing in him never stops at his own person: it leads straight to the Father. He then adds that seeing him is seeing the Father, and that he is the light of the world.

For today: if you trust in Jesus, you trust in God himself. That gives you courage not to hide your faith out of fear of what others think. Today you can decide to speak simply and sincerely of your faith in a place where you usually stay silent.
exp.6:39:
John 7:40 tells us that some people in the crowd, when they heard Jesus's words about rivers of living water, said, "Of a truth this is the Prophet." "Belly" here refers to the innermost part of a person, the heart.

This takes place in Jerusalem, during the Feast of Tabernacles. Jesus had just invited people to believe in him. Many Jews were waiting for a special prophet, perhaps the one mentioned in Deuteronomy 18:15. Not everyone agreed: some said he was the Christ, and others doubted because he came from Galilee. Interpreters debate exactly what each group understood by "the Prophet."

Today we can learn that it is not enough to admire Jesus or to recognize that he says extraordinary things. He invites us to believe in him and to let his Spirit fill us. Let us ask him to guide us into a personal and sincere faith.
exp.5:59:
It says that many of Jesus' disciples, when they heard his teaching, reacted with difficulty. The word rendered as "hard" means hard to accept, not just hard to understand. The question "who can hear it?" means: who can accept or follow this? Here "disciples" does not refer only to the twelve, but to a wider group of followers.

Jesus had just taught in the synagogue at Capernaum that he is the bread from heaven and that whoever eats this bread will live forever. He was asking for complete trust in him, and many felt uneasy. Christians understand the details of this discourse in different ways, but all see that Jesus demanded full faith in himself.

For today: when a teaching of Jesus makes us uncomfortable, let us not dismiss it right away. Better to bring that difficulty to him in prayer and keep listening with humility.
exp.13:21:
Judas, not Iscariot, asks Jesus: "Lord, why is it that you will reveal yourself to us and not to the world?" The word "manifest" here means to make oneself known clearly.

It is the night before the cross, and Jesus has just promised that he will reveal himself to whoever loves him and keeps his commandments. This Judas is probably the same one Luke calls "Judas son of James," though not everyone agrees. He is surprised: he expected a public revelation. Jesus answers that he is speaking of a closeness based on love and obedience, where the Father and he will make their home in the believer.

Today, God is not known only through curiosity or arguments, but through a relationship of love. If you want to sense his presence, begin by obeying today a word of his that you already know.
exp.17:32:
Pilate went back into the governor's residence, the Roman governor's headquarters, and had Jesus called. He asked him directly, "Are you the King of the Jews?" The words "entered again" and "said" in the original are simply the usual way of saying that he went back in and spoke to him.

The Jewish leaders had brought Jesus before Pilate and were bringing charges against him. Apparently they were not allowed to carry out an execution themselves, and John explains that this fulfilled what Jesus had said about how he would die. Pilate, the Roman judge, wants to know whether Jesus is a political threat, because the word "king" sounded like rebellion against Rome.

For today: Jesus is questioned, and he responds without fear or anger. When we are challenged about our faith, we can answer with calm and truth. This question also invites us to decide what place Jesus holds as King in our own lives.
exp.14:13:
Jesus says that his disciples are his friends if they do what he commands. The phrase "you are" appears in the verse, so the reader can match it to the wording they see. Friendship with Jesus is shown through obedience.

Jesus speaks to his disciples the night before his crucifixion. He has just told them to love one another as he has loved them, and that the greatest love is to lay down one's life for friends. Right after this, he explains that he no longer calls them servants but friends, because he has shared with them what he heard from the Father. Their obedience is not that of a frightened slave, but the response of someone who knows they are loved.

Today you might ask yourself: which command of Jesus am I neglecting? Choose one, such as forgiving or serving someone, and practice it this week, trusting in his friendship.
exp.6:20:
Jesus tells them that he did one work and that they were all amazed. The phrase "you marvel" means that they were surprised, and here his annoyance also shows. "Told them" is the same as "said to them."

Jesus speaks in Jerusalem, during the Feast of Tabernacles, before leaders and ordinary people. He refers to the healing of a man on the Sabbath, which happened in chapter 5. Many became angry over it and sought to kill him. Jesus shows them that they themselves circumcise on the Sabbath, so their anger makes no sense.

For today: before criticizing something, let us ask whether we are seeing the good that God is doing. Sometimes we defend rules and forget mercy. Let us pray for a heart that rejoices when someone is healed or helped.
exp.11:30:
Jesus says that the time of judgment on this world has now arrived. By "this world" he means the human system that is turned away from God. He also says that the ruler of this world, an expression commonly understood to refer to Satan, will be cast out, meaning he will be stripped of his power and rule.

Jesus speaks only a few days before his crucifixion. A voice had just come from heaven, and the people thought it was thunder or an angel. He explains that the voice was meant for them. In the verses that follow he speaks of being lifted up, and John makes clear that he is referring to his death on the cross. In this way the cross appears as the moment where the victory is decided.

Today we can live with hope, knowing that Christ has already won the victory on the cross. When you feel pressure, guilt, or fear, remember that the enemy does not have the last word, and draw near to Jesus with confidence.
exp.11:7:
Jesus says that there will always be poor people near the disciples, but that he himself would not be with them for long. The word "á" is the old way of writing "a," and "tenéis" means "tienen."

Jesus speaks these words in Bethany, when Mary pours a very expensive perfume on his feet. Judas criticizes the waste, but the text says he was not concerned about the poor, but about the money he handled. Jesus defends Mary and connects her gesture with his burial, which was already drawing near.

For today: helping the poor is always important, but there are also unique moments to honor Christ and those we love. Let us ask for wisdom to give generously to the needy and, at the same time, not let pass the opportunities to express love and gratitude in time.
exp.6:52:
After the argument, each person went back to his own home. The word "went" in this verse is an old-fashioned form of "went away," and the word "unto" means "to." The meeting ended without any decision.

The religious leaders had gathered because they wanted to arrest Jesus. Nicodemus reminded them that the law requires hearing a person before judging them. They answered with contempt, mocking his origin in Galilee. It should be said that many scholars point out that this verse belongs to a passage (7:53 to 8:11) that does not appear in the oldest manuscripts, and for that reason its original place is debated.

Before judging someone, listen to them patiently and look for the facts. Do not let yourself be carried away by prejudice or by where a person comes from. Justice begins with listening with respect.
exp.15:15:
Jesus says that in a little while his disciples will no longer see him, but that after a short time they will see him again. He gives a reason: he is going to the Father.

Jesus speaks on the night before his crucifixion, while preparing his disciples for his departure. He has just promised them the Holy Spirit. The disciples do not understand his words, as the next verse shows. Scholars often see here the death and resurrection of Jesus, although some also think of his final return. Both readings are possible.

For today: when God seems silent or absent, remember that Jesus already announced that there would be times of waiting, and that his promise to be with us again stands firm. Trust and wait patiently.
exp.2:21:
This verse tells us that, after speaking with Nicodemus, Jesus left Jerusalem and went with his disciples into the region of Judea. There he spent time with them, and he was baptizing. The sentence about the old form of a word is dropped, since that wording does not appear in the verse your reader sees. John 4:2 makes clear that Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples did, so here baptizing is spoken of as happening through them.

The one telling this is John the apostle. He comes from the night conversation with Nicodemus, where Jesus spoke about being born again and coming into the light. Now the account moves from words to action: Jesus lives alongside his disciples, and his ministry grows. Soon John the Baptist is also mentioned as baptizing, and we will see how both ministries existed side by side for a time.

For today: faith is not only hearing ideas, but also walking close to Jesus. Look for time to be with him and with other believers, and let that closeness shape you a little more each day.
exp.1:22:
This verse says that Jesus was in Jerusalem during the Passover feast, and that many people believed in his name when they saw the signs, that is, the miracles he was doing. "Jerusalem" is Jerusalem. "Believing in his name" means trusting in who he is.

Here the writer of the Gospel, John, is speaking. It comes right after the scene where Jesus cleared the temple and spoke about his resurrection. But what follows shows that Jesus did not rely on that faith, because he knew the human heart. Some understand it to have been a shallow faith, based only on the amazement of the miracles.

For today: it is not enough to admire Jesus for what he does. Ask yourself whether you truly trust him and follow him, even when you see no miracles. He knows your heart and invites you to a sincere and firm faith.
exp.5:30:
Here the people remind Jesus that their ancestors ate manna in the desert, and they quote the Scripture that says God gave them "bread from heaven." The manna was the food God gave Israel during their journey through the desert.

The speakers are part of the crowd that Jesus had fed the day before. They ask him for a sign so they can believe him, as if the miracle of the loaves were not enough. By mentioning the manna, they seem to compare Jesus with Moses. Jesus will answer that the true bread from heaven is not the manna, but the one the Father gives now.

For today: it is easy to ask God for more proof, even though he has already shown us his goodness. Today you can thank God for what he has already done and trust in Jesus as your true food, seeking him through prayer and the reading of his Word.
exp.16:24:
Jesus says that the world has not known the Father, but that he does know him, and that his disciples have come to understand that the Father sent him. He calls the Father "righteous," meaning upright and faithful in everything he does. Knowing here is not just having information, but having a real relationship with someone.

Jesus is speaking to the Father in his final prayer, the night before his arrest. He has prayed for himself and now prays for his disciples and for those who would believe later. He contrasts three groups: the world that does not know God, him who knows him perfectly, and the disciples who recognize him through Jesus. His purpose is that they would live in the Father's love.

For today: knowing God does not depend on our intelligence, but on looking to Jesus. Spend a few minutes reading a passage from the Gospels and ask him to show you what the Father is like.
exp.0:32:
John the Baptist says that he did not know with certainty who the Messiah was, until God himself, who sent him to baptize with water, gave him a sign. The one he would see the Spirit come down and stay upon is the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.

John speaks as a witness before the messengers sent by the Jewish leaders. His baptism with water prepared the people and served to present Jesus to Israel. John tells how he saw the promised sign, and for that reason he can declare who Jesus is: the Son of God.

For today: John did not rely on his own ideas, but on what God showed him. We can do the same: trust the Word of God to know Jesus, and then speak about him with humility and honesty.
exp.8:1:
The disciples see a man who has been blind from birth, and they ask Jesus, "Master, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?" The word "Master" is a translation of a term meaning teacher. The sentence about the old form of a word is removed because it does not apply to the verse as your reader sees it.

The ones speaking are the disciples. Many people at that time believed that an illness or disability was a punishment for some sin. That is why they ask in this way. Jesus corrects that idea: neither the man nor his parents are to blame for this blindness, but God wants his works to be shown in him. Then Jesus speaks about the urgency of working while there is time.

When someone suffers, let us avoid looking for someone to blame or offering easy explanations. It is better to approach them with compassion and help in whatever we can, trusting that God can work even in situations we do not understand.
exp.10:19:
This verse tells us that Martha, as soon as she heard that Jesus was coming, went out to meet him. Mary, on the other hand, stayed in the house. The phrase "went out to meet him" means that she went out to meet Him, and "stayed" means that she remained seated or stayed where she was.

Here the narrator, John, speaks. Lazarus, the brother of Martha and Mary, had died, and several Jews were in the house comforting them in their grief. Jesus was arriving late, as they thought. Martha reacts by going out at once and speaks to him frankly. The Bible does not explain why Mary stayed; some think her grief was very deep, but that is only a guess.

Each person draws near to God in a different way when they suffer. Some go out to seek him and speak to him sincerely; others need a moment of quiet. If you are in pain, come to Jesus as you can, with honesty. He knows how to wait, and he also knows how to call you.
exp.6:36:
But on the last day, the greatest day of the feast, Jesus stood up and spoke in a loud voice. The word "cried" means that he spoke loudly, so that everyone could hear him. He invites anyone who is thirsty to come to him and drink.

Jesus speaks in Jerusalem, during the Feast of Tabernacles, when many people were gathered. Some scholars think the last day was the seventh day, and others think it was the eighth. Many connect his words with the water rituals of that feast, although this is debated. The people were discussing who he was, and John explains that he is speaking about the Holy Spirit.

Today, if your soul feels dry or weary, Jesus invites you to come to him with confidence, not to look only in other things. Honor him with a sincere prayer today.
exp.9:5:
This verse says that Jesus told them a parable, that is, a simple comparison about shepherds and sheep, but those who heard it did not grasp what He wanted to teach. The word "but" in the verse links the two parts of the sentence, and the phrase "what things they were which he spake unto them" refers to the meaning of what He was saying.

Jesus speaks with some Pharisees, after healing the man born blind (chapter 9). They considered themselves the guides of the people, yet they rejected Jesus. He uses the image of the shepherd whom the sheep recognize by his voice. Since they did not understand, He immediately explains it by saying: "I am the door of the sheep."

For today: sometimes we do not understand God because our heart is closed or full of pride. We can ask Him for humility, read the Bible with patience, and listen for His voice, trusting that Jesus continues to explain with love to whoever seeks Him sincerely.
exp.6:29:
This verse says that some people wanted to arrest Jesus, but no one managed to touch him. The reason is that "his hour" had not yet come. The phrase "to arrest him" means to seize or capture him, and "no one laid hands on him" means that no one grabbed hold of him.

Jesus was teaching in the temple during the Feast of Tabernacles. He had said that he came from God, and this greatly angered the religious leaders. John uses "his hour" to speak of the moment God had set for the handing over and death of Jesus. As long as that time had not arrived, his enemies could not stop him.

For today: our lives are also in God's hands, and his timing is more sure than the plans of any person. When you face opposition or fear, you can rest in the fact that God is still in control and trust that he will accomplish his purpose at the right moment.
exp.14:22:
It says that rejecting Jesus is no small matter: whoever hates him also hates God the Father.

Jesus speaks to his disciples the night before his crucifixion. He warns them that the world will reject them because of him. Many who heard his words and saw his works refused to believe. Since Jesus came to reveal the Father, rejecting him was rejecting God himself.

For today: we cannot say that we love God and, at the same time, set Jesus aside. Also, if someone rejects us for following him, let us remember that this is nothing new. Let us respond with humility and love, trusting in him.
exp.2:22:
John the Baptist was also baptizing at a place called Aenon, near Salim. That place was chosen because there was "much water," meaning enough water to baptize many people. People kept coming and were being baptized.

The one telling this is the apostle John, who writes the Gospel. He notes that Jesus and his disciples were also baptizing in Judea, so both ministries were going on at the same time. Scholars do not agree on the exact location of Aenon and Salim. What the text makes clear is that John the Baptist was still carrying out his mission of preparing the people, before he was imprisoned.

Today, we can learn from John's faithfulness: he kept simply doing what God had entrusted to him, without competing with anyone. Let us ask God for joy to serve where he has placed us.
exp.11:29:
Jesus explains that the voice from heaven did not sound to help him, but for the benefit of the people who were there.

Jesus had just prayed, and the Father answered from heaven. Some thought it was thunder, and others thought an angel had spoken to him. Jesus makes clear that the voice was a sign for them, so that they would believe. A few words later he speaks of his death and says that he would draw everyone to himself.

God sometimes gives us signs, words, or encouragement through the Bible, and it is not always only for us. Let us ask for an attentive heart, like that of someone who truly wants to listen, and let us share with others what God teaches us so that they too may believe and be encouraged.
exp.17:36:
Pilate asks Jesus whether he really is a king. Jesus answers, "You say so," meaning he does not deny it, but he clarifies what kind of king he is. He says that he was born and came into the world to bear witness to the truth, and that everyone who belongs to the truth hears his voice.

Jesus is in custody, accused before the Roman governor. Pilate wants to know whether Jesus is a political threat. That is why Jesus has just explained that his kingdom is not of this world: it does not advance by weapons or political power. Afterward Pilate asks, "What is truth?" and declares that he finds no crime in him.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we truly want to listen to Jesus, even when his truth makes us uncomfortable. Listening to him in the Bible and in prayer, and obeying him, is a way of living under his kingdom.
exp.5:39:
God the Father wants every person who "sees" the Son and believes in him to have eternal life. Here "seeing" is not only looking with the eyes, but recognizing who Jesus is.

Jesus speaks in Capernaum, after feeding a crowd with bread. He explains that he is the bread that came down from heaven and that his mission is to carry out the Father's will. As the next passage shows, some Jews grumbled because they knew his family and did not understand how he could have come from heaven.

For today: faith in Jesus is not a distant idea but personal trust. If you feel tired today or afraid of death, you can rest in the fact that Jesus promises to sustain those who believe in him, and pray with that hope.
exp.4:7:
Jesus gives the sick man three commands: "Rise," "take up your bed," and "walk." The "bed" is the mat or pallet where he used to sleep. Jesus says these words to him directly.

Jesus speaks with a man who had been sick for a long time beside the pool of Bethesda. The man said that no one helped him into the water. Jesus does not speak to him about the pool, but heals him with his word alone. The account says it was the Sabbath, and that provoked the reaction of the Jews.

For today: sometimes we wait for a solution in our own way, and God invites us to trust his word and take a step of faith. If today you feel you cannot, listen to Jesus, obey what he already shows you, and walk with confidence in his power.
exp.19:27:
Thomas responds to the risen Jesus with a very brief statement: "My Lord and my God." The wording is simple: the verse says "answered and said unto him," and the confession itself is "My Lord and my God." Thomas recognizes Jesus as his Lord and calls him God.

Thomas is one of the twelve disciples. He had said that he would not believe in the resurrection unless he saw and touched the wounds of Jesus. Eight days later, Jesus appears with the doors shut and invites him to check for himself. The text does not say that Thomas touched him; it only records his confession. Jesus responds by blessing those who believe without having seen.

For today: when you have doubts, bring them honestly to Jesus instead of hiding them. He dealt patiently with Thomas. Then let your faith find expression in personal surrender: "My Lord and my God."
exp.19:26:
Jesus speaks directly to Thomas and invites him to touch his hands and his side, where the wounds from the crucifixion were. He asks him to stop doubting and to believe. The word "unbelieving" in the verse means a person who does not believe, and the word "believing" means a person who trusts. "Reach hither thy hand" means "stretch out your hand here."

Risen Jesus appears to his disciples eight days after the first time. Thomas had not been present, and he had said that he would not believe without seeing and touching the wounds. Jesus repeats almost the same words he had used, which shows that he knew Thomas's doubt and treats him with patience. Thomas answers with a statement of faith.

For today: when you have doubts, bring them honestly to Jesus instead of hiding them. He does not turn away from someone who seeks the truth with honesty, and he can turn doubt into a firmer faith.
exp.2:4:
Jesus says that to enter the kingdom of God a person must be born "of water and of the Spirit." "Verily, verily" means "truly, truly." It is a new birth that God himself produces, not something a person achieves by their own effort.

Jesus speaks with Nicodemus, a respected teacher among the Jews, who came to visit him at night. Nicodemus took the idea of being born again in a literal way and became confused. Jesus makes clear that he is speaking of a spiritual birth. The water is understood in several ways: as natural birth, as baptism, or as spiritual cleansing. Christians do not agree on this, but all agree that the Spirit is the one who gives the new life.

Today, do not trust in your record, your titles, or your religiousness. Ask the Holy Spirit to renew your heart, and receive that new life as a gift from God.
exp.3:10:
Here the Samaritan woman answers Jesus with respect, calling him "Sir". She thinks about practical things: the well is very deep, and Jesus has no bucket or rope to draw water. That is why she asks where he would get this "living water". In that time, "living water" could mean running water, or fresh water from a spring.

Jesus has just told her that, if she knew God's gift, she would ask him for living water. The woman takes his words literally. Jesus was speaking of something spiritual, but she is still thinking about Jacob's well. This misunderstanding gives Jesus the opening to explain more.

Today we too can get stuck thinking only about what is visible and practical. Let us ask God to open our understanding so that we can receive what he offers, which goes beyond our daily needs.
exp.5:26:
Jesus tells them not to put all their effort into food that spoils, but into the food that lasts to eternal life. That food is given by the Son of man, a title Jesus uses for himself. The word "labour" means "work hard" or "strive," and the word "sealed" means that the Father has marked him out or given him his approval as his sent one.

Jesus speaks to the crowd that followed him across the lake after he multiplied the loaves. He points out that they are looking for him because they had their fill of bread, not because they understood what the signs showed. They answer by asking what they must do, and Jesus says that the work of God is to believe in the one he has sent.

Today we can ask ourselves what we seek first from God: his blessings or himself. This week set aside a fixed time to read the Gospels and to trust in Jesus, not only to ask him for things.
exp.0:9:
This verse says that Jesus, the Word of God, was in the world. Although the world was made through him, people did not recognize him. The word "knew" here means to recognize who he was, not merely to know that he existed.

John, the author of the gospel, presents Jesus as the true light. He has just mentioned John the Baptist, who came to testify about that light. The apostle John wants to show that, although Jesus is the Creator, many did not accept him. The next verse explains that his own people also rejected him.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we recognize Jesus in our everyday lives. Sometimes we live so busy that we pay him no attention. We can set aside a few minutes each day to pray, read his Word, and receive him with an open heart.
exp.10:22:
Jesus answers Martha with a simple promise: "Thy brother shall rise again." The word "saith" is an old form that simply means "says." Jesus speaks in the future tense and leaves the promise open, without yet explaining when or how it will happen.

Martha is grieving because her brother Lazarus has died, and Jesus arrived when he had already been in the tomb for days. She expresses both pain and an incomplete faith: she trusts Jesus, but she does not imagine what he is about to do. She understands his words as a hope for the last day. Jesus will use that moment to reveal himself as the resurrection and the life.

For today: when grief makes you feel that it is already too late, remember that Jesus is not limited by our timing. Bring him your sorrow honestly and trust that his promises are firm, even when you do not yet understand how he will fulfill them.
exp.8:13:
This verse gives us a very important detail: Jesus healed the blind man on the Sabbath. It says that Jesus made clay, probably with earth and saliva, and with that he opened the man's eyes, that is, he gave him back his sight. The Sabbath is the weekly day of rest for the Jews.

Here the narrator, John, speaks. He makes this clear because the Sabbath was a day when Jewish law and traditions prohibited certain kinds of work. Making clay could be seen as work. That is why the Pharisees, when they learned of it, began to question Jesus and were divided among themselves.

For today: sometimes we focus so much on rules and customs that we fail to see the work of God. Let us ask for a humble heart, so that we can rejoice when God does good, even when it comes in a way we did not expect.
exp.15:31:
Jesus says that the time has already come when his disciples will be scattered, each one going to his own place, and will leave him alone. But he makes clear that he is not really alone, because the Father is with him. "Scattered" means dispersed, separated from one another. Where the verse says "Behold," it is like saying "look" or "pay attention."

Jesus speaks with his disciples the night before his arrest. They have just said that they believe in him, and Jesus answers with a question: "Do you now believe?" He warns them that their faith will soon be tested, for they will run away when he is arrested. Even so, he does not reject them. He speaks to them so that they may have peace and trust, because he has overcome the world.

For today: when we fail or feel alone, we can remember that Jesus does not let us go, even when we hesitate. We can return to him with confidence, seeking his peace and leaning on the presence of the Father.
exp.12:24:
This verse tells that the disciple whom Jesus loved, who was reclining next to Jesus at the supper, leaned back toward his chest and asked him quietly: "Lord, who is it?" "Leaning back on the chest" describes the posture at the table in those days, when people ate reclining, very close to one another.

It is the Last Supper. Jesus had just said that one of the twelve would betray him. Peter, unable to ask directly, motioned to this disciple to find out who it was. Tradition holds that it is John, although the text does not give his name. Jesus answers with the gesture of the piece of bread dipped and given to Judas.

For today: when you have doubts or fear, draw near to Jesus with confidence and ask him sincerely. He is not bothered by the honest questions of someone who is close to him.
exp.3:15:
Jesus tells the Samaritan woman to go and get her husband and come back with him. The word "call" means "call him" or "tell him to come," and "here" is the same as "come here." The forms with the accent and the "come here" style are the old spelling and style of this translation.

Jesus has just offered her a water that gives eternal life, and she asks for that water. Then He touches a very personal point in her life. Many believe He does this to show her that He knows her story and to lead her to be honest, not to humiliate her. Interpreters understand it in several ways, but the conversation continues with tenderness and truth.

For today: Jesus knows our whole life and still invites us to come close. Before receiving His help, we can speak to Him honestly, without hiding anything. His truth does not seek to destroy us, but to heal us.
exp.17:14:
After Jesus was arrested, Simon Peter followed him at a distance, along with another disciple. That other disciple was known to the high priest, which is why he could go in with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest's house. Here "high priest" is the term used for the chief priest.

John, the narrator, tells what happened that night. Jesus was first taken to Annas and then to Caiaphas. It is not known for certain who the other disciple was; many think it was John himself, though the text does not say so. This account sets up the scene where Peter denies Jesus.

For today: following Jesus is easier when everything is going well. When pressure comes, we need humility and dependence on God. Ask him today for the courage to be faithful to Christ, even when it costs you.
exp.5:55:
He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood dwells in me, and I in him, Jesus says. "Dwells" means staying, living united with someone in a constant way. It is a promise of close and mutual fellowship.

Jesus speaks in the synagogue at Capernaum, after feeding the crowd. The people were looking for bread for the stomach, and he presents himself as the bread of life sent by the Father. Eating and drinking is an image of believing in and receiving Christ fully. Christians have understood this in different ways: some see it as a reference to the Lord's Supper, others as an image of faith, and many see both.

For today: do not come to Jesus only when you need something. Seek to be with him every day, in prayer and in his Word, as one who feeds steadily.
exp.11:0:
It says that Jesus arrived in Bethany six days before the Passover feast. Lazarus lived there, the man Jesus had raised from the dead.

Bethany was a village near Jerusalem.

The one speaking is the evangelist John, who tells the events as a narrator. This scene opens the final days of Jesus before his crucifixion. John recalls that Lazarus had been raised to show that Jesus has power over death. The supper and the act of Mary that come right after take place in that atmosphere of gratitude and of growing threat against Jesus.

For today: just as Lazarus sat at the table with Jesus, we can show gratitude by sitting with Him in prayer and in reading His Word, remembering what He has done in our lives.
exp.9:10:
Jesus says that he is the good shepherd, and that this shepherd gives his life for the sheep. The word "good" here speaks of someone genuine and excellent, not merely kind. "Gives" means that he lays down his life willingly, out of love and not out of obligation.

Jesus speaks to a group of Pharisees and ordinary people, after healing a blind man and after the religious leaders had rejected him. He has just said that he is the gate and that he came to give life in abundance. Now he presents himself as the shepherd who truly cares, unlike the leaders who took advantage of the people, and unlike the hired hand who runs away at the first sign of danger.

Today, you can trust that Jesus cares for you with complete love. When you feel alone or insecure, pray and remember how much he has already shown your worth. Also, imitate him: care for others without seeking only your own benefit.
exp.3:19:
Here the Samaritan woman says that her ancestors worshipped on "this mountain," which is Mount Gerizim, and that the Jews claim the right place to worship is Jerusalem. "You say" means "you say," and "is necessary" means "ought."

Jesus has just shown her that he knows her life, and she recognizes him as a prophet. So she raises an old debate between Samaritans and Jews about where worship should take place. Perhaps she wanted to steer the conversation away from her personal life, although the Bible does not say so. Jesus will answer that what matters will not be the place, but worshipping the Father.

For today: let us not keep arguing over secondary differences, such as places or styles, when God invites us into a sincere relationship with him. We can draw near to God anywhere, with an honest heart.
exp.7:16:
Jesus says that in their law it is written that the testimony of two men is true. "Your law" refers to the law of Moses, which the Pharisees knew well. The idea is that a matter is considered firm when two witnesses confirm it (see Deuteronomy 19:15).

Jesus speaks with the Pharisees in the temple, in Jerusalem. They had told him that his testimony about himself was not valid (John 8:13). He answers using their own law: his testimony is not alone, for the Father who sent him also testifies about him. Some scholars discuss how exactly this argument should be understood, but the central idea is clear.

For today: truth does not rest on the opinion of a single voice, not even our own. Before drawing conclusions, let us seek confirmation in the Bible, in wise counsel, and in humble prayer.
exp.4:46:
Jesus asks a question to get his hearers to think. "Writings" refers to what Moses wrote, that is, the first books of the Bible. Jesus says: if you do not trust what Moses wrote, how are you going to trust what I tell you?

Jesus speaks with religious leaders who criticized him for healing on the Sabbath and for saying that God was his Father. They said they trusted Moses and the Scriptures. Jesus explains to them that Moses wrote about him, so rejecting him showed that they had not truly believed what Moses said.

For today: it is not enough to know the Bible or to respect it in words. If we read it sincerely, it will lead us to Jesus. Today you can read a passage from the Old Testament and ask yourself: how does this show me Christ, and what change does it ask of me?
exp.9:8:
Jesus says that he himself is the door. Whoever enters through him will be saved, that is, rescued and kept safe. The phrase about going in and out describes a secure and free life, like sheep that come and go without fear. The phrase about finding pasture speaks of nourishment and care. The word "shall" shows a promise for the one who trusts in him.

Jesus speaks to a group of Pharisees, after healing a man born blind and after they had thrown him out. He explains, using the image of shepherds, that they had been poor guides, and that he is the true way to God. The thieves and robbers are the false leaders who take advantage of the people.

For today: when you feel lost or tired, do not look for security in things that promise much and do not give peace. Come to Jesus simply, trust him, and let him feed you with his Word and his company each day.
exp.12:8:
Peter says to Jesus, "Lord, not only my feet, but also my hands and my head." Earlier he had refused to let Jesus wash his feet, but now he wants to be washed completely.

We are at the Last Supper. Jesus has just washed the feet of his disciples, a servant's task. Peter had resisted, but Jesus told him that without this washing he would have no part with him. Peter swings from one extreme to the other: from refusing to asking for more. Jesus will answer by speaking of a deeper cleansing, and of the fact that one of them was not clean.

Today, we can learn to receive with humility what Christ does for us, even when we do not fully understand it. Peter wanted to do it his own way, but Jesus invites us to trust him and to let ourselves be cleansed every day.
exp.18:25:
Here it says that Jesus, hanging on the cross, saw his mother Mary and, standing beside her, the disciple whom he loved, who is traditionally identified with John. Jesus speaks to his mother and says "Woman," a respectful way of addressing someone at that time. With "behold thy son" he points to the disciple.

Jesus is speaking in his final hours. Although he is suffering greatly, he is thinking about the care of his mother. The verses that follow show that he asks the disciple to receive her as a mother, and the disciple takes her into his home. Many understand that, being a widow, she needed someone to look after her. Some also see a gesture of forming a new family of faith.

For today: look at who God has placed near you and care for them with concrete actions. Even in the midst of your own burdens, you can show practical love to your family or your community.
exp.9:7:
Jesus says that everyone who came before him as supposed guides of the people were "thieves and robbers," that is, people who took advantage of the sheep. Where the phrase "robbers" appears in the verse, it means raiders or plunderers. But the sheep, the faithful people, did not follow them or listen to them.

Jesus speaks to some Pharisees after healing a blind man (chapter 9). They had thrown that man out. Jesus has just said that he is the door of the sheep. He does not condemn God's prophets, but the false leaders who sought their own gain. Scholars agree on this, though they debate exactly who is meant.

For today: learn to recognize the voice of Jesus by reading his Word. In this way you will be able to tell apart those who lead you to use you from those who lead you to true life.
exp.5:27:
The people who were listening to Jesus ask him what they must do to carry out "the works of God." "To work" means to do or practice, and "they said to him" is what they said to him. They understood that Jesus was asking them to make an effort, and they want to know what kind of work pleases God.

These are the crowd who had eaten the bread multiplied the day before. Jesus had just told them not to work only for food that perishes, but for the food that lasts to eternal life. They answer by thinking about merits and tasks, and Jesus will explain to them that the work of God is to believe in the one he sent.

Today we often think we gain God's favor through effort and good deeds. This question invites us to reconsider that: before doing anything for God, let us trust in Jesus. From that trust the good works later grow.
exp.14:21:
Jesus says that if he had not come and spoken to them, they would not be guilty in the same way. But he has already come and spoken, so they have no cloak for their sin. The word "cloke" in the verse means a covering used to hide something or to defend oneself. It does not say that they had no sin before, but that their rejection is now more serious because they have come to know the truth.

Jesus speaks to his disciples the night before his crucifixion. He warns them that the world will reject them, as it rejected him. Those who heard his words and saw his works, and yet hated him, also rejected the Father.

For today: the light we have received brings responsibility. It is not enough to hear the Word of God; we must respond to it with humility and obedience. And if we face rejection for following Christ, let us remember that he has already experienced it.
exp.7:44:
Jesus says that precisely because he tells the truth, they do not believe him. It is a surprising statement: one would normally expect people to believe someone who speaks the truth. But Jesus explains that they are used to lies and, for that reason, the truth is uncomfortable for them. The word that appears in the following verse means to accuse or to show someone to be guilty.

Jesus speaks with some Jewish leaders in the temple, in the middle of a very heated debate. They claimed to be children of Abraham and of God, yet they rejected Jesus. He shows them that their rejection reveals where their heart is inclined. This harsh language was spoken in a specific debate, and we should read it with care.

For today: examine yourself with humility and ask whether you ever reject a truth only because it makes you uncomfortable or corrects you. Ask God for a heart willing to listen, even when it hurts.
exp.9:6:
Jesus repeats firmly what he is teaching. "Verily, verily, I say unto you" means "I assure you, it is true." He says: "I am the door of the sheep." "Then said Jesus unto them again" means "he said to them once more." The door is the way by which the sheep go in and out safely.

Jesus is speaking to some Pharisees, after healing the man born blind (chapter 9). They had not understood the parable of the shepherd and the sheep, so Jesus explains it with another image. He is the only true access to God and to the care of the flock. The verses that follow speak of salvation, freedom, and nourishment.

For today: you do not need to earn God's favor by your own efforts or search for many paths. You can come to Jesus with confidence, speak to him today in prayer, and rest in knowing that he receives you and cares for you.
exp.6:6:
Jesus says that the world cannot hate his brothers, but it does hate him. The reason is that he testifies, that is, he openly declares, that the works of the world are evil. "Hate" here means to despise and reject with strong feeling, and "world" in this passage refers to those who live turned away from God.

Jesus speaks with his brothers, who still did not believe in him. They urged him to go up to the Feast of Tabernacles in Jerusalem and show himself publicly. He explains to them that his time, the moment set by God, has not yet come. They did not trouble the world, but the truth that Jesus spoke did.

For today: speaking the truth in love can bring rejection, and that does not mean we have failed. Let us ask God for courage and humility to speak with kindness, without seeking a fight or applause.
exp.20:13:
He says this was the third time Jesus showed himself to his disciples after he rose from the dead. "Showed himself" means he let himself be seen clearly. The word "to" appears in the verse as written.

The one speaking here is John, the author of the Gospel. He notes this detail at the end of the scene of breakfast by the lake, where Jesus had already given bread and fish to his friends. He is referring to the times Jesus appeared to the disciples when they were gathered together, since other passages record more appearances. After this moment, Jesus will speak with Peter and restore him.

For today: Jesus comes back again and again to seek out his own. If you feel far away or have failed, do not be afraid to draw near. He receives you, feeds you, and gives you a new chance to follow him.
exp.16:21:
Jesus says that he has given his disciples the glory that the Father gave him. The purpose is that they may be one, that they live united, just as Jesus and the Father are one.

Jesus speaks in prayer to his Father, shortly before he is arrested. He prays for his disciples and also for those who would believe later through their message. He wants their unity to be so visible that the world believes the Father sent him. Some think the "glory" refers to his presence and his character; others, to future honor. The text allows for both ideas.

Today, seek unity with other believers. Work to forgive quickly, listen with respect, and serve alongside those who think differently on secondary matters, so that your life shows the love of Christ.
exp.16:17:
Jesus says that his Father sent him into the world, and that in the same way he sends his disciples. The word "sent" speaks of a mission: they are in the world not by chance, but with an assignment received from God.

Jesus is praying to his Father the night before his arrest, in what is known as his high priestly prayer. He prays for the eleven disciples who are with him. He has just said that they are not "of the world," that is, they do not share its values opposed to God, and he asks that the Father sanctify them, that is, set them apart for his service, through his word of truth.

Today, this reminds us that our work, family and neighborhood are places of mission. We do not have to escape the world, but to live in it with the truth of God, with love and with humility, as Jesus did.
exp.11:18:
The Pharisees said to one another that their efforts were getting them nowhere. "You are gaining nothing" explains the phrase "you are gaining nothing" in the verse. With "the world has gone after him" they exaggerate to say that a huge number of people were following Jesus.

This happens right after Jesus enters Jerusalem, when the crowd welcomes him with palm branches. Those who had seen the raising of Lazarus kept telling what had happened, and that drew more people. The Pharisees speak among themselves, frustrated, because they wanted to stop Jesus and could not. Soon after, some Greeks also want to see him, as if his words were being fulfilled in an unexpected way.

For today: sometimes it bothers us to see God at work and others receiving blessing. We can examine our hearts, avoid envy and pride, and rejoice when people draw near to Christ.
exp.7:55:
Jesus says that Abraham, the ancestor of the Jewish people, greatly rejoiced in looking forward to Christ's day, and that in some way he saw it and was filled with joy. The phrase "my day" refers to the coming and the work of Jesus.

Jesus speaks to Jewish leaders who claimed to be children of Abraham, yet rejected him. He tells them that Abraham did believe in what God promised. Scholars explain in several ways how Abraham "saw" that day: through faith, in a promise, or in heaven. The Jewish leaders mock him, and Jesus answers that he existed before Abraham.

Today we can rejoice to see fulfilled what others only hoped for. Take a moment to thank God for Jesus, who is present in your life.
exp.7:49:
Jesus says that He is not looking for people to praise Him or give Him honor. He says there is Someone who does care about His glory, and who is also the one who judges. The phrase "there is one that seeketh" refers to His Father, as seen in the previous verse.

Jesus is speaking in the temple with Jewish leaders who have just insulted Him, saying that He is a Samaritan and that He has a demon. He does not defend Himself to gain prestige. He leaves His cause in the hands of the Father, who knows the truth and will judge with justice.

When we are criticized or misunderstood, we do not have to spend our lives defending our image. We can live with honesty, seek to please God, and entrust the rest to Him, because He sees everything and judges with justice.
exp.4:43:
Jesus asks how it is possible to believe when a person lives seeking the applause of others and does not care about God's approval. "Glory" here means honor, recognition, or good reputation. "Receive" means accept or take in. Jesus points out that this pursuit of human honor gets in the way of faith.

Jesus speaks with religious leaders of Jerusalem, after healing a man on the Sabbath. They rejected him, even though he came in the name of the Father. He tells them that they do not have the love of God and that their own Scriptures, written by Moses, speak of him.

For today: examine what truly moves you. Ask yourself whether you are seeking to please God or to look good in the eyes of others. Ask him to give you a sincere heart, one that values his approval more than applause.
exp.5:0:
This verse says that, after what was told before, Jesus went over to the other side of the Sea of Galilee, which is also called the Sea of Tiberias. The word "went" is an older way of saying it. The "Sea" is the lake of Galilee, which was large, like a small sea. Tiberias was a nearby city, and the lake took another name from it.

Here the narrator, the apostle John, marks the start of a new scene. Soon after comes the crowd and then the miracle of the loaves and the fish. John does not explain why Jesus crossed the lake. The text that follows only says that many people followed him because they saw the signs he did for the sick.

For today: Jesus moved with purpose, even when others followed or sought him. We can ask him to guide us in each step, even when we do not understand the whole road, and trust that he knows where he is leading us.
exp.0:12:
It says that the children of God are not born through family inheritance (blood), nor through human effort (the will of the flesh), nor through the decision of another person (the will of man). Their new birth comes only from God. The explanation also notes that the word "born" in this verse refers to being brought into life.

The apostle John speaks here as he begins his Gospel. He has just said that many rejected Jesus, but that those who received him were made children of God. With this verse he makes clear that this privilege does not depend on lineage, as some believed, but on the work of God.

For today: you do not need to earn God's affection or rely on your family, your church, or your merits. Receive Jesus with simple faith and rest in the fact that God himself gives you a new life. And give thanks, because this is a gift.
exp.7:54:
Jesus says that his hearers do not know God, although they claim that he is their God. He, on the other hand, does know him. He states that to deny it would be to lie, as they lie when they say they know him. "Keeping his word" means that he obeys what the Father says. "Liar" here refers to the one who asserts something false about God.

Jesus speaks in a tense argument with Jewish leaders in Jerusalem. They doubt his authority and compare him with Abraham and the prophets. Jesus answers that his honor comes from the Father, not from himself. Later he will say that Abraham rejoiced to see his day.

Today, knowing God is not only saying that we believe in him, but obeying his word. This week, choose one command of Jesus that you have set aside, such as forgiving or speaking the truth, and begin to practice it sincerely.
exp.3:8:
The Samaritan woman is surprised that Jesus, who is a Jew, asks her, a Samaritan, for water. She explains why it surprises her: "the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans," meaning that they normally had no contact and shared nothing with them.

Jesus is tired beside the well, and his disciples have gone to buy food. Between Jews and Samaritans there was an old religious and cultural hostility. Besides, he is speaking with a woman, and that was also uncommon at that time. Even so, Jesus breaks through those barriers to offer her something much greater: living water.

For today: Jesus draws near to people others avoid. We can ask him to help us set aside prejudices and take the first step toward someone different from us, with respect and kindness.
exp.7:56:
The Jews answer Jesus with astonishment and mockery: "You are not even fifty years old, and you say you have seen Abraham?" The word "said" in the verse means "they said to him." The word "still" is the one used in the verse's phrasing. They understood that Jesus was speaking of having known Abraham in person.

Jesus had just said that Abraham rejoiced to see his day. The Jewish leaders, who were arguing with him, thought in human terms: age. They did not grasp that Jesus was speaking of something greater. So he answers them at once: "Before Abraham was, I am," words that many understand as a declaration that he is eternal and divine. That is why they wanted to stone him.

Today, when something of God seems impossible to us, let us avoid measuring it only by what we understand. Let us ask for humility to listen to Jesus as he is, not as we imagine him.
exp.18:11:
From then on Pilate tried to set him free, but the Jews cried out, "If you let this man go, you are no friend of Caesar. Anyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar." They said that anyone who makes himself a king goes against Caesar. The word "tried" here means he was making an effort, and "set him free" means letting him go free.

Pilate was the Roman governor, and he felt that Jesus did not deserve to die. The Jewish leaders, seeing this, changed their accusation and made it a political one. "Friend of Caesar" was a title of loyalty to the emperor, and losing it could cost Pilate his position. In this way they pressured him through fear.

For today: we often know what is right, but the fear of losing something holds us back. Ask God for the courage to do what is right, even when it costs us.
exp.2:31:
This verse says that Jesus tells what he has seen and heard in heaven, that is, he speaks from what he knows firsthand. Yet, even so, almost no one accepts what he says. The word "testifies" means to give testimony, to affirm something one has witnessed.

The one speaking is John the Baptist, answering his disciples, who were worried because many people were now following Jesus. John feels no envy: he says that Jesus must increase and he must decrease. For this reason he stresses that Jesus comes from above and speaks with authority. Scholars understand "no one" as an exaggerated expression to show that only a few were receiving him.

Today, we can ask ourselves whether we are really listening to Jesus or only hearing opinions about him. A good practice is to read a passage from the Gospels each day, with the attitude of someone receiving a trustworthy testimony.
exp.7:30:
Jesus speaks to some Jews who had believed in him. He tells them that if they continue in his word, that is, if they hold firmly to what he teaches and put it into practice, then they will truly be his disciples.

Jesus is teaching in Jerusalem. He had just spoken about his oneness with the Father, and many believed in him. But he shows them that believing at first is not enough; true faith is proven by perseverance. Later in the passage, we notice that some resist what he says, which shows that not everyone had the same depth of faith.

For today: it is not enough to have believed one day or to feel spiritual emotion. A good practical step is to read a passage from the Gospels each day and ask yourself, "What can I obey today?" In this way your faith grows steadily.
exp.17:5:
He says that when Jesus answered "I am," those who had come to arrest him drew back and fell to the ground. The phrase about drawing back is explained as meaning they moved backward. The phrase about falling to the ground means they fell down onto the floor.

This is John's account of Jesus's arrest in the garden. Jesús knew what awaited him and still stepped forward himself. He spoke to the soldiers and guards who had been sent with Judas. Some think that "I am" recalls the divine name of the Old Testament; others see only their astonishment at his authority. John makes clear that Jesus was in control: no one took his life from him by force.

For today: even when everything seems out of control, Jesus remains Lord. We can trust him in the middle of trials, knowing that he is not taken by surprise and that he cares for us.
exp.1:18:
Jesus tells the Jewish leaders to destroy this temple, and that he will raise it up in three days. "Raise it up" means "build it up again" or "make it stand again." The words "told them" and "they said to him" are older forms of "said to them" and "asked him."

Jesus had just driven out of the temple in Jerusalem those who were selling animals and exchanging money. The leaders asked him for a sign that would prove his authority. He answered with a mysterious statement. They thought he was speaking of the building, but the evangelist later explains that he meant the temple of his body, that is, his death and resurrection.

For today: our faith rests on a Jesus who overcame death. When you face losses or painful endings, trust that he knows how to raise up again what seems destroyed.
exp.7:40:
Jesus tells them that they do the works of their father, without yet naming him. They answer: "We be not born of fornication," that is, they say they are not illegitimate children nor children of doubtful faith, and they declare that they have one Father, God.

Jesus speaks with some Jews who said they believed in him, but who were seeking to kill him. They relied on their descent from Abraham. Jesus shows them that being family of Abraham is not enough if their actions do not resemble the faith and obedience of Abraham. Some think their words hint at a mockery about Jesus' birth, but the text does not make this clear.

Today, it is not enough to say "I am a believer" or to have a good religious heritage. Our actions and attitudes show whom we truly follow. We can ask God to examine us with sincerity.
exp.3:32:
The disciples were asking one another whether anyone had brought Jesus something to eat. The phrase "Hath any man brought him ought to eat?" means "Has anyone brought him something to eat?" They had gone into town to buy food, and when they came back they heard him say that he had food they did not know about.

The disciples are speaking among themselves. Jesus had just been talking with the Samaritan woman at the well. They understood his words in a literal way, thinking only of physical hunger. Jesus was speaking of something deeper, and in the next verse he explains it: his food is to do the will of God.

Often, like the disciples, we focus only on what is material and overlook what God is doing. Today you might ask yourself: what opportunity is God placing before me, in a conversation or in someone's need, to love and to serve?
exp.11:26:
Jesus says that his soul is "troubled," that is, deeply stirred and distressed. He asks himself what he should say, and he considers asking the Father to save him from this hour, the time of his suffering and death. But he quickly recognizes that this is exactly why he came.

Jesus is speaking in Jerusalem, a few days before the cross. He has just taught that whoever gives up their life out of love for God will keep it forever, and that his followers will walk that same path. His anguish shows that he was truly human. Even so, he ends by asking the Father to glorify his name, and the Father answers from heaven.

It is normal to feel fear or anguish before a difficult trial. You can tell God honestly what you are feeling, as Jesus did, and then ask him for strength to follow his will with confidence.
exp.12:6:
Jesus tells Peter that he does not yet understand what Jesus is doing, but that he will understand it later. The word "hereafter" points to a future moment, when everything will become clear.

Jesus speaks with Peter during the Last Supper. He has taken the role of a servant to wash the feet of his disciples. Peter is surprised and questions him, because it seems unfitting to him that his Master should do that work. Many understand that Jesus is teaching humility and also foreshadowing his work of cleansing on the cross, although the text does not explain everything here.

Today, when we do not understand what God allows or does in our lives, we can trust that He is good. Perhaps later we will see His purpose. In the meantime, we can obey Him with humility.
exp.0:45:
Nathanael doubts and asks whether anything good can come out of Nazareth.

Philip had just found Jesus and wanted to share it with his friend Nathanael. He told him that Jesus was the one about whom Moses and the prophets wrote. Nazareth was a small town, and it is not known for certain why Nathanael looked down on it; perhaps it was local prejudice, or perhaps it was because the town is not mentioned in the Scriptures. Even so, Jesus received him with kindness.

When someone has doubts about Jesus, there is no need to win an argument. We can simply invite them to read the Gospels, to come with us to church, and to get to know Jesus for themselves. And if you have doubts, you can come to him honestly.
exp.12:27:
No one at the table understood why Jesus told Judas, "What you are doing, do quickly." The explanation of that verse's wording does not carry over to the King James version your reader sees, so that comment is omitted here.

This is the last supper. Jesus knows that Judas is going to betray him, and he gives Judas the bread dipped in the sauce, a gesture that some understand as a final sign of closeness. John, who tells the scene, explains that the disciples thought Judas was going to buy something for the feast or give to the poor, because he kept the money bag. Jesus is not caught by surprise; he acts with full knowledge and control.

For today: sometimes we do not understand what God is doing while it is happening. We can trust that he sees what we cannot see, and ask him to make us attentive and humble so that we do not judge in haste.
exp.5:4:
This verse tells us that Jesus lifted up his eyes and saw a large crowd coming toward him. Then he asked Philip where they could buy bread to give all those people something to eat. Some old words: the quoted word "saw" in the verse above is the same word, and "these" refers to the people in the crowd.

Here Jesus is speaking, and he is addressing Philip, one of his disciples. The next verse explains that he asked this to test him, since Jesus already knew what he was going to do. Passover was near, and the people were following Jesus because of the signs he performed. Philip answers by thinking about money, and not about what Jesus could do.

For today: when you face a need that seems too big, do not think only about what you have. Bring it to Jesus with confidence, because he can use trials to teach you to depend on him.
exp.3:20:
Jesus tells the Samaritan woman to trust his word: a time is coming when worship of the Father will no longer be tied to this mountain or to Jerusalem.

Jesus is talking with a Samaritan woman at the well. She recognizes him as a prophet and raises the old dispute: the Samaritans worshiped on their mountain, and the Jews worshiped in Jerusalem. Jesus does not enter that argument but takes it further: what matters is not the place, but knowing the Father and worshiping him as he desires.

For today: you do not need a special place, a temple, or a perfect setting to draw near to God. Right now, at home, at work, or on the road, you can speak to him sincerely, because the Father seeks hearts that worship him in truth.
exp.2:26:
John the Baptist says that a person cannot receive anything, whether a gift, a task, or a success, unless God grants it. The word "heaven" here refers to God himself. "Anything" means any blessing or responsibility.

John's disciples were worried because Jesus was baptizing and people were going to him instead of to John. They seemed to be jealous. John answers with humility: his mission came from God, and so did Jesus'. He then compares himself to the friend of the bridegroom, who rejoices when he hears the bridegroom's voice.

Today we can learn not to compare ourselves with others. If someone receives more recognition or success than we do, we can rejoice and trust that God gives each person their place and their calling.
exp.18:7:
This verse says that Pilate, the Roman governor, became even more afraid when he heard what the Jewish leaders had said. "Saying" here means what they had just said: that Jesus "made himself the Son of God." Pilate already felt fear before; now that fear grows.

The chief priests wanted Jesus to die, but they needed Pilate to authorize it. Pilate had already said that he found no fault in Jesus. When he heard that Jesus presented himself as the Son of God, Pilate became troubled. The Bible does not explain in detail everything he thought, so we do not know exactly what he feared; some believe he felt a religious fear, others that he was worried about making an unjust decision.

For today: when we feel uneasy about doing something unjust, let us not ignore it. Let us ask God for courage to do what is right, even when it costs us.
exp.15:21:
Jesus tells his disciples that they now feel sorrow, but that he will see them again. Then their hearts will be filled with joy, and no one will be able to take that joy from them. The first sentence of the quoted phrase in the source refers to "you" as a plural group, and the word "see" appears in the verse as "see you again."

Jesus speaks on the last night before his crucifixion. He announces that he is going away and that they will weep, while the world will rejoice. He uses the image of a woman giving birth: the pain is real, but it passes in the face of the joy of the child. Many understand "I will see you again" as referring to the resurrection; others also think of his return or of the work of the Spirit.

For today: when you go through moments of sorrow, remember that they are not the final word. You can weep honestly and, at the same time, rest on Jesus' promise that the joy he gives is firm and does not depend on circumstances.
exp.3:33:
Jesus says that his "food," that is, what sustains him and gives him strength, is to do what God his Father wants and to bring to completion the work he was entrusted with. "The one who sent me" is the Father. "Finish" means to carry it through to the end.

Jesus has just spoken with a Samaritan woman at a well, and he has given her hope. The disciples return with food and worry that he has not eaten. Jesus uses food as an image: just as the body needs bread, his life is nourished by carrying out God's mission, which includes reaching people like this woman.

For today: ask yourself what truly sustains you. This week, look for one concrete action, even a small one, to obey God, such as helping or speaking with someone, and you will see that obeying also gives strength.
exp.9:11:
Jesus describes a hired hand, that is, someone who looks after the sheep only for pay. Since the sheep are not his own, when he sees the wolf coming he abandons them and runs away. Then the wolf attacks them and scatters them. The word "catcheth" means that it seizes them and carries them off by force.

Jesus speaks in John 10, after healing the man born blind, and he addresses some Pharisees who had treated him harshly. He presents himself as the good shepherd who gives his life for the sheep. Many understand that the hired hand represents leaders who do not truly care for the people, although the text gives no names.

For today: if you lead, teach, or care for others, do it with love and not only out of duty or for gain. And if you feel unprotected, remember that Jesus does not abandon you when difficulties come.
exp.14:26:
Jesus tells his disciples that they too will speak about him. "Ye" here means "you," and the phrase about bearing witness means that they will tell what they have seen and experienced. The reason is that they have been with Jesus from the beginning, that is, from the start of his public ministry.

Jesus speaks on the night before his crucifixion, preparing his friends for the world's rejection. He has just promised that the Spirit of truth will testify about him. Now he adds that the disciples will do so as well, and this is why their voice carries special weight: they are direct witnesses to his words and works.

Today we did not see Jesus walk through Galilee, but we can still tell what he has done in our lives. Simply and without boasting, we can share our experience with him, trusting that the Spirit accompanies our words.
exp.2:29:
It says that Jesus must become more and more important, more known and more honored, while the one speaking must take up an ever smaller place. The word "must" in this verse is the key idea, meaning that this is what is necessary and right. "Decrease" means to become less, to grow smaller. It is like the daylight growing while the light of a lamp loses its importance.

The one speaking is John the Baptist. His disciples told him with concern that Jesus was baptizing and that many were going to him. John felt no envy. He explained that he was only the friend of the bridegroom, the one who rejoices when he hears the bridegroom's voice. His mission was to prepare the way, not to be the center.

Today we can ask ourselves whether what we do seeks our own applause or that others come to know Jesus. A practical way is to sincerely rejoice when someone else is recognized or helps another person, and to give Christ the credit for the good that God does through us.
exp.5:5:
This verse explains why Jesús asked Philip a question. To test him means to put him to the test, to examine his faith. And the phrase "he himself knew what he would do" means that Jesús already knew what He was going to do. The question did not come from doubt, but from a purpose.

The one speaking here is John, the author, who explains in the voice of the narrator what was in Jesus' heart. A great crowd was coming toward Him, and Jesús asks Philip where they could buy bread. Philip answered by thinking about the money and about what seemed impossible. Afterward Jesus fed everyone with the little that was there.

For today: when God allows a situation that is beyond us, He may be inviting us to trust, not to calculate. Before you lose heart over what you lack, remember that Jesus already knows what He will do, and you can ask Him to teach you to look to Him.
exp.2:1:
Nicodemus went to see Jesus during the night. He addressed him as "Rabbi," which means teacher, and acknowledged that Jesus had come from God. His reason was that no one can perform the "signs" (the miracles) that Jesus was doing unless God were with him.

Nicodemus was a Pharisee and a member of the Jewish council. He came at night; some think it was out of fear of his colleagues, others that he wanted a quiet conversation. The Bible does not make this clear. He speaks with respect, but his faith is still incomplete: he sees Jesus as a teacher sent by God. Jesus, in response, takes him deeper and speaks to him about the new birth.

For today: it is not enough to admire Jesus or to recognize that he did good things. Come to him sincerely, even with your doubts, and let yourself be guided toward a deeper faith.
exp.5:62:
It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh by itself is of no use. This verse says that only God's Spirit can truly give life. The phrase about the flesh means that what is merely human, on its own, cannot give us eternal life. Jesus adds that his words are spirit and they are life.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples after saying that they must eat his flesh and drink his blood. Many were offended and grumbled, because they understood it in a literal way. He makes clear to them that what matters is not the physical but what the Spirit does through his words. Some Christians see here a symbolic explanation, and others do not; there is discussion about how this relates to the Lord's Supper.

For today: do not rely only on human effort. Read the words of Jesus every day and ask the Spirit to make them life for you.
exp.18:14:
The leaders and the crowd shout loudly: "Away with him, away with him, crucify him!" Pilate asks them with irony: "Shall I crucify your King?" The chief priests answer: "We have no king but Caesar," that is, the emperor of Rome.

Pilate is sitting on the judgment seat, in the place called the Pavement. It is the day of preparation for the Passover. He knows that Jesus is not guilty, but he gives in to the pressure. The priests, by saying this, reject Jesus as King and also set aside their hope in God as their true King, something very serious for the people of Israel.

For today: it is easy to say "I have no king but..." my work, my comfort, or the opinion of others. Today we can ask ourselves what occupies the place of Jesus in our heart, and put Him first again.
exp.0:43:
Here the verse says that Philip was from Bethsaida, the town of Andrew and Peter. Bethsaida was a town by the Sea of Galilee.

Here John tells how Jesus began gathering his first followers. Jesus had just said to Philip, "Follow me." John notes where Philip came from, perhaps to show that these men already knew each other and were neighbors. The text does not explain more, so we do not know whether that connection influenced Philip's decision. Right after this, Philip goes and finds Nathanael to tell him what he has found.

God often reaches us through people close to us: neighbors, friends, family. Think about who lives near you and might need a simple invitation. Like Philip, you can say, "Come and see."
exp.17:33:
Jesus answers Pilate with a question. He wants to know whether Pilate is saying this on his own, that is, from what he himself thinks, or whether he is only repeating what others have told him about Jesus. The word "or" in the verse is the form used in the King James Version, and it is what this question turns on.

Pilate, the Roman governor, had just asked him: "Art thou the King of the Jews?" The Jewish leaders had brought Jesus before him so that he would condemn him. With his question, Jesus does not avoid anything: he leads Pilate to consider whether he speaks from his own inquiry or from accusations made by others. In this way he prepares his answer about his kingdom.

Today we can also ask ourselves what we think of Jesus. Do we believe in Him because of what we have examined and experienced, or only because of what others have told us? It is good to listen to others, but it is wise to come to Jesus personally, read the Gospels, and pray with sincerity.
exp.7:17:
Jesus says that he himself bears witness to who he is, and that his Father, who sent him, also bears witness about him. So there are two who testify. The word "bear" means to present or declare. "Sent me" means that the Father commissioned him to come into the world with a mission.

Jesus is speaking in the temple with some Pharisees who are questioning him. They said that his testimony was not valid because it came from him alone. Jesus answers with the law of Moses, which required two witnesses to confirm something. He affirms that he is not alone, for the Father is with him. They, however, did not know the Father.

For today: if we want to know God, we should look to Jesus with an open heart. Ask God to help you recognize him in his Word and to trust what he says.
exp.0:46:
Jesus sees Nathanael coming toward him and says of him, "Here comes a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit." The words "saw" and "saith" are older forms of "saw" and "says." "Deceit" means falsehood or duplicity; Jesus is speaking of a sincere man without hypocrisy.

Philip invited Nathanael to meet Jesus, although Nathanael hesitated because Philip was from Nazareth. Even so, he went. Jesus speaks first and praises his honesty. Nathanael is surprised that Jesus knows him, and when Jesus tells him that he saw him under the fig tree, Nathanael confesses that he is the Son of God. We do not know for certain what Nathanael was doing under the fig tree; the text does not explain it.

We can come to Jesus with sincerity, even with doubts. He knows us completely and values an honest heart. There is no need to pretend before God: we can speak to him with openness.
exp.19:16:
Jesus says to Mary Magdalene: "Touch me not," that is, "do not cling to me," because he has not yet ascended to the Father. He asks her to go to his brothers, the disciples, and tell them that he is ascending to his Father, who is also their Father, and to his God, who is also their God.

Mary has just recognized him when he spoke her name, and she is filled with joy. Jesus speaks with her and gives her a mission. Some believe she was holding on to him out of fear of losing him again. Others explain it in a different way, and there is no single agreed opinion.

Jesus invites us not to stop at simply feeling his closeness, but to carry his message to others. Today you can tell someone, simply, the hope you have received.
exp.6:14:
The explanation says that the Jews were amazed when they heard Jesus teaching. They wondered how he could know so much of the Scriptures and of religious teaching if he had never studied with a recognized teacher. The word "marvelled," which appears in the verse above, means "were amazed."

We are at the Feast of Tabernacles, in the middle of the week. Jesus goes up to the temple and begins to teach openly, although many had been speaking about him quietly out of fear. Those speaking here are the leaders and the people of Jerusalem. His wisdom surprises them because he had no training in the schools of the rabbis. Jesus answers that his teaching comes from God, who sent him.

For today: let us not measure the value of a teaching by the titles of the one who gives it, but by whether it agrees with the Word of God. Let us ask God for a heart willing to obey, for Jesus says that in this way we will recognize the truth.
exp.13:19:
Jesus says that "on that day" his disciples will understand something very deep: that he is in the Father, that they are in Jesus, and that Jesus is in them. "You will know" here means to understand through experience, not merely to know a fact. It is a union of life and love.
