Jesus speaks with his disciples the night before his crucifixion, and they are sad and afraid because he is leaving. He promises them that they will not be left as orphans and that he will send the Spirit. "That day" probably points to the resurrection and the gift of the Spirit at Pentecost, though some also see it as something ongoing.

For today: do not live your faith only through rules or your own effort. Begin the day by remembering that Christ is with you and in you, and ask him for guidance in each decision.
exp.9:14:
Jesus says that his knowledge of the sheep is like the knowledge that exists between him and the Father: it is close and personal. He also affirms that he lays down his life for them. In this older version, "lay down" means "give up" or "give", and "sheep" are those who belong to him and follow him.

Jesus speaks to a group of leaders and people from Jerusalem, and presents himself as the good shepherd. He contrasts himself with the hired hand, who runs away when danger comes because he does not truly love the sheep. Jesus, by contrast, does not run away: he gives himself willingly. This anticipates his death, which he himself later explains as a free giving, not as something taken from him.

For today: you can trust that Christ knows you from the inside, with your fears and your failures, and still loves you. When you feel alone or of little worth, remember that someone gave his life for you. Respond by listening to his voice and following him each day.
exp.6:23:
Jesus says: do not judge by appearance, that is, by what is seen at first glance. Rather, judge with a right and just judgment, one that seeks the truth.

Jesus speaks in Jerusalem, during the Feast of Tabernacles. Some were criticizing him because he had healed a man on the Sabbath. He points out their inconsistency: they circumcised on the Sabbath and saw no fault in that. He asks them to look at the heart of the matter: he had restored a person to complete health.

Today, before we form an opinion about someone or something, let us stop to ask, listen, and learn the facts. If we judge only by what seems to be, we can be mistaken and hurt others.
exp.17:26:
Peter denied Jesus for the third time. Right after that, the rooster crowed. In the verse, "then" means "immediately," so the denial and the crowing are presented as happening one right after the other.

John tells what happened while Jesus was being questioned in the house of the high priest. Peter was outside, warming himself by the fire. A servant, a relative of Malchus, asked him whether he had seen him with Jesus in the garden. Peter was afraid and denied it. The crowing of the rooster fulfilled what Jesus had told him earlier: that he would deny him three times.

All of us can fail out of fear, even when we are sincere in our love for Christ. If you have failed, do not stay hidden in shame. Peter's account reminds us that Jesus knows our weakness and that, afterward, He restored Peter. Return to Him with humility.
exp.7:51:
The Jews react with anger to what Jesus said. Now, they say, they are sure that he has a demon, meaning that he is out of his mind, or possessed. Their reason is that Abraham died, and the prophets too, but Jesus claims that whoever keeps his word will never see death. Seeing death means experiencing it.

Jesus was speaking with Jewish leaders who doubted him. They understood his words only as physical death, and so they seemed absurd to them. Jesus was speaking of a deeper life, eternal life with God. His claim led them to wonder who he thought he was.

Today, the words of Jesus invite us to trust him beyond what we are able to understand. Keeping his word means believing it and obeying it each day. If something he says is hard for you, do not reject it right away; instead, ask God for humility to listen to him.
exp.14:3:
Jesus invites his disciples to remain united with him, and he promises that he will remain in them. To "abide" means to stay, to remain. A branch is a part of the vine, and "bearing fruit" means producing grapes, that is, a life that reflects Christ. A branch cannot bear fruit on its own; it bears fruit only when it is joined to the vine. The same is true for us.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the night before his arrest, after the Last Supper. He is preparing them for his absence and teaching them that their spiritual life will depend on staying connected to him, not on their own strength.

For today: set aside a moment each day to pray and read the Bible, not out of obligation, but to stay close to Jesus. Before making decisions or facing the day, say to him: "Lord, without you I can do nothing."
exp.8:38:
Jesus says that he came into the world for judgment, that is, so that it becomes clear who truly receives the light. Those who do not see and admit it will be healed; those who see, that is, those who think they know everything, will be blinded, shut off from the truth.

Jesus speaks after healing a man who was born blind, a man who has just believed in Him and worshiped Him. Some Pharisees, who had rejected Him, listen and feel that they are being pointed out. Jesus is speaking of spiritual blindness, not physical blindness: their pride kept them from recognizing their need.

Today we can ask ourselves with humility: in what area do I think I already know everything? Recognizing our need before God opens the door to his light. Let us ask him every day: "Lord, open my eyes."
exp.3:11:
The Samaritan woman asks Jesus whether he is greater than Jacob, the ancestor who gave us the well. Jacob himself drank from it, and so did his sons and his livestock. The words "gave" and "herds" mean "gave" and "flocks" in the original wording, though your verse above already uses the English words. She thinks Jesus cannot offer anything better than that well.

The woman of Samaria is speaking beside the well at Sychar, where Jesus has asked her for water. She takes the talk of "living water" literally, and so she compares Jesus with Jacob, who was highly respected by the Samaritans. Without knowing it, she raises the key question: who is Jesus? He will answer that his water satisfies thirst forever.

For today: sometimes we hold on to what has always been, such as tradition or custom, and we doubt that Jesus can give us anything more. Today you can bring him honestly your thirst for peace, forgiveness, or meaning, and trust that he can give you more than you imagine.
exp.17:6:
Jesus asks them again: "Whom seek ye?" And they answer: "Jesus of Nazareth." The word "seek" is the one the verse uses, and "asked he them again" means he asked them the question once more. "Of Nazareth" shows that Jesus came from Nazareth.

We are in the garden, on the night of his arrest. Jesus speaks with the soldiers and the officers who had come with Judas. He had just said "I am," and they had fallen to the ground. By repeating the question, Jesus makes clear that he gives himself up of his own will and asks that they let his disciples go. In this way he protects his own.

For today: Jesus placed himself between danger and his friends. If he cared for them in his most difficult hour, we can entrust our fears and our loved ones to him, knowing that he cares for us.
exp.10:48:
This verse introduces Caiaphas, who was high priest that year. He speaks up in a meeting of leaders and tells them bluntly: "Ye know nothing at all," meaning that they do not understand the situation or see the solution.

The chief priests and the Pharisees were alarmed because Jesus had just raised Lazarus, and many were believing in him. They feared that Rome would react and take away their place of power. Caiaphas speaks harshly and proposes getting rid of Jesus. Without knowing it, his words ended up expressing something much deeper, as John explains right after.

For today: God can carry out his plan even through people with bad intentions. If you find yourself facing injustice or decisions you do not understand, trust that God is still at work. And examine your own heart, so that the fear of losing something does not keep you from recognizing Jesus.
exp.11:47:
Jesus says that whoever rejects him and does not receive his words already has a judge: the very words he has spoken. Those words will be the measure on the last day, the final day, when God judges.

Jesus speaks at the close of his public ministry, in Jerusalem, to people who had seen his signs and still doubted. He has just said that he came to save, not to condemn. He adds that his words are not his own but come from the Father who sent him. So rejecting them is rejecting God himself.

For today: do not take lightly what Jesus says. Read a passage from the Gospels slowly and ask yourself: "What is Jesus asking of me today, and how can I obey him with confidence in his grace?"
exp.16:4:
Here Jesus asks the Father to glorify him, that is, to publicly restore to him the honor and splendor that are his as God. "Close to yourself" means in the Father's presence. Jesus says he had that glory "before the world was," that is, before creation.

Jesus speaks in prayer, shortly before he is arrested. He has already said that he finished the work the Father gave him. Now he asks to be received back into his glory, and right after this he prays for his disciples. Many Christians see here the teaching that Christ existed before creation and is one with the Father.

For today: Jesus prayed with confidence and clarity, knowing why he came. We can do the same: finish faithfully what God entrusts to us, and trust that he sustains us even in difficult times, with hope in his final glory.
exp.13:0:
Jesus says: "Let not your heart be troubled," meaning that they should not let their hearts fill with anguish or fear. Then he adds: "ye believe in God, believe also in me." This can be understood either as a statement ("you already believe in God") or as an invitation ("believe in God"); in both cases, Jesus asks them to trust in him just as they trust in God.

Jesus speaks with his disciples during the Last Supper, shortly before he is arrested. He has just told them that he is going away and that Peter will deny him. They are sad and confused. That is why Jesus comforts them with the promise that he is preparing a place for them and will come back for them.

When fear or uncertainty unsettle you, stop and speak to Jesus honestly. Remember what he has promised, and choose to trust him one day at a time, even when you do not understand everything.
exp.7:57:
Jesus says that before Abraham was, he "is." Notice that he does not say "I was," but "I am," in the present tense. With this he affirms that he has existed from forever. The phrase "Verily, verily" means "I assure you in all truth." Where the explanation quotes the words for "was" and "were," the wording in the verse above is "was," so those comments are rewritten below.

Jesus speaks with Jewish leaders who question him. They do not understand how he could have seen Abraham, who lived centuries before. Many understand that "I am" recalls the name God gave himself in Exodus 3:14, and that is why they wanted to stone him, since they saw it as a claim to be equal to God.

For today: if Jesus is eternal and stands above time, we can trust him in the midst of our uncertainties. Today, bring to him in prayer something that worries you, remembering that he already knows your future and walks with you.
exp.13:20:
Jesus says that the one who truly loves him is the one who holds his commandments and keeps them, that is, receives them and puts them into practice. That person is loved by the Father, is loved by Jesus, and Jesus will reveal himself to them, which means making himself known and real in their life. The explanation of the old wording is not needed here, since the verse above already uses the words "manifest myself," which convey this same meaning.

Jesus speaks with his disciples at the Last Supper, shortly before his death. He is preparing them for his absence and promises that they will see him again and that the Spirit will be with them. Judas (not Iscariot) asks how he will reveal himself to them and not to the world.

Today, love for Jesus shows itself in concrete obedience. Choose one of his teachings, such as forgiving or being honest, and practice it this week, trusting that he will become more real in your life.
exp.3:45:
So Jesus went back to Cana in Galilee, the town where he had earlier turned the water into wine. Close by, in Capernaum, there was a royal official, a man who served the king (probably Herod Antipas, though the text does not say so). His son was sick.

Here the narrator, John, speaks. He sets the scene for the second sign Jesus would perform in Galilee. He recalls the first miracle at Cana to show that Jesus was already known there. The Galileans had welcomed him because of what they had seen in Jerusalem, but Jesus knew that a faith based only on miracles is weak.

When our need overwhelms us, we can come to Jesus as this father did. He does not stay far from a family's pain. Let us ask him for help, but also learn to trust him for who he is, not only for what he does.
exp.5:66:
Jesus asks his twelve closest disciples whether they also want to leave. The explanation of the word "want" and the word "leave" has been removed here, since those words do not appear in the verse as your readers see it. It is a sincere question, with no pressure or reproach.

Jesus had just taught hard things about himself as the bread of life. Many who heard him did not accept it and stopped following him. Then Jesus turns to the twelve and asks them. Peter answers that they have nowhere else to go, because only Jesus has words of eternal life. This shows that following Jesus is a free and personal decision.

Today, when some part of the faith costs us something or we do not understand it, we can pause and answer that same question honestly. Instead of pulling away, let us go to Jesus with our doubts, trusting that only he has words of life.
exp.20:16:
Jesus asks Peter a third time whether he loves him. Peter is hurt because of the repeated question, and he answers by appealing to Jesus' knowledge of all things, including his heart. Jesus replies: "Feed my sheep," meaning take care of them and nourish them like a shepherd. "Peter was grieved" means "Peter felt sad."

Jesus speaks with Peter after his resurrection, by the lake, after they have eaten together with his disciples. Peter had denied him three times the night of the arrest. Many understand that the three questions restore him and give him back his place, although the text does not state this so directly.

For today: love for Jesus is shown in caring for others with patience. If you have failed, He does not discard you; He calls you again. Think of one person you can encourage or serve this week.
exp.6:40:
The verse shows that the people were divided. Some said, "This is the Christ," meaning the promised Messiah. Others doubted and asked, "Shall Christ come out of Galilee?"

This happens in Jerusalem, during the Feast of Tabernacles. Jesus had just spoken about living water, and the crowd was reacting. Those who doubted were thinking about Galilee, where Jesus grew up, and they remembered that Scripture points to Bethlehem as the place of the Messiah. They do not seem to have known that Jesus was born in Bethlehem, something the text here does not make clear.

For today: before rejecting Jesus on the basis of partial ideas, it is wise to investigate with humility. We can ask God to show us the full truth and read his Word with an open heart.
exp.15:23:
Jesus tells his disciples that up to that point they had not asked for anything in his name. Now he invites them: ask, and you will receive. The purpose is that their joy be full, complete, filled up.

Jesus speaks on the last night with his disciples, before the cross. They are sad because he is leaving. He promises that they will see him again and that no one will take away their joy. He teaches them that, after his resurrection, they will have a new and direct access to the Father, asking in the name of Jesus, that is, united to him and to what he is.

For today: when you pray, do not do it with fear or distance. Bring your needs to the Father with confidence, in the name of Jesus, and seek his will and his joy more than just quick answers.
exp.11:23:
Jesus uses the image of a grain of wheat. If the grain is kept and not planted, it remains alone, without multiplying. But if it falls into the ground and dies, that is, it is buried and stops being a whole grain, it sprouts and produces much fruit.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples, shortly before his arrest. They have just been told that some Greeks wanted to see him. He answers that the time of his glorification has come, and with this image he announces that his death would bring abundant fruit. Many believers understand here a reference to the salvation of many people.

For today: God often gives fruit when we give up something of our own, such as time, comfort, or pride, out of love for him and for others. Today you can ask yourself what you could plant generously.
exp.19:1:
Here Mary Magdalene sees that the stone has been taken away, and she runs to tell Peter and the other disciple, whom Jesus loved, whom almost everyone takes to be John. She tells them that they have taken the body of the Lord and that they do not know where they have laid him.

María speaks out of pain and confusion. It is still dark, and she is not yet thinking about the resurrection; she assumes someone moved the body. So she runs to find the two disciples, and they go at once to the tomb, as the next passage tells.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening and feel that everything is dark, do not stay alone with your anxiety. Seek out other believers, tell them what worries you, and go together to look for the truth. God often reveals himself to those who keep seeking.
exp.18:28:
This verse tells us that there was a jar there full of vinegar. The soldiers soaked a sponge in that vinegar, put it on a branch of hyssop (a small plant), and held it up to Jesus' mouth. The word "filled" carries the sense of "packed full," and "á" is simply the "a" we use today.

John, who was close to the cross, is the one who tells the story. Jesus had just said, "I thirst," and John explains that he said it so that the Scripture would be fulfilled. Many believe this refers to psalms such as Psalm 69:21, although the text does not quote one in particular. Vinegar was a cheap, common drink among the soldiers.

Jesus knew human suffering in his own body: he experienced thirst, weariness, and anguish. When you go through times of pain, you can speak to him with confidence, because he understands you. You can also help someone who is suffering with a simple gesture, such as a cup of water or a kind word.
exp.14:24:
Jesus says that the rejection he suffers was already foretold in the Scriptures. "Their law" refers to the Hebrew Bible in general, not only the first five books. "Without a cause" means without a just reason. They hated him even though he had done them no wrong. The word "but" introduces the contrast, and "hated" is the verb that describes their attitude toward him.

Jesus speaks with his disciples the night before his arrest. He is preparing them for the rejection of the world. He explains that the hatred against him does not take him by surprise. Many think he is referring to passages such as Psalm 35:19 or Psalm 69:4, although the text does not make this clear.

If someone rejects you unjustly for following Christ, do not lose heart. Jesus went through the same thing and did not lose his way. Ask God for peace and answer with kindness anyone who treats you badly.
exp.10:41:
Jesus speaks with his Father and says that he already knew that the Father always hears him. Even so, he prayed out loud for the people who were there. The phrase "the people who stand by" here means the crowd, the people present. His aim was that they would believe the Father had sent him.

Jesus is standing in front of the tomb of Lazarus, his friend, who had been dead for four days. They have just taken away the stone. His prayer does not ask for a miracle out of doubt, but gives thanks in advance. He does it in public so that the witnesses understand that what is about to happen comes from God. Then he calls Lazarus, and he comes out.

For today: our prayer can be simple and confident, like Jesus', who spoke with his Father with assurance. Also, when we pray in front of others, we can do so with humility, to encourage their faith and not to show ourselves off.
exp.0:1:
This verse repeats and clarifies what the previous one just said: "The same," that is, the Word, already existed "in the beginning" and was with God. The word "Word" here refers to Jesus Christ.

The one speaking is the apostle John, who begins his Gospel by presenting who Jesus is. Before telling of his life on earth, John affirms that Jesus did not begin to exist in Bethlehem, but was with God from eternity. In this way he prepares the reader to understand that everything that follows, creation, life, and light, comes from him.

For today: if Jesus was with God from the beginning, we can trust that he knows the Father well and truly shows him to us. When you doubt what God is like, look to Jesus.
exp.0:31:
John the Baptist tells what he saw: the Spirit came down from heaven "like a dove" and remained on Jesus. The word "bare" in the verse means he gave testimony, and "abode" means it settled and stayed. The phrase "like a dove" describes how the descent looked; it does not say that the Spirit is a dove.

John is speaking here as a public witness to Jesus. God had told him that he would recognize the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit by this sign. In this way John confirms that Jesús is the Son of God, the expected Messiah, and presents him to Israel.

For today: Jesus does not act on human ideas alone, but with the backing of the Spirit. We can ask God to guide us by his Spirit in our daily lives, and, like John, we can also simply tell what we have seen of Jesus in our own lives.
exp.17:39:
The crowd shouted again with force: "Not this man, but Barabbas!" John makes clear that Barabbas was a robber. "They cried out" means that they shouted. The word "robber" can also refer to a bandit or a violent rebel.

Pilate had just said that he found no fault in Jesus. To release him, he offered them the custom of setting a prisoner free at the Passover. Those who shout are the people gathered in front of the governor's hall, including the Jewish leaders who were accusing Jesus. They choose a guilty man instead of the innocent one. John tells it soberly, and lets the injustice of the moment show through.

Today, it is easy to be carried along by the pressure of the crowd and to prefer what is comfortable or popular over the truth. Ask God for courage to choose Christ and to act justly, even when almost everyone around you is shouting something else.
exp.11:38:
This verse says that a certain group of people could not believe in Jesus. John explains it with another phrase from the prophet Isaiah, which continues in the next verse. The word "however" from the earlier context means "but," and "saying" refers to "message."

John, the author, is recounting that Jesus performed many signs (miracles) before the people, and yet many did not believe. To explain this, he quotes the prophet Isaiah, who centuries earlier spoke of the hardening of the people. Christians interpret this passage in several ways: some emphasize the action of God, others the voluntary hardness of the human heart. John shows that the unbelief did not take God by surprise.

For today: do not be discouraged if someone close to you does not believe, even when they see good things. Keep praying, loving, and being a good witness, and ask God to keep your own heart sensitive to his voice.
exp.5:41:
Here the people are puzzled by what Jesus said. They know him as "the son of Joseph," and they say they know his father and mother. That is why they cannot understand how he can claim, "I came down from heaven." The word "murmured" means they were complaining under their breath, with doubt and irritation.

The ones speaking are Jews from Galilee who had seen the bread multiplied. Jesus had just said that he is the bread that came down from heaven. They looked only at his human and family origin, and so they found it hard to believe that he came from God. Jesus answers at once that no one comes to him unless the Father draws him.

For today: let us not judge Jesus or other people only by what we already think we know. Let us ask God for a humble and open heart, so that we may listen with faith to what Jesus truly says.
exp.19:30:
It says that John wrote these signs with a clear purpose: that we may believe that Jesus is the Christ, that is, the promised Messiah, and the Son of God. And that by believing we may have life in his name.

Here John, the author, speaks as he closes his gospel. He has just told how Thomas doubted and then believed when he saw the risen Jesus. John makes clear that he did not write everything Jesus did, but what is needed so that readers, who did not see Jesus, can also believe.

For today: read the gospels not only to learn facts, but to know Jesus and trust him. When you read a story, ask yourself: what does it show me about Jesus, and how can I trust him more today?
exp.19:17:
Mary Magdalene went to where the disciples were and told them that she had seen the Lord. She also repeated to them what Jesus had said to her.

John is the one who recounts this. Mary had gone to the tomb weeping, and there the risen Jesus called her by her name. He charged her to tell the disciples that he was going up to the Father. She obeyed at once. Afterward, the account shows the disciples still living in fear, and Jesus himself appeared to them. Some scholars point out that she was the first to announce the resurrection.

Today, we can learn from Mary: when Jesus becomes real to us, it is not meant to be kept secret. Tell simply what he has done in your life, even when others doubt or are afraid.
exp.10:40:
They took away the stone from the place where Lazarus had been laid. Then Jesus looked up toward heaven and spoke with his Father. He gave thanks because he had heard him.

Jesus stands before the tomb of his friend Lazarus, who had been dead for four days. Martha was doubtful because the body already smelled bad. Jesus reminded her that whoever believes will see the glory of God. His prayer, said out loud, had a purpose: that those present would believe that the Father had sent him. Afterward he called Lazarus to come out.

Jesus gives thanks before he sees the result. Today we can do the same: speak to God with confidence, thank him for listening to us, and follow his guidance even when the situation seems impossible or hopeless.
exp.5:67:
Peter answers Jesus with a question of his own: "Lord, to whom shall we go?" He means that he sees no better option. He recognizes that Jesus' words give eternal life, that is, a life with God that does not end.

Peter speaks on behalf of the twelve apostles. Jesus had just taught hard things about himself as the bread of life, and many disciples had left. Then Jesus asked the twelve whether they also wanted to leave. Peter answers with sincerity and confidence.

For today: when faith becomes difficult or we do not understand everything, we can ask Peter's question. Instead of pulling away, let us draw closer to Jesus, read his Word, and speak with him honestly. Only in him do we find firm hope.
exp.4:13:
Jesus later finds the man he had healed, now in the temple. He reminds him that he is already well and tells him to sin no more. The reason given is so that nothing worse happens to him.

Jesus is the one speaking. The man had been ill for thirty-eight years by the pool of Bethesda, and Jesus healed him on the Sabbath. Jewish leaders questioned him for carrying his mat, and he did not know who had healed him. Jesus seeks him out so that he will come to know him. As for "something worse," it is understood in several ways: more serious consequences, or a greater spiritual harm. The text does not say that his illness was a punishment for a specific sin.

For today: when God gives us a new opportunity, let us respond with gratitude and with a life that honors him, without returning to what was harming us.
exp.7:27:
Jesus says that when the leaders lift up the Son of Man, they will understand who he is. "I am he" recalls the name God gives himself. He also affirms that he does not act on his own: he speaks what the Father has taught him.

Jesus speaks in the temple with religious leaders who doubt him and do not understand that he is speaking about the Father. "Lift up" probably refers to his crucifixion, and perhaps also to his exaltation; John uses that word in both senses. Jesus shows that his mission and his words come from the Father, who is with him. After this, many believed.

For today: imitate Jesus' attitude. Before you speak or decide, ask yourself whether you are seeking to please God and to listen to his word, not just to follow your own ideas.
exp.0:17:
It says that no one has seen God in his full essence. But Jesus, the only Son, is the one who makes him known to us. The phrase "only Son" means one of a kind, a beloved and special Son. "In the bosom of the Father" expresses closeness and complete intimacy. "Made him known" means that he explained him and revealed him.

John, the author of the Gospel, closes this introduction to his book (the prologue) with this verse. He has just said that the law came through Moses, and that grace and truth came through Jesus. Now he affirms that Jesus shows what God is really like. Afterward, the account moves on to the testimony of John the Baptist.

For today: if you want to know what God is like, look to Jesus. Read the Gospels and notice how he treats people, with compassion and truth. In this way you can trust that God is that close and that good to you.
exp.11:45:
Jesus says that he is the light that has come into the world. His purpose is that whoever trusts in him should not remain in darkness, that is, in the gloom of ignorance, sin, and separation from God.

Jesus speaks near the end of his public ministry in Jerusalem. After many signs, some still doubted. So he spoke out loud, to make it clear that believing in him is believing in the Father who sent him. He says that he did not come to condemn but to save, though rejecting his message has consequences.

For today: if there are dark areas in your life, such as fear, guilt, or confusion, bring them to Jesus in prayer and read his words with confidence. He does not seek you to condemn you, but to guide you.
exp.8:26:
Here the man who was once blind answers the Pharisees with a certain irony. He tells them that he already told them how he received his sight, but they did not want to listen. Then he asks them why they want to hear it again, and whether they also want to become disciples of Jesus.

The Pharisees are investigating the healing Jesus did on the Sabbath. They had already questioned the man and his parents. He, tired of the repeated questions, speaks with boldness. His question shows that they were not seeking the truth, but something with which to accuse Jesus. They react with anger and insults.

For today: Let us listen with an open heart when God speaks to us, without seeking only what confirms our own ideas. And if we have experienced the work of Jesus in our lives, we can testify with simplicity and courage, even when others do not want to listen.
exp.1:21:
What it says: After Jesus rose from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said that about the temple. Then they believed the Scripture and what Jesus had said to them. The old forms of two words are not in the verse, so the translation keeps only the meaning.

Context: It is the narrator, John, who is speaking. Jesus had just cleared the temple, and the Jews asked him for a sign. He answered, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." They thought of the building, but he was speaking of his body. The disciples did not understand at that time; they understood after the resurrection. It is not made clear which passages of Scripture John had in mind.

For today: We will not always immediately understand what God does or says. We can keep his word in our hearts with patience, trusting that he will give light in his time.
exp.3:25:
Jesus is talking with a Samaritan woman beside a well. She has just said that she knows the Messiah is coming and will explain everything to them. It is remarkable that Jesus reveals this so clearly to a woman from Samaria, whom many Jews looked down on. Some scholars note that the phrase "I am" also recalls how God presents Himself in other passages of the Bible, although here it is understood mainly as "I am the Messiah."

Today, Jesus still draws close to ordinary people, in the middle of their routines. You do not have to be perfect to speak with Him: you can be sincere and listen for His voice.
exp.5:68:
Peter speaks on behalf of the twelve disciples. He says that they believe and are sure that Jesus is the Christ, that is, the promised Messiah, and the Son of the living God. "Are sure" here means that they are convinced by what they have seen and heard with Him.

Jesús had just taught hard things, and many of his followers had left. Then he asked the twelve whether they too would want to leave. Peter answered with sincerity: there is no one else to go to, because only Jesus has words of eternal life. Even so, Jesus said that one of them would be betrayed by someone close, referring to Judas.

For today: when a teaching of Jesus costs you something or you don't understand it, don't walk away right away. Ask yourself, "Where else would I go?" and stay close to Him, trusting who He is.
exp.6:0:
This verse says that, after the events John has just recounted, Jesus continued traveling through the region of Galilee. He did not want to go to Judea, because the Jewish leaders were looking for a way to kill him. "Were looking for a way" means they were plotting or seeking to put him to death. "Walked" means that he went from one place to another, teaching and serving.

The one speaking here is the writer, John, who sets the scene for us. Shortly before, in John 5, Jesus had healed a man on the Sabbath and had said that God was his Father, and this angered the leaders in Judea a great deal. That is why Jesus keeps his distance from them, since his hour had not yet come.

For today: being prudent is not being a coward. Jesus trusted God's timing and did not throw himself into danger without need. We can ask him for wisdom to know when to move forward and when to wait.
exp.8:35:
Here the man who had been blind answers Jesus with a sincere question: "Who is he, Lord, that I might believe on him?" The word "Lord" here can be a respectful form of address, like "sir," although soon it becomes worship. He wants to believe, but he does not yet know whom he should trust with his faith.

Jesus had just healed him, and the religious leaders insulted him and threw him out of the synagogue. Jesus seeks him out and asks whether he believes in the Son of God. The man speaks openly and without pride, ready to follow whatever is revealed to him.

For today: you do not need to have everything figured out to come to Jesus. An honest question and a willing heart are a good beginning. When you feel rejected or confused, remember that Jesus also goes out to seek you.
exp.8:39:
The Pharisees who were near Jesus heard that some are made to see and others are made blind. Then they ask him, with a tone somewhere between annoyed and mocking: "Are we blind also?"

Jesus had just healed a man who was blind from birth, and that man believed and worshiped him. Jesus is speaking of spiritual blindness: those who recognize their need receive light, but those who think themselves wise close themselves off to the truth. The Pharisees understand that Jesus is talking about them, and they react defensively.

For today: ask God for humility to recognize what you still do not see clearly. Whoever admits their need receives light; whoever boasts of knowing everything closes themselves to change and to forgiveness.
exp.2:14:
This verse says that everyone who trusts in Jesus will not perish, but will receive eternal life. Perishing here means being separated from God forever. Believing here means trusting in Jesus, not merely accepting an idea.

Jesus speaks with Nicodemus, a Jewish teacher who visited him at night. Jesús reminds him of the story of the serpent that Moses lifted up in the desert (Numbers 21): whoever looked at it in faith was healed. In the same way, Jesus says that he himself would be lifted up, a reference that many understand as his death on the cross.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love through effort. You can come to Jesus just as you are and entrust him with your life, your fears, and your future. Today, tell him in prayer that you trust him.
exp.3:6:
This verse tells how a woman of Samaria came to the well to draw water. Jesus, who was sitting there, said to her: "Give me to drink." In the older wording of this edition, the small word for "to" is simply "to," and "draw water" means taking it out of the well with a bucket or jar.

Jesus speaks while tired from the road and close to midday, since the sixth hour is usually understood as twelve o'clock in the day. His disciples had gone away to buy food. Jews and Samaritans had a deep hostility, so the woman is surprised that Jesus speaks to her and asks her for a favor.

For today: Jesus broke down barriers with a simple request. We can ask ourselves whom we avoid because of prejudice, and take a simple step of respect and kindness toward that person, such as an honest conversation, without any sense of superiority.
exp.12:5:
This verse tells how Jesus, after washing the feet of the other disciples, came to Simon Peter. Surprised, Peter asks him: "Lord, dost thou wash my feet?" The word "basin" in the context refers to a vessel or bowl for water.

We are at the Last Supper, shortly before the crucifixion. Jesus does the work of a servant, something that someone of his rank would normally never do. Peter speaks because he does not understand how his Master and Lord could humble himself in this way. His question shows respect, but also surprise. Jesus answers that he will understand later.

For today: sometimes we find it hard to receive help or accept God's love because we feel we do not deserve it. Let us learn to let Christ serve us with humility and, at the same time, to serve others with the same simplicity.
exp.1:1:
This verse says that Jesus and his disciples were also invited to the wedding.

The author, John, tells what happened in Cana of Galilee, where a wedding was being celebrated and Jesus's mother was already present. This is the first scene after Jesus gathered his first disciples. John presents Jesus in the middle of a family celebration, not in a religious setting. This detail prepares the account of the wine, which comes right after.

For today: Jesus accepted the invitation and shared in the joy of others. We can follow his example by joining the celebrations of family and friends, and letting our presence be kind and helpful to others.
exp.7:15:
Jesus says that, if he judges, his judgment is true or just. The reason is that he does not act alone: the Father who sent him is with him. The word "judge" refers to evaluating and giving a verdict.

Jesus speaks with some Pharisees in the temple, during a discussion about his identity. They were saying that his testimony was not worth anything because he spoke about himself. Jesus answers that they judge by outward appearances, that is, by human appearances, while he acts in unity with the Father. In the following verse he appeals to the law, which required two witnesses.

For today: before judging others, let us ask God for his perspective. Our judgments often rest on appearances or prejudices. If we seek the truth with humility and prayer, we can become more just, patient, and compassionate.
exp.1:24:
This verse says that Jesus did not need anyone to tell him what human beings are like, because he himself knew them from within. The phrase "testify of" means to report or give information about someone. "Man" here refers to people in general.

The speaker is John, the writer of the Gospel, who comments on what was happening in Jerusalem during the Passover feast. Many believed in Jesus when they saw his signs, but he did not entrust himself to that faith, because he saw their hearts. Some understand that it was a shallow faith, based only on miracles.

For today: Jesus knows us completely, with our struggles and our motives. We do not have to pretend before him. We can pray with sincerity, ask him to cleanse our hearts, and seek a faith that truly follows him, not only when we see results.
exp.19:18:
The explanation says that on the same day of the resurrection, as evening came, the disciples were gathered behind closed doors because they feared the Jews. Suddenly Jesus arrived, stood in the middle of them, and said to them: "Peace be unto you."

The account in John tells this. That day Mary Magdalene had already told them she had seen the Lord. Even so, the disciples remained afraid, since the authorities had put Jesus to death. He greets them with the common greeting, "peace," but with a deep sense of calm and reconciliation. Then he shows them his wounds and sends them out.

For today: when fear shuts you in, remember that Jesus can come to where you are and give you his peace. Bring your fear to him honestly and trust that he is with you.
exp.5:70:
This verse makes clear who Jesus was speaking about when he called one of the twelve a "devil." He meant Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon. The text explains that Judas was the one who would betray him, even though at that moment he was still one of the twelve. To "betray" means to hand someone over to his enemies.

Here John the writer speaks as the narrator. Peter had just confessed that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God. Jesus answers that he himself chose the twelve, but that one of them was a "devil," that is, someone who worked in the service of the enemy. John adds this note looking back, when he already knew what Judas had done.

For today: being close to the things of God is not the same as having a faithful heart. Let us examine our hearts with humility and ask God to keep us sincere before him.
exp.12:0:
Shortly before the Passover, the explanation says, Jesus knew that the time had come for him to leave this world and go to the Father. Even so, his attention was on his own, his disciples. He had loved them, and he loved them to the end, a phrase that can mean until the last moment or also to the utmost, with complete love.

Here the last supper in the Gospel of John begins. The narrator is John, who presents Jesus as aware that his death is near. What follows is the washing of the feet, an act of service. John wants to show that the cross and that service spring from the same love, even with Judas's betrayal already underway.

For today: love consistently, even in your difficult days. When you are tired or worried, look for a concrete act of service toward someone close to you, as Jesus did.
exp.14:23:
Jesus says that he did among them works that no other man has done, such as healing the sick, giving sight to the blind, and raising the dead. If he had not done them, they would not be guilty of this sin. But they saw them and, even so, rejected both him and his Father. "Hate" here means to reject with hostility.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the night before his crucifixion. He warns them that the world will hate them, as it hated him. He explains that this rejection was not for lack of evidence, since the works spoke clearly. Then he announces that the Holy Spirit will bear witness to him.

For today: do not lose heart if someone rejects Jesus or rejects you for following him. Keep showing love and truth through your life, and trust that the Spirit can open the eyes of those who do not see today.
exp.14:5:
It says that whoever does not remain joined to Jesus is cast out, like a useless branch. That branch is the one that grows from the vine. The branch dries up, they gather it, and they burn it. It is a picture: a branch cut off from the vine has no life and bears no fruit.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the night before his crucifixion. He teaches them that he is the vine and they are the branches, and that all fruit depends on being joined to him. Christians interpret this fire in different ways. Some see a warning about losing salvation; others see people who seemed to be believers but were never truly joined to Christ. Both positions take the text seriously.

For today: look for a moment each day to pray and read the Bible, not as an obligation, but to stay close to Jesus, from whom comes life and fruit.
exp.11:6:
Jesus defends Mary, who has just poured a very costly perfume over his feet. He says to those who criticize her, "Let her alone." He explains that she has kept this perfume for the day of his burial. The sentence about the perfume's name and the coins has been removed, since those words do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

Jesus speaks in Bethany, six days before the Passover. Judas Iscariot had objected that the perfume could have been sold to help the poor, but the text makes clear that he was a thief. Jesus sees in Mary's gesture a preparation for his approaching death. Some think she did not fully understand this; the text does not say so.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we give Jesus the best of ourselves, without calculating too much. Loving God with generosity is not at odds with helping the poor; both come from a grateful heart.
exp.2:10:
Jesus tells Nicodemus, very earnestly, that what he teaches is not an opinion or a rumor. He speaks of what he knows and has seen. But Nicodemus and others do not accept that testimony. The word "witness" means to give solid proof of something as a witness does, and the word "receive" means to take in or accept what is said.

Jesus speaks with Nicodemus, a religious leader who came to him at night. He had just asked how someone can be born again. Jesus is surprised that a teacher of Israel does not understand. The "we" may refer to Jesus together with those who bear witness to God, and some interpret it in other ways.

Today, we can come to Jesus with humility, even if we already know a great deal about religion. Listening to his word with an open heart is the first step to believing and understanding.
exp.7:10:
The woman answers that no one has condemned her. Jesus tells her that he does not condemn her either, and asks her to go and sin no more. The word "no man" means "no one," and "go" is a gentle command: "go on your way."

The scribes and Pharisees had brought this woman, caught in adultery, to set a trap for Jesus. When he invited whoever was without sin to throw the first stone, they left one by one. Jesus and the woman were left alone, and he, who did have the authority to judge, offered her forgiveness and a fresh start. Some scholars point out that this passage does not appear in the oldest manuscripts, though many churches receive it as part of Scripture.

Today, God welcomes us with mercy, not contempt. His forgiveness does not leave us as we were: it invites us to leave sin behind and begin again.
exp.16:6:
Jesus says that the disciples have now understood something important: everything he has, his teachings, his authority, and his work, comes from the Father. The word "now" marks a step forward in their understanding. "Have known" means they recognized it with certainty, not merely by hearing about it.

Jesus is praying to his Father the night before his crucifixion, in what many call his priestly prayer. He speaks of the disciples whom the Father gave him. He showed them who God is, and they kept his word. This prayer presents them before the Father before Jesus departs.

For today: recognize that the good things you receive from Christ, his Word, his forgiveness, and his guidance, have their origin in God. This invites us to trust Jesus with greater confidence and to give him thanks every day.
exp.7:38:
The Jewish people say that their father is Abraham. Jesus replies that if they were truly Abraham's children, they would do what Abraham did. In this context, "works" means the actions and way of life.

Jesus is speaking with some Jews who were listening to him in Jerusalem. He acknowledges that they descend from Abraham, but they seek to kill him because his word finds no place in them. Jesus is referring to Abraham, who believed God and received his word. For this reason, a true relationship with Abraham is shown in obedience and faith, not only in bloodline.

For today: belonging to a church, having a Christian family, or using a religious label is not enough. Real faith shows in how we receive God's truth and in how we live. Today, ask yourself: which part of the Word is hard for me to accept and obey?
exp.18:27:
This verse tells us that Jesus, knowing that everything he had to do was now finished, said: "I thirst." It means he was very thirsty. John explains that he said this "that the scripture might be fulfilled," that is, so that what had been foretold in the Bible would come to pass.

He is the one speaking here, near the end of the crucifixion. He had just asked his mother and his beloved disciple to take care of one another. His thirst shows that he truly suffered as a human being. John does not say which exact passage he has in mind; many think of Psalm 22:15 or 69:21, but this is not certain.

For today: Jesus knows human tiredness and pain, because he lived through them. You can come to him with confidence in your needs, large or small, and remember that he faithfully finished the work the Father had given him.
exp.5:60:
Jesus knew without anyone telling him that his followers were complaining quietly about what he had just taught. He asks them, "Doth this offend you?" That is, does this make you stumble, or does it sit badly with you? The word "murmured" means they were grumbling under their breath.

Jesus was teaching in the synagogue in Capernaum. He had just said that he is the bread of life and that people must eat his flesh and drink his blood. Many disciples, not only the twelve, found it a hard saying. He does not take it back; he confronts them with kindness and with clarity. People read this teaching in different ways, but all agree that it demanded faith.

Today, when a teaching of Jesus makes us uncomfortable, it is best not to grumble or walk away. We can bring that doubt to him honestly, ask him for light, and keep listening to him.
exp.5:69:
Jesus reminds the twelve that he himself chose them, but he warns them that one of them is a "devil." In this verse the word does not mean that Judas is literally the devil; it means he acts like him, as an adversary or accuser.

Jesus speaks right after Peter declares his faith in him. Many disciples had already left because his teachings seemed hard. Jesus does not get carried away by the excitement of the moment, and he shows that he knows the heart of each one. John explains that he was referring to Judas Iscariot, who would later betray him.

For today: being close to Jesus or to the church is not the same as following him from the heart. We can ask God to examine our faith and keep us faithful, rather than judging others.
exp.16:9:
Jesus tells the Father that everything he has belongs to the Father, and everything that belongs to the Father belongs to him. He also states that he has been glorified in his disciples, meaning that they show and honor who he is. The idea of being "glorified" here means that he is recognized and given honor.

Jesus is praying to the Father the night before his crucifixion. He has just said that he is praying for his disciples, the ones the Father gave him. This statement shows the deep unity between the Father and the Son, and why Jesus can pray for them with confidence.

For today: if you believe in Jesus, your life can bring him honor. Today you can ask yourself: does my way of speaking, working, and treating others show Christ? Also, remember that you belong to those whom Jesus prays for and cares for.
exp.20:5:
Jesus, from the shore, tells the disciples to cast the net on the right side of the boat. They do as he says and catch so many fish that they are not able to draw the net in. Here "cast" carries the same sense as the verse above, and the small fishing boat is simply "the ship."

This takes place after the resurrection. The disciples had fished all night and caught nothing. Jesus speaks to them from the beach, but they do not yet recognize him. Afterward, John realizes that it is the Lord. Some think this miracle recalls the first great catch of fish they experienced with Jesus, although the text does not say so directly.

When we are tired and see no results, we can stop and listen to the voice of Jesus and obey him, even when his instruction seems simple. He knows what we do not see, and his word can open paths where we had already given up.
exp.4:9:
They said that some Jewish leaders confronted the man who had just been healed. They reminded him that it was the Sabbath and that, in their view, he was not allowed to carry his mat, that is, the mat or pallet on which he had been lying. "Allowed" means permitted by the law.

The ones speaking are the Jews, probably religious authorities. The man had been ill for thirty-eight years by the pool of Bethesda. The law of Moses commanded rest on the Sabbath, and over time many rules were added about what counted as work. They focused on the rule, not on the miracle. The man answered that the one who healed him told him to carry his mat.

For today: we can keep what God commands without losing sight of people. When someone receives help or improvement, let us first rejoice with them, and ask God to give us a compassionate heart and not only a demanding one.
exp.3:7:
This verse is a note from the narrator. It explains that Jesus' disciples were not there because they had gone into town to buy food. The old-fashioned spelling "á" is simply the older way of writing "a," and "de comer" means "food."

The author, John, tells us that Jesus, tired from the journey, sits down by Jacob's well in Samaria and speaks alone with a woman who has come to draw water. This detail explains why Jesus is alone with her. It keeps the scene vivid, since a difficult conversation between a Jew and a Samaritan woman is about to begin.

Today, we can notice that God sometimes works in quiet moments, in private, while others are busy with necessary tasks. Let us ask him to help us be attentive to the people he places in our path, even in the midst of everyday life.
exp.12:30:
Jesus says that now the Son of man is glorified, and that God is glorified in him. "Glorified" means shown to be of true worth and honored. "Son of man" is a title Jesus used for himself.

Jesus speaks with his disciples at the Last Supper. Judas has just left to betray him, and it was already night. With that departure, the road to the cross is set in motion. It is striking that Jesus speaks of glory at such a dark moment. John shows that the cross, with all its suffering, reveals the love and the plan of God. Some scholars emphasize the surrender; others, the resurrection that follows.

For today: when you go through a difficult night, remember that God can work even there. Entrust your situation to him with confidence, and ask that in it his love and his faithfulness may be seen, even though you do not yet understand how.
exp.6:3:
He says that no one who wants to be known publicly does their things in secret.

The brothers of Jesus are speaking before the Feast of Tabernacles. They ask him to go to Judea, where the disciples and many people were. But John makes clear that they did not yet believe in him. For this reason their words sound more like a challenge or irony than sincere faith. Jesus answers that his time had not yet come, since he was following the Father's plan.

For today: let us not follow the pressure of others to prove who we are. Let us seek to obey God with patience, trusting that he knows the right moment for everything.
exp.15:11:
Jesus says that he still has many more things to teach his disciples, but that for now they cannot bear them, because they are too heavy for them at this moment.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples on the night before his death. He has told them that he is going to the Father, and they are sad and confused. For that reason he does not tell them everything at once. He promises right away that the Spirit of truth will come and will guide them little by little into all truth, and that he will always glorify Christ.

God teaches us with patience and in his own time. Do not be anxious if you do not understand everything about your faith; follow Jesus, pray and read his Word, trusting that the Spirit will guide you step by step.
exp.13:3:
Jesus tells his disciples that they already know where he is going and the way to get there. The phrase "you know" stands in for the verse's wording, and "whither" is the same as "where," which appears in the verse above. "I go" refers to Jesus going to the Father.

Jesus speaks on the night before his crucifixion, during the Last Supper. The disciples are sad and confused because he has told them he will leave. Jesus wants to calm their hearts with the promise that he is preparing a place for them and will come back for them. Thomas answers that they do not understand, so Jesus makes clear that the way is not a place or a route, but himself.

For today: when you feel lost or without direction, remember that you do not need to know every detail of the future. It is enough to trust Jesus and stay close to him, because he already knows the way.
exp.4:27:
This verse says we should not be amazed at what Jesus has just taught. A time is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice. "Do not marvel" means "do not be amazed." "Tombs" are the graves where the dead are buried.

The speaker is Jesus, in a conversation with religious leaders who were upset because he healed a man on the Sabbath and said that God was his Father. Shortly before, he explained that the Father gave him life in himself and authority to judge. Now he adds that this authority will reach the dead, and the next verse speaks of a resurrection to life and another to condemnation.

For today: death is not the last word, because Jesus has authority over it. This invites us to live with hope, without fear, and to do good today, trusting that he is a just judge.
exp.17:24:
Simon Peter was standing and warming himself by the fire. Some people asked him whether he was one of Jesus' disciples, and he denied it, saying, "I am not." The word "high priest" here refers to the chief priest.

While Jesus was being questioned in the house of the high priest, Peter had followed him into the courtyard. The ones speaking are people who were there, perhaps servants and guards. This is the first of three denials that Jesus had foretold. Peter was afraid, and the contrast is strong: Jesus speaks the truth while being struck, and Peter keeps silent about the truth out of fear.

Today we too can feel pressure to hide our faith and to please others. If we fail, let us remember that Jesus forgave and restored Peter. Let us ask for courage and trust in his grace.
exp.15:6:
Jesus says he is speaking to them with complete honesty: it is good for you that I go away. If I do not go away, the Comforter will not come to you; but if I depart, I will send him to you. "Nevertheless" means "but," "Comforter" refers to the Holy Spirit, and "convict" in the following context means "convince."

Jesus speaks with his disciples at the Last Supper, shortly before his arrest. He has announced his departure, and they are full of sorrow. He explains that his going away is not a loss but part of God's plan: the Holy Spirit would be with them and would accompany them in a new way.

When something we love changes or ends, we can feel sadness and fear. This verse invites us to trust that God is still at work, even when we do not understand the moment. Today we can ask the Holy Spirit for comfort and guidance in what we are living through.
exp.9:15:
Jesus says he has other sheep that are not "of this fold," that is, of another pen. He affirms that he must also bring them, meaning it is necessary for him to lead them. They will hear his voice, and in the end there will be one flock and one shepherd. The words for "those" and "will hear" are understood in the same way today.

Jesus speaks to a group of Jews in Jerusalem and presents himself as the good shepherd who gives his life for his sheep. Many understand that the "other sheep" are the Gentiles, people from other nations, but the text does not say so in those words. What is clear is that his work would reach beyond Israel.

Today, we can remember that the church belongs to Christ, not to any one group, country, or culture. This week, approach with respect and affection a believer who is different from you, and listen together to the voice of the same Shepherd.
exp.4:29:
Jesus says that he does not act on his own authority, apart from the Father. When he speaks of judging, he means that he decides according to what he hears from the Father. That is why his judgment is right, meaning upright and correct. And when he says he does not seek his own will, he means that he does not pursue his own desires, but what the Father wants, the Father who sent him.

Jesus speaks in Jerusalem, after healing a man on the Sabbath. Some Jewish leaders were criticizing him for calling God his Father. He explains that his relationship with the Father is one of perfect unity: there is no rivalry, but obedience and trust. He has just spoken about the resurrection and the judgment, and he clarifies that this judgment will be fair because it is aligned with the Father.

For today: before deciding something important, ask God what he wants and not only what is good for you. Pray, read his Word, and seek wise counsel, with a willingness to obey.
exp.9:34:
Jesus says that Scripture called those who received the word of God "gods." This is a phrase from Psalm 82:6. He adds that the Scripture "cannot be broken," that is, it cannot be annulled or disproved.

The Jewish leaders wanted to stone Jesus because they thought that, being a man, he was making himself God. Jesus answers with an argument from the lesser to the greater: if the Bible used that title for men to whom God spoke, how can they accuse him of blasphemy, him whom the Father sent? Scholars debate who the psalm was referring to: human judges, or heavenly beings.

We can trust the Bible as firm and true. Before judging someone, it is wise to listen carefully to what God actually says, and not only to what we already think.
exp.2:34:
It says that the Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand. To have something "in his hand" means to be under his care and authority. Jesús has the Father's love and also the rule over everything.

These words close the testimony of John the Baptist, although some scholars think they could be a comment by the evangelist. His disciples were worried because many people were going to Jesus. John explains to them that Jesus comes from God, speaks the words of God, and that the Father fully backs him. That is why the next verse invites belief in the Son.

For today: if Christ has everything in his hand, you can entrust him with your worries, your future, and your doubts. What you do not control, he holds with love.
exp.5:58:
This verse is a brief note from the writer. It says that Jesus spoke the whole preceding discourse in the synagogue at Capernaum, while he was teaching. A synagogue was the place where Jews gathered to read the Scriptures, pray, and hear teaching.

The Gospel writer John is speaking, and the one teaching is Jesus. Before this, he had said that he is the bread of life and that whoever eats this bread will live forever. John tells us where it happened: in a public place of teaching, before Jews who knew the story of the manna. That is why many were offended, as the following verses show. Christians understand the meaning of "eat" in different ways, but almost all agree that it speaks of receiving Jesus himself.

For today: do not turn away from a teaching of Jesus just because it is hard. Stay with it, listen humbly, and ask God to help you understand it.
exp.4:11:
The Jewish leaders ask the man who had been healed: "Who was it that told you to take up your bed and walk?" The word "bed" refers to the mat or pallet where he had been lying. Notice that they do not ask who healed him, but who told him to carry it.

This happens after Jesus healed a man who had been sick for thirty-eight years by the pool of Bethesda. It was the Sabbath, and the leaders focused on the rule against carrying things on that day, according to their understanding of the law. They are the ones speaking here; the man did not yet know who had healed him.

For today: sometimes we fix our attention so much on the rules that we stop rejoicing in the good that God does. Let us ask for a heart that, when it sees the help and healing of others, first gives thanks and celebrates.
exp.4:6:
Here the sick man calls Jesus "Sir" and explains why he has not been healed. He has no one to help him into the pool when the water is stirred. "Troubled" means "stirred," and "while I am coming" means "while I am on my way." Always someone else gets down ahead of him.

The man speaking had been ill for thirty-eight years, beside the pool of Bethesda. Jesus asked him whether he wanted to be made well, and he answers with his problem rather than with a plain yes. Some older translations add a note about an angel who stirred the water, but many scholars believe it was added later. Jesus will heal him with his word alone.

For today: sometimes we focus so much on what we lack or on what has failed us that we forget Jesus is standing right before us. Tell him honestly what you need, and expect him to act, even if not in the way you imagined.
exp.16:23:
Jesus asks the Father that those who believe in him will one day be with him, where he is, so that they can see his glory. That glory is a gift from the Father, because the Father loved him before the foundation of the world, that is, before the world was created.

Jesus speaks on the night before his arrest, during his final prayer with the disciples, sometimes called the high priestly prayer. He prays for them and for those who will believe later. He asks for unity and protection, and he wants them to know the love that exists between him and the Father. Many understand "where I am" as God's presence after this life, although there is discussion about how to apply it exactly.

For today: if you belong to Christ, you are part of what he desired with all his heart. When you feel alone or insecure, remember that Jesus asked that you be with him. Spend a few minutes today giving thanks for that love and resting in that hope.
exp.5:65:
After hearing the teachings of Jesus, many of his followers left and stopped going with him. Where the explanation says "went back," it means they returned to their former way of life, and where it says "walked with him," it means they followed him closely.

Jesus had just said that he is the bread of life and that it was necessary to believe in him truly. Many had gone after him for the loaves and the miracles, and those words were hard for them. Jesus knew who did not believe from the heart. So he asked the twelve, and Peter answered that they had no one else to go to.

Today, when faith in Jesus is difficult or inconvenient for us, we can choose to stay with him, as Peter did, because only he has words of eternal life.
exp.15:18:
Jesus realizes that his disciples want to ask him something, but they do not dare to. So he asks them a question: whether they are discussing among themselves what he said about "a little while" and "you will not see me."

Jesus speaks with his disciples at the Last Supper, shortly before his death. He had told them that he was going to the Father, and they did not understand. Many believe he is referring to his death and resurrection, though some also see a reference to his final return. He responds to their confusion and promises that their sorrow will turn into joy.

Today we can bring our doubts honestly to Jesus. He already knows what confuses us, and he receives us with patience. When we do not understand what God is doing, we can trust that the difficult moment is not the end of the story.
exp.6:19:
The people answered and said, "You have a demon. Who is trying to kill you?" In the language of that time, saying that someone "had a demon" was a way of accusing him of being out of his mind or possessed. "Tries" means "seeks" or "attempts."

Jesus was teaching in the temple during the Feast of Tabernacles. He had just asked them why they wanted to kill him, since he had healed on the Sabbath (John 5). The ones who answer are people from the crowd, many of them visitors to the feast, who perhaps did not know the plans of the leaders. Some scholars think so; the text does not make this entirely clear.

When something makes us uncomfortable, it is easy to insult or discredit the one who says it. Let us rather listen with humility and let the Word examine our hearts.
exp.10:2:
The sisters of Lazarus, Mary and Martha, sent word to Jesus that their brother was sick. They address him as "Lord" and say "he whom you love," which shows that Lazarus was a dear friend of Jesus.

The sisters speak through a messenger, since Jesus was far away from Bethany. Notice that they do not ask him for anything directly: they simply tell him the situation and trust that he will understand and act. They rely on his love for Lazarus, not on Lazarus's own merits. Afterward Jesus says that this sickness would serve the glory of God.

When you are going through a need, you can do as they did: tell Jesus plainly what is happening, trusting in his love. No elaborate prayer is required. He knows how and when to respond, even though his response is not always the one we expect.
exp.5:54:
Jesus says that his flesh is real food and his blood is real drink. The word "real" shows that only he can truly satisfy the deepest need of the human being: eternal life. Just as the body needs food to live, the soul needs Christ.

Jesus speaks in Capernaum, after feeding the crowd with bread. He presents himself as the bread of life. Many were looking only for physical bread, and he invites them to trust him completely. Eating and drinking is a picture of believing and receiving him. Christians understand their relationship with the Lord's Supper in different ways, but all agree that Jesus is speaking of union with him.

Today, do not live by your own strength. Begin the day by seeking Jesus in prayer and in his Word, and trust him as your true sustenance.
exp.5:24:
This verse tells that the people found Jesus on the other side of the sea of Galilee. They said to him, "Rabbi," which means "teacher," and they asked when he had come there.

The speakers are the people whom Jesus had fed with the loaves and the fish. They searched for him by boat as far as Capernaum, because they no longer saw him. Their question seems curious, but Jesus does not answer about the when. He speaks to them about the reason for their search: they wanted more bread, not the Lord himself.

For today: examine why you seek God. It is natural to ask him for help with what you need, but do not stop at the benefits. Seek Jesus himself, for he gives the food that lasts forever.
exp.4:36:
Jesus says that the Father, who sent him, has borne witness of him. He then adds that his hearers have never heard the Father's voice or seen his shape, the word "shape" here meaning his outward appearance or form.

Jesus is speaking with some Jewish leaders who were questioning him for healing on the Sabbath and for calling God his Father. He reminds them that John the Baptist and his own works bore witness to him. Now he says that the Father himself does so as well. Interpreters understand this in different ways: some see in it Jesus' baptism, others the Scriptures, others the inner work of God. The next verse points to the Scriptures.

For today: having religion or knowledge about God is not enough. If we truly want to hear him, we seek him in his Word and are willing to believe in Jesus, whom he sent.
exp.0:23:
This verse says that the people who went to question John the Baptist belonged to the group of the Pharisees. "Were sent" means that someone else had sent them, and they were going on that person's behalf.

The one speaking is the evangelist John, who clarifies a detail of the account. Earlier, religious leaders from Jerusalem sent messengers to find out who John the Baptist was. The Pharisees were very attentive to the law and to tradition, and they cared about who had the authority to teach and to baptize. Some scholars think their interest was to keep watch, although the text does not state their exact motives.

Today we can learn to receive questions with humility and without fear. John did not speak about himself, but pointed to Jesus. When someone asks us about our faith, let us try to answer with simplicity, pointing to Christ and not to ourselves.
exp.8:17:
This verse says that the Jewish leaders did not want to believe that this man had been blind and now could see. So they called his parents to confirm it. The word "But" at the start of the verse introduces the contrast, and "received his sight" means that he was able to see.

Jesus had just healed the blind man on the Sabbath. The Pharisees were divided: some said Jesus did not come from God, and others wondered how a sinner could perform such signs. The healed man said that Jesus was a prophet. Since they could not deny the sign, they tried to doubt the fact itself, and they looked for witnesses who would contradict it.

For today: sometimes, when the truth makes us uncomfortable, we look for excuses not to accept it. Let us ask God for a humble heart, willing to recognize his work even when it does not fit what we thought.
exp.10:54:
This verse says that the Passover was already drawing near, the great Jewish feast that remembered Israel's deliverance from Egypt. Many people from the countryside went up to Jerusalem before the feast to purify themselves, that is, to carry out the cleansing rites the law required, so that they could celebrate the Passover as it was due.

Here it is not a character speaking; it is the narrator, John, who describes the atmosphere. After raising Lazarus, the leaders wanted to kill Jesus, and he withdrew to Ephraim. John sets the scene: the city fills with people, and everyone wonders whether Jesus will dare to come. Soon the Passover would be fulfilled through his death.

For today: many prepared on the outside for the feast, but what matters is preparing the heart. Before each time of worship, take a moment to ask God to cleanse your heart and draw you close to Jesus.
exp.17:25:
Here a servant of the high priest asks Peter whether he did not see him in the garden with Jesus.

The servant was a relative of Malchus, the man whose ear Peter had cut off. It is the night of Jesus' trial. Peter is warming himself by the fire in the courtyard of the high priest. This servant speaks because he recognizes Peter and has a personal reason: his relative was wounded. This is the third denial, and right away the rooster crows, just as Jesus had foretold.

Peter fell when fear overcame his courage. If today you feel ashamed for having failed to bear witness to your faith, remember that Jesus afterward restored Peter. Return to Him with sincerity; His grace is greater than your fall.
exp.0:29:
John the Baptist points to Jesus and says, "This is he of whom I said." He had announced that someone would come after him but who would be greater than him. The word "man" in the verse refers to a man. The phrase "is preferred before me" means he has higher rank and honor. And "was before me" points to the fact that he existed from before, even though Jesus was born after John.

John the Baptist is speaking beside the Jordan, in Bethabara, the day after calling Jesus "the Lamb of God." His mission was to prepare the way and to direct people's attention toward Christ, not toward himself. Here he recalls what he had already said about Him.

For today: true greatness shows itself in humility. We can serve gladly, even when no one notices us, so that Jesus is the center and He receives the honor.
exp.12:12:
Jesus tells his disciples that they are right to call him "Master" and "Lord." The phrases "ye call" and "ye say well" are the words in the verse, and his reply is simply that they speak truthfully. Jesus confirms without hesitation who he is: he himself affirms that these titles belong to him.

Jesus speaks during the Last Supper, just after washing the feet of his disciples, a task belonging to servants. Before explaining the meaning of this act, he reminds them of his authority. So what follows is all the more surprising: the Master and Lord makes himself a servant, and then asks them to do the same for one another.

For today: if we call Jesus "Lord," our lives should resemble his. Today you can choose one concrete act of humble service, without seeking recognition, toward someone in your family, work, or church.
exp.9:23:
This verse tells how some Jews gathered around Jesus and demanded of him: "How long dost thou make us to doubt?" The original wording says "to keep us in suspense," that is, leaving them unsettled and not knowing what to think. They ask him that, if he is the Christ (the Messiah), he tell them plainly.

This takes place in Jerusalem, during the Feast of the Dedication, in winter, while Jesus was walking in Solomon's porch in the temple. The ones speaking are Jews who were listening to him, but many of them were not open to believing. Jesus had already spoken to them and done signs, and in the verses that follow he answers that his works bear witness to him.

For today: sometimes we ask for more proof when we have already seen enough. Let us ask God for a humble heart, ready to believe and to obey what he has already shown us of Jesus.
exp.12:22:
This verse says that one of the disciples, the one Jesus loved, was reclining very close to Him during the meal. The phrase "leaning on Jesus' bosom" means close beside Him, at His side, near His chest. It was customary to eat reclining at the table, leaning toward the person beside you.

The one speaking in the account is John, and Christian tradition usually identifies this disciple with him, although the text does not give his name. Jesus had just announced sadly that one of the twelve would betray Him. Everyone was confused, and Peter asked this disciple to ask who it was. His closeness allowed him to speak with Jesus in confidence.

For today: Jesus invites us to draw near to Him with sincerity. When you are confused or worried, bring your questions to Him in prayer, resting in the assurance that His love for you is real.
exp.10:44:
This verse says that many of the Jews who had come to comfort Mary, the sister of Lazarus, saw with their own eyes what Jesus did and believed in him.
