The phrase "had come to Mary" means that they had gone to visit her in her grief.

Here the speaker is the narrator, John. He has just told how Jesus raised Lazarus, who had been dead for four days. John shows that seeing so great a sign led many to faith. But the next verse makes clear that not everyone responded the same way: some went to tell the Pharisees, who felt threatened.

For today: faced with the work of God, each person responds in a different way. We can ask him to keep our hearts open to believe and trust, rather than hardening ourselves out of fear or pride.
exp.10:6:
Jesus tells his disciples that the time has come to return to Judea. The phrase "he said to the disciples" in the source means "he told them," and the words "again" and "once more" are rendered here as "back again." Two days had passed since he learned that Lazarus was sick.

Jesus, who loved Martha, Mary, and Lazarus, speaks now. He waited two days and now sets out. The disciples are afraid, because in Judea the leaders had tried to stone him. Jesus answers that he walks in the light of the Father's plan, and so he does not stumble. Some understand that his waiting had a greater purpose, which the text presents later on.

For today: when God seems slow, that does not mean he does not love you. Trust his timing and move forward in obedience, even when the steps you take are frightening, knowing that he goes with you.
exp.15:8:
It says that the Holy Spirit, the Helper, will show the world its sin, and that this sin consists in not believing in Jesus. To convict means to show clearly that someone is wrong. Here "sin" points above all to rejecting Christ, not only to bad actions.

Jesus speaks to his disciples at the Last Supper, shortly before his arrest. They are sad because he is leaving. He explains that his departure will bring the Spirit, who will be with them and will also act upon the world, awakening people's consciences.

For today: when you speak about Jesus with others, you do not have to convince anyone by your own strength. Your part is to live and share the truth with love, and to pray that the Spirit touches the heart. He is the one who convicts and transforms.
exp.5:36:
Jesus says that all who the Father gives him will come to him, and that whoever comes to him, he will in no wise cast out. In the older text, one word is simply the ordinary word, and one phrase is a printing error; the correct form is the one that means "I do not cast out," that is, "I do not reject or dismiss him."

Jesus is speaking to a crowd that was looking for him after the feeding of the multitude. He has just said that he is the bread of life, and he laments that they have seen him and still do not believe. Then he explains that he carries out the will of the Father: not to lose any of those who are given to him. Christians have understood in different ways how God's action and the human response relate in this verse.

If you feel unworthy or weary of your failures, you can come to Jesus with confidence. He promises to receive you, not to reject you. Come to him today in prayer, just as you are.
exp.0:18:
This verse begins the account of the testimony of John the Baptist. The Jewish authorities sent priests and Levites (men who served in the temple) from Jerusalem to ask him, "Who are you?" A testimony is what someone openly declares about what they know. The Jews here refers to the religious leaders of Jerusalem.

The one speaking is the evangelist John, who leaves behind the great hymn about Jesus and moves on to concrete events. Many people were following John the Baptist, and the leaders wanted to know by what authority he was acting. The verses that follow show that he denied being the Christ, Elijah, or the prophet, and so he directed attention to Jesus.

For today: when others ask us who we are, we can answer with humility, without seeking fame. Our greatest worth lies in pointing to Christ with our words and the way we live.
exp.15:22:
Jesus says that on that day you will no longer ask him anything, and he promises that whatever you ask the Father in his name, the Father will give you. The word "ask" in that verse is the same word used for requests, so the verse can be read both ways: as a promise about questions and as a promise about requests. Some readers take it to mean doubts and others take it to mean petitions.

Jesus speaks with his disciples on the last night before his cross. They are sad because he is leaving them. He promises that their sorrow will turn into joy, like the pain of a mother giving birth. The phrase "on that day" is usually understood to mean the time after his resurrection and the coming of the Holy Spirit.

Today you can pray to the Father with confidence, relying on Jesus and not on your own merits. Asking "in his name" means asking in agreement with his character and his will, with a humble heart.
exp.7:52:
The Jewish leaders put a challenging question to Jesus: does he really think he is greater than Abraham and the prophets, who died? They ask him to say who he claims to be. The phrase that means "you present yourself as" or "you think you are" is not used in the verse your reader sees, so it is left out here. The old spelling of "to" is also not relevant to your reader's text.

Some Jewish leaders are arguing with Jesus in Jerusalem. They were scandalized because he said that whoever keeps his word will never see death. They understood him only in a physical sense, and so they accused him of having a demon. Jesus was speaking of eternal life, and right away he answers that his glory comes from the Father.

Today we can ask the same question with humility: who is Jesus to me? It is not enough to admire figures of the faith or traditions; Jesus offers a life that overcomes death. Let us trust his word and obey it.
exp.5:57:
Jesus says that he is the bread that came down from heaven. He compares himself with the manna that the ancestors of Israel ate in the desert: they died, in spite of that food. By contrast, whoever eats of this bread will live forever, that is, for always. "Your fathers" means their ancestors, and "are dead" means that they died.

Jesus speaks in the synagogue in Capernaum, after feeding the crowd. The people were looking for bread for the stomach, and he teaches them that they need something deeper: himself. Eating and drinking is an image of believing in him and being united to him. Christians understand this language in different ways, and many disciples found it hard to accept.

Today we can ask ourselves what we live on each day. Just as the body needs food, the soul needs Christ. Make time to pray, to read the Gospels, and to trust in him.
exp.14:0:
Jesus says that he is the true vine and that his Father is the gardener. The vine is the plant that bears grapes, and the gardener is the person who looks after it and tends it. "True" means that Jesus is the genuine vine, the one that truly gives life.

Jesus speaks with his disciples on the night before his crucifixion, after the Last Supper. He is preparing them for his departure. In the Old Testament, Israel was sometimes compared to a vineyard (for example, Isaiah 5), so Jesus presents himself as the one who fulfills what Israel did not. The disciples are the branches that depend on him.

For today: just as a branch cannot bear grapes on its own, we need to remain joined to Jesus. Set aside a few minutes each day to read his Word and pray, trusting that the Father cares for your life.
exp.5:12:
The disciples gathered up the broken pieces that were left over and filled twelve baskets with the scraps of the five barley loaves. "Filled" is the word for what the verse calls "filled," and "gathered" is the word for what the verse calls "gathered together." After everyone had eaten until they were satisfied, there was still more left over than there had been at the start.

John is the one telling the story. Jesus has just fed a large crowd with five loaves and two fish, and he asks that the leftovers be gathered up so that nothing is wasted. Then the people recognize him as the expected prophet. Some want to make him king by force, but Jesus withdraws. The number twelve may call to mind the tribes of Israel, though the text does not explain it.

For today: God gives abundantly, and he also invites us to take care of what he gives us. We can be thankful for what we have, not waste it, and share what is left over with those who need it.
exp.9:3:
The explanation says that the shepherd, after bringing all his sheep out of the pen, walks at the front of them. The sheep follow him because they recognize his voice. The word "own" means the sheep that belong to him. In that time, the shepherd led his flock from the front; he did not push it from behind.

Jesus speaks during a conflict with some Pharisees after healing the man born blind (chapter 9). He uses this parable to show the difference between the true shepherd and false leaders. He will then say that he himself is the door and the good shepherd. The text makes clear that his listeners did not understand the comparison.

For today: learn to recognize the voice of Jesus by reading his Word faithfully. The more you know it, the easier it will be to tell it apart from other voices that pressure or confuse you. Always compare what you hear with what he taught.
exp.10:26:
Martha answers Jesus: "Yes, Lord, I believe." She is saying what she has come to believe. She confesses that Jesus is the Messiah, the Anointed One God promised. She recognizes that Jesus is the Son of God, the one who was to come into the world.

Martha, the sister of Lazarus, is in mourning because her brother died four days ago. Jesus has just told her that he is the resurrection and the life, and he asks her whether she believes this. She does not answer directly about Lazarus, but instead confesses who Jesus is. Afterward she goes to call her sister Mary.

Today we too can trust who Jesus is, even when we do not understand what is happening. In the middle of grief, Martha did not have all the answers, but she held on to him. We can say to him with sincerity, "Lord, I believe in you," and leave with him what we do not understand.
exp.7:58:
It says that, after hearing Jesus, the people took up stones to stone him. But Jesus hid himself, went out of the temple, passed through the midst of them, and so went on his way. "Hid himself" means that he concealed himself or moved out of their sight. "Went on his way" is written in an older form today, so it reads more naturally as "went out."

Jesus was speaking with some Jews in the temple. They doubted his authority, and he said, "Before Abraham was, I am." With those words he used the name by which God revealed himself to Moses (Exodus 3:14). Many understood that he was declaring himself to be God, and for that reason they wanted to stone him for blasphemy. The text does not explain how he managed to leave; it only says that he did.

When the truth of Christ makes us uncomfortable, we can react with anger or with humility. Today we can open our hearts, listen to what he says, and let him correct us instead of rejecting him.
exp.11:4:
Judas asks why this perfume was not sold for three hundred pence and the money given to the poor. A "perfume" was a fragrant oil, and a "pence" was the normal wage for a day's work, so three hundred pence was almost a year's pay.

Judas Iscariot, one of the disciples, speaks while Mary anoints the feet of Jesus in Bethany. His question sounds generous, but John makes clear that he did not really care about the poor: he was a thief and used to steal from the common purse. Jesus defends Mary and says that she was anticipating his burial.

For today: be wary of arguments that sound pious but hide other intentions. Let us examine our hearts, and learn to value sincere worship, even when others think it excessive.
exp.15:20:
Jesus uses the image of a woman giving birth. When her hour comes, she feels pain and anguish. But once the baby is born, she no longer remembers that suffering, because her joy is so great. The words "travail" and "delivered" in the verse above mean giving birth. "A man" means a person, a human being.

Jesus speaks with his disciples on the night before he is crucified. He has told them that soon they will not see him, and they are confused and sad. He explains that a time of weeping is coming, but that it will not be the end: their sorrow will turn into joy, and this points to his resurrection, when they will see him again.

For today: when you go through a difficult time, remember that God can use pain as a path toward a greater joy. Trust that your sorrow does not have the last word, and keep praying to the Father.
exp.2:33:
He whom God has sent speaks the words of God, and the reason is that God gives him the Spirit without limit, not in a measured or partial way, but fully and completely. What Jesus says is not human opinion but divine word.

These words are part of the testimony of John the Baptist, or, according to some interpreters, a reflection by the evangelist John; the text does not make clear where one ends and the other begins. The passage is explaining why it is worth believing in Jesus: he comes from the Father, with full authority and with the Spirit in his entirety. That is why the verses that follow speak of believing in the Son to have eternal life.

Today we can read the Gospels with confidence, knowing that in Jesus we hear the voice of God. Before seeking advice elsewhere, let us open the Bible and listen first to Christ.
exp.0:26:
It says that Jesus is the one who comes after John in his public ministry, yet he existed before him. "Before me" speaks of his rank and also of his eternal existence. The "strap of the sandal" is the thong of the sandal; loosening it was a servant's task, and John says he is not even worthy to do that.

John the Baptist is speaking. The religious leaders ask him by what authority he baptizes, since he is not the Christ, Elijah, or the prophet. John does not put himself at the center: he says he baptizes with water, but that there is already Someone among them whom they do not recognize. The next day he points to him as the Lamb of God.

For today: practice John's humility. Serve and speak about your gifts without seeking applause, and make sure others see Jesus before they see you. Ask yourself: am I doing this so that people notice me, or so that Christ is honored?
exp.4:18:
Jesus says that the Son can do nothing by himself, but only what he sees the Father doing. And whatever the Father does, the Son also does along with him.

Jesus speaks with Jewish leaders who were pursuing him. He had healed a man on the Sabbath, and they wanted to kill him because he also said that God was his Father, which they understood as making himself equal to God. Jesus does not deny it. He explains that his work comes from a perfect union with the Father, with no rivalry or independence.

For today: Jesus himself lived in dependence on and communion with the Father. If he worked this way, how much more should we. Before we decide or act, we can pray and ask, "Lord, what are you doing here, and how can I join in with it?"
exp.6:48:
The explanation says that the ordinary people, who do not know the law of Moses well, are under a curse. The word "cursed" in the verse means condemned or rejected by God. The Pharisees speak with contempt.

The speakers are the Pharisees. The temple guards had not arrested Jesus, and the people were divided about who He was. The leaders feel annoyed and think that only experts in the law can judge rightly. Their remark is an insult, not a teaching of the law. Soon after, Nicodemus reminds them that the law requires hearing a person before judging them.

Today we can examine ourselves: do we look down on those who know less than we do? Biblical knowledge should lead us to humility, to listening, and to treating every person with respect.
exp.14:18:
Jesus says that if his disciples thought and lived like the world, the world would love them as its own. But they no longer belong to that system, because Jesus chose them and took them out of it. That is why they receive rejection. "Hate" here means rejecting with hostility. "The world" refers to humanity living with its back turned to God.

Jesus speaks to his disciples the night before his crucifixion. He has just commanded them to love one another. Now he prepares them: if they rejected him, they will reject them too. He gives them this warning so that they will not be discouraged or caught by surprise.

If someone mocks you or leaves you out because you follow Jesus, do not think that something is wrong with you. Remember that God chose you and loves you. Respond with love, without bitterness, and seek the support of your brothers and sisters in the faith.
exp.9:0:
Jesus says that whoever enters the sheepfold by another way, and not by the door, is a thief and a robber. The sheepfold is the enclosed place where the sheep were kept safe at night. A robber is someone who takes what belongs to others by force.

Jesus speaks to a group of Pharisees, after he healed a blind man and they threw him out of the synagogue (chapter 9). He uses this comparison to show the difference between those who truly care for the people and those who only take advantage of them. He himself will soon present himself as the good shepherd and as the door.

For today: before you follow a leader or a teaching, ask yourself whether it leads people to Christ and cares for them with humility, or whether it seeks personal gain. Always compare what you hear with what Jesus taught.
exp.10:42:
Jesus finishes his prayer and cries out with a loud voice: "Lazarus, come forth." The word "cried" means that he spoke aloud, with force. "With a loud voice" means "with a very strong voice." It is a direct command addressed to a man who had been dead for four days.

Jesus speaks in front of the tomb of his friend Lazarus. He had just prayed to the Father aloud so that the people present would understand that God had sent him. After the prayer, Jesus acts with authority. Lazarus comes out, and many believe in Jesus.

For today: Jesus has the power to give life where there seems to be no hope left. If there is something in your life that you feel has no way out, bring it to God in prayer with confidence. He can speak to that situation, and he can also give you new life inside.
exp.7:14:
They judge "according to the flesh," that is, by human standards: appearances, what they see on the outside, and their own ideas. Jesus adds that he judges no one.

He is speaking in the temple, in Jerusalem, answering the Pharisees who said that his testimony was not valid. They looked at him only as an ordinary man. Many understand "I judge no one" to mean that on his first coming he did not come to condemn, or that he does not judge in a human way or apart from the Father. Interpreters explain it in several ways.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we judge others by appearances, rumors, or prejudices. Before we give our opinion, let us ask God for his view: more patience, more truth, and more mercy.
exp.6:17:
Jesus says that whoever speaks on his own authority seeks to be admired. By contrast, whoever seeks to honor God, who sent him, is sincere, and there is no falsehood in him. Here "unrighteousness" means falseness or wickedness.

Jesus teaches in the temple during the Feast of Tabernacles. The leaders doubt his authority and where his teaching comes from. He answers that his message comes from the Father and that his aim is not to exalt himself but to honor God. Shortly afterward he confronts them for wanting to kill him.

Today we can ask ourselves why we do what we do: are we seeking applause, or do we want to honor God? Before we serve, speak, or teach, it is good to pray: "Lord, let this give glory to you."
exp.5:28:
Jesus answers that the work God wants is to believe in the one he has sent. "Work" here means what God asks of us. "Believe" means to trust, not merely to accept an idea. "The one he has sent" is Jesus himself.

Jesus speaks to the crowd that followed him after he fed the multitude. He had told them not to seek only the food that perishes. They asked what they should do to please God. Jesus changes their question: he does not give a list of tasks, but invites them to trust in him. Yet they then ask for another sign, which shows that they still doubted.

Today, before you fill yourself with efforts to win God's favor, return to the basics: trust in Jesus. You can say to him simply, "Lord, I believe in you; help me to trust you more." From that trust a life of obedience and love is born.
exp.10:53:
This verse says that Jesus no longer went about openly among the people of Judea. He went to a region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and stayed there with his disciples. "Openly" means in plain view of everyone.

The one telling the story is John. Shortly before, the religious leaders had decided to kill Jesus, after he raised Lazarus. That is why Jesus withdrew for a time, while the Passover was drawing near. It is not known for certain where Ephraim was, though it is usually placed north of Jerusalem.

For today: not every withdrawal is fear; sometimes it is wisdom. There are times to act and times to rest, pray, and be with those we love, waiting for God's timing.
exp.12:14:
Jesus says that what he did with his disciples was an example. The word "ye" in the verse means "you," and "do" is the word used there. He wants them to do the same thing he did: to serve others with humility, as when he washed their feet.

Jesus speaks with his disciples at the last supper, shortly before his arrest. He had just done the work of a servant, washing tired and dirty feet. In this way he showed them that true leadership is lived out by serving. Some understand that Jesus is speaking of a literal act, and others of an attitude of service in general.

Today we can imitate Jesus by looking for a humble task that nobody wants to do, at home, at church or at work, and doing it with joy, without expecting recognition.
exp.6:1:
This verse says that the Jewish feast called the feast of booths was already drawing near, also known as the Feast of Booths or the Feast of Tabernacles. The word for these is a reference to temporary shelters or huts made of branches.

The one speaking here is the writer, John, who sets the scene in time. Jesus was in Galilee, avoiding Judea because people there wanted to kill him. This feast recalled when Israel lived in tents in the wilderness, and it was an occasion when many people went up to Jerusalem. That is why his brothers urge him to go and show himself publicly. Later John notes that they did not believe in him.

For today: Jesus did not let the pressure of others rush him, but waited for the Father's timing. Before making an important decision, we can pray, ask for direction, and not act only because others push us.
exp.10:13:
Here Jesus stops speaking in figures and says things without roundabout language: "Lazarus is dead" means "Lazarus has died." Earlier he had said that Lazarus was sleeping, and the disciples understood it as ordinary sleep. Now Jesus makes clear that he means death.

Jesus speaks with his disciples on the way to Bethany, where Lazarus, his friend, lived. The disciples did not understand his way of speaking, so Jesus tells them plainly. In the verses that follow he explains that he is glad he was not there, so that they may believe. Thomas responds with courage and sorrow: "Let us also go, that we may die with him."

For today: Jesus does not hide the painful truth, but he does not leave us alone in it. We can be honest with God about our pain and trust that he is still at work, even when we do not understand.
exp.5:2:
This verse tells us that Jesus went up a mountain and sat there with his disciples. The word "mountain" here may refer to a hill or raised ground near the lake. Going up and sitting down show a moment of pause, close to his closest followers.

The one telling the story is John, the author of the gospel. A large crowd was following Jesus because they had seen the signs he performed by healing the sick. John mentions that the Passover was near, and right after this comes the account of the loaves and the fish. The texts do not say why Jesus went up to that particular place, so it is better not to invent a reason. What we can see is that Jesus gathered with his disciples before attending to the crowd.

For today: even in the middle of crowds and demands, Jesus made time to be close to his own. We can look for simple spaces to sit with God and with people we love, before facing what lies ahead.
exp.4:38:
Jesus says: "Search the scriptures" means to study carefully and to examine thoroughly. He says that you think that in the Scriptures you have eternal life, and that those same Scriptures testify about him.

Jesus is speaking with Jewish leaders who were questioning him after he healed a man on the Sabbath. They knew the Law and the prophets very well, but they did not accept Jesus. He shows them that the Scriptures point to him, and in the next verse he tells them that they are unwilling to come to him to have life.

For today: read the Bible not only to gather information, but to meet Jesus. Before reading, pray simply: "Lord, show me Christ in these words." Then ask yourself what it teaches you about him and how you will respond with trust and obedience.
exp.0:24:
The Pharisees ask John a question: "Why then do you baptize, if you are neither the Christ, nor Elias, nor the prophet?" The words "they asked him" and "said unto him" are old forms of "asked him" and "said to him."

The ones speaking are messengers sent by the Pharisees, religious leaders from Jerusalem. John had just said that he was only the one who prepares the way for the Lord. They wanted to know by what authority he was baptizing. At that time, a baptism like this was unusual and drew attention. John answers that he baptizes with water and that the Lord was already among them.

For today: John served without seeking fame or titles. We can ask ourselves whether, in what we do for God, we want people to see us or to see Jesus.
exp.8:21:
This verse explains why the blind man's parents answered with such caution. They were afraid of the Jews, that is, of the religious leaders. They had already agreed that if anyone confessed that Jesus was the Messiah (the Christ, the promised Savior), that person would be put out of the synagogue, the community where people gathered to worship and live together.

The one speaking here is the evangelist John, who adds this explanation. The parents confirm that their son was born blind, but they do not dare to say who healed him. Being expelled could mean losing their place in religious and social life. Their son, by contrast, will speak with courage.

Today, the fear of losing esteem or acceptance can silence us. Let us ask God for the courage to be sincere about Jesus, with humility and respect, and not let fear make the decision for us.
exp.2:2:
Jesus tells Nicodemus, with great seriousness, that no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again. The phrase "Verily, verily" in the verse above is rendered simply as "Truly, truly" here, and the original wording's "born again" can also be understood as "from above," and many scholars see both meanings in it.

Nicodemus was a Pharisee and a highly respected Jewish leader. He came at night, perhaps out of caution or fear, and he recognized that Jesus had come from God. Jesus does not speak of signs but of something deeper: a new life that only God gives. Nicodemus does not understand, and so he asks how this is possible.

For today: being religious or having a good reputation is not enough. We can ask God simply for a new life, and trust that he gives it through his Spirit, not through our merits.
exp.20:18:
Jesus explains that Peter would die in a way that would honor God. The phrase "signifying" means "making known" or "showing." To "glorify" means to show the greatness of God. Then Jesus says to Peter, "Follow me," a simple and direct invitation.

Jesus speaks with Peter after his resurrection. Peter had denied him three times, and now Jesus asks him three times whether he loves him, and restores him to care for his people. Jesus tells him that his life would end in suffering. Many understand this to refer to a violent death, although the text gives no further details.

Following Jesus is not always easy, but it has meaning and purpose. If you have failed, Jesus still calls you. Today you can answer him with one concrete step of obedience, trusting that he cares for your path, even in difficulties.
exp.7:34:
This verse compares a servant with a son. The servant works in a house, but he has no secure and permanent place in it; he can be dismissed or sold. The son, by contrast, belongs to the family and stays forever.

Jesus is speaking with some Jews who believed in Him, but who took offense when He said the truth would make them free. They boasted of being descendants of Abraham and of never having been slaves to anyone. Jesus explains to them that sin enslaves. Then He says that only the Son, that is, He Himself, can give true freedom. Many understand the "servant" to represent someone who lives bound to sin.

For today: do not trust your history, your family, or your religion to make you feel secure. Come to Jesus with your chains; He offers you freedom and a permanent place as a child in God's family.
exp.7:31:
Jesus says that those who know the truth will be set free by it. "You will know" speaks of a knowledge that is lived out, not just ideas in the head. "Will set you free" means that the truth breaks chains and gives real freedom.

Jesus is speaking with Jews who had just come to believe in him. He tells them that being his true disciples means remaining in his word. They take offense, because they thought they were already free for being descendants of Abraham. Then Jesus makes clear that whoever practices sin is a slave to it. The freedom he offers is freedom from sin, and the truth is tied to his teaching (in John 14:6 he himself says he is "the truth").

For today: set aside a moment each day to read the Gospels and ask yourself what habit or lie has you bound. Obey what Jesus says, and let his word set you free little by little.
exp.11:28:
The people standing nearby heard the sound and said that it had thundered. Others said that an angel had spoken to him. The people heard the sound, but not everyone understood the message.

Jesus had just prayed, and the Father answered from heaven. It was a real voice, but the crowd understood it in different ways. Afterward Jesus explained that the voice had come not for his sake but for theirs, so that they might believe. His cross was near, and the voice confirmed his mission.

For today: God can speak clearly, but our hearts affect what we understand. Ask him to open your ears and your heart when you read his Word, and do not treat it as something casual or unimportant.
exp.0:19:
This verse says that John the Baptist spoke with complete sincerity. "Confessed" means that he openly declared the truth, and "denied not" means that he hid nothing and did not give evasive answers. "The Christ" is the Messiah, the Savior promised by God. John clearly said that he was not that person.

The Jewish leaders in Jerusalem sent priests and Levites, who assisted in the temple, to ask him who he was. Many people followed John, and they wanted to know whether he presented himself as the Messiah. The evangelist John records this to show that the Baptist pointed to Jesus and not to himself.

Today we can learn from this humility. It is easy to want attention or to appear to be more than we are. John shows us that serving God begins with being honest about who we are and letting Christ be the center.
exp.10:20:
Martha tells Jesus that if he had been there, her brother would not have died. The words "had not died" are an older way of saying it. And the phrase "said unto Jesus" means "said to Jesus." It is a sentence that mixes grief, trust, and also a little bit of reproach.

Martha speaks with Jesus when he arrives in Bethany, four days after Lazarus's death. She goes out to meet him while Mary stays at home with those who were comforting the family. Martha believes Jesus has power, and that is why, in the following verse, she adds that God will give him whatever he asks. Even so, she does not yet imagine what he is about to do.

We can speak to God with complete honesty, even when we feel pain or do not understand why he did not arrive in time. Martha did not pretend; she brought her sadness to Jesus, and he listened to her and led her to a greater hope.
exp.7:22:
Jesus tells his listeners that they and he come from different places. The words "from beneath" and "of this world" describe a life that looks only at earthly things. "From above" shows that Jesus comes from God, from heaven.

Jesus is speaking with some religious leaders in Jerusalem, who doubt him. He has just said that he is going away and that they will not be able to follow him. They think he may take his own life, but he is speaking of his divine origin. That is why he adds that they need to believe in who he is in order to be forgiven.

For today: ask yourself what you are holding on to, whether what happens in this world or Christ. Ask God to help you trust in Jesus and to look at your decisions from a perspective that comes from him.
exp.18:15:
It says that Pilate, the Roman governor, handed Jesus over to the Jewish leaders so that they would crucify him. They took him and led him away. "Therefore then" means "then, after that." "Delivered him unto them" means that he placed him in their hands. "Crucified" means nailed to a cross, a very cruel Roman punishment.

Here the narrator, John, speaks. Pilate had seen that Jesus was not guilty, but he was afraid of losing his position. The chief priests shouted that they had no king but Caesar, and that pressure made him give in. John shows that Jesus was going to the cross without anyone being able to stop him, and that neither Pilate's fear nor the people's hatred thwarted God's plan.

Today, let us think about how often we give in to pressure out of fear of what others think. Let us ask God for courage to do what is right, and let us remember with gratitude that Jesus went to the cross out of love for us.
exp.5:13:
This verse tells us that the people saw the miracle of the bread and the fish, and concluded that Jesus was "this is of a truth that prophet that should come into the world". The word "sign" means a miracle that points to something greater. "Saw" and "said" show that the reaction was immediate.

The speakers here are the crowd, about five thousand men along with their families, who had just eaten until they were full. They were probably thinking of the prophet that Moses foretold (Deuteronomy 18:15). However, the text that follows shows that they wanted to make him king by force, and Jesus withdrew. They recognized something true, but their idea of what He had come to do was incomplete.

For today: it is not enough to admire Jesus for what He gives us. We can ask ourselves whether we seek him only for his blessings, or whether we let him be Lord on his terms, not ours.
exp.10:12:
John's comment here is an explanation from the writer. John tells us that when Jesus said Lazarus was sleeping, he was speaking of his death. His disciples, however, understood him to mean ordinary restful sleep.

Jesus speaks with his disciples before going to Bethany, where his friend Lazarus has died. Calling death a kind of sleep was a gentle way of speaking about it, and the Bible uses this image in other passages. The disciples took his words literally and thought Lazarus would recover. That is why Jesus speaks to them plainly afterward.

For today: we sometimes understand God's words only in part, from what we can see. We can ask him to open our understanding and trust him, even when we do not grasp everything right away. Jesus sees further than we are able to see.
exp.6:30:
Many of the common people, it says, believed in Jesus. Their reasoning was simple: if the Christ (the promised Messiah) should come, would he do more signs, that is, miracles that point to God, than the ones Jesús was already doing?

This takes place in Jerusalem, during the Feast of Tabernacles. Jesus had just taught in the temple and declared that the Father had sent him. The leaders wanted to arrest him, but the people, seeing his works, began to believe. That whispering worried the Pharisees, and so they sent guards.

For today: faith can begin with honest questions in the face of what God has done. Look carefully at how Jesus has worked in your life and in Scripture, and let that lead you to trust him, without letting the opinion of others hold you back.
exp.3:21:
Jesus says that the Samaritans worship without knowing well whom they worship, while the Jews do know whom they worship. The word "salvation" here is what the verse calls "salvation," and Jesus affirms that it comes through the Jews.

Jesus speaks with a Samaritan woman by a well. She raises the long-standing dispute between Samaritans and Jews about the right place to worship. Jesus answers that God had revealed himself to Israel, and that the Savior would come from that people, that is, Himself. Then he announces that worship would no longer depend on a place.

For today: it is not enough to be sincere in worship; it also matters to know God well, as he has been revealed in Jesus. Spend time reading the Gospels to know him better, and let your worship grow out of that knowledge.
exp.4:21:
He says that the Father judges no one by Himself, but has given all judgment to the Son. The word "gave" refers to "given," meaning God has entrusted Jesus with the authority to judge, just as He gave Him the authority to give life.

Jesus is speaking in Jerusalem. Some Jewish leaders wanted to kill Him because He had healed on the Sabbath and said that God was His Father. Jesus answers that He acts in unity with the Father. For this reason He asks to be honored just as the Father is honored, and then He promises eternal life to whoever believes.

For today: the Judge of all is the same Jesus who died for us. You can trust that His judgment is just and full of love. Today, instead of living in fear or judging others, come to Him in faith and honor His word in your decisions.
exp.13:12:
He says that Jesus will do whatever his disciples ask the Father "in his name." Asking in his name means asking in line with who Jesus is and what he wants, not using his name as a magic formula. The ultimate purpose is that the Father be glorified, that is, honored and shown to be great, through the Son.

Jesus speaks to his disciples at the Last Supper, shortly before his death. He has just told them that he is going to the Father and that they will do great works. He promises them that they will not be left alone: they will be able to pray with confidence. Then he joins asking with love and obedience: "If you love me, keep my commandments."

Before you pray, ask yourself: "Would what I am asking honor God?" In this way your prayers will draw closer to the heart of Jesus and farther from your own desires.
exp.4:5:
It says that Jesus saw a sick man lying beside the pool, and knew that he had been that way for a long time.

This happens in Jerusalem, beside a pool where many sick people waited to be healed. Jesus is the one who speaks. This man had been sick for thirty-eight years. Jesus approaches on his own initiative, without the man asking him to. His question is not due to a lack of information: he invites the man to express his desire and his hope. Some think it also draws him out of his habit of waiting without seeing any other way out.

Today, Jesus draws near to our old wounds and asks us, with tenderness, what we long for. We can answer him honestly, without pretending to be strong, and let him show us the next step.
exp.7:12:
The Pharisees tell Jesus that he is testifying about himself, and so, in their view, his testimony is not valid. To "bear witness" means to affirm something as a witness. They reject it because no other person stands behind him to confirm it.

Jesus had just said, "I am the light of the world." The Pharisees, who were highly respected religious teachers, did not want to accept such a great claim. They rely on the principle that testimony needs more than one witness (Deuteronomy 19:15). Jesus answers that his testimony is true because he knows where he came from and where he is going, that is, he knows his origin in God the Father.

For today: sometimes we make excuses so that we do not accept a truth that makes us uncomfortable. Let us ask for humility to listen to Jesus with sincerity and let his light guide us, even when it changes us.
exp.14:19:
Jesus is reminding them of something he had already taught them: a servant is not greater than his master. If they persecuted Jesus, they will also persecute his followers. And if someone kept what Jesus said, they will also keep what they say. The explanation of the words "remember" and "kept" is left out, since those words are not in the verse your reader sees.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the night before his crucifixion, during his farewell. He wants to prepare them for the rejection that is coming. He explains that the world will reject them because they belong to him, not because they have done anything wrong. This saying also appears in John 13:16.

If someone mocks you or rejects you for following Christ, do not lose heart or think that God has abandoned you. Jesus anticipated this. Respond with love and gentleness, and remember that he walked this road before you.
exp.18:33:
It tells that, after Jesus died on the cross, one of the Roman soldiers pierced his side with a spear. Immediately blood and water came out.

John is the one who tells this, the disciple who was present. The soldiers would break the legs of those who were crucified to hasten their death, but they did not do this to Jesus, because he had already died. John stresses that he is an eyewitness so that the readers may believe. Some see in the blood and water a proof of Jesus' real death; others give it a symbolic meaning, such as forgiveness and new life. The Bible does not explain this in detail.

For today: you can trust that Jesus truly gave his life for you. When you doubt, return to the accounts of the witnesses and rest in the fact that his love was real and complete.
exp.6:33:
Jesus says that his hearers will seek him and will not find him, and that they cannot come where he is going. The two words the explanation discusses are "find" (meaning "come upon" or "discover") and "come" (meaning "arrive" or "get there").

Jesus speaks at the Feast of Tabernacles, in Jerusalem. The Pharisees and the chief priests had already sent officers to arrest him. He answers that his time is short and that he will return to the Father who sent him. The Jews do not understand and think that perhaps he will go to the Jews scattered among the Greeks. Many believe Jesus is speaking of his death, resurrection, and ascension, where no one can arrive through pride or unbelief. The text does not explain more.

Today, let us not put off the decision to answer Jesus. If God speaks to us now, let us listen with humility and faith, because the opportunity is today.
exp.20:3:
It says that at daybreak Jesus was standing on the shore of the lake, but the disciples did not realize it was him. Here the narrator is John, who tells of the third appearance of the risen Jesus to his disciples.

The disciples had spent the whole night fishing without catching anything. Jesus had already risen, and they were still learning to live with him in a new way. The Bible does not explain why they did not recognize him; some think it was the distance or the dim light of the morning, and others think their eyes were kept from seeing him, as in other accounts of the resurrection. We do not know for certain.

For today: Jesus may be near in the middle of our weariness and failure, even when we do not notice it. We can ask him for eyes to recognize him and to hear his voice.
exp.17:16:
A young woman who was guarding the gate of the high priest's courtyard asks Peter if he too is one of Jesus' disciples. Peter answers, "I am not." The word "high priest" refers to the chief priest, and the servant girl on the gate was a servant assigned to watch the entrance.

Jesus had just been arrested and taken to the house of Annas, the former high priest. Peter and another disciple followed him. That other disciple knew the priest, so he managed to have Peter let in. The woman at the gate asks the question, perhaps out of curiosity or suspicion, and Peter, out of fear, denies his Master. This is the first of the three denials that Jesus had foretold.

For today: all of us can fail when we feel pressure to follow Christ. If you have been afraid to acknowledge your faith, do not stay sunk in shame. Peter was later restored by Jesus. Ask Him for courage today and return to Him with confidence.
exp.3:23:
This verse says that God is Spirit, that is, he has no physical body and is not limited to one place. For this reason, those who worship him must do so in spirit and in truth. The phrase "must" means that it is not optional but essential.

Jesus speaks with a Samaritan woman by a well. She had asked him whether one should worship on the mountain of Samaria or in Jerusalem. Jesus answers that what matters is no longer the place, but a sincere heart. Interpreters explain "in spirit" in several ways: with the Holy Spirit, or with the deepest part of the person. "In truth" can refer to sincerity and to the truth revealed in Christ.

Today we can ask ourselves: is my worship sincere, or is it only a habit? Before I pray or sing, I can speak to God honestly, without pretending.
exp.20:4:
Jesus, from the shore, addresses the disciples as "Children," a warm, close way of speaking to them. He asks whether they have anything to eat, and they answer with a simple "No." Jesus already knew the answer; the question opens the conversation.

The disciples had fished all night without catching anything. It was dawn, and they did not recognize Jesus, who had already risen. He speaks to them like a friend, not like a distant teacher, and leads them to admit honestly that their hands are empty. His instruction and the abundant catch will come afterward.

For today: when you feel tired and see no results, humbly acknowledge your need before Jesus. He draws near even when you do not recognize him, and from that honesty he can give you a new direction.
exp.19:19:
He says that Jesus, after greeting his disciples with peace, showed them his hands and his side. The wounds of the crucifixion were there. The sentence about the word "shewed" is rewritten here: the verb in the verse means "showed," and the disciples were filled with joy when they saw the Lord alive.

The Gospel of John tells that it was the evening of the day of the resurrection, Sunday. The disciples were shut in for fear of the Jewish authorities. Jesus comes in, greets them, and shows them the marks of his suffering. In this way he confirms that he is the same one who died on the cross. Soon he will send them out into the world and give them the Holy Spirit.

For today: when fear shuts you in, remember that Jesus knows pain and overcame death. His presence can turn your fear into joy. Ask him today to show you his nearness.
exp.8:6:
Jesus tells the blind man: "Go, wash in the pool of Siloam." The text explains that Siloam means "Sent." The man obeyed, washed, and came back seeing. The older wording is easy to follow: "said unto him" means "said to him," "went his way" means "went," and "washed" means "washed himself."

Jesus speaks this after saying that he is the light of the world. He had just put mud on the eyes of a man who had been blind from birth. John highlights the name "Sent," and many connect it to Jesus, whom the Father sent, although the text does not explain this directly. The healing happens when the man obeys.

Today, we can trust Jesus' word even when we do not understand everything. A simple step of obedience, taken in faith, can open our eyes to what God wants to show us.
exp.4:19:
This verse says that the Father loves the Son and therefore shows him everything that he himself does. Moreover, he will show him even greater works, so that those who hear will be amazed. The word "marvel" in the verse is rendered here simply as "be amazed."

Jesus speaks in Jerusalem, after healing a man on the Sabbath. Some Jewish leaders wanted to kill him, because they said he was making himself equal to God. Jesus does not defend himself by denying this, but explains that the Son acts in complete unity with the Father. The "greater works" are understood from the context that follows: giving life and judging.

For today: if God is a Father who loves and relates to us with closeness, we can approach Jesus with confidence and not only with curiosity. Today you can set aside a few minutes to read the Gospels and ask him to show you his work, with a humble heart ready to be amazed.
exp.6:28:
Jesus says that he knows the Father in a direct and personal way. He gives two reasons: "I am from him," meaning he comes from God and belongs to him in a unique way, and "he hath sent me," meaning the Father commissioned him with a mission. "Know" here speaks of a close relationship, not merely of knowing facts.

Jesus speaks in the temple in Jerusalem during the Feast of Tabernacles. The people were saying that they knew where Jesus came from, and that the Christ would appear without anyone knowing his origin. Jesus answers in a loud voice: they know the place where he was raised, but they do not know the true God who sent him. Some became angry and wanted to arrest him.

For today: knowing God is not only knowing things about him. If you want to know him truly, look to Jesus, who shows him clearly. Set aside time to read the Gospels and to speak with God sincerely.
exp.8:25:
The Pharisees, not giving up, ask the man who had been healed the same questions again: what Jesus did to him and how he opened his eyes. The phrase "Then said they to him again" means "they asked him once more." They had already asked these questions earlier in this chapter.

The speakers are the religious leaders who question the man who used to be blind. He has just said that he does not know whether Jesus is a sinner, but he does know that now he sees. Many understand that they repeat the question not because they want to learn, but to find some flaw in his account or in Jesus' work. His answer that follows shows that he was already tired of repeating the same thing.

We can ask ourselves whether we listen to God with an open heart, or only look to confirm what we already think. A simple and honest testimony, like this man's, is worth more than many arguments. Let us ask for humility to receive the truth.
exp.18:17:
This verse says that Jesus was crucified in the place called Golgotha. Two other men were crucified with him, one on each side, and Jesus was in the middle. The word for being crucified here refers to being nailed or tied to a cross, a very cruel and public punishment used by the Romans.

Here John speaks as a witness to these events, telling the story simply and without embellishment. Pilate had already handed Jesus over to be crucified. John does not explain why the other two were there; other gospels call them criminals. Some see in this a fulfillment of Isaiah 53:12, which says that he was numbered with the transgressors, though John does not mention it in this passage.

For today: Jesus did not avoid the place of the despised, but placed himself in the middle of them. If you feel alone or unworthy, remember that Christ draws near to you. Today you can approach him with confidence.
exp.9:19:
Here the text says that many of those who were listening to Jesus thought something was wrong with Him. They said He had a demon and was "beside himself," that is, that He had lost His reason. That is why they asked, "Why do you listen to him?"

Jesus had just spoken of being the good shepherd who gives his life willingly, and of receiving from His Father the authority to give it and to take it up again. Those words were so strong that they divided the Jews. Some rejected them harshly; others, in the next verse, replied that a demon cannot open the eyes of a blind man, recalling the miracle of chapter 9.

For today: when something about Jesus makes us uncomfortable or surprises us, let us not dismiss it with prejudice. Better to look honestly at what He says and does, and let His works and His Word speak to us.
exp.2:12:
This verse says that no one has gone up into heaven to know God's things firsthand, except Jesus, who came down from heaven. He calls himself "the Son of man," a title he used for himself. The phrase "which is in heaven" is understood in several ways: some see that Jesus remains always united with the Father, even while walking on the earth. The words for "went up" and "came down" in this verse mean "ascended" and "descended."

Jesus speaks with Nicodemus, a Jewish teacher who came to him at night to seek him out. Jesus explains to him that the things of God cannot be understood by human intelligence alone. If Nicodemus did not believe earthly things, such as the new birth, he would understand heavenly things even less. That is why Jesus presents himself as the only witness who truly comes from there.

For today: instead of relying only on my own ideas about God, I can turn to Jesus, who truly knows him, and read the Gospels with humility to learn from him.
exp.16:1:
The explanation says that the Father gave Jesus authority over all of humanity. That authority has a purpose: that Jesus give eternal life to all whom the Father has entrusted to him. The word "authority" here corresponds to the power the verse describes, and "all humanity" corresponds to "all flesh."

Jesus is praying to the Father shortly before going to the cross. He asks to be glorified so that he may glorify the Father. In the following verse he explains that eternal life is knowing the Father, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom he sent. Christians have understood in different ways what is meant by "those whom you gave him," but they all agree that eternal life comes from Jesus.

Today we can rest in the fact that our life with God does not depend on our own strength, but on Jesus. Take a moment to know him better: read a passage from the Gospels and speak with him.
exp.8:18:
The Jewish leaders call the parents of the man who was healed and ask them three questions: whether this is their son, whether he was really born blind, and how it is that he now sees.

The Pharisees did not want to believe that Jesus had performed a miracle, because it contradicted their ideas. Since the healed man had declared that Jesus was a prophet, they now look for another explanation. They think that if the parents deny the fact, the miracle will be left in doubt. They are key witnesses, but, as is seen later, they are afraid.

For today: sometimes the evidence is clear, but our pride or our prejudices keep us from accepting it. Let us ask God for a humble heart, ready to recognize his work, even when it does not fit what we had thought.
exp.2:19:
He says that the one who practices evil rejects the light and does not come to it, because he fears that his deeds will be brought into the open. The word "reproved" is old-fashioned and means rebuked, corrected, or exposed. Here "light" represents Jesus and the truth of God.

Jesus is speaking with Nicodemus, a Jewish teacher who visited him at night. After explaining God's love and the need to believe in the Son, Jesus makes clear why some reject him: not always for lack of evidence, but because the light shows what they would prefer to hide. Many interpreters also see here an invitation to Nicodemus to leave the darkness.

Today we can ask ourselves: is there something I hide from God out of shame? Instead of running away, we can bring it to Him with sincerity. His light does not only expose sin; it also offers forgiveness and a fresh start.
exp.10:34:
This is the shortest verse in the Bible. It says that Jesus wept. The word used in the original indicates silent tears, different from the loud weeping of Mary and the others. In the old text, the phrase "was deeply moved in spirit" means that he felt a very deep emotion, and it means that he was shaken inwardly.

Here the narrator, John, is speaking. Jesus is standing before the tomb of Lazarus, his friend. He was about to raise him, but first he pauses to weep with those who are suffering. Some think he wept because of their pain, others because of death itself; the Bible does not make this clear. Those present see his love, though others doubt it.

For today: Jesus is not ashamed to weep with you. You can bring him your pain honestly, and also keep others company in their sadness, without rushing or easy answers, simply with presence and care.
exp.15:10:
Jesus says that the Holy Spirit will convict the world "of judgment," because the "prince of this world," that is, Satan, has already been judged. The word "because" shows the reason. "Has been judged" means that a sentence has already been pronounced against him.

Jesus speaks with his disciples the night before the cross. He prepares them for his departure and promises them the Holy Spirit. The Spirit will show the world its error: not believing in Christ, rejecting his righteousness, and following the one who is already condemned. Many Christians understand that the cross and the resurrection were that defeat, though Satan still acts.

For today: if you face fear, temptation, or evil, remember that the enemy does not have the last word. Pray for the help of the Spirit and trust in the victory of Christ.
exp.18:31:
This verse tells that the Roman soldiers went to the two men crucified alongside Jesus and broke their legs, first one and then the other. The word "broke" means they shattered the bones of their legs.

The one who tells the story is John, an eyewitness to the scene. The Jewish leaders had asked Pilate for this act because the Sabbath was approaching, a very special day during the Passover, and they did not want bodies left on the crosses. Breaking the legs hastened death, because the crucified man could no longer push himself up to breathe. With Jesus it was not necessary, since he had already died, as the next verse shows.

For today: Jesus truly died, out of love for us. We can trust that his giving of himself was complete. Today, give thanks for this and live grateful, caring also for those who suffer around you.
exp.5:8:
Andrew speaks of a boy who is there with five barley loaves and two small fish. Barley loaves were the common, cheap bread of ordinary people. Then Andrew asks, "But what are they among so many?", that is: "How can so little do anything for so many people?"

Andrew is one of Jesus' disciples. Philip has just said that even two hundred denarii (about seven months' wages for a laborer) would not be enough to feed the crowd. Andrew mentions how little there is, though he cannot see how it could help. Jesus, in the following passage, takes that small offering, gives thanks, and distributes it.

Often we think what we have is very little: time, money, or talents. But Jesus can use what we bring him with simplicity. Put in his hands what you have, even if it seems insufficient, and trust that he knows what to do with it.
exp.6:13:
This verse says that when the feast was already halfway through, Jesus went up to the temple in Jerusalem and began to teach. "About the middle of the feast" means in the middle of the celebration. This is the Feast of Tabernacles, which lasted a week, and "went up" is used because Jerusalem sat on high ground.

Before this, people were whispering about Jesus: some said he was good, and others said he was deceiving the people. No one spoke openly because they were afraid of the Jewish leaders. John tells us that Jesus did not arrive with the group at the start but later, and then he taught publicly. The listeners were amazed that he knew so much without having studied with the recognized teachers.

Today, while many people give opinions about Jesus without knowing him well, we can go straight to his words in the Gospels and listen to him carefully, without letting rumors or fear of what others think decide what we believe.
exp.15:26:
This verse says that the Father himself loves the disciples. The reason Jesus gives is that they have loved him and have believed that he came out from God.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples on the night before his arrest. He explains that soon they will be able to pray to the Father in his name, with confidence and closeness. He assures them that the Father does not look on them from a distance, but loves them. The verses that follow show that Jesus is speaking of his coming into the world and of his return to the Father.

For today: if you believe in Jesus and love him, you can pray without fear, knowing that God loves you personally. Come to him with simplicity and confidence, not like someone who fears being rejected.
exp.10:37:
Jesus, again deeply moved within himself, came to Lazarus's tomb. It was a cave with a stone placed at the entrance.

The verse says "groaning in himself," which means feeling a strong emotion. The Greek word may suggest both sorrow and indignation, and it is not known for certain which shade was the main one.

The writer, John, tells us that Jesus has just wept with Mary and those present. Some of the Jews admire his love, but others doubt: if he healed a blind man, why didn't he prevent this death? Jesus goes to the tomb and will soon ask for the stone to be removed so that the glory of God may be shown.

For today: Jesus does not turn away from pain or from people's doubts. You can bring him your sadness and your questions honestly. He understands your pain and remains worthy of trust, even when you cannot yet see how he will act.
exp.20:19:
Peter turns around and sees the disciple whom Jesus loved following them, the same one who at supper had leaned back against Jesus's chest and had asked who was going to betray him. "Young man" means a youth, and "gird himself" means to tie on one's belt or clothing to go out.

Jesus has just restored Peter, and he tells him that his life will end in a death that will bring glory to God. Then he says to him: "Follow me." Peter looks at the other disciple, traditionally identified with John, and wonders what will happen to him. Jesus answers that this is none of Peter's concern.

For today: it is easy to look at the path of others and compare it with our own. Today you can bring that curiosity or that fear to Jesus in prayer, and return to his personal call to you: "Follow me."
exp.7:42:
Jesus asks why his hearers do not understand what he is saying. "Speech" refers to his way of speaking, to what he means. The answer is that they "cannot hear" his word: this is not a problem of the ears but of the heart. They neither want nor are able to receive what he says.

Jesus speaks with some Jews who boast of being children of God. He explains to them that if God were truly their Father, they would love him, since he comes from God. Because they reject him, he shows them that something is wrong within them. His words are harsh, but they aim to open their eyes.

For today: before arguing with the Bible, ask God for a humble and willing heart. If there is something in his Word that makes you uncomfortable, do not avoid it; listen to it sincerely and let God correct you.
exp.13:23:
Jesus says that whoever does not love him also does not obey his teachings. The words "keeps" and "have heard" mean "obeys" and "have listened to." He also makes clear that his message is not his own idea, but comes from the Father, who sent him.

Jesus speaks with his disciples at the Last Supper, shortly before going to the cross. Judas, not Iscariot, asked him why he would reveal himself to them and not to the world. Jesus answers that love shows itself through obedience, and that the Father and he will make their home with the one who loves him. Right after this, he promises to send the Holy Spirit to help them remember.

Today, love for Jesus does not stay in feelings or words alone. Choose one of his teachings that you already know, such as forgiving or speaking the truth, and ask the Spirit to help you live it out this week.
exp.7:50:
Jesus says that whoever keeps his word, that is, whoever obeys it and holds it in the heart, "shall never see death." "Verily, verily" means "I assure you with all truth." He is speaking of a life that physical death cannot destroy.

Jesus speaks with some Jews who doubt him and even accuse him of having a demon. He answers that he honors the Father and does not seek his own glory. They understand death only as the death of the body, and so they are scandalized: Abraham and the prophets died. Jesus is speaking of a deeper death, the separation from God.

Today, hearing Jesus is not enough; one must obey him. Today you can choose one of his teachings and put it into practice with confidence, knowing that he promises a life with God that does not end.
exp.12:23:
Simon Peter gave the disciple beside Jesus a signal with his head or hand, the disciple whom Jesus loved. He wanted him to ask Jesus whom he was talking about. "Gave a signal" means he pointed to something without speaking. The phrase "the one he was talking about" refers to the person Jesus had said would betray him.

We are at the Last Supper. Jesus had just announced that one of the twelve would hand him over, and the disciples were confused and worried. Peter did not dare to ask directly, so he used the disciple who was closest to Jesus. Many believe that disciple was John, although the text does not give his name.

When we do not understand what is happening, we can come to Jesus with sincerity and confidence, and ask those near Him to seek answers together.
exp.0:39:
This verse tells us that one of the first two disciples who followed Jesus was named Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter. Before following Jesus, Andrew had heard John the Baptist. The phrase about having heard John means that they had listened to him speak.

The one telling the story is John, the author of the Gospel. He introduces Andrew to show how the group of Jesus' followers began. The other disciple is not named here, and it is not known for certain who he was; some think it was the author himself. Andrew spent the day with Jesus and then went to find his brother.

For today: when you find something good in Jesus, don't keep it to yourself. Andrew first listened, then drew near, and then shared with his brother. Start with those closest to you.
exp.0:27:
This verse says that everything just described took place in a place called Bethabara, on the other side of the Jordan River, where John was baptizing. "Beyond" means "on the other side." Some ancient manuscripts say "Bethany" instead of Bethabara, and it is not known with certainty where that site was.

The one speaking here is the writer of the gospel, who places the events in a specific location. John the Baptist had just told the religious authorities that he only baptized with water, but that among them stood someone greater, whom they did not know.

For today: God acts in real places and moments, sometimes ordinary ones. Perhaps he is working in the middle of your life without your noticing. Today, ask him for attentive eyes to recognize him in everyday things.
exp.9:29:
Jesus says that He and the Father are "one thing." The old word "are" only means "are" in the present tense. It does not say that they are the same person, but that there is a deep oneness between the two, in power, purpose, and divine nature.

Jesus speaks at the Feast of Dedication, in Jerusalem, and the Jewish leaders ask him to say plainly whether he is the Christ. He has just said that his sheep are safe in his hand and in the Father's hand. When he declares that they are one, his hearers understand that he is making himself equal to God, and that is why they pick up stones. Christians often see his divinity here; some debate the finer points of this "oneness."

For today: if your security rests in Christ, it also rests in the Father. No one can snatch you from that double protection. Trust in Him when you feel fear or doubt.
exp.18:34:
This verse says that someone saw with his own eyes what happened at the cross and reports it just as it happened. The wording of the quoted phrase is not in your verse, so we will simply translate the sense. The witness affirms that his account is true and that he gives it so that the readers may also believe in Jesus.

The author of the Gospel speaks of what happened when the soldier pierced the side of Jesus with a spear, and blood and water came out. Tradition holds that the witness is the apostle John, although the text does not give his name. He makes this clear so that the readers will trust that Jesus truly died and that this fulfilled the Scriptures.

Our faith does not rest on made-up stories but on a testimony given with honesty. Today we can read the Gospels with confidence and, when we share what God has done in our lives, do so simply and truthfully, without exaggeration.
exp.2:16:
This verse says that God did not send his Son to judge people, but to save them. The word "condemn" means to declare someone guilty and punish them. Being "saved" means being rescued from punishment and ruin.

Jesus is speaking at night with Nicodemus, a Jewish teacher who came to find him with sincere questions. Jesus explains to him that God acts out of love. Although judgment is mentioned later on, the purpose of his coming is to offer rescue to everyone.

For today: if you feel judged or ashamed of your past, remember that Jesus came to offer you salvation, not to crush you. Come to him with confidence. And treat others the way God treats you: with grace and hope, not with contempt.
exp.7:26:
This verse says that the people listening to Jesus did not understand that he was speaking to them about God the Father. "But" means "however," or "yet," and it marks a contrast. Jesús had told them that the one who sent him is true and that he spoke what he had heard from him, yet they did not grasp the message.

Jesus talks with some leaders and people of Jerusalem who ask him, "Who are you?" He answers that his words come from God, who sent him. Even so, they did not understand. Later Jesus tells them that when they lift up the Son of Man, they will know who he is. Many interpreters see here a reference to the cross, though some also see in it his exaltation.

We can hear the Word of God without understanding it if our hearts are not open. Today we can ask God for humility and clarity before we read the Bible, and be willing to listen to what Jesus actually says, not only to what we expect to hear.
exp.12:36:
Peter asks Jesus why he cannot follow him right now. He makes a strong promise: "I will lay down my life for thy sake," that is, he will give his life for Jesus.

Jesus has just said that he is going to a place where Peter cannot come with him yet. Peter, sincere and passionate, does not want to be left behind. Jesus answers with a question that shows Peter is misjudging himself: he tells him that before morning he will deny him three times. Peter speaks out of love, but he does not yet know his own weakness.

For today: loving Jesus truly includes recognizing our frailty. Rather than trusting only in our bold promises, we can ask him each day for his help to remain faithful, knowing that he also restores us when we fail.
exp.8:11:
Here some neighbors ask the man who had been blind where Jesus is. He answers simply, "I don't know." The old-style wording in the source's quoted phrases refers to "that man" and "they told him," and those phrases are not used in the verse your reader sees, so they are left out here.

The ones asking are the neighbors and acquaintances of the man who was healed. They are surprised and want to find Jesus, though we do not know their exact intention. The man knows only what he has lived through: Jesus healed him and gave him an instruction. He still does not know where Jesus is or who he truly is. Little by little his faith will grow in the rest of the chapter.

For today: you do not need to know everything in order to bear witness. You can honestly tell what God has done in your life and admit what you still do not understand. That sincerity makes room for your faith to keep growing.
exp.0:14:
This verse tells that John the Baptist spoke about Jesus in a loud voice. He said that Jesus came after him in time, but that he already existed before him, because he is first.

Here the author of the Gospel speaks, recalling within his account what John the Baptist used to say. He has just explained that the Word, that is, Jesus, became human and showed grace and truth. John the Baptist appears to confirm that Jesus is greater than he is, because he existed long before being born.

For today: we do not need to take first place. Like John, we can speak of Jesus with humility and courage, letting him have the most important place in our lives.
exp.5:9:
Jesus asks his disciples to have the people sit down on the ground. "Sit down" here means sitting or settling in to eat, as was the custom at that time. There was a lot of grass in the place, and about five thousand men settled down. The text says "men," that is, adult males; other gospels make clear that there were also women and children.

Jesus speaks right after Andrew mentioned the five barley loaves and two small fish belonging to a boy, and asked what they were among so many people. Jesus does not argue with that doubt; he gives a simple instruction and has everyone seated before he performs the miracle. John tells it to show who Jesus is.

For today: sometimes God asks us to obey one simple step before we see how he will meet the need. Place in his hands the little you have, and trust.
exp.6:16:
Jesus says that whoever sincerely wants to do God's will will be able to recognize whether what He teaches comes from God or whether He speaks on His own authority. The word "will" in the verse means "want," and the teaching itself is the doctrine. The key is the disposition of the heart: obedience opens the eyes to understand.

We are at the Feast of Tabernacles, in Jerusalem. Jesus is teaching in the temple, and the Jews are amazed that He knows so much without having studied with the recognized teachers. He answers that His teaching comes from the Father who sent Him. Then He invites them to test it, not with arguments, but with a heart willing to obey God.

For today: if you have doubts about the faith, do not wait to resolve them all before obeying. Ask God for sincerity, practice what you already understand from His Word, such as forgiving or being honest, and you will see your understanding grow.
exp.10:0:
This verse introduces a man named Lazarus, who was sick. He lived in Bethany, which the verse here calls a village, meaning a small town. It is also the town of his sisters, Mary and Martha. The word that opens the next scene in the story marks the start of a new part of the account.

Here no character speaks; it is John who is narrating. He presents a family that, according to the Gospels, was close to Jesus. The following verse clarifies which Mary is meant, the one who anointed him with perfume, and tells how the sisters sent word to Jesus that the one he loves is sick. John thus prepares the account of Lazarus being raised from the dead.

For today: sickness comes even to those whom Jesus loves. When you are going through a trial, do as these sisters did: tell Jesus your need honestly and trust that he hears you, even when you do not understand his timing.
exp.19:13:
It says that Mary Magdalene, after speaking with the angels, turned around and saw Jesus standing nearby. But she did not realize that it was him. The phrase "turned herself back" means that she turned around, and "saw Jesus standing" is the verse's own wording.

The account is told by John. Mary had gone to the tomb and, weeping, was looking for the body of her Lord, since she thought it had been taken away. She did not expect to see him alive. It is not clearly explained why she did not recognize him; some think her tears blinded her, others that his risen appearance was different. She recognizes him only when he speaks her name.

For today: sometimes Jesus is near even when our grief or our assumptions keep us from seeing him. In times of sadness, stop, pray, and listen carefully. He knows your name and knows how to speak to you.
exp.7:11:
Jesus says that he is the light of the world. Whoever follows him will not walk in darkness, but will have the light that gives life.

Jesus is speaking in Jerusalem during a festival. Many scholars think he was referring to the Feast of Tabernacles, when large lamps were lit in the temple, though this is interpreted in several ways. He had just forgiven the woman who had been accused, and now he declares who he is: the one who brings light and direction. The Pharisees respond by questioning his testimony.

Today, when you do not know which path to take, begin the day with Jesus: read a passage from the Gospels and ask him for direction. Following him means taking the next step with him, even when you cannot see the whole road.
exp.12:32:
Jesus calls his disciples "little children" with great tenderness. He tells them that his time with them is almost over. Later they will look for him, but they will not be able to go where he is going. He had already said something similar to the Jews (John 7:33-34; 8:21). The word "ye" means "you," and "whither" means "where."

Jesus speaks at the Last Supper, after Judas has gone out to betray him. The cross is approaching, along with his return to the Father and his glorification. He speaks to them with tenderness, because he will soon leave them. For them, at that moment, it was not possible to follow him there. His words prepare the new commandment of love.

Today, we do not have to walk alone or depend on our own strength. Jesus leaves us a clear sign: to love one another. This week, look for someone in your church or family and show your affection with a concrete act: a phone call, a visit, or help.
exp.5:48:
Jesus says that the ancestors of his hearers ate the manna in the wilderness, yet they died anyway. "Are dead" is an older way of saying "died." Manna was the food God gave Israel during the years in the wilderness.

Jesus speaks in the synagogue at Capernaum, after feeding the crowd. The people were asking him for a sign and pointed to the manna as proof of Moses. Jesus answers that this bread fed the body, but it did not prevent death. Then he presents himself as the living bread that gives eternal life to whoever believes in him.

For today: God cares for our daily needs, and that is a gift. But we should not be content only with what sustains this life. Today you can seek Jesus in prayer and in his Word, trusting in him as the source of life that lasts forever.
exp.10:51:
