It says that Jesus' death would not be only for the Jewish people. It would also serve to gather into one people the children of God who were "scattered abroad," that is, dispersed and spread out in different places. The phrase "gather together in one" means to bring together into one family.

The speaker is John, the author, explaining the words of Caiaphas, the high priest. He said it was better that one man should die so that the nation would not be lost, thinking in terms of political reasons. John comments that, without knowing it, Caiaphas prophesied something much greater. This happens after Jesus raised Lazarus and the leaders decided to kill him.

For today: God wants to unite people of every kind and place in Christ. We can approach those who are different from us with respect and affection, in the church or outside it, remembering that Jesus died to gather us together.
exp.4:22:
This verse says that God wants all people to honor the Son in the same way they honor the Father. It adds that whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father either, because it was the Father who sent him. The word "honor" here means to respect, to recognize, and to give the highest value.

Jesus speaks in Jerusalem, after healing a man on the Sabbath. Some Jewish leaders criticized him because he said God was his Father. Jesus answers by explaining that the Father gave him authority to give life and to judge. His unity with the Father is so close that rejecting the Son is rejecting God himself.

For today: we cannot say we honor God while ignoring Jesus. Today you can honor him by listening to his word, trusting him, and obeying him in everyday life.
exp.10:36:
This verse records the question of some of those present at Lazarus's mourning. They remember that Jesus had restored sight to a blind man, and they wonder why he did not keep his friend from dying. It is a question shaped by both grief and doubt.

The ones speaking are some of the Jews who had come with Mary and Martha. They have just seen Jesus weeping. Some take it as a sign of affection; others doubt his power. John refers to the miracle in chapter 9. They do not know that Jesus is about to raise Lazarus.

Today we too may ask why God allows suffering. Honest questions like these can be brought to him in prayer. Jesus does not turn away from the one who suffers, and his purposes sometimes reach further than we can see.
exp.3:13:
Jesus says that whoever drinks of the water he gives will never thirst again. That water becomes inside the person a spring that keeps flowing up to eternal life.

Jesus speaks with a Samaritan woman by Jacob's well. She has mentioned the water of the well, and Jesus uses that daily need to speak to her about a deeper need of the soul. The water of the well quiets thirst for a while, but what he offers is life that remains. Many understand that he is referring to the Holy Spirit, as is explained later in the Gospel (John 7:37-39).

For today: when you feel emptiness, weariness or anxiety, do not run first to what only satisfies for a moment. Go to Jesus in prayer, ask him to fill your heart, and trust that he can give you a life that never runs dry.
exp.13:29:
Jesus says that he will not talk with his disciples for much longer, because "the prince of this world" is coming, that is, Satan. He says "you" to them, and he affirms that the prince of this world "hath nothing in me," meaning that he finds in Jesus no sin and no foothold of control.

Jesus speaks at the Last Supper, shortly before going to the cross. He wants to prepare his disciples so that, when everything happens, they will not lose heart but will believe. He says he will obey the Father out of love. Then he invites them: "Arise, let us go hence." Some believe this is where the way to Gethsemane begins; others think the discourse continued afterward.

For today: when you face trials or pressure, remember that Jesus overcame where we fail. Trust in him, ask him for help to obey God, and do not give the enemy ground in your life.
exp.10:11:
The disciples answer Jesus with simple logic: if Lazarus is sleeping, it is a good sign, because rest helps a sick person recover. "Shall do well" is an old way of saying "will get better."

Jesus had just said that Lazarus was sleeping and that he was going to wake him. But he was speaking of death, using sleep as an image. The disciples understood him in a literal way. Besides, going to Judea frightened them, because there they had tried to stone Jesus. Perhaps that is why they clung to an explanation that would make the journey unnecessary.

For today: sometimes we understand God's words only with human eyes, and so we fall short. Let us ask him to open our understanding, and trust that he sees beyond what we are able to see.
exp.7:6:
Jesus answers those who kept asking him. He stands up and tells them that whoever among them is without sin should throw the first stone at the woman. "Persisted" means they kept insisting; "rose up" refers to him standing; "throw" means to hurl.

The scribes and Pharisees brought him a woman caught in adultery. They reminded him that the law of Moses commanded that such people be stoned, and they wanted to set a trap to accuse him. If he said not to stone her, he would seem to go against the law; if he said to stone her, he would clash with the authorities. Jesus does not deny the law, but he examines the hearts of the accusers. What he was writing on the ground is not known for certain.

Before pointing out the faults of others, look honestly at your own. This does not justify sin, but it invites us to correct with humility, compassion, and a desire to restore, not to humiliate.
exp.18:30:
The Jewish leaders asked Pilate to have the legs of those crucified broken and their bodies taken away. The day of preparation before the sabbath, and that sabbath was a high day because it coincided with the Passover feast. Breaking the legs hastened death.

John, who witnessed the scene, tells that the leaders spoke with Pilate, the Roman governor. The Law said that a body hanging on a tree should not remain overnight (Deuteronomy 21:22-23). They wanted to keep the sabbath from being defiled.

For today: caring for religious customs is good, but it should not harden us against the suffering of others. Let us ask God for a heart that loves mercy as much as duty.
exp.6:4:
It says that Jesus's brothers, that is, the sons of Mary and Joseph who grew up with him, still did not trust in him as the Messiah. "Not even" means "not even": even those closest to him were doubting. Here "believe" means to trust in who Jesus was, not merely to know that he existed.

The speaker is the evangelist John. He explains why the brothers give him that advice at the Feast of Tabernacles. They seem to push him to become famous, perhaps with mockery or human interest. Jesus replies that his time, set by the Father's will, has not yet come. Some scholars debate the exact tone of the brothers, but John makes clear that they had no faith.

For today: do not lose heart if close family members do not believe. Keep loving them patiently and give them a good witness. Later, the Bible shows that James came to be a leader in the church.
exp.8:40:
Jesus says to the Pharisees that if they were blind, they would have no sin. But because they say "We see," their sin remains. The phrase "would have" is an older way of saying "would have," and "remains" means their guilt is not taken away.

Jesus is speaking with some Pharisees, after healing a man who had been blind from birth. That man recognized Jesus and believed, while the leaders rejected him. Here "blind" refers to spiritual blindness: whoever admits they need light can receive it. The Pharisees believed they could see clearly, and so they did not seek help. Some scholars understand that Jesus holds them responsible because they had knowledge and still rejected him.

For today: humbly acknowledge that you need Jesus. Do not hide behind your knowledge or your religion. Ask him to open your eyes and show you where you need forgiveness and change.
exp.10:23:
Martha answers Jesus with a statement of faith: she knows that her brother Lazarus will rise again at the resurrection, "at the last day," that is, the final day, at the end of time. It is a belief that many Jews of her time shared.

Martha has just lost her brother, and Jesus told her, "Your brother shall rise again." She takes those words as a distant promise, not as something immediate. There is comfort in her answer, but also a certain distance. Jesus will respond in the next verse by leading her further: the resurrection is not only a future event but a person, Himself.

Today we can hold good beliefs about God and still see them as far away. This verse invites us to bring our hope from "someday" into the present, trusting that Jesus is near in the midst of our pain.
exp.1:6:
Jesus tells the servants to fill the water jars with water. "Fill" is the word used in the verse, and the jars were large stone containers. The servants filled them right up to the top, leaving no room.

We are at a wedding in Cana of Galilee. The wine had run out, and Mary, the mother of Jesus, told the servants to do whatever He told them. Those jars were used for Jewish purification washings. Each one held two or three measures, which means a great deal of water. The text does not say how the change happened, only that what was drawn out afterward was wine.

For today: sometimes God asks us for something simple that seems small, like filling a jar. Obeying with your whole heart, without leaving it half done, makes room for Him to act. Trust Him and take the step that is yours to take today.
exp.16:16:
He says that Jesus asks the Father to sanctify his disciples, that is, to set them apart and make them holy, for God. This happens through the truth, and Jesus explains that this truth is the word of God. Here, to sanctify means to set apart for a sacred purpose and to transform character.

The speaker is Jesus, in his prayer to the Father the night before his crucifixion. He prays for his disciples, who will remain in a world that will reject them. He does not ask to take them out of the world, but to keep them from evil and to prepare them to be sent, as he himself was sent.

For today: if you want to grow in a clean and steadfast life, devote constant time to reading the Bible, meditating on it, and putting it into practice. Start with a short passage each day and ask God to apply it to your life.
exp.10:17:
This verse says that the town of Bethany was very close to Jerusalem, about fifteen furlongs away. A furlong was an ancient measure of distance, roughly 185 meters, so the distance would be almost three kilometers (about two miles). The name "Bethany" appears here in an older form, and "Jerusalem" is spelled the same way the reader sees it in the verse above.

Here the narrator, John, gives a practical detail. He explains that Bethany was so near the capital that many Jews from Jerusalem could easily go to comfort Martha and Mary. He also reminds us that Jesus arrived at a place close to those who wanted to arrest him, and yet he went anyway.

For today: the pain of others is often close to us, just a few steps away. We can draw near to someone who is suffering through a visit, a phone call, or a simple prayer, as those neighbors did and as Jesus did.
exp.20:2:
Simon Peter says, "I am going fishing." The others answer, "We will go with you too." They set out and get into a boat, but that night they catch nothing.

Peter speaks with six other disciples, after Jesus' resurrection. They were on the Sea of Tiberias, which is the Lake of Galilee. The text does not explain why Peter wanted to fish. Some think he went back to his old trade while he waited; others believe he was confused or looking for a living. The text does not say, so it is not wise to state any of this with certainty. The empty night prepares what Jesus will do at dawn.

There are nights when, even after working hard, we see no fruit. That does not mean God is absent. While you wait for answers, stay faithful in everyday things, and keep your eyes open: Jesus may come in the morning.
exp.11:48:
Jesus says that he does not speak on his own authority. The Father who sent him gave him a command, that is, a clear instruction, about what to say and how to speak.

Jesus speaks at the end of his public ministry in Jerusalem. He has just said that he did not come to condemn but to save, yet that whoever rejects his words will be judged by them on the final day. With this verse he explains why his words carry such weight: they come from the Father himself. He then adds that the Father's command is eternal life.

For today: when you read the Bible, receive the words of Jesus not as mere advice, but as the voice of the Father inviting you to live. Listen to them with humility, and put one of them into practice today.
exp.20:23:
This verse says that the disciple being spoken of is the one who gives testimony to what is told in this Gospel, and that he also left it in writing. Those around him affirm: "we know that his testimony is true." The word "wrote" indicates that the account was set down in a text.

The one speaking here is the narrator of the Gospel, together with a "we" who confirms what was said. The disciple is the one who appears in the text as "the disciple whom Jesus loved," and tradition identifies him with John, although some scholars debate how the book was written. The comment comes after a rumor spread that this disciple would not die, and it seeks to clear things up and support the account.

For today: our faith rests on witnesses who saw and left a record. Read the Gospels with confidence, and in your own way, give a simple and honest testimony of what Jesus has done in your life.
exp.1:10:
This verse says that the miracle of turning water into wine was the first sign Jesus performed, and that it happened in Cana of Galilee. A "sign" means an extraordinary event that points to something greater. There Jesus revealed his glory, that is, his power and who he truly is. And his disciples believed in him.

The one who tells the story is John, who wrote his gospel so that readers would believe in Jesus. We are at a wedding, where the wine had run out. Jesus acted without drawing attention: only the servants knew what had happened. John calls this miracle a "sign" because it is not merely a favor to the newlyweds; it reveals who Jesus is.

Today we can notice that Jesus also shows himself in everyday life. If we feel that something is lacking, we can bring it to him with confidence and watch with faith how he works, even in silence.
exp.16:12:
Jesus says that he is now going to the Father, and that he speaks these things while he is still in the world. His purpose is that his disciples would have his joy made full and complete within themselves.

Jesus is praying for his disciples on the night before his crucifixion. He knows that he will soon leave them and that they will face rejection. So he asks the Father to keep them, and he leaves them this prayer as a promise they hear spoken aloud, so that they may be strengthened.

For today: Christ's joy does not depend on everything going well. When you are going through difficulties, set aside a few minutes to read the words of Jesus and to pray. Ask him to fill your heart with his joy, a joy that comes from knowing you are kept by the Father.
exp.0:13:
The explanation says that the Word, who is Jesus, became a human being and lived among us. The word "was" is the plain past tense, and "lived" can literally suggest that he pitched his tent among the people. Those who saw him noticed his glory, the glory of the only Son of the Father. "Only begotten" means one of a kind. He perfectly showed grace (love given without being earned) and truth.

John, one of Jesus' disciples, writes this to explain who Jesus is. Earlier he spoke of God giving those who believe the right to be his children. Now he shows that God himself came near to us. Afterward, John the Baptist gives testimony about him.

For today: if God wanted to come near to us, we can speak to him with confidence, without fear, just as we are. And we can imitate Jesus by treating others with grace and truth together.
exp.10:47:
This verse shows the fear of the religious leaders. They say that if they let Jesus keep doing miracles, everyone will believe in him, and then the Romans will come and take away "our place" (probably the temple or their position of authority) and "the nation" (the Jewish people).

The chief priests and the Pharisees, gathered in council, are the ones speaking. Jesus had just raised Lazarus. Instead of asking whether God was working through him, they were worried about losing power and security under Roman rule. Interpreters see here both political fear and the defense of their own interests.

For today: when we feel afraid of losing something, we can close our eyes to the truth. Let us ask God for humility to accept what he shows us, even when it changes our plans.
exp.13:18:
Jesus says that in a very little while the world will no longer see him, but his disciples will see him. His life is the foundation of their life.

Jesus speaks with his disciples the night before his crucifixion. They are sad and confused because he is leaving. He promises them the Holy Spirit and assures them that he will not leave them as orphans. Many understand "ye see me" to refer to the appearances after the resurrection, while others also think of his constant spiritual presence. It probably includes both ideas.

When you feel alone or without strength, remember that your life does not depend on you, but on Christ, who is alive. Spend a few minutes today speaking with him, trusting that he is with you.
exp.7:19:
He says Jesus spoke this whole discourse in the treasury area of the temple, a section where the offering boxes stood and people left their gifts. He taught there openly, in plain view of everyone, and no one laid hands on him, meaning no one arrested him. The verse gives the reason: his hour had not yet come, the appointed time for his being handed over and put to death.

Jesus had just been speaking with the Pharisees, who were questioning his testimony. He told them that the Father had sent him and that they knew neither the Father nor him. Although there was hostility, nothing happened outside God's plan. John shows that Jesus was not a victim of circumstances; the Father set his hour.

For today: we can rest in the knowledge that our lives are also in the hands of God and his timing. When there is opposition or waiting, let us trust and keep obeying with courage.
exp.10:18:
It says that many of the Jews had gone to the home of Martha and Mary to comfort them over the death of their brother Lazarus. The word "comfort" here means giving them encouragement and company in their grief. The words "á" and "de" are read here as "to" and "for."

Here the narrator, John, is speaking. Bethany was near Jerusalem, about three kilometers away, and that is why it was easy for a large crowd to come. Four days had already passed since the burial, which shows that the mourning was still going on. This sets up the scene: Jesus arrives and finds the sisters surrounded by people who were weeping with them. Commentators note that this was a Jewish custom of accompanying family members in mourning.

For today: when someone suffers a loss, great speeches are not needed. Accompanying, visiting, and simply being present is already a real form of comfort. Think of someone who is grieving and make them a visit or a phone call this week.
exp.11:2:
It says that Mary took a pound of pure spikenard perfume, very costly, and with it anointed the feet of Jesus. Then she wiped his feet with her hair, and the whole house was filled with the fragrance. The word "pound" is a measure of weight, about 300 grams, and the ointment in the verse is the costly, fragrant oil itself.

This happens in Bethany, six days before the Passover, at a dinner in honor of Jesus. Lazarus, whom Jesus had raised, was there. John, the narrator, tells Mary's act as an expression of love and gratitude. Soon Judas will criticize the expense. Jesus will later explain that she did it in connection with his burial (John 12:7).

For today: loving Jesus may cost us something. Offer him today the best of your time, your attention, or your resources, with sincere gratitude, without worrying about what others think.
exp.9:13:
Jesus says that he is the good shepherd. He affirms that he knows his sheep, that is, those who follow him, and that they also know him. Here "know" does not mean only knowing facts, but having a close and personal relationship. The hired hand was the worker who looked after the sheep only for the pay.

Jesus speaks to a group of Jews in Jerusalem, after healing a blind man. He compares the bad leaders, who abandon the people in danger, with himself, who cares for his own. In the following verse he connects this knowledge with his relationship with the Father and announces that he will give his life for the sheep.

For today: you can trust that Jesus knows you completely, with your fears and your failures, and still cares for you. Spend a few minutes each day listening to his voice by reading the Gospels and praying with sincerity.
exp.7:46:
Jesus says that whoever belongs to God listens attentively to what God says. Therefore, those who reject him are not showing that they belong to God. "Hear" here means to listen and receive, not merely to perceive the sound. The word "reprove" in the previous verse means to accuse or to show someone to be guilty.

Jesus is speaking with some leaders and Jews who were questioning him in the temple. He has just asked them who can prove him guilty of sin, and since they do not answer, he points to the real problem: it is not a lack of evidence, but a closed heart. They react with insults, which confirms their hardness.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we truly want to hear God or only want him to tell us we are right. Before reading the Bible, we can pray: "Lord, I want to listen to you and obey you, even when you correct me."
exp.2:25:
John's disciples are about to tell him that Jesus, whom John had pointed to as a witness, is now baptizing and people are going to him. The sentence about "Rabbi" and the sentence about the other side of the Jordan and the sentence about "they said" are not in the reader's verse, so they are removed.

The ones speaking are John's disciples. They had come from a discussion about purification and seem worried, perhaps with some jealousy, because John had fewer followers. John answers in the next verse with humility: his task was to prepare the way, not to be the center.

For today: when others grow or receive more attention than we do in serving God, we can rejoice instead of competing. Every gift comes from God, and our calling is to point to Christ, not to ourselves.
exp.0:28:
John the Baptist sees Jesus coming toward him and points him out to everyone present. He calls him "the Lamb of God" and says that he takes away the sin of the world. The word "takes" here means carrying away or bearing the sin on himself.

John the Baptist is speaking a day after the religious leaders had asked him who he was. He was preaching and baptizing by the Jordan to prepare the people. Now he presents Jesus as the one who was to come. Christians often see here a reference to the sacrificial lambs of the Old Testament, though scholars debate which exact image John has in mind.

For today: if you carry guilt for something you have done, you can bring it to Jesus with confidence. He came precisely to take that burden away. Today you can pray sincerely, ask for forgiveness, and rest in his mercy.
exp.12:20:
This verse says that Jesus, after speaking with his disciples, was deeply troubled within himself. The phrase "was troubled in spirit" means that he felt strong anguish. The word "testified" means that he declared something with seriousness and firmness. Then he told them that one of them was going to betray him.

Jesus is at the Last Supper with his twelve disciples, shortly before his arrest. He had just washed their feet and told them that he is the one the Father sent. Now he announces the betrayal of one of them. The disciples are left confused, not knowing who he meant.

Jesus did not pretend to be strong or hide his pain. He felt the wound of betrayal and spoke about it with honesty. You too can bring your sadness, your disappointments, and the hurts that others cause you to God, knowing that he truly understands you.
exp.14:9:
Jesus says that if we obey his commandments, we will remain in his love. Since the source's comment explains archaic verb forms that do not appear in the King James wording, I have rewritten that sentence to refer to the verse's own words instead: "keep" and "abide," which are the terms the verse actually uses. Jesus gives himself as an example: he obeyed his Father and lives in the Father's love.

Jesus speaks to his disciples the night before his crucifixion. He has just told them that he is the vine and they are the branches. He wants them to stay joined to him in order to bear fruit. Obedience is not the way to earn his love, but the way of living within that love, as he lived with the Father.

Today, when it is hard to obey God in a specific matter, such as forgiving or being honest, remember that you are already loved. Obey not out of fear, but in order to stay close to Jesus and enjoy his company.
exp.2:7:
The explanation says the wind blows wherever it wants. You hear its sound, but you cannot tell where it comes from or where it goes. Jesus says that this is how it is with everyone who has been born of the Spirit. In Greek, the same word (pneuma) can mean both "wind" and "Spirit," and Jesus plays on that double meaning. The phrase "wherever it goes" is an older way of saying the same thing in today's English.

Jesus is speaking with Nicodemus, a Jewish teacher who came to visit him at night. Jesus has just told him that he must be born again. Nicodemus does not understand, and Jesus explains that this new birth is the work of God's Spirit, not of human effort.

For today: you cannot fully control or explain how God works in a person's heart. You can trust that He is at work, watch for the fruit, and pray for others with hope, without needing to manage the process.
exp.14:20:
Jesus says that his followers will suffer rejection and mistreatment "for my name's sake," that is, for belonging to him and bearing his name. The reason is that those who reject them do not know him who sent him, that is, they do not know God the Father.

Jesus speaks to his disciples the night before his crucifixion. He warns them that the world, which rejected him, will also reject them. He does not say this to frighten them, but to prepare and comfort them: if the Master was persecuted, the disciples should not be surprised.

If someone ever criticizes you, shuts you out, or mocks you for living your faith sincerely, do not lose heart or become bitter. Jesus already foretold this. Respond with patience and love, and remember that those who reject Christ often simply do not yet know God.
exp.9:1:
This verse says that the true shepherd of the sheep is the one who enters by the door, that is, openly and legitimately. It contrasts him with someone who climbs in some other way, like a thief. The phrase "the shepherd of the sheep is" is an older way of saying: "that one is the shepherd of the sheep."

Jesus is speaking within his teaching that follows the healing of the man born blind (John 9). The Pharisees had just thrown that man out, and Jesus contrasts the leaders who harm the people with the shepherd who truly cares for them. Afterward he presents himself as the door and the good shepherd.

For today: before following a teacher or leader, look to see whether his life and message point to Christ, with humility and service, and not to his own gain. Compare what he teaches with the Bible.
exp.11:44:
Jesus says that whoever sees him is seeing the Father who sent him. "Seeing" here does not only mean looking with the eyes, but recognizing and understanding who he really is. Jesus shows what God is like.

He speaks at the end of his public ministry in Jerusalem. He had just pointed out that many did not confess their faith for fear of the Pharisees, because they loved the praise of men more than the glory of God. Then he cries out loudly to make it clear that believing in him is believing in God himself, because he comes from the Father with his light and his words.

For today: if you want to know what God is like, look at Jesus. Read the Gospels and notice how he treats the weary, the sinners, and those who suffer. That is the character of God, and you can trust it.
exp.11:37:
John says that the unbelief of the people matched what Isaiah had written. The prophet asked, "Who hath believed our report?" and "to whom hath the arm of the Lord been revealed?" The words "saying" and "arm of the Lord" mean the message that was announced and the strength with which God acts.

The one speaking is the evangelist John. Jesus had already done many signs, but most people did not believe in him. John quotes Isaiah 53:1, a passage that speaks of the suffering Servant. He does not say that God forced anyone not to believe; he shows that the rejection did not catch God by surprise, and that the Scriptures had already foretold it. Christians understand this theme in different ways.

Today, do not be discouraged if you share your faith and few respond. Keep speaking with love and confidence, asking God to open the eyes and hearts of people.
exp.9:18:
This verse says that once again there was a division among the people because of what Jesus had just said. The word "division" here means a disagreement or a split in opinions. The phrase "there was again" shows that this had already happened before, and "the Jews" here refers mainly to the people and leaders of that place who were listening to Jesus.

Jesus was speaking as the good shepherd. He had just said that he gives his life of his own free will, and that he has power to take it up again, by the command of the Father. These were strong words, and the people responded differently: some rejected him, and others saw in his works something good, such as healing a blind man.

For today: Jesus still stirs up different opinions. Do not lose heart if others do not believe. Listen to his words with honesty, look at what he does, and ask God to show you the truth.
exp.10:21:
Martha tells Jesus that she knows, even now, that God will give you whatever you ask of him.

Martha speaks with Jesus shortly after the death of her brother Lazarus. She is hurt, because she thinks Jesus could have prevented his death. Even so, she expresses trust in him. She does not say exactly what she expects Jesus to do, and people have understood her words in different ways: as a hope that Lazarus will live again, or as a general expression of faith. Jesus responds by speaking about the resurrection.

For today: we can bring our pain and our questions to God honestly, without ceasing to trust him. Martha did not hide her sorrow, but she did not let go of her faith either.
exp.2:11:
Jesus tells Nicodemus that if he does not believe when Jesus speaks of earthly things, he will certainly not believe if Jesus speaks of heavenly things. The earthly things are truths that happen here on earth; the heavenly things are truths about God and his plan that come from heaven.

Jesus speaks with Nicodemus, a teacher of the law, who came to see him at night. Shortly before, Jesus explained that a person must be born again. Many think the earthly things are that new birth, which happens on earth, though some understand it differently. Nicodemus did not understand, and Jesus shows that the problem is a lack of faith.

For today: it is not enough to know a lot about religion. If you find it hard to believe what Jesus has already shown you, ask God for a humble heart that is willing to trust in him.
exp.6:18:
Jesus says that Moses gave you the law, yet none of you truly keeps it. Then he asks why you want to kill him. The source's quoted words about giving and about seeking are not in the reader's verse, so they are removed.

Jesus speaks in the temple in Jerusalem during the Feast of Tabernacles. Earlier he had healed a man on the Sabbath (John 5), and some of the leaders wanted to kill him because of it. He shows them that their anger does not come from true obedience to the law, since the same law teaches us to do good and not to kill. The crowd, who perhaps did not know about those plans, reacts with surprise.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we defend the Bible with words but do not practice it. Obeying God includes mercy and love for our neighbor. Let us ask him to give us a sincere heart, one that listens and also lives out what it hears.
exp.4:34:
He says John the Baptist was like a lit lamp: he burned, that is, he had a passion for God, and he gave light, showing the way. The word "willing" in the verse means that the hearers were glad for a while to take pleasure in that light, but it did not last.

Jesus speaks in Jerusalem with religious leaders who were questioning him. They had sent to ask John, and John pointed to Jesus as the truth. Jesus reminds them of that testimony, not because he needs it, but so that they may be saved. Later he will say that his works and the Father himself speak about him.

For today: it is not enough to admire someone who speaks about God or to enjoy a moment of inspiration. The light is there to guide us toward Jesus. Today you can ask yourself: what truth have I already heard that I need to obey?
exp.9:32:
The Jews answer Jesus that they do not want to stone him for his good works, but for blasphemy. In their view, Jesus is a mere man who makes himself out to be God. The phrase "they answered him" is rendered here in the verse as "the Jews answered him," and "to stone" means to kill someone by throwing stones at them.

Jesus was in Jerusalem, at the Feast of the Dedication, and had just said: "I and the Father are one." The leaders understood that he was claiming to be equal to God, and for them that was a serious crime. Jesus asks them about his works, but they focus on his words. Many Christians see here evidence that his listeners understood his claim well.

For today: it is not enough to admire the works of Jesus; we must ask ourselves who he is. Decide today to trust him as Lord, not only as a good teacher.
exp.11:25:
Jesus says that serving him means following him. Where he is, there also will be the one who serves him. And to the one who serves him, the Father will give honor.

Jesus speaks with his disciples a few days before his crucifixion. He has just spoken about the grain of wheat that dies in order to bear fruit, and in this way he announces his own death. Following him includes walking the same path of self-giving. Right after this, he himself confesses that his soul is troubled, yet he chooses to obey the Father.

Serving Jesus is not only doing tasks for him, but walking with him in obedience and self-giving. Today you can ask yourself: "Where is Jesus calling me to serve with humility this week?" And then take one concrete step, even if it is hard.
exp.3:29:
This verse says that the people of Samaria left their town and went to where Jesus was. The phrase "came unto him" means that they drew near to Him. The word "town" refers to Sychar, a village near the well where Jesus was sitting.

No one is speaking here; it is the narrator, John, who tells what happened. A Samaritan woman had talked with Jesus by the well. Then she ran to the village and told everyone to come and see a man who had told her everything she had ever done. Her invitation stirred the people's curiosity, and that is why they went out to find him.

For today: you do not need to have all the answers to speak to others about Jesus. This woman simply told what she had experienced and invited them to see for themselves. A simple and sincere testimony can lead someone to encounter Christ.
exp.6:45:
The temple guards said they did not dare to arrest Jesus because no one had ever spoken the way he did. "Officers" here means guards or temple police, and the phrase "like this man" refers to how this man speaks.

We are at the Feast of Tabernacles, in Jerusalem. The chief priests and the Pharisees had sent these guards to seize Jesus, but they came back empty-handed. When asked why, they gave this answer. They do not explain exactly what impressed them; the text only shows that his words left them unwilling to arrest him. The leaders reacted with anger and contempt.

For today: approach the words of Jesus with an open heart, reading the Gospels without prejudice. Let yourself be moved by what he says, even if others around you reject it.
exp.6:32:
Jesus says that he will be with the people only a little longer. After that he will return to the Father, whom he calls "him that sent me." The explanation of the wording: the phrase in the source refers to the one who sent Jesus, and "é" would simply be "and." It is an announcement that his time on earth is short.

Jesus speaks in Jerusalem during the Feast of Tabernacles. Some believed in him, but the Pharisees and the chief priests sent officers to arrest him. He answers calmly: his life is not in their hands, but follows the Father's plan. His hearers do not understand and think he will go somewhere else.

Today we can learn to value the time in which God speaks to us and gives us opportunities. We should not put off the decision to listen to Jesus and follow him. Today is a good day to pray, read his Word, and respond to him with sincerity.
exp.1:3:
Jesus answers his mother with a question: "What have I to do with thee?" It is an old way of speaking that can be understood as "What do you and I have to do with this?" Calling her "woman" was not a sign of disrespect in that time. He adds that "mine hour is not yet come," meaning the moment set by God for his work.

We are at a wedding in Cana. The wine has run out, and Mary tells Jesus. He makes clear that his mission does not depend on human pressure, but on the Father's timing. Even so, Mary trusts him and says to the servants: "Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it." Some see in the phrase a necessary distance; others, an invitation to faith.

Today we can bring our needs to Jesus with confidence, accepting that his timing and his way may be different from ours. Meanwhile, obeying him is the best course.
exp.20:6:
That disciple whom Jesus loved recognized the Lord when he saw the catch, and he told Peter. Peter tucked in his clothing and fastened it with his belt, because he was wearing only his light work clothes, and he threw himself into the sea.

The account takes place after the resurrection. The disciples had fished all night without success. A man on the shore told them to cast the net on the right side of the boat, and the catch was enormous. That sign reminded them of Jesus. John recognizes him, and Peter reacts with impulse: he wants to reach Jesus quickly.

For today: when you see the hand of God in your life, do not stop at admiring it. Draw near to Him promptly and sincerely, even with your imperfections. And help others recognize Him, as John did.
exp.12:33:
Jesus says he gives a new commandment: that we love one another. The measure of this love is the love he himself has shown us. The words "os" and "á" are old forms; today we would say "les doy" and "a".

Jesus speaks with his disciples at the last supper, shortly before going to the cross. He warns them that he is going to a place where they cannot yet go. Before leaving, he gives them a sign that will identify them: mutual love. It is "new" because now the model is Christ's own love, which gives itself up for others, and not merely loving as one loves oneself.

Today we can choose someone close to us, perhaps someone who is hard to get along with, and serve them in concrete ways: listening to them patiently, forgiving them, or helping them without expecting anything in return.
exp.13:1:
Jesus says that in his Father's house there are many dwelling places, that is, many rooms or places to live. He adds that if this were not so, he would have told them. Then he announces that he is going to prepare a place for his disciples. "Prepare" and "get ready" mean the same thing: to make everything ready.

Jesus speaks at the Last Supper, shortly before his arrest. He has just announced that he is going away and that Peter will deny him. The disciples are sad and afraid. That is why he begins by saying: "Do not let your hearts be troubled." His words aim to give them calm and hope.

For today: when you feel fear or uncertainty about the future, or grief over someone you have lost, remember that Jesus is preparing a place for you and promises to come back for you. You can rest in his word and pray with confidence, today.
exp.3:16:
Jesus confirms that what she said is true, though it was only part of the truth.

Context: Jesus speaks with a Samaritan woman by a well. She has just asked him for the water that quenches thirst forever. Jesus asks her to call her husband, and so he gently touches a painful area of her life. Afterward he will tell her that she has had five husbands and that the man she now lives with is not her husband. He does not humiliate her; he opens a door for her to be honest.

For today: Jesus knows our whole story and still draws near with kindness. We can be honest with God about our wounds and mistakes, hiding nothing. His truth does not seek to shame us, but to heal us and give us a new life.
exp.0:38:
Jesus answers the question of the two disciples with an invitation: "Come and see." They went, saw where he was staying, and remained with him that day. It was about the tenth hour, by the Jewish way of counting the hours, though some think it refers to four in the afternoon, by the Roman way.

The two disciples were followers of John the Baptist, who had just pointed to Jesus as the Lamb of God. They ask where Jesus lives because they want to get to know him up close. According to the next verse, one of them was Andrew, who then tells his brother that they have found the Messiah.

For today: knowing Jesus is not just hearing about him, but spending time with him. You can accept his invitation by setting aside a moment to read his Word and pray sincerely.
exp.5:50:
Jesus says that he is the living bread that came down from heaven. Whoever eats of this bread will live forever. That bread is his own flesh, which he will give for the life of the world.

Jesus is speaking to a crowd that had been following him because he had given them bread. They mentioned the manna from Moses, but Jesus says that bread did not prevent death. He presents himself as the true food that gives eternal life. The Jews are astonished, and Christians have understood his words in different ways: some see them as a call to faith in Christ, others also as the Lord's Supper.

Today we can nourish our souls with Jesus, not only with passing things. Set aside a moment each day to pray and read the Gospels, trusting that he gave himself up for you.
exp.5:53:
Jesus says that whoever eats his flesh and drinks his blood has eternal life, and that he himself will raise that person up at the last day. The words "last day" are the wording used in the verse above. Raising up means bringing someone back from death.

Jesus speaks in Capernaum, after feeding thousands of people with bread. The crowd was looking for more bread, but he presents himself as the bread of life. The Jews are scandalized by his words. Many Christians understand this as trusting fully in Jesus and his sacrifice; others also connect it with the Lord's Supper. There are different interpretations.

Today we can nourish our faith in Christ every day: by praying, by reading his Word, and by remembering that his self-giving gives us hope. We do not depend on our own strength, but on him, who promises life and resurrection.
exp.0:6:
This verse says John came as a witness. His mission was to speak about the light, that is, about Jesus, so that everyone might believe through his message.

The one speaking is the apostle John, the author of this gospel. In his introduction he explains who Jesus is: the Word and the light. Here he introduces John the Baptist, a different man, sent by God. He mentions him to make clear that John pointed to Jesus, but was not the light. His role was to direct people's attention toward Christ.

For today: we can be simple witnesses. We do not have to be the center or have all the answers. It is enough to honestly share what Jesus has done in our lives and point to Him, so that others may come to know Him for themselves.
exp.4:12:
The explanation says that the man whom Jesus had healed at the pool of Bethesda did not know who had healed him. Jesus had withdrawn, that is, he had quietly slipped away into the crowd that was there. "Wist not who it was" means "did not know who it was."

The one who tells the story is John. The Jewish leaders were asking the man who had told him to carry his mat on the Sabbath. He only knew that someone had healed him, but he did not know his name. Jesus slipped away, and later the man found him in the temple. Some think Jesus acted discreetly so as not to make a spectacle; the text does not explain the reason with certainty.

God often works in our lives without our noticing right away. We can stop to recognize his blessings, seek him, and thank him, instead of receiving his help and moving on without knowing where it came from.
exp.4:2:
Here the text describes a great number of sick people lying on the porches of the pool: blind, lame, and "withered," that is, people whose limbs were paralyzed or wasted away. All of them were waiting for the water to be stirred, since they believed that this would allow them to be healed. The word about them lying down means they were stretched out, unable to care for themselves.

The one speaking is the narrator of the gospel, traditionally John. He tells that Jesus went up to Jerusalem for a Jewish feast and arrived at this place full of suffering. Some early manuscripts do not include the explanation of the angel who stirs the water, and scholars explain this in different ways.

For today: Jesus did not avoid places where there was suffering. We can ask for eyes to see those near us who are waiting for help, and take a concrete step: visit, listen, or pray for someone.
exp.4:41:
Jesus says: "But I know you, that you do not have the love of God in you." The word "mas" means "but," and "os conozco" means "I know you." He is not speaking of a passing impression, but of seeing into their hearts.

Jesus is speaking with religious leaders from Jerusalem who criticized him for healing on the Sabbath and for calling himself the Son of God. They studied the Scriptures, but they were not willing to come to him to receive life. According to the context, they preferred the applause of the people over the approval of God.

Today we can ask ourselves: do I do religious things to love God, or so that others will admire me? Let us ask him to heal our motives and bring us close to Jesus with sincerity.
exp.2:32:
He who accepts and believes what Jesus testifies confirms, as one who sets his seal or signature to a document, that God is true. "Confirmed" comes from the idea of putting a seal on something: it is firmly declaring that something is certain. "Testimony" is what Jesus says he has seen and heard from the Father.

These words are part of the final speech of John the Baptist (or, according to some scholars, a comment by the evangelist; interpreters do not agree). They speak of Jesus, who comes from above. Shortly before, John laments that almost no one receives his testimony. Here the other side is shown: whoever does receive it honors God.

For today: believing in Jesus is not just an idea; it is saying "yes" to God and trusting that his word is true. Today you can do this by obeying a teaching of Jesus that you already know, even when it is costly.
exp.6:25:
This verse shows the surprise of some people of Jerusalem. Jesus was speaking in public, without hiding, and the authorities were not saying anything to him. So they ask whether perhaps the rulers, that is, the leaders and religious authorities, had already recognized that Jesus is the Christ, that is, the promised Messiah.

These are the words of the people of Jerusalem, during the Feast of Tabernacles. They knew that the authorities wanted to kill Jesus, but they saw him teaching freely. Their doubt was sincere, though confused. Soon they think Jesus cannot be the Christ because they believe they know where he comes from. Jesus answers that they do not truly know God, who sent him.

For today: it is not enough to look only at what others do or say, or at what seems to be the case. Let us seek Jesus for ourselves, with humility, reading his Word and asking God to give us understanding.
exp.8:32:
It says that if Jesus were not from God, he would have no power to do anything he did. The phrase "could do nothing" is taken straight from the verse. The speaker maintains that Jesus' miracles show that God is with him.

The man speaking is the one who was born blind and whom Jesus healed. The Pharisees are questioning him, because they say Jesus is a sinner for having healed on the Sabbath. The man, who has no religious training, reasons simply: something so extraordinary could not have happened without God. The leaders become angry, insult him, and throw him out. Later, Jesus looks for him and finds him.

For today: be honest about what God has done in your life, even when others argue about it or reject you. Your simple and sincere testimony has value, and Jesus does not abandon someone who stands up for him.
exp.5:22:
This verse says that other small boats had come from Tiberias, a city on the lake, to a place near where the people had eaten the bread. There the Lord had given thanks before distributing it. The word "boats" in the verse refers to small boats, and the verse's phrase "had come" means that they had arrived.

The one speaking here is John, the narrator. He is explaining how the crowd could cross the lake the next day. Jesus had already fed thousands of people with a few loaves and fish, and then He left without being seen. The crowd noticed that He was not there, so they got into those boats to look for Him in Capernaum.

For today: the people made a great effort to find Jesus, but later we will see that they were looking for him mainly because of the bread. We can ask ourselves honestly: do I seek Jesus for who He is, or only for what He gives me? Let us ask Him for a heart that desires Him.
exp.5:56:
Jesus says that the Father is "living," that is, the source of all life, and that he sent him into the world. Jesus lives because of the Father, meaning he depends on Him and is united with Him. In the same way, whoever eats me, that is, whoever joins themselves to Jesus and receives him by faith, will live because of him. The word "even" in this verse points to this same pattern, so that the one who receives Jesus shares in the same kind of life.

Jesus speaks in the synagogue at Capernaum, after feeding the crowd with bread. The people were looking for more food, and he teaches them that he wants to give them eternal life. Christians understand these words in different ways: some see them as faith in Christ, others as a reference to the Lord's Supper, and others as both.

Today, do not live by your own strength. Begin the day by seeking Jesus in prayer and in his Word, so that he may be your sustenance.
exp.15:14:
Jesus says that everything the Father has also belongs to him. For this reason he states that the Holy Spirit will take from what belongs to Jesus and make it known to the disciples.

Jesus speaks on the last night with his disciples, before his arrest. He sees them sad because he has told them he is going away. He promises them they will not be left alone: the Spirit of truth will guide them and help them understand Jesus more fully. Later, they will not clearly grasp his statement about "a little while."

For today: when you read the Bible, ask the Holy Spirit to help you know Jesus better. He does not seek to draw attention to himself, but to lead you to Christ and his truth.
exp.19:3:
It says that Peter and the other disciple were running together toward Jesus' tomb, but the other one ran faster and got there first. Traditionally the "other disciple" is understood to be John, although the text does not give his name.

The one telling the story is the author of the Gospel, who recounts what happened on the morning of the resurrection. Mary Magdalene had seen the tomb opened and went to tell them, thinking someone had taken the body away. The two disciples set out right away to check it for themselves. Some think the detail about who arrived first shows that the writer was an eyewitness.

For today: when we hear news about Jesus, let us not stand still. We can respond with interest and seek the truth for ourselves, without comparing ourselves to others, because each person comes to Christ at their own pace.
exp.7:20:
Jesus tells them again that he is going away, that they will look for him, but that they will die in their sin. He adds that where he is going, they cannot come.

Jesus speaks in the temple with Jewish leaders who reject him. Shortly before, he had told them that they do not know the Father. They do not understand and think he will kill himself. Jesus explains that he comes from above, from heaven. Many believe that "you will seek me" speaks of a late search, without true faith, although the text does not spell this out.

Today, let us not postpone faith. If Jesus calls us, let us respond with humility and trust, acknowledging our need for forgiveness. He himself is the way that leads us to the Father.
exp.2:24:
This verse tells of an argument that arose between some of John the Baptist's disciples and a Jew (or several Jews, according to the ancient text) about "purifying." A "question" means a debate or dispute. The "purifying" refers to religious washings, that is, to their meaning and value.

The one who narrates is the apostle John. He records this because John the Baptist and Jesus were baptizing at the same time, and the question arose of which baptism or which purifying was better. The text does not say exactly what the point of the dispute was. But this dispute leads John's disciples to complain that everyone was going to Jesus.

For today: when a religious discussion turns into a competition, we lose sight of what matters most. Let us ask God for a humble heart, one that rejoices when Christ is honored, even when we are not the ones in the spotlight.
exp.8:9:
The neighbors put a direct question to the man who had once been blind: "How were thine eyes opened?" They want to know how it is possible that he now sees. The archaic form and quoted phrases in the source are not reproduced here.

The ones speaking are the neighbors and those who knew him as a beggar. They are surprised, and they even doubt whether he is the same person. He had already told them, "I am he." Now they want an explanation, because a change like this was not something people saw every day. His answer, in the verses that follow, is simple: he tells what Jesus did, without embellishing anything.

For today: when someone asks you what has changed in your life, you do not need to give a complicated speech. Honestly tell what God has done for you, just as you lived it. A sincere and humble testimony can stir up questions and open doors to talk about Jesus.
exp.6:24:
This verse says that some people living in Jerusalem were asking one another, "Is this not the one they are looking to kill?" The explanation's comment about the old spelling of the city's name does not apply to the verse as your reader sees it, so it is left out.

Jesus was teaching in the temple during the Feast of Tabernacles. Shortly before, he had argued that healing a man on the Sabbath was a good thing. The people of Jerusalem knew that the leaders wanted to kill him, but now they saw him speaking openly and no one was stopping him. This caused them amazement and confusion.

For today: when something does not fit what we expect, let us not rely only on rumors or on what others say. As Jesus asked, let us judge with righteous judgment: let us listen to his Word and let it make clear to us who he is.
exp.19:8:
This verse says that the disciples had not yet understood what the Scripture foretold: that the Messiah had to rise from the dead. The phrase "for as yet they knew not" means that they still did not grasp it. "Must" shows that the resurrection was part of God's plan.

The one speaking is John, who tells what he experienced that morning. He has just said that he saw the empty tomb and believed. Here he explains that this faith came from seeing the signs, before he fully understood the Scriptures. He does not say which passages he had in mind; some think of Psalm 16:10 or Isaiah 53, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: do not be discouraged if you do not yet understand everything. The disciples began believing with little, and God gradually opened their understanding. Keep reading the Bible with humility and trust that He will teach you little by little.
exp.1:5:
The explanation says that at the wedding feast there were six stone water jars. They were used for the purification of the Jews, that is, for washing hands and utensils according to their religious customs. The words that are rendered as small jars and pitchers in the source are simply jars, and the measure of liquid each one held was about two or three measures. This is usually calculated at roughly 80 to 120 liters, although the exact figure is uncertain.

The narrator, John, describes the scene right after Mary notices that the wine has run out and tells the servants to do whatever Jesus says. John presents the jars first to show that the miracle that follows will be real and visible, involving a large quantity of water.

For today: God can use the ordinary things we have at hand. If He asks us for something simple, like filling some jars, we should obey with confidence, even when we do not yet understand what He is going to do.
exp.19:7:
This verse tells that the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first but stayed outside, now went in. He saw the linen cloths and the cloth that had been over Jesus' head, and he believed. The sentence about the old form of a word is removed, since that word does not appear in the verse as your reader sees it. The text does not say exactly what he believed: many think he believed that Jesus had risen, while others think that at least he believed what Mary Magdalene had told him, that the tomb was empty.

John, who tells the scene in the third person, describes the morning of the resurrection. Mary had reported that the body had been taken away, and Peter and this disciple ran to see it. Tradition identifies this disciple with John, although the text does not give his name. The following verse explains that they still did not understand the Scripture about the resurrection.

For today: faith sometimes begins with little understanding. You can take a step of trust in the signs God shows you, and ask him to keep making the rest clear to you.
exp.3:3:
This verse says that Jesus "had to" pass through Samaria. The word "must" in the verse is an older way of saying "necessary." The verb "pass" is used here in the sense of "go through."

Here it is not Jesus speaking, but the narrator, John. Jesus was traveling from Judea to Galilee. Geographically, the most direct route crossed Samaria, although many Jews took a detour to avoid it because of the hostility between the two peoples. Some think the necessity was only one of route; others also see a divine purpose, since soon Jesus meets a Samaritan woman. The text does not fully explain it.

For today: sometimes the paths that seem like simple routes hide encounters with purpose. We can walk attentively and be willing to love those others avoid, trusting that God can use our ordinary day.
exp.15:0:
Jesus says he has told you these things so that you would not be offended. The word "offended" here does not mean being upset by gossip. It means stumbling or falling away in faith, like someone who trips over a stone on the road. Jesus wants his disciples not to turn away from him when difficulties come.

Jesus speaks with his disciples on the night before his arrest. He has just explained to them that the world will hate them, as it hated him (John 15). He warns them ahead of time about the rejection and persecution that will come, so that it does not catch them by surprise or lead them to think that God has abandoned them.

Today, Jesus does not promise a life without problems. He prepares us honestly. If, for following him, you face mockery, rejection, or hardship, it does not mean you were wrong. Remember his words, stay close to him in prayer, and trust that he is still with you.
exp.8:2:
Jesus answers that this man's blindness was not a punishment for any sin of his own or of his parents. He says it happens "so that the works of God should be made manifest in him," that is, so that God's power and care can be seen in his life. The word "but" in the verse means "rather," which is the same idea as "instead."

The disciples asked Jesus why the man was born blind. In that time many people thought that every illness came from some sin. Jesus corrects that idea and changes the question: instead of looking for someone to blame, he looks at what God can do. Right away he says that he is the light of the world and will heal the man.

Today, when someone suffers, let us avoid pointing at people to blame or offering easy explanations. Better to walk alongside them with compassion and trust that God can work, even in what we do not understand.
exp.3:5:
This verse says that Jacob's well was there. Jesus was tired from walking, so he sat down by the well. It was around noon. "Well" here means the well, and "the sixth hour" is the sixth hour of the Jewish day, which is usually understood as noon, although some scholars place it differently.

The one telling the story is the apostle John, who narrates Jesus' journey through Samaria. Jesus was on the road and stopped at a place with historical roots for the people of Israel, near Sychar. While his disciples went to buy food, Jesus stayed alone, preparing for the meeting with the Samaritan woman.

For today: Jesus really grew tired, like any person. If you are exhausted today, you can come to God without shame. Resting is also part of a healthy life, and God can meet you right in those moments of pause.
exp.20:21:
Jesus answers Peter: "If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me." The phrase "what is that to thee?" means "what does it have to do with you?" And "until I come" refers to his return.

Jesus had just restored Peter and told him how his life would end. Peter, seeing the beloved disciple, asked: "And this one, what about him?" Jesus does not respond with curiosity or with details, but turns him back to his own calling. Afterward, the text makes clear that Jesus did not say that disciple would not die; some people misunderstood his words.

Each person has a different path with God. Comparing ourselves with others distracts us. Today, instead of asking what belongs to others, ask yourself what Jesus is asking of you, and follow Christ faithfully.
exp.4:33:
Jesus says that he does not depend on the testimony of any human being to be who he is. The explanation of "but" in this verse is simply that it means "but," and the word translated "but" here also means "but." When he mentions John's testimony, it is so that they might be saved, that is, so that they might believe and receive life.

Jesus is speaking with religious leaders who were questioning him after he healed a man on the Sabbath. He reminds them that they themselves sent people to ask John the Baptist, who spoke the truth. Jesus does not need human approval, but he uses that testimony as a help so that they might recognize the truth.

Today we can thank the people God uses to bring us closer to Jesus, but without stopping at them. What matters most is going personally to Christ, reading his Word, and trusting in him.
exp.7:36:
Jesus acknowledges that his listeners are physical descendants of Abraham. Yet he tells them that they want to kill him. The reason is that his word has no place in them: it does not find room in their hearts, and they do not receive it.

Jesus is speaking with Jews who had in some way believed in him, but who resist his teaching. He has just told them that the Son gives true freedom. They are offended because they think they are free by virtue of their lineage. Jesus shows them that being Abraham's family is not enough if they reject what God says through him.

For today: having a good religious heritage or attending church is not enough. Ask yourself whether God's Word has room in your heart. Ask the Lord to help you receive it with humility, even when it corrects you.
exp.5:29:
Here the crowd asks Jesus for a sign so that they may believe in him. A "sign" means a miracle that proves who he is. They ask him: "What do you do?" The words that begin the verse and the phrase about what they are willing to accept are older forms of "They said" and "we may see, and believe thee."

The speakers are people from the crowd that Jesus had fed with bread the day before. He had just told them that the work of God is to believe in the one the Father sent. Instead of accepting this, they ask for more proof and mention the manna their ancestors ate. Some understand that they were looking for a sign even greater than the multiplication of the loaves, although the text does not fully explain this.

For today: it is easy to want proof before trusting God, even after seeing his help. We can remember what he has already done in our lives and respond with simple trust in Jesus, not only when everything seems clear to us.
exp.18:41:
This verse says that Jesus was placed in that tomb for two reasons: it was the eve of the Jewish Passover, that is, the day of preparation, and the tomb was close by. "Eve" means the day before. "They laid Jesus" means that they buried him there.

The one telling this is John, a witness to the crucifixion. He explains that Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus had little time, because at nightfall a very solemn day of rest was about to begin. So they did not look for a distant place, but the new tomb in the garden. John also shows that Jesus' death was real and that his burial was carried out with reverence.

For today: God can work through the simple and the urgent. Even if you have little time or few resources, offer with love what you have, as these men did. God can use that faithful act.
exp.17:23:
The verse says that Annas, after questioning Jesus, sent him bound to Caiaphas, the high priest. Jesus had already been arrested in the garden and was first taken before Annas, an influential old man who had been high priest before.

John tells this simply, without comment. Annas was Caiaphas's father-in-law, and Caiaphas held the office that year. Scholars debate a little how the questioning was divided between the two, since the Gospels do not detail it completely. What is clear is that Jesus is passed from hand to hand, bound, while Peter waits outside.

For today: Jesus faced injustice bound and in silence, without returning the blow. When you are treated unfairly, you can trust that God sees everything, and respond with truth and calm, not with revenge.
exp.12:4:
Jesus pours water into a basin, a wide bowl used for washing. Then he begins to wash his disciples' feet and dries them with the towel he had tied around his waist.

The account in John takes place at the last supper, shortly before the crucifixion. The text says that Jesus knew the Father had given him all things and that he was returning to God. Even so, he does the work of a servant, a task that at that time was normally left to household servants. Many understand that he teaches humility in this way; Jesus himself explains it later in the chapter.

Today we can ask ourselves whom we might serve in simple ways and without seeking recognition: helping at home, listening to someone who is weary, or doing a task that no one wants to do. True Christian leadership is shown in humble service.
exp.7:39:
Here Jesus says that the people listening to Him want to kill Him, even though He has only told them the truth He received from God. Jesus points out that Abraham never acted this way.

Jesus is speaking with some leaders and Jews who boast that they are children of Abraham. They reject His message and are already trying to take His life. Jesus shows them that being descendants of Abraham by blood is not enough: Abraham believed and received the word of God, and they are doing the opposite.

For today: having a good heritage or belonging to a church is not enough. True faith shows in how we respond to the truth of God. If something in His Word makes us uncomfortable, let us ask for humility to listen and obey, instead of hardening ourselves.
exp.6:47:
The Pharisees ask a question meant to silence the guards: "Has any of the rulers or of the Pharisees believed on him?" Here "rulers" refers to the leaders or religious authorities, and "the officers" are the temple guards. By this they mean that no one important believes in Jesus.

The Pharisees speak out of irritation, because the guards came back without arresting Jesus. The guards had been impressed by his words. The leaders respond with pressure: if the authorities do not believe, neither should you. It is an argument from prestige, not from truth. Shortly after, Nicodemus, who was one of them, begins to speak with more care.

For today: let us not measure truth by fame, position, or the opinion of the majority. Let us examine humbly what Jesus says and respond honestly, even when others do not.
exp.3:12:
Jesus says that whoever drinks of this well will thirst again. The word "drinketh" means "drinks," and "shall thirst again" means that the thirst will come back. It is a simple truth: the water from the well quenches thirst only for a little while.

Jesus speaks with a Samaritan woman by Jacob's well. She thinks of ordinary water and wonders how He could give her living water without even having a bucket. Jesus does not correct her harshly, but uses the water of the well as a picture to lead her to think about a deeper need. Many understand that this living water represents the life that God gives through Him.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we seek again and again to fill the emptiness of the heart: success, approval, money or entertainment. Today you can bring that thirst to Jesus in prayer, with honesty.
exp.7:25:
Jesus says that he has many things to say and to judge about them, but that he does not speak on his own authority. The one who sent him, the Father, is trustworthy, that is, worthy of trust. And what Jesus announces to the world is what he has heard from him.

Jesus is speaking in the temple with religious leaders who doubt him. They have just asked him who he is, and he warns them that they will die in their sins if they do not believe in him. His answer insists that his message comes from the Father. The text says that they did not understand this.

For today: before trusting a teaching, ask yourself whether it points to the truth of God. We can read the Gospels with humility, listening to Jesus and not only to what we already think, and letting him correct our hearts.
exp.18:4:
Jesus comes out before the crowd wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe, a dark red cloak that the soldiers put on Him to mock Him. Pilate says, "Behold the man!" that is, "Look at this man."

Pilate is the Roman governor. He had already said that he found no crime in Jesus. He presents Him wounded and humiliated, perhaps hoping that the people would feel pity. Commentators differ about his exact intentions. The chief priests, by contrast, demand that He be crucified.

Jesus accepted being humiliated out of love for us. When someone despises you or treats you badly and unjustly, remember that Christ knows that pain. Ask Him to give you patience, and look to Jesus before responding in anger.
exp.15:24:
Jesus says that until now he has spoken to them in parables, that is, with comparisons and figurative language that was hard to understand. But a time is coming when he will no longer speak this way, and he will tell them openly about the Father. To make known to you is to give you the knowledge of something.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples at the last supper, shortly before going to the cross. He has told them about his departure and the coming of the Spirit. Many understand that "that day" refers to the time after the resurrection and the coming of the Holy Spirit, when they would understand better. Some also see it as something that continues in the life of the church.

For today: if there are things about God that you do not fully understand, do not be discouraged. Keep reading the Bible and praying with humility, trusting that God gives you light little by little, and draw near to the Father in the name of Jesus.
exp.9:27:
Jesus says that he himself gives eternal life to his sheep, that is, to those who belong to him. He affirms that they will never be lost and that no one will be able to take them out of his hand. The word "perish" means to be lost or destroyed. "Pluck" means to take away by force.

Jesus speaks in Jerusalem, during a conversation with religious leaders who doubted him and asked him to say plainly whether he was the Messiah. He uses the image of the shepherd and his sheep: the sheep hear his voice, he knows them, and they follow him. His promise is tied to the security that comes from his unity with the Father.

Today, if you trust in Christ and try to follow him, you can live with peace rather than constant fear. When you doubt or feel weak, listen again to his voice in the Bible and in prayer, and remember that your security rests on his strength, not on your own.
exp.10:7:
The disciples speak to Jesus with concern. Their word for him is a respectful title meaning "teacher." Their description of the danger refers to the Jewish leaders who had been trying to kill him, and they remind him that those leaders had recently wanted to kill him in Judea. They ask whether he really intends to go back there.

The disciples speak out of fear and out of affection for Jesus. He has just learned that his friend Lazarus is sick, and he decides to go to Judea. They remember the danger from John 10:31, when people picked up stones against Jesus. Their worry is understandable, but they do not yet understand that Jesus walks according to the timing and purpose of the Father.

When God calls us to obey, the path sometimes seems dangerous, and our fear can make us doubt. We can bring those fears to Jesus honestly, as the disciples did, and ask him to help us trust that his guidance is safe, even when we do not understand everything.
exp.7:32:
They answered him, "We are Abraham's descendants, and we have never been slaves to anyone. How can you say, 'You will be made free'?" They do not understand why He says they will be set free, since they believe they have never been slaves to anyone.

Jesus had just spoken to Jews who had come to believe in Him, and He told them that the truth would set them free. They feel insulted, as if He were saying they lacked freedom. This is striking, because their people had lived under Egypt, Babylon, and Rome. Perhaps they are speaking of their inner freedom or of their identity as God's people; scholars understand this in different ways. Jesus answers them by speaking of slavery to sin.

For today: do not rest on your heritage, your church, or your good name. Ask Jesus to show you the areas where you are still bound, and remain in His word to receive His freedom.
exp.18:23:
The Roman soldiers did not want to tear Jesus' tunic, because it was made of one piece, woven without seams. So they decided to cast lots, something like a drawing, to see who would keep it. "Garment" means an item of clothing, and "fulfilled" means that it came true.

The ones speaking are the soldiers who crucified Jesus. They had already divided his other clothes into four parts. John explains that this fulfilled what Psalm 22:18 said, written centuries before. The soldiers did not know they were fulfilling a prophecy; they were only dividing up the little they had at hand.

For today: God keeps working even in the midst of what is unjust and cruel. If your situation today seems out of control, trust that He is still guiding the story, even if you cannot see it yet.
exp.11:32:
This verse is a note added by the writer, John. When Jesus spoke of being lifted up from the earth, John explains that by this Jesus was showing the way in which he would die. The phrase "showing" here means pointing out or making clear. "Lifted up" points to the crucifixion, when Jesus would be raised up on a cross.

Jesus speaks in Jerusalem, a few days before his death, and announces that his hour has come. John adds this note so that his readers will understand that Jesus knew what awaited him. The crowd, however, did not grasp his words well and became confused, because they expected a Messiah who would remain forever.

For today: Jesus was not caught off guard by suffering; he accepted it out of love. When you go through difficult moments, trust that God can bring something good even out of pain, and let the cross remind you of how much he loves you.
exp.8:22:
These words repeat what the parents of the man born blind had already said. "He is of age" means that he is already an adult, and "ask him" means "ask him yourselves." With this, the parents avoid giving explanations about their son's healing.

The parents spoke before the Jewish leaders, who were investigating how Jesus had given sight to their son. They confirmed that he was their son and that he had been born blind, but they did not want to give an opinion about Jesus. John explains that they were afraid, because it had been decided to put out of the synagogue anyone who acknowledged Jesus as the Messiah. Being put out meant losing life in the community.

For today: fear of rejection can silence us when we ought to testify to what God has done. Let us ask him for courage, and remember that his care is worth more than the approval of others.
exp.7:45:
Jesus asks: "Which of you convinces me of sin?" The verse is asking who among them can prove that he is guilty of any wrongdoing. Jesus challenges his hearers to point out a single fault in him. Then he asks why, if he speaks the truth, they do not believe him.

Jesus is speaking with some Jews who opposed him in Jerusalem. He has just told them that their desires resemble those of the devil, a liar and a murderer. They were already looking for a way to kill him. He does not answer them with anger, but with a question that shows their rejection has no fair reason behind it. They respond with insults, not by proving anything.

For today: when the truth makes us uncomfortable, it is wise to ask ourselves honestly whether we reject it for solid reasons or out of pride and habit. Let us ask God for a humble heart to listen.
exp.3:4:
