Jesus came to a town in Samaria called Sychar, near the piece of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph. The reference to the parcel of ground points to a family property passed down to the children.

John, the narrator, places the scene in a place with a history. Jesus was traveling from Judea to Galilee, and it was necessary for him to pass through Samaria. Some think it was the shortest route; others also see a purpose from God. Jews and Samaritans usually had a bad relationship, and yet Jesus enters that land. This place prepares the encounter with the woman by the well.

God can prepare important encounters in ordinary and even uncomfortable places. Today, when faced with an unexpected path or a person different from us, we can ask: "Lord, what do you want to do here?"
exp.17:34:
Pilate answers with some irritation: "Am I a Jew?" He means that he does not know, and does not care about, the religious disputes of that people. He reminds them that it was Jesus' own nation and the chief priests who handed him over to him. Then he asks directly: "What have you done?"

Jesus has just asked him whether he was speaking on his own or repeating what others said. Pilate, the Roman governor, is questioning Jesus inside the praetorium, his place of government. The Jewish leaders had accused Jesus of being a king. Pilate seeks to understand whether Jesus is really a danger. With this question, Jesus goes on to explain the nature of his kingdom.

Today, before repeating what others say about Jesus, we can ask ourselves what we think of him. Reading the Gospels for ourselves helps us know him truly.
exp.5:21:
This verse tells what the crowd noticed the day after the miracle of the loaves. They were on the east side of the lake, which is called here "the sea." They saw that there was only one small boat there, and that Jesus had not gone into it with his disciples. The disciples had left by themselves. The crowd realized that Jesus was not there.

Here the narrator, John, is speaking. He has just recounted that Jesus fed thousands of people and then walked on the water to reach his disciples. The crowd did not see that miracle at night, and that is why they wonder where Jesus is. The verses that follow say they searched for him as far as Capernaum.

For today: seeking Jesus is good, but it is worth asking ourselves why we seek him. Let it be because of who he is, and not only because of what he gives us.
exp.4:8:
The man who had been ill was made well at once. "Immediately" means "right away." Then he took up his bed, which was his mat or pallet, and walked off. The verse adds that this day was the Sabbath, the day of rest for the Jews.

The narrator, John, tells what happened beside the pool of Bethesda. That man had been sick for many years and was waiting for help. Jesus commanded him to get up, and he obeyed. John mentions the Sabbath because it will lead to an argument: the Jewish authorities held that carrying his bed on the Sabbath broke the law of rest.

For today: when God asks us for a step of faith, we do not need to understand everything. This man obeyed, and in that act he received the strength to walk. Today we can take that simple step, trusting the word of Jesus.
exp.7:47:
Here the Jews, who opposed Jesus, respond with insults. They call him "a Samaritan," which was a form of contempt, and say that he "has a devil," that is, that he is possessed or out of his mind. The word for "rebukes" in the earlier wording means accuses or shows someone to be guilty.

Jesus had just told them that whoever is of God hears the words of God, and that they did not listen. Feeling singled out, instead of answering with reasons, they attack the person. Many Jews of that time despised the Samaritans. Jesus does not return the insult; he answers calmly that he honors his Father.

For today: when a truth makes us uncomfortable, it is easy to defend ourselves by attacking the one who says it. Let us ask God for humility to examine what we hear, and if someone offends us, let us imitate the calm of Jesus.
exp.17:4:
Here the crowd that came to arrest Jesus tells him they are looking for "Jesus of Nazareth," that is, Jesus of Nazareth. He answers, "I am he." Judas, who betrayed him, was standing there with them.

It is the night of the arrest, in a garden. Judas arrived with soldiers and guards sent by the religious leaders, carrying lanterns and weapons. John stresses that Jesus knew everything that awaited him and still stepped forward. No one caught him by surprise. Some see in "I am he" a reference to the divine name in the Old Testament; others, only a simple identification. Perhaps both are true, and the soldiers' reaction suggests something more than a plain answer.

For today: Jesus faced the most difficult moment with courage and willing self-giving. When you are afraid of something you must face, remember that he walked that path already and can walk with you.
exp.8:37:
He says that the man who had been born blind answered Jesus, "Lord, I believe," and then he worshipped him.

The man healed by Jesus is speaking. The Pharisees had thrown him out for insisting that Jesus had healed him. Jesus finds him, asks whether he believes in the Son of Man, and reveals himself to him. His physical sight was restored first, but now his spiritual eyes are opened. Some scholars note that here "worship" shows a deep recognition of who Jesus is, though this man was perhaps only beginning to understand it.

Today, you do not need to have all the answers to respond to Jesus. When He makes himself known to you, the simple response is to believe and surrender your life to Him with gratitude, even when others do not understand.
exp.11:19:
This verse says that among the people who had gone up to Jerusalem to worship God during the feast of Passover, there were some Greeks. "Gone up" refers to traveling to Jerusalem, which is set on high ground. "Greeks" here probably means Gentiles, that is, people who were not Jews, who showed respect for the God of Israel.

Here the narrator, John, is speaking. Jesus had just entered Jerusalem, and the crowd was welcoming him. The Pharisees complained that "the world" was going after him. John presents these Greeks as a sign that Jesus would draw people beyond the Jewish people. Although we do not know with certainty exactly who they were, the account shows their desire to see Jesus.

For today: God invites everyone to come near to Jesus, no matter their background. We can be like Philip and Andrew: helping those who seek Christ to find him, without putting up barriers in their way.
exp.20:10:
Simon Peter went up into the boat and dragged the net to land, full of large fish. There were a hundred and fifty-three of them. Although there were so many, the net was not torn.

The disciples had fished all night without catching anything. Jesus, now risen, told them from the shore to cast the net on the other side, and a huge catch came in. Then he asked them to bring some of the fish for breakfast. John records the detail with care. The number 153 has been given many interpretations, but the text does not explain its meaning, so it is not known for certain.

Jesus can care for and sustain what he himself gives us. When he blesses our work, he also gives strength to carry it. We can obey his word even when we are tired, and trust that he provides, without living in fear that everything will fall apart.
exp.4:20:
This verse says that God the Father has the power to raise the dead and give them life, and that Jesus, the Son, does the same for whomever he chooses. The phrase "whom he will" means "those he decides." Jesus presents himself with the same authority as God to give life.

Jesus speaks in Jerusalem, after healing a sick man on the Sabbath. The religious leaders became angry and criticized him. Jesus responds by explaining that he does not act on his own, but in unity with the Father. For this reason he affirms that his work and the Father's work go together, and that he shares that authority to give life.

For today: if Jesus gives life, we can come to him with hope in our "dead" areas, such as discouragement, sin, or sadness. Today you can pray to him with confidence and ask him to renew your heart.
exp.15:4:
Jesus says that he is now going to the Father, the one who sent him. He points out that none of them asks him where he is going.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples on the last night before the cross. He has just warned them that they will suffer rejection and persecution. Earlier, Peter and Thomas had asked something similar (John 13:36; 14:5), so perhaps Jesus means that they were now so sad that they were not thinking about the meaning of his departure. Some understand it this way, others in different ways.

When we are sad or afraid, we tend to look only at our own pain. Today we can stop and ask Jesus: "What are you doing, Lord, and what do you want to teach me?" He knows the way, and he walks with us through his Spirit.
exp.7:9:
Jesus stands up, looks around, and sees that only the woman is left. He asks her where her accusers are and whether anyone has condemned her. The word for "standing up straight" means to rise up and stand upright. The old spelling "á" is just an older way of writing "to."

Jesus speaks. The religious leaders had brought this woman, caught in adultery, to set a trap for him. Jesus made them think about their own consciences, and they left one by one. Some scholars point out that this passage does not appear in the oldest manuscripts of John, but the church has kept it and read it for centuries.

Jesus does not ignore sin, but he does not crush the one who repents. When we feel singled out for our mistakes, we can come to him with confidence. And when we are tempted to judge others, let us remember that we too need mercy.
exp.17:15:
Peter stood outside, near the door of the courtyard of the high priest. Another disciple, who was acquainted with the high priest, went out, spoke with the woman who guarded the door, and brought Peter in.

The narrator, John, recounts the arrest and trial of Jesus. Jesus was being taken before the Jewish authorities. The other disciple is not named; many think it was John himself, but the Bible does not say so. What follows shows that once inside, Peter denied Jesus.

For today: getting close to Jesus carelessly can lead us into places where it is hard to remain faithful. Before entering certain environments, it is wise to pray and ask God for strength, knowing that He forgives and restores anyone who repents.
exp.1:0:
This verse tells us that a wedding was held in Cana, a town in Galilee, on the third day. The phrase about the wedding taking place means that there was a wedding celebration. The mother of Jesus was there, that is, Mary.

The one speaking is John, the author of the Gospel, who narrates the beginning of Jesus' ministry. The expression "the third day" probably counts from the events of the previous chapter, although some interpret it in other ways. John presents this wedding as the setting for Jesus' first miracle, where He would reveal His glory.

For today: Jesus is present in everyday moments, such as a family wedding. Invite Him into your joys, your plans, and your needs, for He cares about your daily life and not only about religious moments.
exp.10:14:
Jesus says he is glad that he was not in Bethany when Lazarus died. The word "glad" in the verse is the one he uses here, and the verse itself says he is glad "for your sakes," meaning for the sake of his disciples, "to the intent ye may believe," that is, so that their faith would grow. Then he invites them: "let us go unto him," that is, let us go to where Lazarus is.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples. He has just told them plainly that Lazarus died, because they had misunderstood his words about "sleep." He does not rejoice in death or in the family's grief; he is glad that, through this situation, they will see his power over death and believe more firmly.

For today: when God seems slow or does not act the way we expect, we can trust that he is still at work. Sometimes what we do not understand becomes an opportunity for our faith to grow.
exp.7:35:
It says that if Jesus, the Son of God, sets us free, then we are truly free. The word that is rendered "shall make you free" in the reader's verse is the one to watch: the explanation's own word for it is an old form meaning "to set free" or "to bring to freedom." "Indeed" means in a real and complete way, not just in appearance.

Jesus speaks with Jews who believed in him, but who took pride in being descendants of Abraham and said they had never been slaves to anyone. He explains that whoever practices sin is a slave to sin. A servant has no fixed place in the house, but the son does, so only the Son can give freedom and a permanent place.

Today, if you feel tied to a bad habit, to guilt, or to fear, come to Jesus with sincerity. Ask him for forgiveness and help, and trust that his freedom is real and does not depend on your own strength.
exp.13:24:
Jesus says that he has taught them all of this while he was still physically with them. "Os" and "vosotros" are the old way of addressing a group; today we would say "I have said" and "you." With these words he marks that he has already given them important teaching, but that a change will come soon.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples at the Last Supper, shortly before he is arrested. They are sad and confused because he has told them that he is going away. So he reminds them of what he has already taught and, right after, promises them the Holy Spirit, who will help them remember and understand, and he leaves them his peace.

For today: God does not leave us alone with his words from the past. Read the Bible regularly and ask the Holy Spirit to remind you of it and make it clear to you when you face fear or doubt.

sum.8: Jesus heals a man who has been blind from birth and tells him to wash the mud from his eyes in the pool of Siloam. The Pharisees question him and throw him out because he acknowledges that Jesus comes from God. Jesus finds him, and the man believes and worships him, while those who claim "we see" remain blind in their sin.
sum.1: At a wedding in Cana, Jesus turns water into wine, his first sign, and his disciples believe in him. Then, in Jerusalem, he drives the sellers out of the temple and speaks of the temple of his body, which he would raise up in three days. Many believe when they see his signs, but Jesus knows the human heart well.
sum.2: Nicodemus visits Jesus at night, and Jesus teaches him that a person must be born again, born of the Spirit, to enter the kingdom of God. He explains that God loved the world so much that he gave his Son, so that whoever believes in him may have eternal life. John the Baptist says that Jesus must increase and he must decrease.
sum.14: Jesus presents himself as the true vine and teaches his disciples to remain in him so that they will bear fruit, since without him they can do nothing. He calls them friends and commands them to love one another as he has loved them. He warns them that the world will reject them, but promises to send the Spirit of truth to bear witness about him.
sum.4: Jesus heals a man on the Sabbath who had been ill for thirty-eight years, and some Jews pursue him for this and because he says God is his Father. Jesus explains that the Son works in unity with the Father, gives life, and will judge. He affirms that the works, the Scriptures, and Moses bear witness to him.
sum.6: Jesus goes up to the Feast of Tabernacles in secret, and he teaches in the temple that his teaching comes from God, who sent him. The crowd is divided: some believe in him and others doubt. Jesus invites the thirsty to come to him, and the authorities want to arrest him, but Nicodemus asks for a fair trial.
sum.12: At the Last Supper, Jesus, knowing that Judas would betray him, washed his disciples' feet as an example of humility and service. He announced the betrayal, and Judas went out into the night. Then he gave them a new command: to love one another as he had loved them, and he told Peter that he would deny him three times.
sum.18: Pilate had Jesus flogged, and though he found no crime in him, he handed him over to be crucified under pressure from the Jewish leaders. Jesus suffered on the cross, took care of his mother, said "It is finished," and died, fulfilling the Scriptures. Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus buried him in a new tomb.
sum.17: Jesus goes to the garden, where Judas arrives with soldiers to arrest him, and he calmly gives himself up and protects his disciples. Peter denies him three times, while Jesus is questioned by the priests. Before Pilate, Jesus says that his kingdom is not of this world and that he came to testify to the truth; Pilate finds no fault in him, but the crowd asks for Barabbas.
sum.7: Jesus forgives a woman accused of adultery when no one dares to throw the first stone, and he tells her to sin no more. He then presents himself as the light of the world, says that the truth will set people free, and claims that he existed before Abraham. The leaders reject him and try to stone him, but Jesus leaves the temple.
sum.13: At the Last Supper, Jesus comforts his disciples. He tells them that he is going to prepare a place for them in his Father's house and that he will come back to take them with him. He teaches them that he is the way, the truth, and the life, and that anyone who has seen him has seen the Father. He promises the Holy Spirit, who will teach them, and he leaves them his peace.
sum.5: Jesus feeds more than five thousand people with five loaves of bread and two fish, and later walks on the sea to calm his disciples' fear. He then teaches that he is the bread of life who comes down from heaven, and that whoever believes in him has eternal life. Many turn away because of his hard words, but Peter confesses that only Jesus has words of eternal life.
sum.9: Jesus presents himself as the gate and the good shepherd, who knows his sheep, lays down his life for them, and offers them abundant and eternal life, secure in the Father's hand. He says that he and the Father are one, and some want to stone him because of it. He then goes to the Jordan, and many there believe in him.
sum.16: In John 17, Jesus prays to the Father. He asks to be glorified, says that eternal life means knowing the Father and Jesus Christ, and states that he has finished the work he was given to do. He prays for his disciples, asking that the Father keep them from evil and make them holy through the truth. He also prays for future believers, that they may all be one in love.
sum.20: Jesus, risen from the dead, appeared to his disciples at the Sea of Tiberias. He gave them an enormous catch of fish and prepared bread and fish for them to eat. Then he asked Peter three times whether he loved him, and he entrusted him with caring for his sheep. He said to him, "Follow me," and asked him not to focus on what would happen to others.
sum.10: Jesus arrives in Bethany when Lazarus has already been dead for four days. He tells Martha and Mary that he is the resurrection and the life, weeps with them, and commands Lazarus to come out of the tomb, and Lazarus comes out alive. Many believe, but the leaders decide to kill Jesus.
sum.3: Jesus travels through Samaria and talks with a Samaritan woman beside a well. He offers her "living water," shows her that he knows the details of her life, and reveals that he is the Christ, and that God seeks worshipers who worship in spirit and in truth. Many Samaritans believe, and then Jesus heals from a distance the son of a royal official.
sum.0: John presents Jesus as the eternal Word, who was God, created all things, and became a human being full of grace and truth. John the Baptist testifies that Jesus is the Lamb of God and the Son of God. Then Jesus calls his first disciples: Andrew, Peter, Philip, and Nathanael.
sum.11: In Bethany, Mary anoints Jesus' feet, and then the crowd welcomes him with palm branches as King in Jerusalem. Jesus teaches that, like a grain of wheat, he must die in order to bear much fruit, and he calls people to believe in the light. Even so, many do not believe, but Jesus says that he came to save, not to judge.
sum.19: Mary Magdalene finds the tomb empty, and Peter and John go in to see for themselves. The risen Jesus appears to Mary, then to the disciples, and sends them all out with his peace and the Holy Spirit. Thomas doubts at first, but when he sees Jesus he believes, and John explains that he wrote these things so that we may believe and have life.
sum.15: Jesus warns his disciples that they will be persecuted, and that their sorrow will turn into joy, just as a mother forgets her pain when her child is born. He promises them the Spirit of truth, who will guide them, and he encourages them to ask the Father in his name. He gives them peace, because he has overcome the world.
